name: Human Anatomy
description: Complete study manual · 30 practical class topics (Part I — the musculoskeletal system, Part II — the internal organs and the cardiovascular system)

topics.title: General osteology. General concept of the skeleton. Planes and basic terminology. Structure of bones. Cervical, thoracic, lumbar and sacral vertebrae and their age-related features

goals.text: To introduce the student to the basic concepts of anatomy and to the terms denoting anatomical planes and directions; to teach the structure and functions of the skeleton and the classification, structure, chemical composition and development of bones; to master the general structure of a vertebra and the distinctive features and age-related characteristics of the cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and coccygeal vertebrae.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the anatomical position, the three main planes (sagittal, frontal, horizontal) and the directional terms (medial, lateral, proximal, distal, etc.);
the conventional vertical lines on the body surface;
the parts of the skeleton, the number of bones and the functions of the skeleton;
the classification of bones by shape, with examples for each group;
the parts of a long (tubular) bone (diaphysis, metaphysis, epiphysis, apophysis), the compact and spongy substance of bone, the periosteum, and the red and yellow bone marrow;
the chemical composition of bone and the features of children's bones;
the types of ossification (endesmal, perichondral, periosteal, endochondral);
the general structure of a vertebra and the distinctive features of each region of the vertebral column;
the structure of the atlas and the axis, and the surfaces and foramina of the sacrum and coccyx;
the timing of ossification of the vertebrae and their age-related changes.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: show the main planes and directions on the skeleton and on individual bones;
determine the group a bone belongs to from its shape;
identify the region an individual vertebra belongs to and name its parts in Latin;
place the sacrum in the anatomical position and show its surfaces, borders and foramina;
palpate the spinous process of the VII cervical vertebra and the processes of the lumbar vertebrae in a living person.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The conventional lines are used daily in clinical practice: in adults the apex beat is found in the 5th intercostal space 1–1.5 cm medial to the left **midclavicular line**; pleural puncture is usually performed along the **scapular** or **posterior axillary line**. That is why these lines are also needed in classes on percussion and auscultation.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: If a bone is placed in a strong acid, the mineral salts dissolve and ossein remains — the bone keeps its shape but becomes so flexible that it can be tied in a knot. If a bone is burned, the organic matter burns away — the bone keeps its shape but becomes brittle and crumbles to powder when pressed. Thus, **organic matter gives elasticity, mineral matter gives hardness**.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Because children's bones are flexible and their periosteum is thick and strong, children often have **“greenstick” fractures** (*subperiosteal fractures*): the bone breaks, but the periosteum stays intact and the fragments are not displaced. The rich blood supply helps bones heal quickly, but also lets inflammation (osteomyelitis) spread quickly. With **vitamin D** deficiency, bone mineralization is impaired and **rickets** develops (bowing of the legs, the “rachitic rosary”). In the elderly, mineral content decreases, leading to **osteoporosis** and easy fractures (femoral neck, vertebral bodies).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the number of vertebrae by mealtimes: **breakfast at 7 a.m.** (7 cervical), **lunch at 12** (12 thoracic), **dinner at 5** (5 lumbar). The sacrum also consists of **5** vertebrae, and the coccyx of **3–5**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **7 processes** arise from the vertebral arch: **1** spinous + **2** transverse + **2** superior articular + **2** inferior articular processes. The vertebral foramina form the vertebral **canal**, while the notches of adjacent vertebrae form the **intervertebral foramen** — do not confuse them.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: If the halves of the arch fail to fuse, the vertebral canal remains open posteriorly — **spina bifida** (most often in the lumbosacral region). The hidden form (*spina bifida occulta*) is asymptomatic and is often found incidentally on X-ray; in severe forms the meninges or the spinal cord itself herniate (meningocele, meningomyelocele). Taking **folic acid** before pregnancy and in its first weeks is important in preventing this defect.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The VII cervical vertebra is the main landmark for counting vertebrae: when the head is bent forward, the most prominent process at the lower part of the neck belongs to this vertebra. The spinous processes of the thoracic vertebrae are counted downward from it.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: A strong blow to the top of the head (for example, diving head first into shallow water) can fracture the arches of the atlas — a **Jefferson fracture**. Sharp flexion or extension of the neck can cause a **fracture of the dens** of the axis. These injuries are life-threatening because they lie close to the upper spinal cord, i.e., to the respiratory center and the segments of the phrenic nerve (C~III~–C~V~). Therefore, a patient with a neck injury must never be moved without immobilizing the neck.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: To distinguish a thoracic vertebra from the others, look for the **costal facets**. To identify which thoracic vertebra it is: a **whole superior + half inferior** facet — T~I~; **only a superior half** facet — T~X~; **one whole** facet on the body and **no** facet on the transverse process — T~XI~ and T~XII~.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In adults the spinal cord ends at the L~I~–L~II~ level; below it the vertebral canal contains only nerve roots (the “cauda equina”). Therefore, a **lumbar (spinal) puncture** is performed between the spinous processes of L~III~–L~IV~ or L~IV~–L~V~ — since the processes of the lumbar vertebrae are horizontal and the spaces between them are wide, the needle passes easily. Landmark: the line joining the highest points of the two iliac crests (Jacoby's line) passes through the L~IV~ process.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: An anesthetic is injected into the epidural space through the **sacral hiatus** — **caudal (sacral) anesthesia**; this method is used especially in pediatric surgery and obstetrics. The two **sacral cornua**, palpable under the skin, serve as landmarks for finding the hiatus. In women the sacrum is wider, shorter and less curved — reflecting the adaptation of the pelvis to childbirth.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: When counting vertebrae in a living person, do not rely on a single landmark: the C~VII~ process sometimes protrudes as much as that of T~I~. When the head is bent forward and backward, **the C~VII~ process moves, whereas that of T~I~ hardly moves** — this distinguishes them. Additional landmarks: the inferior angle of the scapula — T~VII~; the line of the iliac crests — L~IV~.

sections.title: 1. Anatomy as a science. Anatomical position, planes and directions

blocks.text: **Anatomy** (Greek *anatome* — cutting up, dissection) is the science that studies the form, structure and development of the human body in relation to the mutual position of the organs and the functions they perform. Anatomy is the foundation of medicine: making a diagnosis, performing surgery, injections and punctures, and reading X-rays and CT scans are impossible without knowledge of anatomy. Anatomy is taught in the I–III semesters at TMA and other medical universities.

All anatomical descriptions are given relative to the **anatomical position**: a person standing upright, head and gaze directed forward, arms hanging at the sides of the body with the **palms facing forward**, legs together and feet pointing forward. The forward-facing palms are important: in this position the radius is lateral and the ulna is medial.
The three main planes

items: The **sagittal plane** (Latin *sagitta* — arrow) passes through the body from front to back and divides it into right and left parts. The sagittal plane passing through the exact middle of the body is called the **median (midsagittal) plane** — it divides the body into equal right and left halves.
The **frontal plane** (Latin *frons* — forehead) runs parallel to the forehead and divides the body into anterior and posterior parts.
The **horizontal (transverse) plane** is perpendicular to both of the above planes and divides the body into upper and lower parts.

blocks.text: Additional terms are used for the upper limb: **palmaris** (on the palm side) and **dorsalis** (on the back of the hand), **radialis** (on the radius side — lateral) and **ulnaris** (on the ulna side — medial). For the foot, the terms **plantaris** (on the sole side) and **dorsalis** (the dorsum of the foot) are used.
Conventional vertical lines on the body surface

Conventional lines are drawn to determine the surface projection of organs such as the heart, lungs, pleura and liver: the **anterior median line** (*linea mediana anterior*), the **sternal line** (*linea sternalis*), the **parasternal line** (*linea parasternalis*), the **midclavicular line** (*linea medioclavicularis*), the **anterior, middle and posterior axillary lines** (*linea axillaris anterior, media, posterior*), the **scapular line** (*linea scapularis*), the **paravertebral line** (*linea paravertebralis*) and the **posterior median line** (*linea mediana posterior*).

parts.text: The conventional lines are used daily in clinical practice: in adults the apex beat is found in the 5th intercostal space 1–1.5 cm medial to the left **midclavicular line**; pleural puncture is usually performed along the **scapular** or **posterior axillary line**. That is why these lines are also needed in classes on percussion and auscultation.

blocks.text: **Osteology** (Greek *osteon* — bone, *logos* — study) is the study of bones. The set of bones forming the solid framework of the body is called the **skeleton** (Greek *skeletos* — dried). The adult skeleton consists of **more than 200** (usually 206) separate bones, weighs 5–6 kg and makes up about 10 % of body weight in men and 8.5 % in women. The bones, their joints and the muscles together form the **musculoskeletal (locomotor) system**: bones and joints are its passive part, and muscles are its active part.

The skeleton is divided into two parts: the **axial skeleton** — the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum; and the **appendicular skeleton** — the bones of the upper and lower limbs together with their girdles.

blocks.text: Each bone has elevations on its surface — **apophyses** — where muscles, tendons, fasciae and ligaments originate or insert: a **tuber** (*tuber*), **tubercle** (*tuberculum*), **tuberosity** (*tuberositas*), **crest** (*crista*), **process** (*processus*). Bone surfaces are bounded by **borders** (*margo*); where blood vessels and nerves lie there is a **groove** (*sulcus*), where they pass through there is a **foramen** (*foramen*) and a **canal** (*canalis*), and where a joint is formed there is an **articular surface** (*facies articularis*) covered with cartilage. The **nutrient foramen** (*foramen nutricium*), through which a blood vessel enters the bone, is located on the diaphysis.

sections.title: 4. Structure and chemical composition of bone

blocks.text: The following parts are distinguished in a long tubular bone: the **diaphysis** (*diaphysis*) — a cylindrical or triangular body containing the **medullary cavity** (*cavitas medullaris*); the **epiphysis** (*epiphysis*) — the expanded ends, which bear articular surfaces covered with articular cartilage; the **metaphysis** (*metaphysis*) — the transition from the diaphysis to the epiphysis; in children the **epiphyseal (growth) cartilage** is located here, and the bone grows in length at its expense; the **apophysis** (*apophysis*) — an elevation near the epiphysis to which muscles attach (for example, the greater tubercle of the humerus).

There are two kinds of bone substance. **Compact substance** (*substantia compacta*) forms a thick layer in the diaphyses and a thin layer in the epiphyses and in flat and spongy bones. Its structural unit is the **osteon (Haversian system)**: 4–20 bone lamellae arranged concentrically around a central canal, through which blood vessels and nerves pass. The spaces between osteons are filled with **interstitial lamellae**, and **outer and inner circumferential lamellae** lie at the bone surfaces. **Spongy substance** (*substantia spongiosa*) consists of intersecting **bony beams (trabeculae)**; the trabeculae are arranged along the lines of compression and tension acting on the bone, which makes the bone light yet very strong.

blocks.label: Figure 1.4
blocks.caption: Structure of the compact and spongy substance of bone: 1 — compact substance (*substantia compacta*); 2 — outer circumferential lamellae; 3 — inner circumferential lamellae; 4 — osteon; 5 — periosteum (*periosteum*); 6 — spongy substance (*substantia spongiosa*); 7 — bony trabeculae; 8 — nutrient canal; 9 — blood vessels. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

blocks.text: The outer surface of a bone (except the articular surfaces) is covered by the **bone membrane** — the **periosteum** (*periosteum*). It consists of two layers: an outer **fibrous** layer and an inner **cambial (osteogenic)** layer adjacent to the bone. Thanks to the osteoblasts of the cambial layer, bone **grows in width** and **is restored after a fracture**. The periosteum is firmly attached to the bone by collagen fibers that penetrate into it (Sharpey's fibers) and is very rich in blood vessels and nerves — which is why bone fractures and periostitis are very painful. The medullary cavity is lined from inside by the thin **endosteum**.

blocks.label: Figure 1.5
blocks.caption: Structure of an osteon: 1 — osteon lamellae; 2 — bone cells (osteocytes); 3 — central (Haversian) canal. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

blocks.text: There are two kinds of **bone marrow**: **red marrow** (*medulla ossium rubra*) — hematopoietic and immune tissue; **yellow marrow** (*medulla ossium flava*) — consisting mainly of fat cells. In the fetus and in early childhood all bones contain red marrow. In adults, red marrow is preserved in the flat bones (sternum, ilium, vertebral bodies), the spongy bones and the spongy substance of the epiphyses of tubular bones, while the medullary cavity of the diaphyses is occupied by yellow marrow.

parts.text: If a bone is placed in a strong acid, the mineral salts dissolve and ossein remains — the bone keeps its shape but becomes so flexible that it can be tied in a knot. If a bone is burned, the organic matter burns away — the bone keeps its shape but becomes brittle and crumbles to powder when pressed. Thus, **organic matter gives elasticity, mineral matter gives hardness**.

blocks.text: **Radiological anatomy.** On an X-ray the bone image is produced by the inorganic substances. Compact substance appears as a uniform, dense, smooth band-like shadow, while spongy substance appears as a reticular (meshed) shadow formed by the intersecting trabeculae. In children the **growth cartilage** between the metaphysis and the epiphysis is seen as a light band — it must not be confused with a fracture line.

sections.title: 5. Development of bones and age-related features

blocks.text: Bone tissue appears from mesenchyme in the middle of the second month of prenatal development. By their mode of development bones are of two kinds: **primary bones** develop directly from connective tissue and pass through two stages (membrane → bone) — most bones of the cranial vault and face and part of the clavicle. **Secondary bones** pass through three stages (membrane → cartilage → bone) — the bones of the cranial base, trunk and limbs.

blocks.text: The primary ossification center of tubular bones appears in the **diaphysis** in the 2nd month of fetal life. Ossification centers in the epiphyses appear mainly after birth (some — for example, in the distal epiphysis of the femur — just before birth). **Secondary ossification centers** appear in the apophyses from 8–9 years. The cartilage between the diaphysis and the epiphysis ossifies after puberty (**synostosis**), and growth of the bone in length stops — at about 22–25 years in men and 20–22 years in women.

The skeleton of a **newborn** consists of about 270 separate bones (172 in the trunk and head, 98 in the limbs); later many bones fuse with each other. A newborn's bone consists of coarse-fibered (woven) bone tissue; it contains few mineral salts and much water and many blood vessels, and its periosteum is thick with a well-developed cambial layer. In the first 6 years of life woven bone is replaced by **lamellar** bone and osteons are formed; part of the spongy substance is resorbed, the medullary cavity widens, and red marrow gradually turns into yellow marrow.

parts.text: Because children's bones are flexible and their periosteum is thick and strong, children often have **“greenstick” fractures** (*subperiosteal fractures*): the bone breaks, but the periosteum stays intact and the fragments are not displaced. The rich blood supply helps bones heal quickly, but also lets inflammation (osteomyelitis) spread quickly. With **vitamin D** deficiency, bone mineralization is impaired and **rickets** develops (bowing of the legs, the “rachitic rosary”). In the elderly, mineral content decreases, leading to **osteoporosis** and easy fractures (femoral neck, vertebral bodies).

sections.title: 6. The vertebral column and the general structure of a vertebra

blocks.text: The **vertebral column** (*columna vertebralis*) is the axial skeleton of the body and consists of **33–34** vertebrae: **7 cervical**, **12 thoracic**, **5 lumbar**, **5 sacral** (fused to form the sacrum) and **3–5 coccygeal** vertebrae. Its length averages 73–75 cm in men and 69–71 cm in women. The vertebral column serves as a support, protects the spinal cord in the vertebral canal and takes part in movements of the trunk and head.

parts.text: Remember the number of vertebrae by mealtimes: **breakfast at 7 a.m.** (7 cervical), **lunch at 12** (12 thoracic), **dinner at 5** (5 lumbar). The sacrum also consists of **5** vertebrae, and the coccyx of **3–5**.

blocks.text: Each vertebra (*vertebra*) consists of two main parts: the anterior **vertebral body** (*corpus vertebrae*) and the posterior **vertebral arch** (*arcus vertebrae*). The body bears the main load, so its size increases downward and is greatest in the lumbar region; its posterior surface has nutrient foramina. The arch is attached to the body by two **pedicles** (*pediculus arcus vertebrae*), and its posterior part is called the **lamina** (*lamina arcus vertebrae*). The body and arch bound the **vertebral foramen** (*foramen vertebrale*); all the foramina together form the **vertebral canal** (*canalis vertebralis*), which contains the spinal cord and its meninges.

**Seven processes** arise from the arch: posteriorly — the unpaired **spinous process** (*processus spinosus*); laterally — the paired **transverse processes** (*processus transversi*); upward and downward — the paired **superior and inferior articular processes** (*processus articulares superiores et inferiores*), whose articular surfaces form joints with the adjacent vertebrae. The upper and lower borders of the pedicles bear the **vertebral notches** (*incisura vertebralis superior et inferior*); the notches of adjacent vertebrae form the **intervertebral foramen** (*foramen intervertebrale*), through which the spinal nerves and blood vessels pass.

blocks.label: Figure 1.6
blocks.caption: A vertebra (thoracic vertebra), superior view: 1 — vertebral body; 2 — superior costal facet; 3, 11 — pedicle; 4 — superior articular surface; 5 — transverse costal facet; 6 — transverse process; 7 — vertebral arch; 8 — spinous process; 9 — vertebral foramen; 10 — superior articular process. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

parts.text: **7 processes** arise from the vertebral arch: **1** spinous + **2** transverse + **2** superior articular + **2** inferior articular processes. The vertebral foramina form the vertebral **canal**, while the notches of adjacent vertebrae form the **intervertebral foramen** — do not confuse them.

blocks.text: Development and age-related features of the vertebrae

Each vertebra develops from three main ossification centers: one in the **body** and two in the **two halves** of the arch. In the newborn the cervical (III–VII), thoracic and lumbar vertebrae resemble those of the adult in shape, but most of their parts are cartilaginous and the ossification centers are separated from each other by layers of cartilage.

blocks.label: Figure 1.7
blocks.caption: Parts of a thoracic vertebra of a newborn: 1 — spinous process; 2 — transverse costal facet; 3 — superior articular process; 4 — superior costal facet; 5 — vertebral body; 6 — pedicle; 7 — transverse process; 8 — lamina. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

blocks.title: Table 1.6. Timing of ossification of the vertebrae
head: Age
Process
rows: Each half-arch ossifies; the articular processes are formed
The half-arches fuse to form the spinous process, and the vertebral canal closes posteriorly (successively from the III cervical to the IV lumbar vertebra)
The arches fuse with the vertebral body; widening of the vertebral canal stops

parts.text: If the halves of the arch fail to fuse, the vertebral canal remains open posteriorly — **spina bifida** (most often in the lumbosacral region). The hidden form (*spina bifida occulta*) is asymptomatic and is often found incidentally on X-ray; in severe forms the meninges or the spinal cord itself herniate (meningocele, meningomyelocele). Taking **folic acid** before pregnancy and in its first weeks is important in preventing this defect.

blocks.text: There are 7 **cervical vertebrae** (*vertebrae cervicales*, C~I~–C~VII~). Because they bear little weight, their bodies are small and elliptical, with saddle-shaped curved upper and lower surfaces; the vertebral foramen is large and triangular. Their main distinctive feature is the **foramen transversarium** (*foramen transversarium*) in the transverse processes: the **vertebral artery** and vein pass through the foramina of C~I~–C~VI~. The tip of the transverse process bears **anterior and posterior tubercles**, between which the **groove for the spinal nerve** (*sulcus nervi spinalis*) runs above. The anterior tubercle of the VI cervical vertebra is large and is called the **carotid tubercle** (*tuberculum caroticum*) — in bleeding, the common carotid artery can be compressed against this tubercle.

The articular processes are short and their articular surfaces are oblique: the superior one faces backward and upward, the inferior one forward and downward. The spinous processes of vertebrae II–VI are short and **bifid** (split in two). The spinous process of the **VII cervical vertebra** is long, not bifid and clearly palpable under the skin, so it is called the **vertebra prominens** (*vertebra prominens*).

blocks.label: Figure 1.8
blocks.caption: A cervical vertebra, superior view: 1 — vertebral body; 2 — transverse process; 3 — superior articular surface; 4 — vertebral arch; 5 — spinous process (bifid); 6 — vertebral foramen; 7 — superior articular process; 8 — posterior tubercle; 9 — groove for the spinal nerve; 10 — anterior tubercle; 11 — foramen transversarium. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

parts.text: The VII cervical vertebra is the main landmark for counting vertebrae: when the head is bent forward, the most prominent process at the lower part of the neck belongs to this vertebra. The spinous processes of the thoracic vertebrae are counted downward from it.

blocks.text: The atlas — the I cervical vertebra

The **atlas** (*atlas*) is a vertebra without a body: during development its body fuses with the II vertebra, forming its dens. The atlas consists of two **lateral masses** (*massa lateralis*) and the **anterior and posterior arches** (*arcus anterior et posterior*) connecting them. The anterior arch has an **anterior tubercle** on its front surface and, on its inner surface, the **facet for the dens** (*fovea dentis*), which articulates with the dens of the II vertebra. The posterior arch bears the **posterior tubercle** (a remnant of the spinous process) and, on its upper surface, the **groove for the vertebral artery** (*sulcus arteriae vertebralis*). The oval, concave superior articular surfaces of the lateral masses articulate with the occipital condyles, and their flat inferior surfaces with the II vertebra.

blocks.label: Figure 1.9
blocks.caption: The I cervical vertebra — the atlas, superior view: 1 — anterior tubercle; 2 — anterior arch; 3 — superior articular surface; 4 — transverse process; 5 — foramen transversarium; 6 — posterior tubercle; 7 — posterior arch; 8 — lateral mass; 9 — facet for the dens. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

blocks.text: A pair of ossification centers appears in the lateral masses and posterior arch of the atlas, and two additional centers appear in the anterior arch at 1 year. The posterior half-arches fuse at 2–5 years, and the anterior and posterior arches fuse with each other at 5–9 years.
The axis — the II cervical vertebra

The **axis** (*axis*) is distinguished by the cylindrical **dens** (*dens*) projecting upward from the upper surface of its body; the dens has an **apex** (*apex dentis*) and anterior and posterior articular surfaces. The dens articulates with the anterior arch of the atlas and serves as the **axis** around which the atlas, together with the head, rotates to the right and left. 3 main ossification centers appear in the axis in the 4th month of fetal life (2 in the arch, 1 in the body); they fuse at 2 years, while the cartilage at the base of the dens persists until 3–6 years.

blocks.label: Figure 1.10
blocks.caption: The II cervical vertebra — the axis, posterior view: 1 — apex of the dens; 2 — dens; 3 — superior articular surface; 4 — spinous process; 5 — vertebral body. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

blocks.text: **Radiological anatomy.** In the anteroposterior projection, vertebrae I–II are covered by the shadow of the mandible, so usually only vertebrae III–VII are visible; the upper ones are examined in a special open-mouth projection. In the lateral projection all cervical vertebrae are well seen: the arches of the atlas, the dens of the axis, the vertebral bodies and the intervertebral spaces 4–5 mm high are clearly distinguished.

blocks.label: Figure 1.11
blocks.caption: X-ray of the cervical spine, lateral projection: 1 — posterior arch of the atlas; 2 — spinous process of the V cervical vertebra; 3 — VII cervical vertebra; 4 — intervertebral space; 5 — body of the V cervical vertebra. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

parts.text: A strong blow to the top of the head (for example, diving head first into shallow water) can fracture the arches of the atlas — a **Jefferson fracture**. Sharp flexion or extension of the neck can cause a **fracture of the dens** of the axis. These injuries are life-threatening because they lie close to the upper spinal cord, i.e., to the respiratory center and the segments of the phrenic nerve (C~III~–C~V~). Therefore, a patient with a neck injury must never be moved without immobilizing the neck.

blocks.text: There are 12 **thoracic vertebrae** (*vertebrae thoracicae*, T~I~–T~XII~); their bodies increase in size from above downward, and the vertebral foramen is relatively small and round. Their main distinctive feature is the **costal facets**: the posterolateral surface of the bodies of vertebrae II–IX bears **superior and inferior costal demifacets** (*fovea costalis superior et inferior*) — the demifacets of two adjacent vertebrae together form one articular surface for the head of a rib. Vertebra I has a **whole** superior facet for the I rib and an inferior demifacet for the II rib, vertebra X has only a superior demifacet, and vertebrae XI and XII each have one **whole** facet.

The anterior surface of the transverse processes of vertebrae I–X bears a **transverse costal facet** (*fovea costalis processus transversi*), which articulates with the tubercle of the rib; vertebrae XI–XII lack this facet. The spinous processes are long, triangular and directed obliquely downward, overlapping each other like roof tiles (especially in the mid-thoracic region). The articular processes lie in the frontal plane: the superior articular surface faces backward, the inferior one forward.

blocks.label: Figure 1.12
blocks.caption: A thoracic vertebra, lateral view: 1 — superior costal facet; 2 — superior articular process; 3 — transverse costal facet; 4 — transverse process; 5 — inferior articular process; 6 — spinous process; 7 — inferior articular surface; 8 — inferior vertebral notch; 9 — inferior costal facet; 10 — vertebral body. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

parts.text: To distinguish a thoracic vertebra from the others, look for the **costal facets**. To identify which thoracic vertebra it is: a **whole superior + half inferior** facet — T~I~; **only a superior half** facet — T~X~; **one whole** facet on the body and **no** facet on the transverse process — T~XI~ and T~XII~.

blocks.text: **Radiological anatomy.** In the anteroposterior projection the bodies are rectangular and the intervertebral spaces are 4–5 mm; the transverse processes overlap the posterior ends of the ribs (whereas the transverse processes of the I thoracic vertebra are clearly visible). In the lateral projection the bodies are rectangles with smooth borders, and the intervertebral foramina are seen as round lucencies at the posteroinferior margin of the body.

There are 5 **lumbar vertebrae** (*vertebrae lumbales*, L~I~–L~V~). Because they bear the greatest load, their bodies are the largest and **bean-shaped**, and the vertebral foramen is triangular. Since the transverse process is a rudimentary rib, it is called the **costal process** (*processus costalis, s. costiformis*); on the posterior surface of its base lies a small **accessory process** (*processus accessorius*) — a remnant of the true transverse process. Lateral to the superior articular process is the **mammillary process** (*processus mamillaris*).

The spinous processes are short, flat, broad, thickened at the tip and directed **horizontally** backward — so the spaces between them are wide. The articular processes are well developed, and their articular surfaces lie in the **sagittal** plane: the superior ones face medially and the inferior ones laterally; this allows flexion and extension in the lumbar region but limits rotation.

blocks.label: Figure 1.13
blocks.caption: A lumbar vertebra, superior view: 1 — vertebral body; 2 — superior vertebral notch; 3 — costal process; 4 — superior articular process; 5 — spinous process; 6 — vertebral arch; 7 — superior articular surface; 8 — mammillary process; 9 — accessory process; 10 — vertebral foramen. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

parts.text: In adults the spinal cord ends at the L~I~–L~II~ level; below it the vertebral canal contains only nerve roots (the “cauda equina”). Therefore, a **lumbar (spinal) puncture** is performed between the spinous processes of L~III~–L~IV~ or L~IV~–L~V~ — since the processes of the lumbar vertebrae are horizontal and the spaces between them are wide, the needle passes easily. Landmark: the line joining the highest points of the two iliac crests (Jacoby's line) passes through the L~IV~ process.

blocks.text: **Radiological anatomy.** In the anteroposterior projection the bodies of the lumbar vertebrae are wider than they are high, and the intervertebral spaces are up to 10 mm; the oval shadows of the pedicles and, in the midline, a double vertical row of spinous processes are superimposed on the shadow of the body.

The **sacrum** (*os sacrum*) is a triangular bone formed by the fusion of 5 sacral vertebrae. Its broad **base** (*basis ossis sacri*) faces upward and its **apex** (*apex ossis sacri*) downward and forward. Where the base joins the V lumbar vertebra, an anteriorly projecting **promontory** (*promontorium*) is formed — an important landmark in measuring the pelvis.

The **anterior — pelvic surface** (*facies pelvica*) is concave and smooth: it bears 4 **transverse lines** (*lineae transversae*) — traces of fusion of the vertebral bodies — and at their ends 4 pairs of **anterior sacral foramina** (*foramina sacralia anteriora*). The **posterior surface** (*facies dorsalis*) is convex and rough and bears 5 longitudinal crests: the unpaired **median sacral crest** (*crista sacralis mediana*) — from the fusion of the spinous processes; the paired **medial crests** (*cristae sacrales mediales*) — from the articular processes; and the paired **lateral crests** (*cristae sacrales laterales*) — from the transverse processes. Between the medial and lateral crests lie 4 pairs of **posterior sacral foramina** (*foramina sacralia posteriora*).

blocks.label: Figure 1.14
blocks.caption: Sacrum and coccyx, pelvic surface: 1 — base of the sacrum; 2 — superior articular processes; 3 — lateral part; 4 — anterior sacral foramina; 5 — apex of the sacrum; 6 — coccyx; 7 — transverse lines. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

blocks.text: Lateral to the foramina lies the **lateral part** (*pars lateralis*); the **auricular surface** (*facies auricularis*) on its side articulates with the corresponding surface of the ilium, and behind it is the **sacral tuberosity** (*tuberositas ossis sacri*), to which ligaments attach. The vertebral foramina join to form the **sacral canal** (*canalis sacralis*); the canal opens below by the **sacral hiatus** (*hiatus sacralis*), on either side of which stand the **sacral cornua** (*cornua sacralia*) — remnants of the articular processes.

blocks.label: Figure 1.15
blocks.caption: Sacrum and coccyx, posterior surface: 1 — superior articular processes; 2 — sacral canal; 3 — sacral tuberosity; 4 — medial sacral crest; 5 — median sacral crest; 6 — sacral hiatus; 7 — sacral cornu; 8 — coccygeal cornu; 9 — coccyx; 10 — posterior sacral foramina; 11 — lateral sacral crest; 12 — auricular surface. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

blocks.text: The **coccyx** (*os coccygis*) is formed by the fusion of 3–5 rudimentary vertebrae; it is triangular and curved forward. The I coccygeal vertebra has a small body that joins the sacrum and upward-directed **coccygeal cornua** (*cornua coccygea*).

**Age-related features.** In the newborn the sacrum is wedge-shaped and consists mainly of cartilage. At 3–8 years the ossification centers of each vertebra fuse; during this period vertebra I shifts forward and vertebrae II–IV backward, forming the **sacral kyphosis**. The sacral vertebrae fuse with each other into a single bone at **17–25 years**. In the newborn the coccygeal vertebrae are 4–5 cartilaginous vertebrae consisting only of bodies; the ossification center of the I coccygeal vertebra appears at 1–7 years, and the coccyx ossifies completely at ≈30 years.

parts.text: An anesthetic is injected into the epidural space through the **sacral hiatus** — **caudal (sacral) anesthesia**; this method is used especially in pediatric surgery and obstetrics. The two **sacral cornua**, palpable under the skin, serve as landmarks for finding the hiatus. In women the sacrum is wider, shorter and less curved — reflecting the adaptation of the pelvis to childbirth.

skills.title: Practical skill: algorithm for identifying the region of a vertebra

items: Place the vertebra in the **anatomical position**: the body in front, the spinous process facing backward and downward, the vertebral foramen directed vertically.

Look at the transverse process: if it **has a foramen**, it is a **cervical** vertebra. If it has no body and two arches — the **atlas**; if a dens projects from the body — the **axis**; if the spinous process is long and not bifid — **C~VII~**.
If there are **costal facets** on the side of the body, it is a **thoracic** vertebra; distinguish T~I~, T~X~ and T~XI–XII~ by whether the facets are whole or half facets.
If the body is large and bean-shaped, there are no foramina or costal facets, and the spinous process is horizontal and broad — it is a **lumbar** vertebra.
Name and show the parts of the vertebra in Latin: *corpus, arcus, pediculus, lamina, foramen vertebrale, processus spinosus, transversus, articularis superior et inferior, incisura vertebralis*.

Hold the sacrum with its base upward and its concave pelvic surface facing forward; show the transverse lines, the anterior and posterior foramina, the three crests, the auricular surface, the sacral canal and the hiatus.

parts.text: When counting vertebrae in a living person, do not rely on a single landmark: the C~VII~ process sometimes protrudes as much as that of T~I~. When the head is bent forward and backward, **the C~VII~ process moves, whereas that of T~I~ hardly moves** — this distinguishes them. Additional landmarks: the inferior angle of the scapula — T~VII~; the line of the iliac crests — L~IV~.

skills.title: Practical skill: palpation in a living person

items: Ask the seated patient to bend the head forward; find the most prominent process at the lower part of the neck — **C~VII~**.
Count the spinous processes of the thoracic vertebrae downward from it; with the arms hanging down, the inferior angle of the scapula lies at the level of the T~VII~ process.
With the patient standing, join the highest points of the two iliac crests — the line passes through the **L~IV~** process or the L~IV~–L~V~ interspace.
Palpate the median sacral crest and the sacral cornua at its lower end, and show the location of the sacral hiatus.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: An 8-year-old child fell from a tree and complains of pain in the forearm. The X-ray shows a fracture of the radial diaphysis, but the fragments are not displaced and the periosteum is intact.
cases.ask: What type of fracture is this? Why is it common in children and how does it heal?
cases.answer: This is a **“greenstick” (subperiosteal) fracture**. Children's bones contain relatively more organic matter and fewer mineral salts — the bone is flexible; the periosteum is thick and strong, so it holds the fragments together. The cambial layer of the periosteum is well developed and the bone is rich in blood vessels — so the fracture heals faster than in adults.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: After an injury, the neck X-ray of a patient shows that a vertebra without a body and with two arches has fractures of its anterior and posterior arches in several places. The patient had dived head first into a shallow pool.
cases.ask: Which vertebra is injured? Why is this injury dangerous?
cases.answer: The vertebra without a body is the **atlas (C~I~)**; with a vertical blow to the head, the occipital condyles force the lateral masses of the atlas apart — a **Jefferson fracture**. The injury is dangerous because it lies close to the upper cervical segments of the spinal cord and to the vertebral artery (which passes through the foramen transversarium of the atlas and lies in the groove on its posterior arch); if C~III~–C~V~ are damaged, diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory arrest may occur.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A physician is going to perform a diagnostic lumbar puncture. The patient is lying on his side with his knees drawn up to his abdomen.
cases.ask: Between which vertebrae is the needle inserted? How can the site be found, and why is it performed at this level?
cases.answer: The puncture is performed between the spinous processes of **L~III~–L~IV~** or **L~IV~–L~V~**. The landmark is the line joining the highest points of the two iliac crests, which passes through the L~IV~ process. In adults the spinal cord ends at the L~I~–L~II~ level and below it there are only nerve roots — so there is no risk of injuring the spinal cord. The spinous processes of the lumbar vertebrae are horizontal and the spaces between them are wide, and in the flexed position the space widens further.

topics.title: The ribs, sternum and thoracic cage and their age-related features

goals.text: To introduce the student to the structure of the ribs and sternum, the formation of the thoracic cage, its apertures, shapes and age-related changes; to relate this knowledge to examination of the heart and lungs, punctures and injuries.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the classification of the ribs (true, false, floating) and the features of their attachment to the sternum;
the parts of a rib: head, neck, tubercle, body (shaft), angle, costal groove;
the distinctive features of ribs I, II, XI and XII;
the parts and notches of the sternum and the sternal angle;
the composition of the thoracic cage, its superior and inferior apertures, the infrasternal angle and the costal arch;
the shapes of the thoracic cage and their relation to body build (constitution);
the age-related features and ossification timing of the ribs, sternum and thoracic cage;
the appearance of the thoracic cage on an X-ray.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: distinguish a left rib from a right one and show its parts in Latin;
count the II rib and the intercostal spaces in a living person using the sternal angle;
show the apertures of the thoracic cage, the costal arch and the infrasternal angle on the skeleton;
distinguish the anterior and posterior parts of the ribs on a chest X-ray.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the classification of the ribs by the number **“7 – 3 – 2”**: **7** pairs of true, **3** pairs of false and **2** pairs of floating ribs. 12 pairs in total. In the newborn, however, rib X has not yet joined the costal arch — the classification is **7 – 2 – 3**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In the costal groove the blood vessels and nerve lie from above downward in the order **VAN**: **V**ein — **A**rtery — **N**erve; the nerve is lowest and projects slightly from the groove. Therefore, in pleural puncture and intercostal block the needle is inserted along **the upper border of the lower rib** — so that the vessels and nerve are not injured.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Sometimes an additional **cervical rib** develops from the transverse process of the VII cervical vertebra (in ≈0.5–1 % of the population). It may compress the subclavian artery and fibers of the brachial plexus over the I rib — **thoracic outlet syndrome**: pain, numbness and weakness in the arm and a weakened pulse. The compression most often occurs in the region of the tubercle of the anterior scalene muscle.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The sternal angle is the “key” to counting the ribs.** It is easily palpated under the skin as a transverse ridge; the **II rib** lies beside it, and below that is the **II intercostal space**. The I rib cannot be palpated under the clavicle, so counting begins with the II rib. At the level of the sternal angle lie, posteriorly, the T~IV~–T~V~ intervertebral space and, internally, the tracheal bifurcation and the beginning and end of the aortic arch.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Sternal puncture** (piercing the sternum to obtain red marrow) is performed in the upper part of the sternal body at the level of the III rib, or in the manubrium: here the bone is superficial and its spongy substance is rich in red marrow. A special needle with a stop (Arinkin needle) is used, because the posterior plate of the sternum is thin and the heart and great vessels lie behind it. In children the sternum is thin, so marrow is usually taken from the ilium or the tibia.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Pathological shapes of the thoracic cage are important in diagnosis: **“pigeon chest”** (*pectus carinatum*) — the sternum protrudes forward, often after rickets; **funnel chest** (*pectus excavatum*) — the lower sternum is sunken inward (congenital); **emphysematous (barrel) chest** — the anteroposterior diameter is increased and the ribs are horizontal (in pulmonary emphysema); **rachitic rosary** — thickenings at the junctions of the bony and cartilaginous parts of the ribs. In the elderly the costal cartilages calcify and the mobility of the thoracic cage decreases.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: To avoid mistakes when counting ribs on an X-ray, count them by their **posterior parts**, starting next to the spine: the posterior parts are horizontal and distinct, while the anterior parts are oblique and their cartilaginous portion is not visible. The shadows of the scapulae fall on the upper lateral part of the lung fields — do not interpret them as changes in the lung.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Because a newborn's ribs are horizontal, the thoracic cage expands little during inspiration — infants breathe mainly **with the diaphragm (abdominal type)**. That is why abdominal distension (meteorism) or tight swaddling makes breathing difficult for an infant. Once the child begins to walk upright, the ribs slope downward and thoracic-type breathing is added.

blocks.text: The **ribs** (*costae*) are 12 pairs of flat, long, arched spongy bones. Each rib consists of two parts: a long posterior **bony part** (*os costale*) and a short anterior **costal cartilage** (*cartilago costalis*). Posteriorly the ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae, and anteriorly they attach to the sternum through their cartilages or end freely.

parts.text: Remember the classification of the ribs by the number **“7 – 3 – 2”**: **7** pairs of true, **3** pairs of false and **2** pairs of floating ribs. 12 pairs in total. In the newborn, however, rib X has not yet joined the costal arch — the classification is **7 – 2 – 3**.

blocks.text: At the posterior end of the rib lies the **head of the rib** (*caput costae*); its **articular surface** (*facies articularis capitis costae*) articulates with the costal facets on the bodies of the thoracic vertebrae. Because the heads of ribs II–X articulate with two adjacent vertebrae, their articular surface is divided in two by the **crest of the head** (*crista capitis costae*); ribs I, XI and XII lack this crest.

The head is followed by the narrowed **neck of the rib** (*collum costae*), whose upper border bears the **crest of the neck** (*crista colli costae*). At the junction of the neck with the body lies the **tubercle of the rib** (*tuberculum costae*); its articular surface (*facies articularis tuberculi costae*) articulates with the costal facet of the transverse process (ribs XI and XII lack an articular surface on the tubercle).

The longest part — the **body (shaft) of the rib** (*corpus costae*) — is flat and has external and internal surfaces and superior and inferior borders. Slightly lateral to the tubercle the body bends sharply to form the **angle of the rib** (*angulus costae*): in ribs I–II the angle almost coincides with the tubercle, and in the lower ribs the distance between them increases. Along the inferior border of the inner surface of the body runs the **costal groove** (*sulcus costae*), which contains the intercostal vein, artery and nerve.

blocks.label: Figure 2.1
blocks.caption: A left rib: 1 — angle of the rib; 2 — tubercle of the rib; 3 — neck of the rib; 4 — head of the rib; 5 — articular surface of the head; 6 — crest of the head; 7 — articular surface of the tubercle; 8 — body of the rib; 9 — costal groove. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

parts.text: In the costal groove the blood vessels and nerve lie from above downward in the order **VAN**: **V**ein — **A**rtery — **N**erve; the nerve is lowest and projects slightly from the groove. Therefore, in pleural puncture and intercostal block the needle is inserted along **the upper border of the lower rib** — so that the vessels and nerve are not injured.

blocks.text: Features of individual ribs

items: The **I rib** (*costa prima*) is the shortest, widest and most curved; instead of external and internal surfaces it has **superior and inferior surfaces** and medial and lateral borders. Its superior surface bears the **tubercle for the anterior scalene muscle** (*tuberculum musculi scaleni anterioris*); behind it runs the **groove for the subclavian artery** (*sulcus arteriae subclaviae*), and in front of it the **groove for the subclavian vein** (*sulcus venae subclaviae*). Its head has no crest.
The **II rib** (*costa secunda*) bears the **tuberosity for the serratus anterior muscle** (*tuberositas musculi serrati anterioris*) on its outer surface.
**Ribs XI and XII** have no crest on the head and no articular surface on the tubercle; their angle and groove are poorly developed and their anterior end is free. Rib XII is shorter than rib XI.

blocks.label: Figure 2.2
blocks.caption: Ribs I and II (superior view): *Caput, collum, tuberculum costae I et II* — head, neck and tubercle of ribs I and II; *Sulcus arteriae subclaviae* — groove for the subclavian artery; *Tuberculum m. scaleni anterioris* — tubercle for the anterior scalene muscle; *Sulcus v. subclaviae* — groove for the subclavian vein; *Tuberositas m. serrati anterioris* — tuberosity for the serratus anterior muscle. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: Sometimes an additional **cervical rib** develops from the transverse process of the VII cervical vertebra (in ≈0.5–1 % of the population). It may compress the subclavian artery and fibers of the brachial plexus over the I rib — **thoracic outlet syndrome**: pain, numbness and weakness in the arm and a weakened pulse. The compression most often occurs in the region of the tubercle of the anterior scalene muscle.

blocks.text: The **sternum** (*sternum*) is a long flat (spongy) bone located in the anterior wall of the thoracic cage in the frontal plane. It consists of three parts: above — the **manubrium** (*manubrium sterni*), in the middle — the **body of the sternum** (*corpus sterni*), and below — the **xiphoid process** (*processus xiphoideus*).

The **manubrium** is the widest and thickest part of the bone. Its upper border bears the **jugular notch** (*incisura jugularis*); on either side are the **clavicular notches** (*incisurae claviculares*), which articulate with the clavicle, and below them are notches for the cartilage of the I rib. Where the manubrium joins the body, the anteriorly projecting **sternal angle** (*angulus sterni*, angle of Louis) is formed; the cartilage of the **II rib** attaches on each side of it.

The **body of the sternum** is its longest part and widens downward; its anterior surface shows transverse lines left by the fusion of its ossification segments (sternebrae). Its lateral borders bear **costal notches** (*incisurae costales*) for ribs III–VII; the notch for the VII rib lies at the junction of the body and the xiphoid process. The **xiphoid process** is the smallest part and variable in shape: its tip may be bifid or perforated, and it remains cartilaginous for a long time.

blocks.caption: The sternum, anterior view: *Incisura jugularis* — jugular notch; *Incisura clavicularis* — clavicular notch; *Incisura costalis I, II* — costal notch for ribs I, II; *Manubrium sterni* — manubrium; *Angulus sterni* — sternal angle; *Corpus sterni* — body of the sternum; *Incisurae costales III–VII* — costal notches; *Processus xiphoideus* — xiphoid process; *Ossa suprasternalia* — suprasternal ossicles (inconstant). Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.label: Figure 2.4
blocks.caption: The sternum, right lateral view: the sternal angle projecting forward between the manubrium and the body is clearly visible. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: **The sternal angle is the “key” to counting the ribs.** It is easily palpated under the skin as a transverse ridge; the **II rib** lies beside it, and below that is the **II intercostal space**. The I rib cannot be palpated under the clavicle, so counting begins with the II rib. At the level of the sternal angle lie, posteriorly, the T~IV~–T~V~ intervertebral space and, internally, the tracheal bifurcation and the beginning and end of the aortic arch.

**Sternal puncture** (piercing the sternum to obtain red marrow) is performed in the upper part of the sternal body at the level of the III rib, or in the manubrium: here the bone is superficial and its spongy substance is rich in red marrow. A special needle with a stop (Arinkin needle) is used, because the posterior plate of the sternum is thin and the heart and great vessels lie behind it. In children the sternum is thin, so marrow is usually taken from the ilium or the tibia.

blocks.text: The **thoracic cage** (*cavea thoracis, compages thoracis*) is formed by the union of the 12 thoracic vertebrae, 12 pairs of ribs and the sternum. It protects the organs of the thoracic cavity — the heart, lungs, esophagus and great vessels — and takes an active part in respiratory movements. In humans the thoracic cage has the shape of a **truncated cone** flattened from front to back: its transverse diameter is greater than its anteroposterior diameter (associated with upright walking; in quadrupeds it is the reverse).

blocks.label: Figure 2.5
blocks.caption: The thoracic cage, anterior view: *Apertura thoracis superior* — superior aperture; *Manubrium, corpus sterni* — manubrium and body of the sternum; *Spatia intercostalia* — intercostal spaces; *Costae verae, spuriae, fluctuantes* — true, false and floating ribs; *Cartilagines costales* — costal cartilages; *Processus xiphoideus* — xiphoid process; *Apertura thoracis inferior* — inferior aperture; *Angulus infrasternalis* — infrasternal angle; *Arcus costalis* — costal arch. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: The right and left costal arches form the **infrasternal angle** (*angulus infrasternalis*) below the xiphoid process. The space between adjacent ribs — the **intercostal space** (*spatium intercostale*) — numbers 11 pairs and contains the intercostal muscles, vessels and nerves. On the inner surface of the thoracic cage, between the vertebral bodies and the angles of the ribs, there are broad **pulmonary grooves** (*sulci pulmonales*) on both sides, in which the posterior parts of the lungs lie.

blocks.text: The shape of the thoracic cage depends on muscle development, the position of the internal organs, occupation and physical exercise. In women the thoracic cage is shorter and narrower, with a wider upper part — women breathe mainly by the **thoracic type**, and men by the **abdominal (diaphragmatic) type**.

parts.text: Pathological shapes of the thoracic cage are important in diagnosis: **“pigeon chest”** (*pectus carinatum*) — the sternum protrudes forward, often after rickets; **funnel chest** (*pectus excavatum*) — the lower sternum is sunken inward (congenital); **emphysematous (barrel) chest** — the anteroposterior diameter is increased and the ribs are horizontal (in pulmonary emphysema); **rachitic rosary** — thickenings at the junctions of the bony and cartilaginous parts of the ribs. In the elderly the costal cartilages calcify and the mobility of the thoracic cage decreases.

blocks.text: On an anteroposterior X-ray the bones of the thoracic cage visible are mainly the ribs; the sternum is covered by the shadow of the heart and great vessels and can only be seen in the lateral projection. The **posterior parts** of the ribs run almost horizontally lateral to the spine and are seen more clearly; the **anterior parts** start from the lateral edge of the thoracic cage and slope medially and downward. The shadows of the anterior and posterior parts intersect and divide the lung field into quadrangular “cells.” The costal cartilages are not visible on X-ray (they are visible if calcified in the elderly).

blocks.label: Figure 2.8

Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: To avoid mistakes when counting ribs on an X-ray, count them by their **posterior parts**, starting next to the spine: the posterior parts are horizontal and distinct, while the anterior parts are oblique and their cartilaginous portion is not visible. The shadows of the scapulae fall on the upper lateral part of the lung fields — do not interpret them as changes in the lung.

blocks.text: Ribs

In the newborn the ratio of the bony and cartilaginous parts of the rib is similar to that in the adult, but the **head and tubercle are cartilaginous**; the body is rounded, and the angle and groove of the rib are poorly defined. A newborn has 7 pairs of true, 2 pairs of false and 3 pairs of floating ribs. In early childhood the ribs grow rapidly, their anterior part flattens and turns downward, and the angle becomes distinct. In the second period of childhood secondary ossification centers appear in the head and tubercle and fuse with the body at **18–25 years**; during this period the cartilage of rib X joins the costal arch.
The sternum

In the newborn there is one ossification center in the manubrium and 4–5 in the body (sometimes one also at the base of the xiphoid process); they are separated by layers of cartilage. The parts of the body (sternebrae) fuse with each other **at puberty**, forming a single body. The xiphoid process ossifies and fuses with the body **at ≈30 years**; the manubrium and the body fuse very late — **after 40 years** — or remain separate for life.
The thoracic cage

parts.text: Because a newborn's ribs are horizontal, the thoracic cage expands little during inspiration — infants breathe mainly **with the diaphragm (abdominal type)**. That is why abdominal distension (meteorism) or tight swaddling makes breathing difficult for an infant. Once the child begins to walk upright, the ribs slope downward and thoracic-type breathing is added.

skills.title: Practical skill: studying a rib and the sternum

items: Place the rib in the anatomical position: the head posterior and medial, the groove on the **lower** border of the inner surface, the convex outer surface facing laterally. From this, determine whether it is a right or left rib.
Show the parts of the rib in sequence: *caput, crista capitis, collum, crista colli, tuberculum, angulus, corpus, sulcus costae*.
Distinguish the I rib from the others: the shortest and widest, with superior and inferior surfaces; show the tubercle and the two grooves on its superior surface.
On the sternum, show the manubrium, body, xiphoid process, jugular and clavicular notches, costal notches and the sternal angle.
On the skeleton, show the superior and inferior apertures of the thoracic cage, the costal arch and the infrasternal angle, and determine its shape.

skills.title: Practical skill: counting ribs in a living person

items: Run your finger down from the jugular notch and find the transverse ridge — the **sternal angle**.

Move the finger laterally — this is the **II rib**; the depression below it is the II intercostal space. Count downward in this way (in women counting below the breast is harder — continue along the midaxillary line).

Posterior landmark: with the arms hanging down, the **inferior angle of the scapula** lies at the level of the VII rib (or the VII intercostal space); the XII rib can be found by palpating from lateral to medial.
Measure the infrasternal angle: place both thumbs along the costal arches and estimate the angle between them (acute, right or obtuse) — this is used to determine the body build.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient injured in a car accident has pain on the left lateral surface of the chest that increases on inspiration. The X-ray shows fractures of the bodies of ribs VII–IX along the midaxillary line.
cases.ask: Which structures may be injured in a rib fracture? How is an intercostal block performed to relieve the pain?
cases.answer: The **intercostal vein, artery and nerve** lying in the costal groove may be injured, as well as the intercostal muscles, parietal pleura and lung (pneumothorax, hemothorax). In the block, the anesthetic is injected at the **lower border of the rib** in the region of the angle of the rib or the midaxillary line — the nerve lies just below the groove. In pleural puncture, by contrast, the needle is inserted along the upper border of the lower rib.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: The physician asked a student to find the patient's apex beat. The student began counting the ribs below the clavicle but could not palpate the I rib.
cases.ask: From which landmark should rib counting begin? Why?
cases.answer: The I rib is hidden behind the clavicle and cannot be palpated. Counting starts from the **sternal angle** (the transverse ridge at the junction of the manubrium and body): the **II rib** lies beside it, and below it the II intercostal space. Counting in this way down to the V intercostal space, the apex beat is found 1–1.5 cm medial to the left midclavicular line.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: Parents are worried about bead-like thickenings along the anterior ends of the ribs on the chest of their 1-year-old child. The child went out little during the winter, and the sternum protrudes slightly forward.
cases.ask: What are these changes and what causes them? In which part of the rib are they located?
cases.answer: These are signs of **rickets**: the **“rachitic rosary”** — widening of the growth cartilage at the **junction of the bony and cartilaginous parts** of the ribs — and forward protrusion of the sternum (“pigeon chest”). The cause is impaired mineralization of bone tissue due to **vitamin D** deficiency (lack of sunlight). Because children's bones contain few mineral salts and grow intensively, the changes develop quickly.

topics.title: Bones of the shoulder girdle and free upper limb: structure and age-related features

goals.text: To introduce the student to the structure of the bones of the shoulder girdle (clavicle and scapula) and the free upper limb (humerus, ulna, radius, bones of the hand), the points palpable in a living person, the timing of ossification and the principles of determining bone age; to explain the clinical significance of the nerves running along the bones and of typical fractures.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the divisions of the upper limb skeleton and the bones of each division;
the ends, surfaces and elevations of the clavicle;
the surfaces, borders and angles of the scapula, its spine, acromion and coracoid process;
the structures of the proximal end of the humerus (head, anatomical and surgical necks, tubercles), its body and its distal end;
the ends, borders and articular surfaces of the ulna and radius;
the two rows of carpal bones, the metacarpal bones and the phalanges of the fingers;
the timing of ossification of the upper limb bones and the order of appearance of ossification centers in the carpal bones.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: place each bone in the anatomical position and determine whether it is right or left;
show the main structures of the bones and name them in Latin;
palpate in a living person the clavicle, acromion, spine and inferior angle of the scapula, the epicondyles of the humerus, the olecranon and the styloid processes;
identify the carpal bones on an X-ray of the hand and roughly estimate the bone age.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Growth of the upper limb bones **“runs away from the elbow”**: in the humerus the more active growth cartilage is at the top (near the shoulder joint), and in the radius and ulna — at the bottom (near the wrist joint). Therefore, in children injuries of the proximal metaphysis of the humerus and the distal metaphysis of the radius most often lead to growth disturbances.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Fracture of the clavicle** is one of the most common fractures: from a fall on the outstretched hand or the shoulder, usually at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds (where the bone is thinnest and curves). The medial fragment is pulled **upward** by the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and the lateral fragment is displaced **downward** by the weight of the arm. Because the subclavian vessels and the brachial plexus lie beneath the clavicle, they may be injured. In newborns, clavicle fracture is **the most common birth injury**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In adolescents the ossification center of the acromion appears on an X-ray as a separate bone fragment — do not mistake it for a fracture. Sometimes the acromion never fuses with the scapula (*os acromiale*); this is a normal variant but may cause shoulder pain.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the nerves along the humerus from above downward in the order **“A–R–U”**: the **A**xillary nerve — at the surgical neck, the **R**adial nerve — in the middle of the shaft (in the spiral groove), the **U**lnar nerve — behind the medial epicondyle.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Rule for distinguishing the two forearm bones: **the ulna is thick at the top** (it mainly forms the elbow joint), **the radius is thick at the bottom** (it mainly forms the wrist joint). Both bones have a head, but at opposite ends: the head of the radius is **at the top**, the head of the ulna is **at the bottom**.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Fracture of the radius “at the typical site”** (Colles' fracture) occurs 2–3 cm above the distal end, from a fall on the outstretched palm; in this region the compact substance is thin and the spongy substance is sparse, i.e., the resistance of the bone is reduced. The distal fragment is displaced backward and laterally — the forearm takes on a “dinner fork” shape. It is especially common in elderly women because of osteoporosis. In children, **epiphysiolysis** (separation along the growth cartilage) occurs in this region.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the carpal bones from lateral (thumb side) to medial, first the proximal and then the distal row: **“Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle”** — **S**caphoid, **L**unate, **T**riquetrum, **P**isiform; **T**rapezium, **T**rapezoid, **C**apitate, **H**amate.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Fracture of the scaphoid** is the most common carpal fracture (from a fall on the outstretched palm). Pain is felt in the **“anatomical snuffbox”** — the depression formed at the base of the thumb when it is extended. Because the bone receives its blood supply mainly from its distal part, after a fracture the proximal fragment may be **left without blood and undergo necrosis**. The fracture may not be visible on the initial X-ray — so if it is suspected, the hand is immobilized and imaging is repeated after 10–14 days.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The carpal bones ossify **starting with the capitate and proceeding counterclockwise** (looking at the left hand from the palm): capitate → hamate → triquetrum → lunate → scaphoid → trapezium → trapezoid, and last — the pisiform. A rough rule: **after 1 year, the child's age ≈ the number of visible carpal bones** (for example, 3 at 3 years, 4 at 4 years).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In an injury of the elbow region, disruption of **Hueter's triangle** (a change in the position of the three points) indicates a fracture or dislocation. Because children have many ossification centers in this region, always evaluate the X-ray **in comparison with the healthy side**.

sections.title: 1. The upper limb skeleton: general information

blocks.text: The upper limb skeleton consists of two divisions: the **shoulder girdle** (*cingulum membri superioris*) — the clavicle and scapula, and the **free part of the upper limb** (*pars libera membri superioris*). The free part is in turn divided into three: proximal — the **humerus**; middle — the **forearm bones** (radius and ulna); distal — the **bones of the hand** (carpal bones, metacarpal bones and phalanges). In humans the upper limb has been freed from its supporting function and has become an organ of labor: the shoulder girdle is mobile, the joints have a wide range of motion, and the thumb can be opposed to the other fingers.

All upper limb bones except the clavicle pass through three stages of development (membrane → cartilage → bone): their diaphyses ossify in fetal life, and their epiphyses and apophyses after birth. In the newborn the upper limb is short relative to the trunk and long relative to the lower limb; the arm is short, and the forearm and especially the hand are long. By puberty the arm lengthens ≈4 times, the forearm 3–5 times and the hand ≈3 times; at ≈20 years the proportions of the upper limb resemble those of the adult. The humerus grows in length mainly at its **proximal** epiphysis, and the forearm bones at their **distal** epiphysis.

parts.text: Growth of the upper limb bones **“runs away from the elbow”**: in the humerus the more active growth cartilage is at the top (near the shoulder joint), and in the radius and ulna — at the bottom (near the wrist joint). Therefore, in children injuries of the proximal metaphysis of the humerus and the distal metaphysis of the radius most often lead to growth disturbances.

blocks.text: The **clavicle** (*clavicula*) is a short tubular bone curved in an S shape; it lies horizontally between the clavicular notch of the sternum and the acromion of the scapula and acts as a “strut” holding the upper limb away from the trunk. It has a **body** (*corpus claviculae*) and two ends. The medial **sternal end** (*extremitas sternalis*) is thick and triangular and joins the sternum by its **sternal articular surface** (*facies articularis sternalis*). The lateral **acromial end** (*extremitas acromialis*) is flat and wide and bears the **acromial articular surface** (*facies articularis acromialis*), which joins the acromion.

The medial 2/3 of the bone is convex forward, and the lateral 1/3 is concave forward. Its upper surface is smooth and palpable under the skin along its entire length. On the lower surface are: medially, the **impression for the costoclavicular ligament** (*impressio ligamenti costoclavicularis*); in the middle, the **groove for the subclavius muscle** (*sulcus musculi subclavii*); laterally, the **conoid tubercle** (*tuberculum conoideum*) and the **trapezoid line** (*linea trapezoidea*) — the attachment sites of the parts of the coracoclavicular ligament.

blocks.label: Figure 3.1
blocks.caption: The clavicle: A — superior view, B — inferior view: 1 — acromial articular surface; 2 — sternal articular surface; 3 — sternal end; 4 — impression for the costoclavicular ligament; 5 — body of the clavicle; 6 — groove for the subclavius muscle; 7 — conoid tubercle; 8 — trapezoid line; 9 — acromial end. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** The clavicle is **the first bone in the body to ossify** (in the 6th week of fetal life) and the only upper limb bone that develops by the **endesmal** route (without a cartilaginous stage). In the newborn it is S-shaped and its sternal end is cartilaginous. In the first 7 years of life the clavicle grows in length and width. A secondary ossification center appears in the sternal end at 16–18 years and fuses with the body at **20–25 years** — one of the last growth zones in the skeleton to close.

parts.text: **Fracture of the clavicle** is one of the most common fractures: from a fall on the outstretched hand or the shoulder, usually at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds (where the bone is thinnest and curves). The medial fragment is pulled **upward** by the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and the lateral fragment is displaced **downward** by the weight of the arm. Because the subclavian vessels and the brachial plexus lie beneath the clavicle, they may be injured. In newborns, clavicle fracture is **the most common birth injury**.

blocks.text: The **scapula** (*scapula*) is a triangular flat bone; it lies on the posterolateral surface of the thoracic cage at the level of ribs II–VII and is attached to the trunk by muscles. It has three **borders** — **medial** (*margo medialis*, facing the vertebral column), **lateral** (*margo lateralis*, facing the axilla) and **superior** (*margo superior*) — and three **angles** — **superior** (*angulus superior*), **inferior** (*angulus inferior*) and the thickened **lateral** (*angulus lateralis*).

The **anterior — costal surface** (*facies costalis*) is concave and forms the **subscapular fossa** (*fossa subscapularis*). The **posterior surface** (*facies posterior*) is convex; it is divided in two by the transversely running **spine of the scapula** (*spina scapulae*): above — the **supraspinous fossa** (*fossa supraspinata*), below — the larger **infraspinous fossa** (*fossa infraspinata*); each contains the muscle of the same name. Laterally the spine widens and ends in the **acromion** (*acromion*), which overhangs the shoulder joint — the highest point of the shoulder.

At the lateral angle lies the shallow oval **glenoid cavity** (*cavitas glenoidalis*), which articulates with the head of the humerus; above it is the **supraglenoid tubercle** (*tuberculum supraglenoidale* — the origin of the long head of the biceps), and below it the **infraglenoid tubercle** (*tuberculum infraglenoidale* — the origin of the long head of the triceps). The cavity is followed by the narrowed **neck of the scapula** (*collum scapulae*). On the superior border is the **scapular notch** (*incisura scapulae*), and lateral to it the forward-curving **coracoid process** (*processus coracoideus*).

blocks.label: Figure 3.2
blocks.caption: Right scapula, posterior view: 1 — superior angle; 2 — superior border; 3 — spine of the scapula; 4 — scapular notch; 5 — coracoid process; 6 — acromion; 7 — lateral angle; 8 — infraspinous fossa; 9 — lateral border; 10 — inferior angle; 11 — medial border; 12 — supraspinous fossa. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

blocks.label: Figure 3.3
blocks.caption: Right scapula, anterior view: 1 — coracoid process; 2 — scapular notch; 3 — superior border; 4 — superior angle; 5 — subscapular fossa; 6 — medial border; 7 — costal surface; 8 — inferior angle; 9 — lateral border; 10 — infraglenoid tubercle; 11 — glenoid cavity; 12 — supraglenoid tubercle; 13 — acromion. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** The first ossification center appears at the end of the 2nd month of fetal life in the region of the neck of the scapula, and the body and spine ossify from it. In the newborn the scapula lies higher and more laterally than in the adult; the coracoid process, acromion, glenoid cavity, medial border and inferior angle are cartilaginous. An ossification center appears in the coracoid process at the end of the first year, and in the acromion, inferior angle and medial border at 10–15 years. The acromion and coracoid process fuse with the body of the scapula at **18–21 years**, and the medial border and inferior angle at **20–21 years**.

parts.text: In adolescents the ossification center of the acromion appears on an X-ray as a separate bone fragment — do not mistake it for a fracture. Sometimes the acromion never fuses with the scapula (*os acromiale*); this is a normal variant but may cause shoulder pain.

blocks.text: The **humerus** (*humerus*) is the longest tubular bone of the upper limb; it has a body and two ends. At the **proximal end** lies the spherical **head of the humerus** (*caput humeri*), facing medially, upward and slightly backward. The head is separated from the rest of the bone by a shallow groove — the **anatomical neck** (*collum anatomicum*). Lateral to it is the **greater tubercle** (*tuberculum majus*), and in front the **lesser tubercle** (*tuberculum minus*); the **crests of the greater and lesser tubercles** (*crista tuberculi majoris et minoris*) continue downward from them. Between the tubercles and crests lies the **intertubercular groove** (*sulcus intertubercularis*), through which the tendon of the long head of the biceps passes. Below the tubercles is the narrowed part of the bone — the **surgical neck** (*collum chirurgicum*) — the most common site of fracture.

The **body** (*corpus humeri*) is cylindrical above and triangular below; it has **anteromedial**, **anterolateral** and **posterior surfaces** and **medial** and **lateral borders**. In the middle of the body, on the anterolateral surface, is the **deltoid tuberosity** (*tuberositas deltoidea*). On the posterior surface the **groove for the radial nerve** (*sulcus nervi radialis*) spirals from medial to lateral and downward.

The **distal end** widens to form the **condyle of the humerus** (*condylus humeri*). Its medial part bears the **trochlea** (*trochlea humeri*), which articulates with the ulna, and its lateral part the **capitulum** (*capitulum humeri*), which articulates with the radius. Anteriorly, above the trochlea is the **coronoid fossa** (*fossa coronoidea*) and above the capitulum the **radial fossa** (*fossa radialis*); posteriorly, above the trochlea, is the deep **olecranon fossa** (*fossa olecrani*). On either side of the condyle are the **medial and lateral epicondyles** (*epicondylus medialis et lateralis*), palpable under the skin; the **supracondylar ridges** continue upward from them. The **groove for the ulnar nerve** (*sulcus nervi ulnaris*) runs on the posterior surface of the medial epicondyle.
