Middle of the body (groove for the radial nerve)
Paralysis of the extensors of the wrist and fingers — **“wrist drop”**
**“Claw hand”**, impaired sensation in fingers IV–V; an “electric shock” pain when struck

parts.text: Remember the nerves along the humerus from above downward in the order **“A–R–U”**: the **A**xillary nerve — at the surgical neck, the **R**adial nerve — in the middle of the shaft (in the spiral groove), the **U**lnar nerve — behind the medial epicondyle.

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** The primary ossification center appears in the diaphysis in the 8th week of fetal life. In the newborn the bone is relatively short and its ends are cartilaginous. In the proximal epiphysis, ossification centers appear in the head in the first months of life, in the greater tubercle at ≈2 years and in the lesser tubercle at 2–3 years; they merge into a single bony mass at ≈8 years, and the proximal epiphysis fuses with the diaphysis at **20–24 years**. The centers of the distal epiphysis (capitulum, trochlea, epicondyles) appear in childhood and fuse with the diaphysis early — at **16–18 years**.

The **ulna** (*ulna*) lies on the medial side of the forearm (the little-finger side); its proximal end is thick and its distal end thin. Its **proximal end** bears the deep **trochlear notch** (*incisura trochlearis*), which articulates with the trochlea of the humerus; it is bounded posterosuperiorly by the large **olecranon** (*olecranon*) and anteriorly by the **coronoid process** (*processus coronoideus*). On the lateral surface of the coronoid process is the **radial notch** (*incisura radialis*) for the head of the radius, and below it the **tuberosity of the ulna** (*tuberositas ulnae*), to which the brachialis muscle attaches.

The **body** is triangular: it has **anterior**, **posterior** and **medial** surfaces and **anterior**, **posterior** and sharp **interosseous borders** (*margo interosseus*), the latter facing the radius. At the **distal end** lies the **head of the ulna** (*caput ulnae*) — its **articular circumference** (*circumferentia articularis*) articulates with the ulnar notch of the radius — and posteromedially the **styloid process** (*processus styloideus ulnae*).

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** The primary center appears in the diaphysis in the 8th week of fetal life. In the newborn the proximal end is cartilaginous and there is no medullary cavity yet. An ossification center appears in the distal epiphysis at ≈7 years and in the olecranon at 8–11 years; the olecranon fuses with the diaphysis at **16–17 years**, and the distal end at **20–24 years**.

The **radius** (*radius*) lies on the lateral side of the forearm (the thumb side); unlike the ulna, its proximal end is thin and its distal end thick. At the **proximal end** is the cylindrical **head of the radius** (*caput radii*): its upper concave surface (*fovea articularis*) articulates with the capitulum of the humerus, and the **articular circumference** (*circumferentia articularis*) on its side articulates with the radial notch of the ulna. Below the head is the narrowed **neck** (*collum radii*), and below that, on the medial side, the **radial tuberosity** (*tuberositas radii*), to which the tendon of the biceps attaches.

The **body** is triangular and has a sharp **interosseous border** facing the ulna. The widened **distal end** bears on its medial side the **ulnar notch** (*incisura ulnaris*) for the head of the ulna, on its inferior surface the **carpal articular surface** (*facies articularis carpalis*), which articulates with the carpal bones, and on its lateral side the **styloid process** (*processus styloideus radii*), palpable under the skin. The posterior surface of the distal end bears a tubercle (*tuberculum dorsale*) and grooves for muscle tendons.

In A: 1 — head of the radius; 2 — neck; 3 — tuberosity; 4 — interosseous border; 5 — styloid process; 6 — anterior border; 7 — anterior surface; 8 — nutrient foramen; 9 — articular circumference. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

parts.text: Rule for distinguishing the two forearm bones: **the ulna is thick at the top** (it mainly forms the elbow joint), **the radius is thick at the bottom** (it mainly forms the wrist joint). Both bones have a head, but at opposite ends: the head of the radius is **at the top**, the head of the ulna is **at the bottom**.

**Fracture of the radius “at the typical site”** (Colles' fracture) occurs 2–3 cm above the distal end, from a fall on the outstretched palm; in this region the compact substance is thin and the spongy substance is sparse, i.e., the resistance of the bone is reduced. The distal fragment is displaced backward and laterally — the forearm takes on a “dinner fork” shape. It is especially common in elderly women because of osteoporosis. In children, **epiphysiolysis** (separation along the growth cartilage) occurs in this region.

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** The primary center appears in the diaphysis in the 8th week of fetal life; in the newborn both ends are cartilaginous and the neck is poorly defined. The ossification center of the distal epiphysis appears at the end of the first year and fuses with the diaphysis at **19–22 years**; the ossification center of the head appears at 5–6 years and fuses at **17–18 years**.

The skeleton of the hand (*ossa manus*) consists of three parts: the **carpal bones** (*ossa carpi*) — 8, the **metacarpal bones** (*ossa metacarpi*) — 5, and the **phalanges of the fingers** (*ossa digitorum, phalanges*) — 14.
Carpal bones

The 8 small spongy bones are arranged in two rows. The **proximal row** (from lateral to medial): the **scaphoid** (*os scaphoideum*), **lunate** (*os lunatum*), **triquetrum** (*os triquetrum*) and **pisiform** (*os pisiforme*). The first three together form an ellipsoid articular surface that articulates with the radius; the pisiform is a sesamoid bone lying within the tendon of the ulnar flexor muscle. The **distal row**: the **trapezium** (*os trapezium*), **trapezoid** (*os trapezoideum*), **capitate** (*os capitatum* — the largest carpal bone) and **hamate** (*os hamatum* — with a hook, *hamulus*, on its palmar surface). On the palmar side the carpal bones form a concave, trough-like **carpal groove** — closed by the flexor retinaculum, it becomes the **carpal tunnel**.

parts.text: Remember the carpal bones from lateral (thumb side) to medial, first the proximal and then the distal row: **“Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle”** — **S**caphoid, **L**unate, **T**riquetrum, **P**isiform; **T**rapezium, **T**rapezoid, **C**apitate, **H**amate.

blocks.text: Metacarpal bones and phalanges

The **metacarpal bones** (*ossa metacarpi I–V*) are short tubular bones; each has a **base** (*basis*), **body** (*corpus*) and **head** (*caput*). The I metacarpal is the shortest and thickest, and its base bears a **saddle-shaped** articular surface for the trapezium — which allows the thumb to be opposed to the other fingers (opposition). The bases of metacarpals II–V bear lateral surfaces that articulate with their neighbors. The **phalanges** are also short tubular bones: fingers II–V have three each — **proximal**, **middle** and **distal** phalanges — and the thumb has two (proximal and distal). Each phalanx has a base, body and head (*trochlea*); the tip of the distal phalanx bears the **tuberosity of the distal phalanx** (*tuberositas phalangis distalis*). In the region of the I metacarpophalangeal joint there are 2 **sesamoid bones** within the tendons.

Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

parts.text: **Fracture of the scaphoid** is the most common carpal fracture (from a fall on the outstretched palm). Pain is felt in the **“anatomical snuffbox”** — the depression formed at the base of the thumb when it is extended. Because the bone receives its blood supply mainly from its distal part, after a fracture the proximal fragment may be **left without blood and undergo necrosis**. The fracture may not be visible on the initial X-ray — so if it is suspected, the hand is immobilized and imaging is repeated after 10–14 days.

blocks.text: **Radiological anatomy.** On an X-ray of the hand the shadows of the trapezium and trapezoid overlap, and the shadow of the pisiform is superimposed on that of the triquetrum. In the diaphyses of the metacarpals and phalanges the compact substance and the medullary canal are visible, and the heads are covered by a thin compact layer.

Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

sections.title: 8. Ossification of the upper limb bones and bone age

blocks.text: In the newborn the carpal bones are formed but are **entirely cartilaginous** — on an X-ray the carpal region looks “empty.” Their ossification centers appear in a strict order, so the child's **bone (biological) age** is determined from an X-ray of the hand and compared with the chronological age (growth delay, endocrine diseases, forensic medical examination).

blocks.title: Table 3.2. Appearance of ossification centers in the carpal bones
head: Bone
Time of appearance

parts.text: The carpal bones ossify **starting with the capitate and proceeding counterclockwise** (looking at the left hand from the palm): capitate → hamate → triquetrum → lunate → scaphoid → trapezium → trapezoid, and last — the pisiform. A rough rule: **after 1 year, the child's age ≈ the number of visible carpal bones** (for example, 3 at 3 years, 4 at 4 years).

blocks.label: Figure 3.9
blocks.caption: X-ray of the left hand of a 3-year-old child: 1 — distal phalanx; 2 — middle phalanx; 3 — proximal phalanx; 4 — metacarpal bones; 5 — I metacarpal; 6 — capitate; 7 — radius; 8 — ulna; 9 — hamate. In the carpal region only the capitate and hamate (and the initial center of the triquetrum) are visible so far; the epiphyses of the phalanges and metacarpals are separated by cartilage. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

blocks.text: Ossification centers appear in the diaphyses of the metacarpals in the 9th–11th weeks of fetal life; the epiphyseal centers appear at 2.5–3 years (in the I metacarpal — in the base, in II–V — in the head) and fuse with the body at **15–20 years**. The diaphyses of the phalanges appear in the 2nd–3rd months of fetal life, and the epiphyseal centers (in the base) at 2–3 years; they fuse at **18–20 years**.

skills.title: Practical skill: determining the side of the upper limb bones

items: **Clavicle:** place the flat (acromial) end laterally, the convex medial 2/3 forward and the smooth surface upward — this shows which side it belongs to.
**Scapula:** orient the glenoid cavity laterally, the spine backward and upward and the inferior angle downward.
**Humerus:** turn the head upward and medially and the intertubercular groove forward; the trochlea is then medial and the capitulum lateral.
**Ulna:** turn the thick end (olecranon) upward, the trochlear notch forward and the radial notch laterally.
**Radius:** turn the thick end downward, the styloid process laterally, the ulnar notch medially and the tuberosity forward and medially.

skills.title: Practical skill: palpation in a living person

items: Palpate the clavicle along its entire length from the sternal to the acromial end; at its lateral end find the acromion, and deep, in front of and below it, the coracoid process.
Palpate the spine, medial border and inferior angle of the scapula (at the level of the VII rib); observe the movement of the scapula when the arm moves.

In the elbow region find the medial and lateral epicondyles and the olecranon: with the elbow extended they lie on one straight line, and with the elbow flexed to 90° they form an isosceles triangle (Hueter's triangle).
Roll the ulnar nerve under your finger behind the medial epicondyle.
Find the styloid processes of the radius and ulna: that of the radius lies ≈1 cm lower than that of the ulna.
Have the thumb extended and palpate the anatomical snuffbox and the scaphoid at its floor.

parts.text: In an injury of the elbow region, disruption of **Hueter's triangle** (a change in the position of the three points) indicates a fracture or dislocation. Because children have many ossification centers in this region, always evaluate the X-ray **in comparison with the healthy side**.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 65-year-old woman slipped on ice and fell on her outstretched palm. The distal forearm has a “dinner fork” deformity, and the styloid processes lie at the same level.
cases.ask: Which bone is fractured and where? Why at this particular site and at this age?
cases.answer: This is a **fracture of the radius “at the typical site” (Colles' fracture)** — 2–3 cm above the distal end, with the distal fragment displaced backward and laterally. Normally the styloid process of the radius lies ≈1 cm lower than that of the ulna; their being at the same level indicates shortening of the radius. In this region the compact substance is thin and the spongy substance sparse, and in elderly women **postmenopausal osteoporosis** further reduces the strength of the bone.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A young man fell on his shoulder while playing football. There is pain in the shoulder joint region; the X-ray shows a fracture of the narrowed part of the humerus below the tubercles. The patient cannot raise his arm to the side, and sensation on the lateral surface of the shoulder is reduced.
cases.ask: Which part of the humerus is fractured? Which nerve is injured?
cases.answer: The **surgical neck** of the humerus is fractured. The **axillary nerve** (*n. axillaris*) winds around this region from behind: it innervates the deltoid muscle (abduction of the arm is impaired) and supplies sensory innervation to the skin of the lateral surface of the shoulder. It must not be confused with the anatomical neck (the border of the head) — which lies much higher.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: Parents complain that their 6-year-old son is much shorter than his peers. The endocrinologist ordered an X-ray of the left hand; in the carpal region only the capitate, hamate and triquetrum were found.
cases.ask: Estimate the child's bone age. What is this examination based on?
cases.answer: Ossification centers appear in the carpal bones in a strict order: capitate (2–3 months), hamate (3–4 months), triquetrum (≈3 years), lunate (≈4), scaphoid (≈5), trapezium and trapezoid (5–6 years). The presence of only three bones corresponds to a **bone age of ≈3 years**, i.e., 3 years behind the chronological age. This indicates delayed ossification and requires a search for endocrine causes such as hypothyroidism or growth hormone deficiency.

topics.title: Bones of the pelvic girdle and free lower limb: structure and age-related features

goals.text: To introduce the student to the structure of the hip bone and the bones of the free lower limb (femur, patella, tibia, fibula, bones of the foot), the points palpable in a living person, the structure of the pelvis as a whole, its sex differences and dimensions, and the timing of ossification.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the three parts of the hip bone (ilium, ischium, pubis) and their structures;
the structure of the acetabulum;
the greater and lesser pelvis, the terminal line, and the sex differences and main dimensions of the pelvis;
the structures of the head, neck, trochanters, body and distal end of the femur; the neck-shaft angle;
the structure of the patella, tibia and fibula;
the bones of the foot (tarsal bones, metatarsal bones, phalanges) and the arches of the foot;
the timing of ossification of the lower limb bones and the signs of fetal maturity.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: place each bone in the anatomical position and determine whether it is right or left;
show the main structures of the bones and name them in Latin;
palpate in a living person the iliac crest, anterior superior iliac spine, greater trochanter, patella, tibial tuberosity and malleoli;
explain the measurement of the external dimensions of the pelvis with a pelvimeter and calculate the true conjugate.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The **anterior superior iliac spine** is the main landmark for measuring leg length (from it to the medial malleolus), for the projection of the inguinal ligament and for surgical incisions of the abdominal wall. Bone marrow biopsies and trephine biopsies are taken from the **iliac crest** (its posterior part), and in children marrow puncture is also performed here. The **upper outer quadrant of the gluteal surface** is the safe site for intramuscular injection: the sciatic nerve passes through the lower inner quadrant.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Because the acetabulum is shallow in the newborn, **congenital hip dislocation (developmental dysplasia of the hip)** occurs. To detect it early, all newborns undergo ultrasound examination of the hip joint and special tests (Ortolani, Barlow); if detected early, it is fully cured with wide swaddling and a special splint.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the subpubic angle with your fingers: the obtuse angle of the female pelvis resembles the angle between the **thumb and index finger** (≈90°), and the acute angle of the male pelvis the angle between the **index and middle fingers** (≈70°).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The **true conjugate** is not measured directly — it is calculated: **9 cm is subtracted from the external conjugate** or **1.5–2 cm from the diagonal conjugate** (20 − 9 = 11 cm; 13 − 2 = 11 cm). If the true conjugate is less than 11 cm, the pelvis is considered **contracted** and natural delivery may be difficult.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Fracture of the femoral neck** is common in the elderly (especially in women with osteoporosis) from a fall on the side. The neck lies inside the joint capsule, and the vessels supplying the head run along the neck — in a fracture they are torn, and the risk of **avascular necrosis of the head** and nonunion of the fracture is high. Therefore, **joint replacement (arthroplasty)** is often performed. The patient's leg is externally rotated and shortened, and the greater trochanter is displaced upward.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Around the neck of the fibula the **common fibular nerve** (*n. fibularis communis*) lies just under the skin, pressed against the bone. A blow here, a tight cast or prolonged sitting with crossed legs can injure the nerve, leading to **“foot drop”** (inability to dorsiflex the foot and extend the toes, “steppage gait”). Because the anterior surface of the tibia lies directly under the skin, fractures here are often **open**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In adolescents (10–15 years) the apophysis of the tibial tuberosity may become strained by the pull of the quadriceps muscle and form a painful bump — **Osgood–Schlatter disease** (common in adolescent athletes). The X-ray shows fragmentation of the apophysis — this must not be misinterpreted as a fracture.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: There are 7 tarsal bones: **2 + 1 + 3 + 1** — posteriorly **2** large ones (talus and calcaneus), in the middle medially **1** (navicular), in front **3** cuneiform and laterally **1** cuboid. That is one fewer than the 8 bones of the hand: the pisiform has no “counterpart.”

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: If the ligaments and muscles supporting the arches weaken, **flatfoot** develops (longitudinal or transverse): rapid fatigue and pain in the foot and lower leg. In infants and young children the plantar fat pad is thick, so the foot looks flat — this is normal; the arch forms by 4–6 years. Therefore, flatfoot is usually diagnosed after 6–7 years (plantography, podometry).

sections.title: 1. The lower limb skeleton: general information

blocks.text: The lower limb skeleton consists of two divisions: the **pelvic girdle** (*cingulum membri inferioris*) — the paired hip bones, and the **free part of the lower limb** (*pars libera membri inferioris*) — the femur, patella, tibia and fibula, and the bones of the foot. The main function of the lower limb bones is to support the body weight with little expenditure of energy and to move the body in space. Therefore they are larger and more massive than the upper limb bones, their joints are stronger and their range of motion smaller. When standing, the body's center of gravity lies in the pelvis, in front of the II sacral vertebra.

In the newborn the lower limb is short relative to the upper limb, and the thigh is short. The lower limb grows especially quickly in the second period of childhood and at puberty; by puberty the thigh lengthens ≈4.5 times, the leg ≈4 times and the foot ≈3 times.

The **hip bone** (*os coxae*) is formed by the fusion of three bones — the **ilium** (*os ilium*), **ischium** (*os ischii*) and **pubis** (*os pubis*). Until 14–16 years they are joined by cartilage, after which they ossify into a single bone. Where the bodies of the three bones meet, the deep **acetabulum** (*acetabulum*), into which the head of the femur fits, is formed on the outer surface. The acetabulum is surrounded by a **rim** (*limbus acetabuli*); its articular part is the horseshoe-shaped **lunate surface** (*facies lunata*), its center is the rough **acetabular fossa** (*fossa acetabuli*), and on its inferomedial side is the **acetabular notch** (*incisura acetabuli*).

blocks.label: Figure 4.1
blocks.caption: Components of the hip bone (outer surface): the ilium (white), ischium (pink) and pubis (blue) meet in the acetabulum. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: The ilium

The ilium consists of a **body** (*corpus ossis ilii*) and a broad **ala (wing)** (*ala ossis ilii*). The thickened upper border of the ala — the **iliac crest** (*crista iliaca*) — is S-shaped and bears an **outer lip**, **intermediate line** and **inner lip**, to which the abdominal muscles attach. Anteriorly the crest ends in the **anterior superior iliac spine** (*spina iliaca anterior superior*), below which lies the **anterior inferior spine**; posteriorly there are the **posterior superior** and **posterior inferior iliac spines**. On the outer — **gluteal surface** (*facies glutea*) of the ala, three rough lines — the **anterior, posterior and inferior gluteal lines** — delimit the origins of the gluteal muscles. The inner surface is concave — the **iliac fossa** (*fossa iliaca*); behind it lie the **auricular surface** (*facies auricularis*), which articulates with the sacrum, and the **iliac tuberosity**. On the inner surface the fossa is bounded below by the **arcuate line** (*linea arcuata*).
The ischium and pubis

The body of the **ischium** forms the posteroinferior part of the acetabulum; the **ramus** (*ramus ossis ischii*) continues downward from it. The posterior border of the body bears the **ischial spine** (*spina ischiadica*); above it lies the **greater sciatic notch** (*incisura ischiadica major*), and below it the **lesser sciatic notch**. At the junction of the ramus and body is the thick **ischial tuberosity** (*tuber ischiadicum*), which serves as a support when sitting.

The **pubis** consists of a body and **superior** and **inferior rami**. The upper border of the superior ramus is a sharp crest — the **pecten of the pubis** (*pecten ossis pubis*) — which ends anteriorly in the **pubic tubercle** (*tuberculum pubicum*). Medially the two pubic bones face each other by their **symphyseal surfaces** (*facies symphysialis*). Together the pubis and ischium bound the large **obturator foramen** (*foramen obturatum*); at its upper border is the **obturator groove**, through which vessels and nerves pass.

parts.text: The **anterior superior iliac spine** is the main landmark for measuring leg length (from it to the medial malleolus), for the projection of the inguinal ligament and for surgical incisions of the abdominal wall. Bone marrow biopsies and trephine biopsies are taken from the **iliac crest** (its posterior part), and in children marrow puncture is also performed here. The **upper outer quadrant of the gluteal surface** is the safe site for intramuscular injection: the sciatic nerve passes through the lower inner quadrant.

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** The hip bone develops from three main ossification centers: in the body of the **ischium** in the 4th month of fetal life, the **pubis** in the 5th month and the **ilium** in the 6th month. In the newborn the three bones are separate and joined in the acetabulum by **Y-shaped cartilage**; the acetabulum is shallow and oblique. The rami of the ischium and pubis fuse at 7–8 years; the Y-shaped cartilage of the acetabulum ossifies at **14–16 years**. Additional centers in the iliac crest, spines and ischial tuberosity appear at puberty and fuse at **20–25 years**.

parts.text: Because the acetabulum is shallow in the newborn, **congenital hip dislocation (developmental dysplasia of the hip)** occurs. To detect it early, all newborns undergo ultrasound examination of the hip joint and special tests (Ortolani, Barlow); if detected early, it is fully cured with wide swaddling and a special splint.

sections.title: 3. The pelvis as a whole: structure, sex differences and dimensions

blocks.text: The **pelvis** (*pelvis*) is formed by the two hip bones, the sacrum and the coccyx. The **terminal line** (*linea terminalis*) — a line passing through the sacral promontory, the arcuate lines, the pecten of the pubis and the upper border of the symphysis — divides it into two parts: above — the **greater pelvis** (*pelvis major*), bounded by the alae of the ilia, a support for the abdominal organs; below — the **lesser pelvis** (*pelvis minor*), the cavity containing the urinary bladder, rectum and internal genital organs — in women it is the **birth canal**. The **superior aperture** of the lesser pelvis (*apertura pelvis superior*) corresponds to the terminal line, and the **inferior aperture** (*apertura pelvis inferior*) is bounded by the coccyx, ischial tuberosities, inferior pubic rami and the symphysis.

parts.text: Remember the subpubic angle with your fingers: the obtuse angle of the female pelvis resembles the angle between the **thumb and index finger** (≈90°), and the acute angle of the male pelvis the angle between the **index and middle fingers** (≈70°).

blocks.text: The dimensions of the pelvis are needed in obstetrics to plan delivery. In a living woman the external dimensions are measured with a **pelvimeter**, and the internal dimensions are estimated from them.

parts.text: The **true conjugate** is not measured directly — it is calculated: **9 cm is subtracted from the external conjugate** or **1.5–2 cm from the diagonal conjugate** (20 − 9 = 11 cm; 13 − 2 = 11 cm). If the true conjugate is less than 11 cm, the pelvis is considered **contracted** and natural delivery may be difficult.

blocks.text: The **femur** (*femur*) is the longest and strongest tubular bone of the human skeleton. Its **proximal end** bears the spherical **head** (*caput femoris*); in its center lies the **fovea of the head** (*fovea capitis femoris*), to which the ligament of the head attaches. The head is joined to the body by the obliquely directed **neck of the femur** (*collum femoris*): the angle between the neck and the axis of the body is **≈130°** in adults (larger in children, smaller in the elderly). Where the neck passes into the body there are, laterally, the large **greater trochanter** (*trochanter major*) and, posteromedially, the **lesser trochanter** (*trochanter minor*); they are connected anteriorly by the **intertrochanteric line** (*linea intertrochanterica*) and posteriorly by the **intertrochanteric crest** (*crista intertrochanterica*). On the medial surface of the greater trochanter is the **trochanteric fossa** (*fossa trochanterica*).

The **body** (*corpus femoris*) is slightly convex forward and rounded; along its posterior surface runs the two-lipped **rough line** (*linea aspera*) — its **lateral and medial lips** continue upward to form the **gluteal tuberosity** (*tuberositas glutea*) and the **pectineal line** (*linea pectinea*), and below they diverge to bound the **popliteal surface** (*facies poplitea*). The **distal end** widens to form two condyles — the **medial** and **lateral condyles** (*condylus medialis et lateralis*); posteriorly they are separated by the deep **intercondylar fossa** (*fossa intercondylaris*), and anteriorly they are joined by the **patellar surface** (*facies patellaris*) for the patella. On the lateral surfaces of the condyles lie the **medial and lateral epicondyles**.

parts.text: **Fracture of the femoral neck** is common in the elderly (especially in women with osteoporosis) from a fall on the side. The neck lies inside the joint capsule, and the vessels supplying the head run along the neck — in a fracture they are torn, and the risk of **avascular necrosis of the head** and nonunion of the fracture is high. Therefore, **joint replacement (arthroplasty)** is often performed. The patient's leg is externally rotated and shortened, and the greater trochanter is displaced upward.

blocks.text: The **patella** (*patella*) is the largest **sesamoid bone** in the body; it develops within the tendon of the quadriceps femoris. It is triangular: its broad **base** (*basis patellae*) faces upward and its **apex** (*apex patellae*) downward; its posterior articular surface articulates with the patellar surface of the femur. Its ossification center appears at 2–6 years.

**Age-related features.** The primary center appears in the diaphysis at the end of the 2nd month of fetal life. In the newborn the femur is relatively short, its ends are cartilaginous, and the neck-shaft angle is large (≈150°). **The ossification center in the distal epiphysis appears just before birth** (in the 9th month of fetal life) — its presence is a **sign of fetal maturity** (Béclard's nucleus). A center appears in the head in the 1st year (at 3–6 months), in the greater trochanter at ≈4 years and in the lesser trochanter at ≈8 years. The trochanters fuse with the body at **16–18**, the head at **17–19**, and the distal epiphysis at **20–22 years** in women and **22–24 years** in men.

The **tibia** (*tibia*) lies on the medial side of the leg and bears the full body weight. Its **proximal end** widens to form the **medial and lateral condyles**; their upper **articular surfaces** (*facies articularis superior*) articulate with the condyles of the femur. Between the articular surfaces is the **intercondylar eminence** (*eminentia intercondylaris*) with two tubercles, and in front of and behind it the **anterior and posterior intercondylar areas** (where the cruciate ligaments and menisci attach). The posteroinferior surface of the lateral condyle bears an **articular surface** (*facies articularis fibularis*) for the head of the fibula.

The **body** is triangular; its **anterior border** (*margo anterior*) is sharp and palpable under the skin along its whole length; at its upper part is the **tibial tuberosity** (*tuberositas tibiae*), to which the quadriceps tendon (patellar ligament) attaches. The lateral border is the interosseous border; on the posterior surface the **soleal line** (*linea musculi solei*) runs obliquely. At the **distal end** are the downward-projecting **medial malleolus** (*malleolus medialis*) and the **inferior articular surface**, which articulates with the talus, and laterally the **fibular notch** (*incisura fibularis*) for the fibula.

The **fibula** (*fibula*) is a thin long bone on the lateral side of the leg; it bears almost no body weight and serves mainly as a site of muscle attachment and as the lateral wall of the ankle joint. At its proximal end are the **head** (*caput fibulae*) and its **apex** (*apex*), and at its distal end the **lateral malleolus** (*malleolus lateralis*), clearly palpable under the skin; the lateral malleolus extends **lower** than the medial malleolus. On the posterior surface of the malleolus is the **malleolar groove** (*sulcus malleolaris*), through which the tendons of the fibular muscles pass.

parts.text: Around the neck of the fibula the **common fibular nerve** (*n. fibularis communis*) lies just under the skin, pressed against the bone. A blow here, a tight cast or prolonged sitting with crossed legs can injure the nerve, leading to **“foot drop”** (inability to dorsiflex the foot and extend the toes, “steppage gait”). Because the anterior surface of the tibia lies directly under the skin, fractures here are often **open**.

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** An ossification center also appears in the proximal epiphysis of the tibia **just before birth** (a sign of maturity), and in the distal epiphysis in the 2nd year; a secondary center appears in the tuberosity at 10–13 years. The distal epiphysis fuses with the diaphysis at **16–19**, and the proximal epiphysis at **19–24 years**. In the fibula the center of the distal epiphysis appears at ≈2 years and that of the head at 3–5 years; they fuse at **20–22** and **≈24 years**.

parts.text: In adolescents (10–15 years) the apophysis of the tibial tuberosity may become strained by the pull of the quadriceps muscle and form a painful bump — **Osgood–Schlatter disease** (common in adolescent athletes). The X-ray shows fragmentation of the apophysis — this must not be misinterpreted as a fracture.

blocks.text: The skeleton of the foot (*ossa pedis*) consists of three parts: the **tarsal bones** (*ossa tarsi*) — 7, the **metatarsal bones** (*ossa metatarsi*) — 5, and the **phalanges of the toes** — 14.
Tarsal bones

The **proximal row** is formed by two large bones. The **talus** (*talus*) is the “link” between the leg and the foot: it has a **head**, **neck** and **body**; the upper part of the body — the **trochlea** (*trochlea tali*) — forms the ankle joint with the leg bones. No muscles attach to the talus. The **calcaneus** (*calcaneus*) is the largest bone of the foot; posteriorly it ends in the large **calcaneal tuberosity** (*tuber calcanei*) (where the Achilles tendon attaches), and medially it bears a process supporting the talus — the **sustentaculum tali** (*sustentaculum tali*).

**Distal row**: medially the **navicular bone** (*os naviculare*) — between the head of the talus and the three cuneiform bones; its medial-inferior surface bears a tuberosity. In front of it are the three **cuneiform bones** — **medial, intermediate and lateral** (*ossa cuneiformia*); laterally, in front of the calcaneus, is the **cuboid bone** (*os cuboideum*), whose inferior surface bears a groove for the tendon of the fibularis longus muscle.
Metatarsal bones and phalanges of the toes

The **metatarsal bones** (*ossa metatarsi I–V*) are short tubular bones (base, body, head). The I metatarsal is the shortest and thickest, the II the longest; the lateral side of the base of the V metatarsal bears a **tuberosity** (*tuberositas ossis metatarsi V*), palpable under the skin. The **phalanges of the toes** resemble those of the hand but are shorter; the big toe (*hallux*) has two phalanges and the other toes three each. Two sesamoid bones lie beneath the I metatarsophalangeal joint.

parts.text: There are 7 tarsal bones: **2 + 1 + 3 + 1** — posteriorly **2** large ones (talus and calcaneus), in the middle medially **1** (navicular), in front **3** cuneiform and laterally **1** cuboid. That is one fewer than the 8 bones of the hand: the pisiform has no “counterpart.”

blocks.text: Arches of the foot

The bones of the foot do not lie flat — they form upwardly convex **arches**, and when standing the foot rests mainly on three points — the **calcaneal tuberosity** and **the heads of the I and V metatarsals**. The **longitudinal arch** (its medial part is high — support and shock absorption; its lateral part is low — support) and the **transverse arch** (at the level of the bases of the metatarsals) are distinguished. The arches cushion impact during walking and jumping; they are maintained by the shape of the bones, the ligaments (especially the long plantar ligament and the plantar aponeurosis) and the muscles.

parts.text: If the ligaments and muscles supporting the arches weaken, **flatfoot** develops (longitudinal or transverse): rapid fatigue and pain in the foot and lower leg. In infants and young children the plantar fat pad is thick, so the foot looks flat — this is normal; the arch forms by 4–6 years. Therefore, flatfoot is usually diagnosed after 6–7 years (plantography, podometry).

blocks.text: **Radiological anatomy and age-related features.** In the newborn the tarsal bones are mainly cartilaginous; ossification centers are present only in the **calcaneus** (from the 6th month of fetal life), **talus** (7th–8th month) and **cuboid** (9th month). After birth centers appear in the lateral cuneiform (1st year), intermediate cuneiform (3–4 years), medial cuneiform (2–4 years) and navicular (3–5 years). An additional center appears in the calcaneal tuberosity at 7–10 years and fuses with the body at **16–17 years**. Centers in the epiphyses of the metatarsals and phalanges appear at 2–4 years and fuse at **16–19 years**.

skills.title: Practical skill: determining the side of the lower limb bones

items: **Hip bone:** turn the acetabulum laterally, the obturator foramen downward and forward and the iliac crest upward; the pubis is then in front and the ischial tuberosity posteroinferior.
**Femur:** turn the head upward and medially and the linea aspera backward.
**Tibia:** turn the wide end upward, the sharp anterior border forward and the medial malleolus medially.
**Fibula:** turn the triangular flattened malleolus downward, the articular surface of the malleolus medially and the malleolar groove backward.
**Foot:** turn the calcaneal tuberosity backward, the trochlea of the talus upward and the big toe medially.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 78-year-old woman slipped at home and fell on her side. Her right leg is externally rotated and 2 cm shorter than the left, there is pain in the hip joint, and she cannot lift her leg.
cases.ask: Which part of which bone may be fractured? Why is this fracture dangerous?
cases.answer: This is a **fracture of the femoral neck** — common in the elderly against a background of osteoporosis. The neck lies inside the joint capsule, and the blood supply of the head depends on vessels running along the neck; in a fracture they are torn, and the risk of **avascular necrosis of the head** and nonunion of the fracture is high. Therefore a hip replacement (endoprosthesis) is often performed. Prolonged bed rest leads to pneumonia, thrombosis and pressure sores.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: On examination of a pregnant woman, the following were measured with a pelvimeter: *distantia spinarum* — 23 cm, *distantia cristarum* — 26 cm, *distantia trochanterica* — 29 cm, *conjugata externa* — 18 cm.
cases.ask: Evaluate the pelvic dimensions. What is the true conjugate? How does this affect delivery?
cases.answer: Normal: 25–26, 28–29, 30–31 and 20–21 cm. All dimensions are 2–3 cm smaller — a **generally (uniformly) contracted pelvis**. True conjugate = 18 − 9 = **≈9 cm** (normal 11 cm). Because the true conjugate is reduced, the fetal head may be unable to pass through the superior aperture of the lesser pelvis — cesarean section is considered when planning delivery.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A newborn was sent for forensic medical examination. It must be determined whether the baby was mature (full-term) or premature. The X-ray shows ossification centers 5–7 mm in diameter in the distal epiphysis of the femur and the proximal epiphysis of the tibia; centers are also present in the calcaneus, talus and cuboid.
cases.ask: Is the newborn mature? Justify your answer.
cases.answer: Yes, the newborn is **mature**. The ossification center in the distal epiphysis of the femur (Béclard's nucleus) appears in the 9th month of fetal life, i.e., just before birth; its presence (and that of the center in the proximal epiphysis of the tibia) indicates that the fetus was full-term. The center in the cuboid also appears in the 9th month. In a premature infant these centers are absent or very small.

topics.title: The skull. Bones of the neurocranium: occipital, parietal, frontal and ethmoid bones and their age-related features

goals.text: To introduce the student to the divisions and development of the skull, the structure of the occipital, parietal, frontal and ethmoid bones of the neurocranium, and the features of the newborn's skull (fontanelles); to relate this knowledge to examination of children, head injuries and diseases of the ENT organs.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the neurocranium and viscerocranium and the bones that belong to them;
the stages of development of the skull bones and their groups by origin;
the parts of the occipital bone, the foramen magnum, the condyles, canals and structures on its internal and external surfaces;
the borders, angles and surfaces of the parietal bone;
the parts of the frontal bone, the frontal sinus and the structures of its orbital part;
the parts of the ethmoid bone, the labyrinth cells and the nasal conchae;
the types, location and closure times of the fontanelles.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: place an individual bone in the anatomical position and show its structures, naming them in Latin;
show the boundaries of the bones of the neurocranium and the sutures on a skull;
find the fontanelles on a newborn's skull (on a mannequin or picture) and state when they close;
palpate in a living person the external occipital protuberance, superciliary arches, glabella and supraorbital notch.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: When intracranial pressure rises sharply (edema, hemorrhage), the cerebellar tonsils and the medulla oblongata may **herniate into the foramen magnum** — this compresses the respiratory and circulatory centers and leads to death. That is why lumbar puncture is dangerous when intracranial pressure is high. The **external occipital protuberance** is a landmark for measuring the head (head circumference) and for blocking the occipital nerves.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In the region of the **sphenoidal angle** of the parietal bone (the temporal region — the **pterion**) the bone is thin, and the **middle meningeal artery** lies on its inner surface. When a blow falls here, the artery ruptures and blood collects between the bone and the dura mater — an **epidural hematoma**. The patient may initially regain consciousness (the “lucid interval”), after which the condition deteriorates sharply — emergency trepanation is required.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Inflammation of the frontal sinus — **frontal sinusitis** — is accompanied by pain in the forehead and supraorbital region; pressure over the supraorbital foramen (where the nerve emerges) is painful. Because the sinus opens into the nose by a narrow passage, drainage is difficult during inflammation. Infection may spread into the cranial cavity through the thin posterior wall of the frontal sinus (meningitis, brain abscess).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: On adult X-rays a thin light line along the midline of the frontal bone is often a **persistent metopic suture** — do not confuse it with a fracture. The suture is **serrated, symmetric** and exactly in the midline, whereas a fracture line is irregular and usually deviates from the midline.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In a fracture of the anterior cranial fossa (usually through the **cribriform plate**), the meninges tear and cerebrospinal fluid leaks from the nose — **CSF leak** (rhinorrhea); loss of smell (anosmia) and “spectacle” bruising around the eyes are also typical. If clear fluid flows from the nose, it should be tested with the blood-mixed spot (halo) test and for glucose. Such a patient must not blow the nose hard or have a nasal tube inserted — infection may spread into the cranial cavity. Because the orbital plate is very thin, **inflammation of the ethmoid cells** (ethmoiditis, especially in children) easily spreads to the orbit.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Remember the fontanelles by **“4 – 2 – 1 – 0”**: there are **4** types (6 in total) of fontanelles; **2** are unpaired (anterior and posterior), and two pairs are lateral (sphenoidal and mastoid). The anterior fontanelle closes at **1–1.5 years**, the posterior at **2–3 months**, and the lateral fontanelles are often already **closed at birth (0)**.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The **anterior fontanelle** serves as a “window” for the pediatrician. A **bulging, tense** fontanelle indicates increased intracranial pressure (meningitis, hydrocephalus, hemorrhage); a **sunken** fontanelle is a sign of dehydration (exsiccosis). **Early closure** of the fontanelle and premature ossification of the sutures (**craniosynostosis**) lead to deformity of the head and restriction of brain growth; **late closure** is seen in rickets, hypothyroidism or hydrocephalus. In infants, ultrasound examination of the brain (neurosonography) is performed precisely through the anterior fontanelle.

blocks.text: The **skull** (*cranium*) protects the brain and the sense organs and serves as a support for the initial parts of the digestive and respiratory tracts. It is divided into two parts: the **neurocranium** (*neurocranium*) — forming the cavity containing the brain, and the **viscerocranium (facial skeleton)** (*viscerocranium*) — the skeleton of the orbits and the nasal and oral cavities. The neurocranium is formed by **8** bones: unpaired — the **occipital, sphenoid, frontal and ethmoid** bones, and paired — the **parietal** and **temporal** bones. In the neurocranium the **cranial vault (calvaria)** (*calvaria*) and the **cranial base** (*basis cranii*) are distinguished.

blocks.label: Figure 5.1
blocks.caption: The skull, right lateral view; the bones are shown in different colors: *os frontale* — frontal, *os parietale* — parietal, *os occipitale* — occipital, *os temporale* — temporal, *os sphenoidale* — sphenoid bone, *os zygomaticum* — zygomatic bone, *maxilla* — maxilla, *mandibula* — mandible; *sutura coronalis, squamosa, lambdoidea* — coronal, squamous and lambdoid sutures. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: Development of the skull bones

The skull bones pass through three stages: **membranous** (end of the 1st — beginning of the 2nd month of fetal life), **cartilaginous** (end of the 2nd — beginning of the 3rd month, when the cranial base becomes cartilage) and **bony**. Most bones of the **cranial vault and face** do not pass through a cartilaginous stage but ossify directly from connective tissue by the **endesmal** route (primary bones); the bones of the **cranial base** ossify via cartilage (secondary bones). The facial bones develop from the **visceral (branchial) arches** of the embryo: arch I — the mandibular arch (maxilla and mandible, malleus, incus), arch II — the hyoid arch (stapes, lesser horns of the hyoid bone), and so on.

blocks.title: Table 5.1. Groups of skull bones by origin
head: Group
Primary (endesmal) bones
Secondary (via cartilage) bones
rows: Upper part of the occipital squama, parietal and frontal bones, squamous and tympanic parts of the temporal bone
Sphenoid bone, basilar and lateral parts of the occipital bone, petrous part of the temporal bone

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** In the newborn the cranial vault is very large relative to the base (the neurocranium is ≈8 times larger than the facial skeleton, compared with ≈2 times in adults). In the first year the vault grows rapidly, and at 1 year its length reaches half that of an adult's head; at 20 years it takes its permanent shape. Until one year the vault bones are elastic, with no clear boundary between the outer table, diploe and inner table; the diploe forms from 4–5 years. Grooves for the meningeal vessels and venous sinuses appear on the inner surface of the vault bones from 5–6 months. The inner surface of the cranial vault bones has no periosteum — its role is performed by the dura mater.

The **occipital bone** (*os occipitale*) forms the posteroinferior wall of the neurocranium. It consists of four parts surrounding the **foramen magnum** (*foramen magnum*) — through which the cranial cavity communicates with the vertebral canal (the medulla oblongata, the vertebral arteries and the spinal roots of the accessory nerve pass through it). Its parts are: posteriorly — the **occipital squama** (*squama occipitalis*), anteriorly — the **basilar part** (*pars basilaris*), and on the sides — the paired **lateral parts** (*partes laterales*).

In the center of the external surface of the **occipital squama** is the **external occipital protuberance** (*protuberantia occipitalis externa*), clearly palpable under the skin; the **external occipital crest** (*crista occipitalis externa*) descends from it to the foramen magnum. On either side of the protuberance run the **superior** and **inferior nuchal lines** (*linea nuchae superior et inferior*), to which muscles and ligaments attach, and above them the **highest nuchal line**. On the internal surface there is a cross-shaped elevation — the **cruciform eminence** (*eminentia cruciformis*); at its center is the **internal occipital protuberance**, from which the **groove for the superior sagittal sinus** runs upward, the **grooves for the transverse sinuses** run to either side and the **internal occipital crest** runs downward. The eminence divides the internal surface of the squama into four fossae: the occipital lobes of the cerebrum lie in the upper ones, and the cerebellar hemispheres in the lower ones.

blocks.label: Figure 5.2
blocks.caption: Occipital bone, external surface: *Squama occipitalis* — occipital squama; *Protuberantia occipitalis externa* — external occipital protuberance; *Linea nuchae suprema, superior, inferior* — highest, superior and inferior nuchal lines; *Crista occipitalis externa* — external occipital crest; *Foramen magnum* — foramen magnum; *Condylus occipitalis* — occipital condyle; *Canalis condylaris* — condylar canal; *Fossa condylaris* — condylar fossa; *Processus jugularis* — jugular process; *Incisura jugularis* — jugular notch; *Tuberculum pharyngeum* — pharyngeal tubercle; *Pars basilaris* — basilar part. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: On the inferior surface of the **lateral parts** lie the oval **occipital condyles** (*condyli occipitales*), which articulate with the atlas; the base of the condyles is pierced by the **hypoglossal canal** (*canalis nervi hypoglossi* — for cranial nerve XII), and behind the condyles is the inconstant **condylar canal** (*canalis condylaris* — for an emissary vein). On the outer border of the lateral part is the **jugular notch** (*incisura jugularis*) — together with the corresponding notch of the temporal bone it forms the **jugular foramen** (through which the internal jugular vein and cranial nerves IX, X and XI pass) — and behind it the **jugular process**.

The **basilar part** is a quadrangular segment in front of the foramen magnum; it fuses with the body of the sphenoid bone at **18–20 years**. Together with the body of the sphenoid its internal surface forms the sloping **clivus** (*clivus*), on which the pons and medulla oblongata lie. Its inferior surface bears the **pharyngeal tubercle** (*tuberculum pharyngeum*), to which the pharynx attaches, and along its lateral border runs the groove for the inferior petrosal sinus.

blocks.label: Figure 5.3
blocks.caption: Occipital bone, internal surface: *Eminentia cruciformis* — cruciform eminence; *Protuberantia occipitalis interna* — internal occipital protuberance; *Sulcus sinus sagittalis superioris* — groove for the superior sagittal sinus; *Sulcus sinus transversi* — groove for the transverse sinus; *Sulcus sinus sigmoidei* — groove for the sigmoid sinus; *Crista occipitalis interna* — internal occipital crest; *Margo lambdoideus, mastoideus* — lambdoid and mastoid borders; *Canalis condylaris* — condylar canal; *Tuberculum jugulare* — jugular tubercle; *Clivus* — clivus; *Sulcus sinus petrosi inferioris* — groove for the inferior petrosal sinus. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: When intracranial pressure rises sharply (edema, hemorrhage), the cerebellar tonsils and the medulla oblongata may **herniate into the foramen magnum** — this compresses the respiratory and circulatory centers and leads to death. That is why lumbar puncture is dangerous when intracranial pressure is high. The **external occipital protuberance** is a landmark for measuring the head (head circumference) and for blocking the occipital nerves.

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** In the newborn the occipital bone consists of **four parts** around the foramen magnum, separated from each other by layers of cartilage. The squama and lateral parts fuse at **3–4 years**, and the basilar part with the lateral parts at **6–10 years**; growth of the bone ends at ≈20 years.

The **parietal bone** (*os parietale*) is a paired, quadrangular flat bone, convex outward; it forms the upper lateral parts of the cranial vault. It has **four borders**: the **sagittal border** (*margo sagittalis*) — forms the sagittal suture with the opposite parietal bone; the **frontal border** (*margo frontalis*) — the coronal suture with the frontal bone; the **occipital border** (*margo occipitalis*) — the lambdoid suture with the occipital bone; and the **squamous border** (*margo squamosus*) — the squamous suture with the squama of the temporal bone. Between the borders **four angles** are distinguished: the **frontal**, **occipital**, **sphenoidal** and **mastoid angles**.

In the center of the **external surface** is the most prominent point — the **parietal tuber** (*tuber parietale*); below it run the arched **superior and inferior temporal lines**, to which the temporal fascia and muscle attach. Near the sagittal border there may be a **parietal foramen**, through which an emissary vein passes. The **internal surface** is concave; it bears **arterial grooves** (*sulci arteriosi*) left by the branches of the middle meningeal artery, half of the groove for the superior sagittal sinus along the sagittal border, and the groove for the sigmoid sinus in the region of the mastoid angle.

blocks.label: Figure 5.4
blocks.caption: Right parietal bone, external surface: *Margo sagittalis, frontalis, occipitalis, squamosus* — sagittal, frontal, occipital and squamous borders; *Angulus frontalis, occipitalis, sphenoidalis, mastoideus* — frontal, occipital, sphenoidal and mastoid angles; *Tuber parietale* — parietal tuber; *Foramen parietale* — parietal foramen; *Linea temporalis superior et inferior* — superior and inferior temporal lines; *Facies externa* — external surface. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.label: Figure 5.5
blocks.caption: Right parietal bone, internal surface: the grooves of the middle meningeal artery (*sulci arteriosi*), the groove for the superior sagittal sinus (*sulcus sinus sagittalis superioris*) and the groove for the sigmoid sinus at the mastoid angle (*sulcus sinus sigmoidei*). Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: In the region of the **sphenoidal angle** of the parietal bone (the temporal region — the **pterion**) the bone is thin, and the **middle meningeal artery** lies on its inner surface. When a blow falls here, the artery ruptures and blood collects between the bone and the dura mater — an **epidural hematoma**. The patient may initially regain consciousness (the “lucid interval”), after which the condition deteriorates sharply — emergency trepanation is required.

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** The parietal bone develops by the endesmal route from one or two ossification centers in the region of the parietal tuber. In the newborn it is quadrangular, with smooth edges and rounded, unossified angles — they bound the fontanelles. Vascular grooves appear on its inner surface at 3 years, and suture serrations on its edges at 4 years.

The **frontal bone** (*os frontale*) forms the anterior part of the cranial vault and the roofs of the orbits. It consists of three parts: the vertical **frontal squama** (*squama frontalis*), the horizontal paired **orbital parts** (*partes orbitales*) and the **nasal part** (*pars nasalis*) between them.

On the external surface of the **squama** are the two **frontal tubers** (*tubera frontalia*), below them, above the orbital margins, the arched **superciliary arches** (*arcus superciliares*), and between them a smooth area — the **glabella**. The squama passes into the orbital part at the **supraorbital margin** (*margo supraorbitalis*); in its medial third is the **supraorbital notch (foramen)** (*incisura/foramen supraorbitale*), through which the nerve and vessels of the same name pass. Laterally the margin ends in the **zygomatic process** (*processus zygomaticus*), from which the temporal line runs upward. On the internal surface the **groove for the superior sagittal sinus** runs along the midline, and below it the **frontal crest** (*crista frontalis*).

blocks.label: Figure 5.6
blocks.caption: Frontal bone, anterior view: *Squama frontalis* — frontal squama; *Tuber frontale* — frontal tuber; *Arcus superciliaris* — superciliary arch; *Glabella* — glabella; *Margo supraorbitalis* — supraorbital margin; *Foramen supraorbitale, incisura frontalis* — supraorbital foramen, frontal notch; *Processus zygomaticus* — zygomatic process; *Linea temporalis* — temporal line; *Facies temporalis* — temporal surface; *Pars nasalis* — nasal part; *Spina nasalis* — nasal spine; *Margo parietalis* — parietal border. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: The **orbital parts** are thin triangular plates; their inferior surface forms the roof of the orbit and their superior surface the floor of the anterior cranial fossa (where the frontal lobes of the brain lie, hence the impressions of the gyri). At the lateral angle of the inferior surface is the **fossa for the lacrimal gland** (*fossa glandulae lacrimalis*), and medially the **trochlear fovea**, to which the trochlea attaches. Between the two orbital parts is the **ethmoidal notch** (*incisura ethmoidalis*), into which the ethmoid bone fits. From the middle of the **nasal part** the **nasal spine** (*spina nasalis*) projects downward. In the thickness of the lower part of the squama lies the air-filled **frontal sinus** (*sinus frontalis*) — it is divided in two by a septum and opens into the **middle nasal meatus**; therefore the frontal bone is a **pneumatic** bone.

blocks.label: Figure 5.7
blocks.caption: Frontal bone, inferior view: *Facies orbitales* — orbital surfaces; *Fossa glandulae lacrimalis* — fossa for the lacrimal gland; *Spina trochlearis, fovea trochlearis* — trochlear spine and fovea; *Incisura ethmoidalis* — ethmoidal notch; *Sinus frontalis* — frontal sinus (opened); *Margo nasalis, spina nasalis* — nasal border and spine; *Incisura supraorbitalis* — supraorbital notch. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: Inflammation of the frontal sinus — **frontal sinusitis** — is accompanied by pain in the forehead and supraorbital region; pressure over the supraorbital foramen (where the nerve emerges) is painful. Because the sinus opens into the nose by a narrow passage, drainage is difficult during inflammation. Infection may spread into the cranial cavity through the thin posterior wall of the frontal sinus (meningitis, brain abscess).

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** In the newborn the frontal bone consists of **two symmetric halves** joined in the midline by the **frontal (metopic) suture**; the frontal tubers are prominent, and there are no superciliary arches or frontal sinus. The two halves begin to fuse **in the 2nd year** and usually fuse completely **by 7–8 years**; in some people (about 5–10 %) the **metopic suture persists for life**. The frontal sinus appears in the 1st–2nd year of life, becomes clearly visible on X-rays after 7 years, and completes its development at ≈25 years.

parts.text: On adult X-rays a thin light line along the midline of the frontal bone is often a **persistent metopic suture** — do not confuse it with a fracture. The suture is **serrated, symmetric** and exactly in the midline, whereas a fracture line is irregular and usually deviates from the midline.

blocks.text: The **ethmoid bone** (*os ethmoidale*) is an unpaired, light pneumatic bone; it fits into the ethmoidal notch of the frontal bone and takes part in forming the anterior cranial base and the walls of the nasal cavity and orbits. Its parts:

items: The **cribriform plate** (*lamina cribrosa*) — a horizontal plate with many foramina; through them the **olfactory nerves** (cranial nerve I) pass from the nasal cavity into the cranial cavity. In the midline the **crista galli** (*crista galli*) projects upward from it — the falx cerebri of the dura mater attaches to it.
The **perpendicular plate** (*lamina perpendicularis*) — directed downward, it forms the upper part of the nasal septum.

The **ethmoidal labyrinth** (*labyrinthus ethmoidalis*) — paired, consisting of air-filled **ethmoidal cells** (*cellulae ethmoidales*: anterior, middle, posterior); they open into the superior and middle nasal meatuses. The lateral surface of the labyrinth — the thin **orbital plate** (*lamina orbitalis*) — forms the medial wall of the orbit; from its medial surface the **superior and middle nasal conchae** (*concha nasalis superior et media*) hang into the nasal cavity. Below the middle concha lie the **uncinate process** and the **ethmoidal bulla**.

blocks.label: Figure 5.8
blocks.caption: Ethmoid bone, superior view: *Lamina perpendicularis* — perpendicular plate; *Crista galli, ala cristae galli* — crista galli and its ala; *Lamina et foramina cribrosa* — cribriform plate and its foramina; *Labyrinthus ethmoidalis (cellulae ethmoidales)* — ethmoidal labyrinth (ethmoidal cells); *Lamina orbitalis* — orbital plate. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: In a fracture of the anterior cranial fossa (usually through the **cribriform plate**), the meninges tear and cerebrospinal fluid leaks from the nose — **CSF leak** (rhinorrhea); loss of smell (anosmia) and “spectacle” bruising around the eyes are also typical. If clear fluid flows from the nose, it should be tested with the blood-mixed spot (halo) test and for glucose. Such a patient must not blow the nose hard or have a nasal tube inserted — infection may spread into the cranial cavity. Because the orbital plate is very thin, **inflammation of the ethmoid cells** (ethmoiditis, especially in children) easily spreads to the orbit.

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** In the newborn the ethmoid bone is cartilaginous, and only part of the labyrinth is ossified; the ethmoidal cells are present at birth but small — that is why in children **ethmoiditis** is the earliest sinusitis to develop. In the first year the cribriform plate ossifies and fuses with the labyrinth. At ≈3 years the nasal mucosa grows into the labyrinth cells and the cells enlarge; by puberty the bone resembles that of the adult.

sections.title: 6. The newborn's skull: fontanelles and sutures

blocks.text: In the newborn the bones of the cranial vault are not joined by sutures: between them there are wide **connective tissue membranes**. Where several bones meet, these membranes widen to form unossified areas — the **fontanelles** (*fonticuli cranii*). During delivery the fontanelles allow the skull bones to overlap, making it easier for the head to pass through the narrow birth canal, and in the first years they allow rapid growth of the brain.

blocks.label: Figure 5.9
blocks.caption: The newborn's skull, lateral view: *Fonticulus anterior* — anterior fontanelle; *Fonticulus sphenoidalis* — sphenoidal fontanelle; *Fonticulus posterior* — posterior fontanelle; *Fonticulus mastoideus* — mastoid fontanelle; *Tuber parietale, tuber frontale* — parietal and frontal tubers; *Ala major* — greater wing of the sphenoid bone; *Squama occipitalis, pars lateralis ossis occipitalis* — occipital squama and lateral part; *Anulus tympanicus* — tympanic ring; *Squama temporalis* — temporal squama. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: Remember the fontanelles by **“4 – 2 – 1 – 0”**: there are **4** types (6 in total) of fontanelles; **2** are unpaired (anterior and posterior), and two pairs are lateral (sphenoidal and mastoid). The anterior fontanelle closes at **1–1.5 years**, the posterior at **2–3 months**, and the lateral fontanelles are often already **closed at birth (0)**.

The **anterior fontanelle** serves as a “window” for the pediatrician. A **bulging, tense** fontanelle indicates increased intracranial pressure (meningitis, hydrocephalus, hemorrhage); a **sunken** fontanelle is a sign of dehydration (exsiccosis). **Early closure** of the fontanelle and premature ossification of the sutures (**craniosynostosis**) lead to deformity of the head and restriction of brain growth; **late closure** is seen in rickets, hypothyroidism or hydrocephalus. In infants, ultrasound examination of the brain (neurosonography) is performed precisely through the anterior fontanelle.

blocks.text: As the child grows, the fontanelles are replaced by sutures. The bones of the cranial vault are joined mainly by serrated sutures: the **sagittal** (between the two parietal bones), **coronal** (between the frontal and parietal bones), **lambdoid** (between the parietal and occipital bones) and **squamous** (between the parietal and temporal bones). The serrations of the sutures appear from 3–4 years; after 30–40 years the sutures gradually ossify (synostosis) and begin to disappear — this is used in forensic medicine for approximate age estimation.

skills.title: Practical skill: studying the bones of the neurocranium

items: Show the 8 bones forming the neurocranium on a skull; distinguish the unpaired and paired bones.

Place the occipital bone with the foramen magnum facing down and the squama backward; show its four parts, the condyles, the hypoglossal canal, the jugular notch, the clivus, the cruciform eminence and the sinus grooves.
Place the parietal bone with its convex surface outward and the sphenoidal angle, where the arterial grooves branch, forward and downward, and determine its side; name its borders and angles.
On the frontal bone show the squama, the orbital and nasal parts, the superciliary arches, glabella, supraorbital notch, zygomatic process, ethmoidal notch and frontal sinus.
On the ethmoid bone show the cribriform and perpendicular plates, the crista galli, the labyrinth, the orbital plate and the nasal conchae.
On a mannequin of a newborn's skull find all the fontanelles, and name the bones bounding them and their closure times.

skills.title: Practical skill: palpation in a living person and examination of a newborn

items: Palpate the external occipital protuberance, the superior nuchal line, the superciliary arches, the glabella and the notch on the supraorbital margin (a slightly tender point when pressed).

In an infant, palpate the anterior fontanelle with a fingertip while the child is calm and held upright: assess its size (along the diagonals), the state of its edges and its tension (bulging, flat, sunken), and feel for pulsation.
Measure the head circumference with a centimeter tape through the occipital protuberance and the superciliary arches (34–35 cm in a full-term newborn).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 9-month-old child was brought to the pediatrician by his mother: for 2 days he has had diarrhea and vomiting, he urinates little and his lips are dry. On examination the anterior fontanelle is sunken below the level of the bone edges.
cases.ask: What does this state of the fontanelle indicate? Where is the anterior fontanelle located and when does it close?
cases.answer: A sunken fontanelle is a sign of **dehydration (exsiccosis)** — the body has lost fluid, and the intracranial volume and pressure have decreased. The anterior fontanelle lies **between the two frontal and two parietal bones**, where the sagittal, coronal and metopic sutures intersect, and is diamond-shaped; it closes at **1–1.5 years** (by 2 years). Urgent replacement of fluid losses (rehydration) is needed.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: After a car accident, symmetric bruising appeared around both eyes of a patient (“spectacle sign”); when the patient bends forward, clear fluid drips from the nose, and he says he cannot smell.
cases.ask: Which bone and which structure are injured? What is the fluid flowing from the nose?
cases.answer: This is a **fracture of the anterior cranial fossa**, specifically of the **cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone** (hence the tearing of the olfactory nerves — anosmia). The clear fluid flowing from the nose is **cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)**: the meninges are torn, and the subarachnoid space communicates with the nasal cavity (rhinorrhea). There is a risk of infection (meningitis) — blowing the nose and nasal packing are forbidden.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A young man was hit in the temporal region by a baseball and lost consciousness for a few minutes, then came to and felt well. 3 hours later his headache worsened, he vomited and then lost consciousness again; the pupil on the side of the blow is dilated.
cases.ask: What complication has developed? What is its anatomical basis?
cases.answer: This is an **epidural hematoma**. In the temporal region (the pterion — where the frontal, parietal and temporal bones and the greater wing of the sphenoid bone meet) the bone is thin; the **middle meningeal artery** lies on the inner surface of the **sphenoidal angle** of the parietal bone. In a fracture the artery ruptures, and blood collects between the bone and the dura mater and compresses the brain. The period of regained consciousness is the “lucid interval.” Emergency trepanation and removal of the hematoma are required.
