topics.title: The sphenoid and temporal bones: structure and age-related features. Canals of the temporal bone

goals.text: To introduce the student to the structure of the central bones of the cranial base — the sphenoid and temporal bones — the vessels and nerves passing through their foramina, fissures and canals, and their age-related features; to relate this knowledge to conditions in neurosurgery, otorhinolaryngology and neurology.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the body, sella turcica, lesser and greater wings and pterygoid processes of the sphenoid bone;
the foramina and fissures of the sphenoid bone and the structures passing through them;
the parts of the temporal bone (squama, petrous part — the pyramid, tympanic part) and the mastoid process;
the surfaces, borders and apex of the pyramid and the structures on it;
the canals of the temporal bone, where they begin and end, and the vessels and nerves passing through them;
the age-related features of the sphenoid and temporal bones.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: place the sphenoid bone in the anatomical position and show its parts, foramina and fissures, naming them in Latin;
determine the side of a temporal bone and show its parts and the surfaces of the pyramid;
find the entry and exit openings of the canals of the temporal bone and state what passes through them;
palpate in a living person the mastoid process, the zygomatic arch and the external acoustic opening.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Pituitary tumors** (adenomas) enlarge the sella turcica and thin its floor — this can be seen on a lateral skull X-ray and on MRI. When the tumor grows upward, it compresses the **optic chiasm** above the sella, and the patient loses the outer halves of the visual fields (**bitemporal hemianopia**). Pituitary tumors are often removed through the nose via the **sphenoidal sinus** (the transsphenoidal approach).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the three foramina of the greater wing and the branches of the trigeminal nerve as **“R-O-S — 2-3-artery”**: foramen **R**otundum — the **2**nd branch of cranial nerve V, foramen **O**vale — the **3**rd branch, foramen **S**pinosum — the **artery** (middle meningeal artery). The first branch (the ophthalmic nerve) passes not through a foramen but through the **superior orbital fissure**.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Because the **mastoid antrum** communicates with the tympanic cavity, inflammation of the middle ear (otitis) may spread to the mastoid cells and cause **mastoiditis**: pain and swelling behind the ear, with the auricle pushed forward. The inflammation may spread through the thin walls of the cells to the sigmoid sinus (thrombosis) and to the posterior and middle cranial fossae (meningitis, brain abscess). Surgery here (antromastoidotomy) is performed in the triangle behind the suprameatal spine (Chipault's triangle).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Course of the facial canal:** internal acoustic opening → horizontally forward → **geniculum** (the greater petrosal nerve branches off here) → backward along the medial wall of the tympanic cavity (below the lateral semicircular canal) → vertically downward → **stylomastoid foramen**. The canal lies very close to the middle ear, and its wall is sometimes very thin or dehiscent.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Because the facial nerve runs in a long, narrow bony canal, it becomes **compressed** in inflammation and edema — **peripheral facial nerve palsy** (Bell's palsy): one side of the face “droops,” the patient cannot close the eye or wrinkle the forehead, and the corner of the mouth drops. The nerve may also be injured in middle ear inflammation and surgery and in fractures of the temporal bone. Depending on the level of injury, additional signs (impaired taste — chorda tympani; reduced lacrimation — greater petrosal nerve) help locate the lesion.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In newborns and young children the mastoid process is undeveloped, so the **stylomastoid foramen lies very superficially** — the facial nerve emerges close to the skin. Therefore the facial nerve can easily be injured when obstetric forceps are used or an incision is made behind the ear. The short, straight auditory tube is the reason why middle ear inflammation is common in children.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In a fracture of the middle cranial fossa (through the pyramid), blood or cerebrospinal fluid leaks from the ear (**otoliquorrhea**), and after 1–2 days bruising appears behind the ear over the mastoid process (**Battle's sign**). If these signs appear, the ear must not be irrigated or packed.

blocks.text: The **sphenoid bone** (*os sphenoidale*) is an unpaired bone in the center of the cranial base, wedged like a “wedge” between the occipital and frontal bones. It borders almost all the bones of the skull and resembles a bat in flight. The sphenoid bone consists of four parts: the **body** (*corpus*), the paired **lesser wings** (*alae minores*), the paired **greater wings** (*alae majores*) and the paired downward-directed **pterygoid processes** (*processus pterygoidei*).

blocks.label: Figure 6.1
blocks.caption: Sphenoid bone, anterior view: 1 — orbital surface of the greater wing; 2 — lesser wing; 3 — opening of the sphenoidal sinus; 4 — dorsum sellae; 5 — hypophyseal fossa; 6 — optic canal; 7 — superior orbital fissure; 8 — greater wing; 9 — infratemporal crest; 10 — sphenoidal spine; 11 — pterygoid canal; 12 — sphenoidal rostrum; 13 — sphenoidal crest; 14 — medial plate of the pterygoid process; 15 — lateral plate; 16 — pterygoid process; 17 — foramen rotundum; 18 — temporal surface of the greater wing. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

blocks.text: The body and the sella turcica

The **body** is cube-shaped and contains the air-filled **sphenoidal sinus** (*sinus sphenoidalis*) — divided in two by a septum, it opens through an aperture on the anterior surface of the body (*apertura sinus sphenoidalis*) into the **sphenoethmoidal recess** of the nasal cavity (the region of the superior nasal meatus); therefore the sphenoid bone is also a pneumatic bone. On the upper — cerebral surface of the body is a saddle-like depression — the **sella turcica** (*sella turcica*). In its center is the **hypophyseal fossa** (*fossa hypophysialis*), which holds the endocrine gland the **hypophysis (pituitary gland)**; in front is the **tuberculum sellae** (*tuberculum sellae*), and behind the wall-like **dorsum sellae** (*dorsum sellae*); together with the basilar part of the occipital bone, the dorsum forms the **clivus** (*clivus*). In front of the tuberculum sellae runs the transverse **prechiasmatic sulcus** (*sulcus prechiasmaticus*), in which the optic chiasm lies, and on the lateral surfaces of the body runs the **carotid sulcus** (*sulcus caroticus*), in which the internal carotid artery lies. Around the sella are the **anterior, middle and posterior clinoid processes** (*processus clinoidei*).

parts.text: **Pituitary tumors** (adenomas) enlarge the sella turcica and thin its floor — this can be seen on a lateral skull X-ray and on MRI. When the tumor grows upward, it compresses the **optic chiasm** above the sella, and the patient loses the outer halves of the visual fields (**bitemporal hemianopia**). Pituitary tumors are often removed through the nose via the **sphenoidal sinus** (the transsphenoidal approach).

blocks.text: The wings

The **lesser wings** arise from the anterosuperior part of the body by two roots; between the roots lies the **optic canal** (*canalis opticus*), through which the **optic nerve** (cranial nerve II) and the **ophthalmic artery** pass. The posterior border of the lesser wing is free, and its medial end terminates in the anterior clinoid process. Between the lesser and greater wings is the **superior orbital fissure** (*fissura orbitalis superior*), which opens into the orbit.

The **greater wings** arise from the lateral surfaces of the body and extend laterally and upward. Four surfaces are distinguished on them: the **cerebral surface** (*facies cerebralis* — part of the middle cranial fossa, with digital impressions and arterial grooves), the **orbital surface** (the lateral wall of the orbit), the **temporal surface** (the wall of the temporal fossa; it is separated from the infratemporal surface by the **infratemporal crest**) and the **maxillary surface**. At the base of the greater wing three foramina lie from front to back: the **foramen rotundum** (*foramen rotundum*), the **foramen ovale** (*foramen ovale*) and the **foramen spinosum** (*foramen spinosum*); the **sphenoidal spine** (*spina ossis sphenoidalis*) projects downward from the posterior angle of the wing.

blocks.label: Figure 6.2
blocks.caption: Sphenoid bone, posterior view: *Corpus ossis sphenoidalis* — body (the site of union with the occipital bone); *Ala minor, ala major* — lesser and greater wings; *Canalis opticus* — optic canal; *Dorsum sellae* — dorsum sellae; *Processus clinoideus anterior, posterior* — anterior and posterior clinoid processes; *Fissura orbitalis superior* — superior orbital fissure; *Foramen rotundum* — foramen rotundum; *Canalis pterygoideus* — pterygoid canal; *Sulcus caroticus* — carotid sulcus; *Spina ossis sphenoidalis* — sphenoidal spine; *Processus pterygoideus: lamina lateralis, lamina medialis* — lateral and medial plates of the pterygoid process; *Fossa pterygoidea* — pterygoid fossa; *Hamulus pterygoideus* — pterygoid hamulus; *Incisura pterygoidea* — pterygoid notch. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: The pterygoid processes

The **pterygoid processes** descend from the junction of the body and the greater wing; each consists of a **medial** and a **lateral plate**, between which is the posteriorly open **pterygoid fossa** (*fossa pterygoidea*); below, the plates are separated by the **pterygoid notch**. The medial plate ends below in the **pterygoid hamulus** (*hamulus pterygoideus*) — the tendon of the tensor veli palatini muscle winds around it. The base of the process is pierced from front to back by the **pterygoid canal** (*canalis pterygoideus*). The masticatory muscles (pterygoid muscles) originate from the outer surface of the lateral plate.

The first branch (the ophthalmic nerve) passes not through a foramen but through the **superior orbital fissure**.

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** The sphenoid bone develops from many (12–14) ossification centers: the medial plates of the pterygoid processes ossify endesmally, and the remaining parts via cartilage. In the newborn the bone consists of three parts: the body (its anterior and posterior segments separated by thin cartilage) with the attached lesser wings, and on each side the greater wing with the pterygoid process. The two segments of the body fuse **in the 1st year**, and the greater wings with the body at **≈3 years**. The sphenoidal sinus is very small at birth, begins to enlarge from 3–4 years and takes shape at puberty. The cartilage between the sphenoid and occipital bones (**spheno-occipital synchondrosis**) ossifies in adolescence (15–20 years) — it is the main zone providing growth of the cranial base in length.

The **temporal bone** (*os temporale*) is a paired bone; it forms part of the lateral wall and base of the neurocranium, contains the **organ of hearing and balance**, and articulates with the mandible. The temporal bone consists of three parts arranged around the **external acoustic opening** (*porus acusticus externus*): above — the **squamous part** (*pars squamosa*), medially — the **petrous part** or **pyramid** (*pars petrosa*), and below and in front — the **tympanic part** (*pars tympanica*).

blocks.label: Figure 6.4
blocks.caption: Right temporal bone, lateral view: *Pars squamosa* — squamous part; *Facies temporalis* — temporal surface; *Sulcus arteriae temporalis mediae* — groove for the middle temporal artery; *Processus zygomaticus* — zygomatic process; *Tuberculum articulare* — articular tubercle; *Fossa mandibularis* — mandibular fossa; *Fissura petrosquamosa, petrotympanica, tympanomastoidea* — petrosquamous, petrotympanic and tympanomastoid fissures; *Pars tympanica* — tympanic part; *Porus et meatus acusticus externus* — external acoustic opening and meatus; *Spina suprameatica, foveola suprameatica* — suprameatal spine and fovea; *Processus mastoideus* — mastoid process; *Incisura mastoidea* — mastoid notch; *Foramen mastoideum* — mastoid foramen; *Processus styloideus* — styloid process; *Incisura parietalis* — parietal notch; *Margo parietalis, sphenoidalis* — parietal and sphenoidal borders. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: The squamous part

The **squamous part** is a thin plate directed upward and convex outward; its upper border forms the **squamous suture** with the parietal bone and the greater wing of the sphenoid bone. On its outer — **temporal surface** runs the groove for the middle temporal artery. The **zygomatic process** (*processus zygomaticus*) projects forward from it; it joins the temporal process of the zygomatic bone to form the **zygomatic arch** (*arcus zygomaticus*). At the base of the zygomatic process is the **mandibular fossa** (*fossa mandibularis*), in which the head of the mandible lies, and in front of it the **articular tubercle** (*tuberculum articulare*). The inner — cerebral surface bears digital impressions and arterial grooves.
The petrous part (pyramid)

The **pyramid** is the hardest part of the temporal bone; it is shaped like a three-sided pyramid, its **base** continuing laterally into the mastoid process and its **apex** (*apex partis petrosae*) directed forward and medially toward the body of the sphenoid bone. The pyramid has **three surfaces** — anterior, posterior and inferior — and **three borders** — superior, posterior and anterior.

items: **Anterior surface** (facing the middle cranial fossa): near the apex is the **trigeminal impression** (*impressio trigeminalis*), in which the trigeminal ganglion lies; in the middle is the **arcuate eminence** (*eminentia arcuata*), formed by the anterior semicircular canal of the inner ear; lateral to it is the thin roof of the tympanic cavity — the **tegmen tympani** (*tegmen tympani*); and there are the hiatuses and grooves of the canals of the greater and lesser petrosal nerves.

**Posterior surface** (facing the posterior cranial fossa): in its middle is the **internal acoustic opening** (*porus acusticus internus*), leading into the **internal acoustic meatus** (through which cranial nerves VII and VIII and the labyrinthine artery pass); above and lateral to it is the **subarcuate fossa**, and below it the **external aperture of the vestibular aqueduct**.

**Inferior surface** (facing the external surface of the cranial base): the **external opening of the carotid canal**, behind it the **jugular fossa** (which with the occipital bone forms the jugular foramen), between them the **petrosal fossula**; laterally the thin **styloid process** (*processus styloideus*) and behind it the **stylomastoid foramen** (*foramen stylomastoideum*).

blocks.text: Grooves for venous sinuses run along the borders of the pyramid: on the **superior border** — the groove for the superior petrosal sinus, and on the **posterior border** — the groove for the inferior petrosal sinus. Behind the base of the pyramid, on the inner surface of the mastoid part, is the broad **groove for the sigmoid sinus**.

blocks.label: Figure 6.5
blocks.caption: Right temporal bone, internal (medial) view: *Facies posterior partis petrosae* — posterior surface of the pyramid; *Porus acusticus internus* — internal acoustic opening; *Apex partis petrosae* — apex of the pyramid; *Eminentia arcuata* — arcuate eminence; *Tegmen tympani* — tegmen tympani; *Impressio trigemini* — trigeminal impression; *Sulcus sinus petrosi superioris, inferioris* — grooves for the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses; *Sulcus sinus sigmoidei* — groove for the sigmoid sinus; *Fossa subarcuata* — subarcuate fossa; *Apertura externa aqueductus vestibuli* — external aperture of the vestibular aqueduct; *Apertura externa canaliculi cochleae* — external aperture of the cochlear canaliculus; *Processus styloideus* — styloid process; *Foramen mastoideum* — mastoid foramen. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: The mastoid process and tympanic part

The **mastoid process** (*processus mastoideus*) is the outer part of the base of the pyramid; it lies behind the external acoustic opening and is clearly palpable under the skin. The sternocleidomastoid muscle attaches to it; the posterior belly of the digastric muscle arises from the **mastoid notch** on its medial side. Inside the process are air-filled **mastoid cells** (*cellulae mastoideae*); the largest of them — the **mastoid antrum** (*antrum mastoideum*) — communicates with the tympanic cavity.

The **tympanic part** is a thin, horseshoe-shaped curved plate; it forms the anterior, inferior and posterior walls of the **external acoustic meatus** (*meatus acusticus externus*). The tympanic part is separated from the squamous part by the **petrosquamous** and **petrotympanic fissures**; the **chorda tympani** emerges from the petrotympanic fissure.

blocks.label: Figure 6.6
blocks.caption: Right temporal bone, superior view (anterior surface of the pyramid): *Facies anterior partis petrosae* — anterior surface of the pyramid; *Eminentia arcuata* — arcuate eminence; *Tegmen tympani* — tegmen tympani; *Hiatus canalis n. petrosi majoris, minoris* — hiatuses of the canals for the greater and lesser petrosal nerves; *Sulcus n. petrosi majoris, minoris* — grooves for these nerves; *Impressio trigemini* — trigeminal impression; *Canalis caroticus* — carotid canal; *Fissura petrosquamosa* — petrosquamous fissure; *Sulcus sinus sigmoidei, petrosi superioris* — grooves for the sigmoid and superior petrosal sinuses; *Margo superior partis petrosae* — superior border of the pyramid. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: **Course of the facial canal:** internal acoustic opening → horizontally forward → **geniculum** (the greater petrosal nerve branches off here) → backward along the medial wall of the tympanic cavity (below the lateral semicircular canal) → vertically downward → **stylomastoid foramen**. The canal lies very close to the middle ear, and its wall is sometimes very thin or dehiscent.

Because the facial nerve runs in a long, narrow bony canal, it becomes **compressed** in inflammation and edema — **peripheral facial nerve palsy** (Bell's palsy): one side of the face “droops,” the patient cannot close the eye or wrinkle the forehead, and the corner of the mouth drops. sections.title: 4. Age-related features of the temporal bone

blocks.text: In the newborn the temporal bone consists of **three parts** (squama, pyramid, tympanic ring) separated by layers of cartilage. The squamous part is thin and consists only of two compact plates; the spongy substance has not formed. The **tympanic part** is not yet a complete ring but has the form of the **tympanic ring** (*anulus tympanicus*), so the **external acoustic meatus is short and mainly cartilaginous**, and the tympanic membrane lies more superficially and more horizontally. **The mastoid process is almost absent** — it develops from the 2nd year, after the child begins to walk, under the pull of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and cells appear within it; the mastoid antrum, however, is present at birth and relatively large. The styloid process develops from two ossification centers (one before birth, the other at ≈2 years).

In the first year of life the parts of the temporal bone fuse with each other. Up to three years the bone grows evenly; the tympanic part grows rapidly and forms the bony part of the external acoustic meatus, which takes shape at ≈5 years. The mastoid cells enlarge during childhood and at puberty come to resemble those of the adult.

parts.text: In newborns and young children the mastoid process is undeveloped, so the **stylomastoid foramen lies very superficially** — the facial nerve emerges close to the skin. Therefore the facial nerve can easily be injured when obstetric forceps are used or an incision is made behind the ear. The short, straight auditory tube is the reason why middle ear inflammation is common in children.

In a fracture of the middle cranial fossa (through the pyramid), blood or cerebrospinal fluid leaks from the ear (**otoliquorrhea**), and after 1–2 days bruising appears behind the ear over the mastoid process (**Battle's sign**). If these signs appear, the ear must not be irrigated or packed.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 45-year-old woman complains that the outer parts of her visual field on both sides have “disappeared”; her menstrual cycle is disturbed, and milk is discharged from the breast. Brain MRI shows an enlarged sella turcica with a tumor in it.
cases.ask: From which organ has the tumor arisen? What is the anatomical cause of the visual disturbance? By which route can the tumor be reached?
cases.answer: This is a **pituitary tumor** (prolactinoma) — the pituitary gland lies in the **hypophyseal fossa** of the sella turcica. Growing upward, the tumor compresses the **optic chiasm**, which lies in the prechiasmatic sulcus above the tuberculum sellae: in the chiasm the fibers from the medial (nasal) halves of the retinas cross, and they serve the outer (temporal) halves of the visual fields — **bitemporal hemianopia**. The tumor is usually removed through the nose via the **sphenoidal sinus** (transsphenoidally), because the hypophyseal fossa lies directly above the sinus.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: After a winter cold, a student woke up in the morning and noticed that the right side of his face had “frozen”: he cannot close his right eye or wrinkle his forehead, the right corner of his mouth droops, and his sense of taste has changed when eating.
cases.ask: Which nerve is affected? What is the course of its canal, and why is this nerve so often affected?
cases.answer: This is **peripheral palsy of the facial nerve (VII)** (Bell's palsy). The nerve passes through the long, narrow and bent **facial canal** in the pyramid of the temporal bone: from the fundus of the internal acoustic meatus → horizontally forward → geniculum → backward along the medial wall of the tympanic cavity → downward → **stylomastoid foramen**. With exposure to cold or a viral infection the nerve swells and, unable to expand in the bony canal, becomes compressed. The change in taste indicates that the nerve is damaged above the origin of the **chorda tympani**.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: 2 weeks after acute otitis media, a 5-year-old child's temperature rose again; redness and a painful swelling appeared behind the ear, and the auricle is pushed forward and downward.
cases.ask: What complication has developed? By which route has the inflammation spread, and where else can it spread?
cases.answer: This is **acute mastoiditis**. The inflammation of the middle ear has spread from the tympanic cavity via the **mastoid antrum** into the **cells of the mastoid process**. Through the thin walls of the cells the inflammation can spread to the **sigmoid sinus** (thrombosis), to the **posterior and middle cranial fossae** (meningitis, cerebellar or temporal lobe abscess), and also beneath the neck muscles. Treatment — antibiotics and, if necessary, antromastoidotomy.

topics.title: Bones of the facial skeleton: maxilla and mandible, small bones of the face

goals.text: To introduce the student to the structure and age-related changes of the bones of the facial skeleton — the maxilla and mandible, the palatine, zygomatic, nasal and lacrimal bones, the inferior nasal concha, the vomer and the hyoid bone; to relate this knowledge to practical problems in dentistry, ENT and maxillofacial surgery.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the list of facial bones (paired and unpaired);
the four surfaces of the body of the maxilla, the maxillary sinus and its four processes;
the plates and processes of the palatine bone and the formation of the hard palate;
the structure of the zygomatic, nasal and lacrimal bones, the inferior nasal concha and the vomer;
the body, ramus, processes, foramina and canal of the mandible;
the parts of the hyoid bone;
the age-related changes of the facial bones, especially the jaws.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: place the maxilla and mandible in the anatomical position, determine their side and name their structures in Latin;
show the boundaries of the facial bones on a skull;
show the location of the infraorbital, mental and mandibular foramina (points for conduction anesthesia);
palpate in a living person the base, angle and head of the mandible and the hyoid bone.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The roots of the upper **second premolar and first and second molars** lie very close to the floor of the maxillary sinus and sometimes protrude into it. Therefore inflammation of these teeth may spread into the sinus causing **odontogenic maxillary sinusitis**, and extraction of a tooth may leave the sinus open (an oroantral fistula). Because the outlet of the sinus (hiatus) lies in its upper part, pus does not drain well on its own.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The maxillary sinus is the **largest** paranasal sinus. Openings of the sinuses into the nose: into the **middle nasal meatus** — the maxillary and frontal sinuses and the anterior and middle ethmoidal cells; into the **superior nasal meatus** — the posterior ethmoidal cells; into the **sphenoethmoidal recess** — the sphenoidal sinus; into the **inferior nasal meatus** — the nasolacrimal duct.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The hard palate is formed by the union in the midline of the right and left parts of the maxillae and palatine bones. If this union fails during fetal life, a **cleft palate** develops — the oral and nasal cavities communicate, the infant has difficulty sucking and food comes out of the nose; it is often combined with a cleft lip and is corrected surgically. In the region of the **greater palatine foramen**, palatal anesthesia is performed to anesthetize the upper teeth.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The **nasal bones** are the most frequently fractured facial bones (boxing, falls). **Deviation of the nasal septum** (at the junction of the vomer and the perpendicular plate) makes breathing difficult and is corrected surgically (septoplasty). When the lacrimal passages are blocked, **dacryocystitis** develops; because the lacrimal bone is very thin, during surgery a new passage between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity is made precisely through it (dacryocystorhinostomy).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In dentistry, **mandibular (inferior alveolar) nerve block** is used to anesthetize the lower teeth: the anesthetic is injected around the **mandibular foramen** (the region of the lingula) on the inner surface of the ramus — here the inferior alveolar nerve enters the canal. For the anterior teeth and the chin region the anesthetic is injected in the region of the **mental foramen**, and for the upper anterior teeth and upper lip in the region of the **infraorbital foramen**. The mandible most often fractures at the **angle**, the **canine region** and the **neck of the condylar process** (the bone is weaker at these sites).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The angle of the mandible changes over life like a **“U”**: large in the newborn (**≈150°**) → small in adults (**120–130°**) → large again in edentulous elderly people (**≈140°**). The reason is the load from the teeth and the masticatory muscles: when teeth are present and chewing is strong, the ramus stands more upright.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Fracture of the hyoid bone** is an important sign in forensic medicine: it is often seen in cases of **strangulation** (manual compression of the neck). In young people the parts of the bone are joined by cartilage and are flexible, so it fractures less often, whereas in the elderly the fused, brittle bone fractures more easily.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: On X-rays of children's facial bones, do not misinterpret the shadows of **tooth buds and unerupted permanent teeth** in the body of the jaw as a tumor or cyst. Knowing the eruption times of the teeth (deciduous — 6 months–2.5 years, permanent — 6–12 years, wisdom teeth — 17–25 years) is necessary for reading jaw X-rays correctly.

sections.title: 1. Bones of the facial skeleton: general information

blocks.text: The **facial skeleton** (*viscerocranium*) forms the skeleton of the orbits and the nasal and oral cavities and serves as a support for the masticatory and facial muscles. It includes **paired** bones — the **maxilla** (*maxilla*), **palatine bone** (*os palatinum*), **zygomatic bone** (*os zygomaticum*), **nasal bone** (*os nasale*), **lacrimal bone** (*os lacrimale*) and **inferior nasal concha** (*concha nasalis inferior*) — and **unpaired** bones — the **vomer** (*vomer*), **mandible** (*mandibula*) and **hyoid bone** (*os hyoideum*). The facial bones develop mainly from the visceral arches (maxilla, mandible, hyoid bone) and the nasal capsule; most ossify by the endesmal route.

blocks.text: The **maxilla** (*maxilla*) is a paired, central bone of the face; it articulates with almost all the bones of the face. It has a **body** and **four processes**. The **body** (*corpus maxillae*) contains the largest paranasal sinus — the **maxillary sinus** (*sinus maxillaris*, antrum of Highmore); it opens into the **middle nasal meatus** of the nasal cavity through the **maxillary hiatus** (*hiatus maxillaris*).

The body has four surfaces. The **anterior surface** (*facies anterior*) — below the infraorbital margin is the **infraorbital foramen** (*foramen infraorbitale*), and below it the **canine fossa** (*fossa canina*); its medial boundary — the **nasal notch** (*incisura nasalis*) — ends below in the **anterior nasal spine** (*spina nasalis anterior*). The **orbital surface** (*facies orbitalis*) is the floor of the orbit; from its posterior border the **infraorbital groove** begins, becoming a **canal** in front and opening by the above-mentioned foramen. The **infratemporal surface** (*facies infratemporalis*) faces backward; it bears the prominent **maxillary tuberosity** (*tuber maxillae*) and the **alveolar foramina**, through which vessels and nerves enter the molars. The **nasal surface** (*facies nasalis*) is the lateral wall of the nasal cavity; it bears the maxillary hiatus and, in front of it, the **lacrimal groove** (*sulcus lacrimalis*) — which, with the lacrimal bone and the inferior concha, forms the **nasolacrimal canal**.

Therefore inflammation of these teeth may spread into the sinus causing **odontogenic maxillary sinusitis**, and extraction of a tooth may leave the sinus open (an oroantral fistula). Because the outlet of the sinus (hiatus) lies in its upper part, pus does not drain well on its own.

The maxillary sinus is the **largest** paranasal sinus. Openings of the sinuses into the nose: into the **middle nasal meatus** — the maxillary and frontal sinuses and the anterior and middle ethmoidal cells; into the **superior nasal meatus** — the posterior ethmoidal cells; into the **sphenoethmoidal recess** — the sphenoidal sinus; into the **inferior nasal meatus** — the nasolacrimal duct.

sections.title: 3. The palatine, zygomatic and small facial bones

blocks.text: Palatine bone

The **palatine bone** (*os palatinum*) is a paired, L-shaped bone consisting of two plates. The **horizontal plate** (*lamina horizontalis*) joins its fellow of the opposite side to form the **posterior 1/3 of the hard palate**; in the middle of its posterior border is the **posterior nasal spine**. The **perpendicular plate** (*lamina perpendicularis*) forms the lateral wall of the posterior part of the nasal cavity; its upper border bears the orbital and sphenoidal processes, with the **sphenopalatine notch** between them. Between the perpendicular plate and the maxilla and pterygoid process runs the **greater palatine canal**; it opens at the posterolateral angle of the hard palate by the **greater palatine foramen**. The **pyramidal process** projects backward and laterally from the junction of the plates.

blocks.caption: The hard palate — maxillae and palatine bones, inferior view: *Processus palatinus maxillae* — palatine process of the maxilla; *Lamina horizontalis ossis palatini* — horizontal plate of the palatine bone; *Sutura palatina mediana, transversa* — median and transverse palatine sutures; *Foramen incisivum, os incisivum* — incisive foramen and incisive bone; *Foramina palatina majora* — greater palatine foramina; *Spina nasalis posterior* — posterior nasal spine; *Arcus alveolaris, alveoli dentales, septa interalveolaria* — alveolar arch, dental alveoli, interalveolar septa; *Torus palatinus* — palatine torus. parts.text: The hard palate is formed by the union in the midline of the right and left parts of the maxillae and palatine bones. If this union fails during fetal life, a **cleft palate** develops — the oral and nasal cavities communicate, the infant has difficulty sucking and food comes out of the nose; it is often combined with a cleft lip and is corrected surgically. In the region of the **greater palatine foramen**, palatal anesthesia is performed to anesthetize the upper teeth.

blocks.text: Zygomatic bone

The **zygomatic bone** (*os zygomaticum*) is a paired bone, the strongest in the lateral part of the face; it forms the cheek prominence and connects the facial bones with the neurocranium. It has **lateral**, **temporal** and **orbital surfaces** and three processes — the **frontal process** (to the frontal bone), the **temporal process** (which forms the **zygomatic arch** with the zygomatic process of the temporal bone) and the part that joins the maxilla. The bone is pierced by small foramina through which nerves pass.

blocks.label: Figure 7.6
blocks.caption: Right zygomatic bone, lateral surface: *Processus frontalis* — frontal process; *Processus temporalis* — temporal process; *Facies lateralis* — lateral surface; *Foramen zygomaticofaciale* — zygomaticofacial foramen; *Tuberculum marginale* — marginal tubercle. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: The nasal and lacrimal bones, the inferior nasal concha and the vomer

items: The **nasal bone** (*os nasale*) is a paired, small quadrangular plate; the two join in the midline to form the bony part of the **bridge of the nose**. Above it joins the frontal bone and laterally the frontal process of the maxilla; its lower border continues into the nasal cartilages.

The **lacrimal bone** (*os lacrimale*) is a paired bone, the smallest and most delicate facial bone; it lies in the medial wall of the orbit. The **posterior lacrimal crest** on its lateral surface ends below in a **hamulus**; the **lacrimal groove** in front of the crest, together with the corresponding groove of the maxilla, forms the **fossa for the lacrimal sac**.

The **inferior nasal concha** (*concha nasalis inferior*) is a paired, independent thin curved plate; it attaches to the conchal crests of the maxilla and palatine bone and bounds the inferior nasal meatus from above. Its lacrimal process takes part in forming the nasolacrimal canal.

The **vomer** (*vomer*) is an unpaired, thin quadrangular plate; it forms the posteroinferior part of the nasal septum. Its upper border joins the body of the sphenoid bone by two **alae**, its anterosuperior border joins the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone, and its posterior border is free and separates the choanae.

blocks.label: Figure 7.7
blocks.caption: Left — right lacrimal bone (A — lateral, B — medial surface): *Sulcus lacrimalis* — lacrimal groove; *Crista lacrimalis posterior* — posterior lacrimal crest; *Fossa sacci lacrimalis* — fossa for the lacrimal sac (part of it); *Hamulus lacrimalis* — lacrimal hamulus. Right — the vomer, right lateral view: *Ala vomeris* — ala of the vomer. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: The **nasal bones** are the most frequently fractured facial bones (boxing, falls). **Deviation of the nasal septum** (at the junction of the vomer and the perpendicular plate) makes breathing difficult and is corrected surgically (septoplasty). When the lacrimal passages are blocked, **dacryocystitis** develops; because the lacrimal bone is very thin, during surgery a new passage between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity is made precisely through it (dacryocystorhinostomy).

blocks.text: The **mandible** (*mandibula*) is the **only movable** unpaired bone of the skull; it forms the paired temporomandibular joint with the temporal bones. It has a horizontal horseshoe-shaped **body** (*corpus mandibulae*) and two **rami** (*rami mandibulae*) rising from it; at the junction of the body and ramus is the **angle of the mandible** (*angulus mandibulae*).

The thick lower border of the **body** is the **base** (*basis mandibulae*), and its upper border is the **alveolar part** (*pars alveolaris*), which bears 8 **dental alveoli** for the lower teeth on each side. On the **outer surface** of the body: in the middle — the **mental protuberance** (*protuberantia mentalis*) with the **mental tubercles** on either side; below the second premolar (or between the first and second premolars) — the **mental foramen** (*foramen mentale*), through which the mental nerve and vessels emerge; and the **oblique line** (*linea obliqua*), running obliquely backward into the ramus. On the **inner surface**: in the midline — the **mental spine** (*spina mentalis*, where the genioglossus and geniohyoid muscles attach); below and lateral to it — the **digastric fossa** (*fossa digastrica*); the **mylohyoid line** (*linea mylohyoidea*), running obliquely backward and upward; above it in front — the **sublingual fovea** (*fovea sublingualis*), and below it behind — the **submandibular fovea** (*fovea submandibularis*).

blocks.label: Figure 7.8
blocks.caption: Mandible, left anterolateral view (canal opened): *Caput mandibulae* — head of the mandible; *Collum mandibulae* — neck; *Processus condylaris* — condylar process; *Processus coronoideus* — coronoid process; *Incisura mandibulae* — mandibular notch; *Ramus mandibulae* — ramus of the mandible; *Lingula, foramen mandibulae* — lingula and mandibular foramen; *Canalis mandibulae* — mandibular canal; *Angulus mandibulae* — angle; *Tuberositas masseterica* — masseteric tuberosity; *Corpus mandibulae* — body; *Linea obliqua* — oblique line; *Foramen mentale* — mental foramen; *Protuberantia mentalis* — mental protuberance; *Tuberculum mentale* — mental tubercle; *Pars alveolaris, juga alveolaria* — alveolar part and alveolar yokes. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: The upper part of the **ramus** is divided by the **mandibular notch** (*incisura mandibulae*) into two processes: the anterior **coronoid process** (*processus coronoideus*), to which the temporalis muscle attaches; and the posterior **condylar process** (*processus condylaris*), which consists of the **neck** (*collum*) and the ellipsoid **head** (*caput mandibulae*); on the anterior surface of the neck is the **pterygoid fovea**, to which the lateral pterygoid muscle attaches. In the middle of the inner surface of the ramus is the **mandibular foramen** (*foramen mandibulae*) — partly covered in front by the **lingula** (*lingula*); the foramen leads into the **mandibular canal** (*canalis mandibulae*) within the bone, which ends at the mental foramen (inferior alveolar nerve and vessels). The **mylohyoid groove** runs downward and forward from the foramen. In the region of the angle there is the **masseteric tuberosity** on the outer side and the **pterygoid tuberosity** on the inner side.

blocks.label: Figure 7.9
blocks.caption: Mandible, internal (posterior) view: *Foramen mandibulae, lingula mandibulae* — mandibular foramen and lingula; *Sulcus mylohyoideus* — mylohyoid groove; *Linea mylohyoidea* — mylohyoid line; *Spina mentalis* — mental spine; *Fossa digastrica* — digastric fossa; *Fovea sublingualis* — sublingual fovea; *Fovea submandibularis* — submandibular fovea; *Torus mandibularis* — mandibular torus; *Tuberositas pterygoidea* — pterygoid tuberosity; *Angulus mandibulae* — angle of the mandible. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: In dentistry, **mandibular (inferior alveolar) nerve block** is used to anesthetize the lower teeth: the anesthetic is injected around the **mandibular foramen** (the region of the lingula) on the inner surface of the ramus — here the inferior alveolar nerve enters the canal. For the anterior teeth and the chin region the anesthetic is injected in the region of the **mental foramen**, and for the upper anterior teeth and upper lip in the region of the **infraorbital foramen**. The mandible most often fractures at the **angle**, the **canine region** and the **neck of the condylar process** (the bone is weaker at these sites).

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** The mandible develops from the first branchial arch — mainly by the endesmal route from connective tissue around **Meckel's cartilage** (with additional cartilaginous foci in the condylar and coronoid processes). In the newborn the mandible consists of **two halves** joined in the midline by connective tissue, which ossify and fuse **during the 1st year**. In the newborn most of the body is occupied by tooth buds, the alveolar part and mental protuberance are not defined, the ramus is short, the **angle is obtuse (≈150°)** and the mental foramen lies near the lower border. With tooth eruption the alveolar part develops, the ramus lengthens and the angle decreases to **120–130°** in adults. **In the elderly**, after the teeth are lost, the alveolar part is resorbed (atrophy), the body becomes lower, the mental foramen moves near the upper border and the angle increases again (≈140°).

blocks.label: Figure 7.10
blocks.caption: Age-related changes of the mandible: A — the newborn's mandible (two halves, tooth buds, obtuse angle); B — the adult mandible (boundaries of the ramus and body, angle, processes). Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: The angle of the mandible changes over life like a **“U”**: large in the newborn (**≈150°**) → small in adults (**120–130°**) → large again in edentulous elderly people (**≈140°**). The reason is the load from the teeth and the masticatory muscles: when teeth are present and chewing is strong, the ramus stands more upright.

blocks.text: The **hyoid bone** (*os hyoideum*) is an unpaired, horseshoe-shaped bone; it lies in the anterior region of the neck between the mandible and the larynx (at the level of the III–IV cervical vertebrae) and does not articulate with other bones — it is suspended from the cranial base and the larynx by muscles and ligaments. It consists of a **body** (*corpus*), paired **greater horns** (*cornua majora*) and paired **lesser horns** (*cornua minora*). The suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles and the muscles of the tongue attach to it; it serves as an important support in swallowing and speech.

blocks.label: Figure 7.11
blocks.caption: Hyoid bone, left anterolateral view: *Corpus* — body; *Cornu majus* — greater horn; *Cornu minus* — lesser horn. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** The hyoid bone develops from the II and III branchial arches. Ossification centers appear in the body and greater horns just before birth, and in the lesser horns at puberty. The parts of the bone fuse with each other at **25–30 years** (sometimes later).

parts.text: **Fracture of the hyoid bone** is an important sign in forensic medicine: it is often seen in cases of **strangulation** (manual compression of the neck). In young people the parts of the bone are joined by cartilage and are flexible, so it fractures less often, whereas in the elderly the fused, brittle bone fractures more easily.

sections.title: 6. Age-related features of the facial skeleton

blocks.text: In the newborn the facial skeleton is very small relative to the neurocranium (≈1:8), because the jaws, teeth and paranasal sinuses have not yet developed. The **maxilla** is low, and most of its body is occupied by tooth buds, so the lower margin of the orbit lies close to the alveolar process; the **maxillary sinus** looks like a small groove. During infancy the bone grows rapidly, and alveoli and septa appear in the alveolar process. The eruption of the deciduous teeth (from 6 months) and especially **their replacement by permanent teeth** (6–12 years) enhance the vertical growth of the facial skeleton; the maxillary sinus enlarges rapidly after the permanent teeth erupt and at puberty resembles that of the adult.

The zygomatic, nasal and lacrimal bones are ossified at birth and grow in proportion with the skull as a whole; the processes of the inferior nasal concha are cartilaginous at birth and resemble those of the adult at ≈13 years. At puberty **individual and sex characteristics** appear in the facial bones (especially the jaws, chin and cheek prominences) — men have a more massive jaw and chin. In old age, with loss of the teeth, the alveolar processes are resorbed and the lower third of the face shortens.

parts.text: On X-rays of children's facial bones, do not misinterpret the shadows of **tooth buds and unerupted permanent teeth** in the body of the jaw as a tumor or cyst. Knowing the eruption times of the teeth (deciduous — 6 months–2.5 years, permanent — 6–12 years, wisdom teeth — 17–25 years) is necessary for reading jaw X-rays correctly.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: 3 days ago a patient had the upper left first molar extracted. Now there is a feeling of heaviness in the left cheek, purulent discharge from the left side of the nose and fever. When drinking water, fluid comes out of the left nostril.
cases.ask: What complication has developed? What is its anatomical basis?
cases.answer: This is **odontogenic maxillary sinusitis** with an **oroantral fistula** (perforation). The roots of the upper first and second molars and the second premolar lie very close to the **floor of the maxillary sinus** (sometimes separated from it only by mucosa). When the tooth was extracted, the floor of the sinus was perforated and the oral cavity came to communicate with the maxillary sinus; fluid passes from the sinus through the **maxillary hiatus** into the middle nasal meatus and from there out through the nose. Infection entered the sinus and inflammation developed.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: After a blow to the chin, a boxer cannot close his mouth completely, his teeth do not meet properly (the bite is disturbed), there is pain in front of his left ear, and numbness is felt in the left half of the lower lip.
cases.ask: Where in the mandible can fractures occur? What is the numbness of the lip related to?
cases.answer: With a blow to the chin, the mandible often breaks **in two places**: at the site of impact (the chin or canine region) and at the **neck of the condylar process** on the opposite or the same side (pain in front of the ear). Numbness of the lower lip is due to injury of the **inferior alveolar nerve**: it enters the canal through the mandibular foramen, runs within the body and emerges from the **mental foramen** as the mental nerve (lower lip and skin of the chin). Because the fracture line passes through the canal, the nerve has been crushed or stretched.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: To treat a lower left molar, a dentist performed an inferior alveolar nerve block. After the injection the left half of the lower lip, the teeth and the left anterior 2/3 of the tongue became numb.
cases.ask: Where was the anesthetic injected, and why did the tongue also become numb?
cases.answer: The anesthetic was injected on the inner surface of the mandibular ramus, in the region of the **mandibular foramen and lingula** — where the inferior alveolar nerve enters the canal. Here the **lingual nerve** also passes slightly anterior and medial to the inferior alveolar nerve, so it is anesthetized too — numbness appears in the anterior 2/3 of the tongue. The inferior alveolar nerve supplies all the lower teeth of that side, and through the mental nerve the lower lip and the skin of the chin.

topics.title: The skull as a whole. The cranial base. Topography of the skull: the orbit, nasal cavity, temporal, infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae; their clinical significance

goals.text: To acquaint the student with the skull as a whole — its views from different sides, the inner and outer surfaces of the calvaria and cranial base, the cranial fossae, and the walls and communications of the orbit, nasal cavity, and temporal, infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae; to explain the routes by which infection, hemorrhage and tumors spread through these communications.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the main structures and sutures seen in the superior, anterior, lateral and posterior views of the skull;
the structures on the inner surface of the calvaria;
the anterior, middle and posterior fossae of the internal cranial base, their boundaries and foramina;
the parts and foramina of the external cranial base;
the walls, foramina and fissures of the orbit;
the walls of the nasal cavity, the nasal meatuses and the openings into them;
the walls and communications of the temporal, infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae;
age and sex changes of the skull and the cranial index.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find all the sutures, fossae, foramina and canals on the skull and name them in Latin;
name the nerves and vessels passing through the foramina of the cranial base;
show the seven communications of the pterygopalatine fossa with a probe;
calculate the cranial index and determine the shape of the skull.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: When the calvaria is fractured, the **inner table** breaks over a wider area and into more fragments than the outer table (it is more brittle) — so even with an injury that looks small from outside, bone fragments inside may damage the meninges and brain. Through the diploic veins, infection of the scalp can spread into the cranial cavity (emissary and diploic veins).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The cranial nerves leave the cranial base in the order **"anterior fossa — 1, middle — 2 to 6, posterior — 7 to 12"**: anterior fossa — CN I; middle fossa — II (optic canal), III, IV, V1, VI (superior fissure), V2 (foramen rotundum), V3 (foramen ovale); posterior fossa — VII, VIII (internal acoustic opening), IX, X, XI (jugular foramen), XII (hypoglossal canal).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Fractures of the cranial base present differently depending on which fossa is injured: **anterior fossa** — "raccoon eyes" (periorbital bruising), CSF leak from the nose, loss of smell; **middle fossa** — blood or CSF leaking from the ear, bruising over the mastoid process (Battle's sign), injury to CN VII and VIII (facial palsy, deafness); **posterior fossa** — bruising in the occipital region and neck, injury to CN IX–XII (disturbed swallowing and speech), the most dangerous because of proximity to the vital centers.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: When a blunt blow (a ball, a fist) strikes the eye region, pressure inside the orbit rises sharply and the thinnest walls break — the **inferior wall** (into the maxillary sinus) or the **medial wall** (into the ethmoidal cells) — a **"blow-out" fracture** (*blow-out*). Orbital tissue and the inferior rectus muscle become trapped in the fracture, causing inability to look upward and double vision; injury to the infraorbital nerve causes numbness of the cheek and upper lip.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The middle nasal meatus is the "crossroads" of the paranasal sinuses: **three** sinuses open into it — the frontal, maxillary, and anterior and middle ethmoidal cells. So swelling of the mucosa in this meatus (rhinitis) can block the outflow of several sinuses at once and cause **sinusitis**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the **7** routes of the pterygopalatine fossa as "**C-O-N-M-I-P and L**": **C**ranial cavity (foramen rotundum), **O**rbit (inferior orbital fissure), **N**asal cavity (sphenopalatine foramen), **M**outh (greater palatine canal), **I**nfratemporal fossa (pterygomaxillary fissure), **P**harynx (pharyngeal canal) and the foramen **L**acerum region (pterygoid canal).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Because of the many communications of the pterygopalatine fossa, infections and tumors in this region (for example, juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma in young people) can spread into the nasal cavity, orbit, infratemporal fossa and cranial cavity. Block of the pterygopalatine ganglion is used in some types of headache; maxillary nerve block is performed through the greater palatine canal in operations on the maxilla.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The shape of a newborn's head may change during delivery (the skull bones overlap one another — **molding**, caput succedaneum) — this resolves within a few days. In a child who always lies on the back, the occiput flattens (positional deformity); it must be distinguished from **craniosynostosis** (premature closure of sutures) — in craniosynostosis the head shape changes characteristically along a particular suture, and surgery is required.

sections.title: 1. Views of the skull from different sides

blocks.text: **From above** (*norma verticalis*) the skull is ovoid; it shows the **frontal**, two **parietal** and the **occipital** bones and the **coronal**, **sagittal** and **lambdoid** sutures joining them. The points where sutures meet are used in craniometry: **bregma** (intersection of the coronal and sagittal sutures — site of the anterior fontanelle) and **lambda** (intersection of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures — site of the posterior fontanelle).

**From the front** (*norma frontalis*) one sees the frontal bone, the openings (aditus) of the two orbits, between them the **piriform aperture** (*apertura piriformis*) of the nasal cavity, and below the alveolar processes of the maxilla and mandible with the teeth. **From behind** one sees the occipital squama, the external occipital protuberance, the nuchal lines, the lambdoid suture and the mastoid processes.

blocks.label: Figure 8.1
blocks.caption: Skull, anterior view: frontal bone, orbits, piriform aperture of the nasal cavity, zygomatic bones, maxilla and mandible. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: **From the side** (*norma lateralis*) the wide **temporal fossa** (*fossa temporalis*) is seen: it is bounded above by the **temporal line** and below by the **zygomatic arch**, and the temporalis muscle lies in it. On the wall of the temporal fossa, the H-shaped area where the parietal, frontal and temporal bones and the greater wing of the sphenoid meet — the **pterion** — is one of the thinnest places of the skull. Below the zygomatic arch lies the **infratemporal fossa** (*fossa infratemporalis*), and deeper to it the **pterygopalatine fossa** (*fossa pterygopalatina*).

blocks.label: Figure 8.2
blocks.caption: Skull, lateral view — temporal, infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae (zygomatic arch removed): *Fossa temporalis* — temporal fossa; *Fossa infratemporalis* — infratemporal fossa; *Crista infratemporalis* — infratemporal crest; *Fossa pterygopalatina* — pterygopalatine fossa; *Foramen sphenopalatinum* — sphenopalatine foramen; *Fissura orbitalis inferior* — inferior orbital fissure; *Tuber maxillae* — maxillary tuberosity; *Foramina alveolaria* — alveolar foramina; *Lamina lateralis processus pterygoidei* — lateral plate of the pterygoid process; *Hamulus pterygoideus* — pterygoid hamulus; *Sutura sphenosquamosa, sphenozygomatica, frontozygomatica* — sutures. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: The bones of the calvaria (*calvaria*) consist of two compact tables — the **outer** (*lamina externa*) and the more brittle **inner table** (*lamina interna, lamina vitrea* — "glassy") — and the spongy substance between them, the **diploe**; the diploe contains **diploic canals** through which veins pass. On the inner surface, along the midline, there is the **groove for the superior sagittal sinus**; beside it are **granular foveolae** (*foveolae granulares*) formed by arachnoid granulations, as well as **arterial grooves** (branches of the middle meningeal artery) and impressions of the cerebral gyri — **digitate impressions**.

blocks.label: Figure 8.3
blocks.caption: Calvaria, inner surface: *Os frontale, os parietale, os occipitale* — frontal, parietal, occipital bones; *Sutura coronalis, sagittalis, lambdoidea* — coronal, sagittal, lambdoid sutures; *Lamina externa, lamina interna, diploe* — outer and inner tables, diploe; *Sulcus sinus sagittalis superioris* — groove for the superior sagittal sinus; *Foveolae granulares* — granular foveolae; *Sulci arteriosi* — arterial grooves; *Ossa suturalia* — sutural bones. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: When the calvaria is fractured, the **inner table** breaks over a wider area and into more fragments than the outer table (it is more brittle) — so even with an injury that looks small from outside, bone fragments inside may damage the meninges and brain. Through the diploic veins, infection of the scalp can spread into the cranial cavity (emissary and diploic veins).

blocks.text: The **internal cranial base** (*basis cranii interna*) is divided into three step-like fossae: the **anterior**, **middle** and **posterior cranial fossae**. The boundary between the anterior and middle fossae is the posterior borders of the lesser wings of the sphenoid and the tuberculum sellae; the boundary between the middle and posterior fossae is the superior borders of the petrous parts of the temporal bones and the dorsum sellae.

blocks.label: Figure 8.4
blocks.caption: Internal cranial base (bones colored): *Fossa cranii anterior* — anterior cranial fossa (frontal — blue, ethmoid — red); *Lamina cribrosa, crista galli, foramen caecum* — cribriform plate, crista galli, foramen cecum; *Ala minor, canalis opticus* — lesser wing, optic canal; *Sella turcica, fossa hypophysialis, dorsum sellae* — sella turcica; *Foramen rotundum, ovale, spinosum, lacerum* — foramen rotundum, ovale, spinosum and lacerum; *Impressio trigemini* — trigeminal impression; *Porus acusticus internus* — internal acoustic opening; *Clivus* — clivus; *Foramen jugulare* — jugular foramen; *Canalis hypoglossi* — hypoglossal canal; *Foramen magnum* — foramen magnum; *Sulcus sinus transversi, sigmoidei* — grooves for the transverse and sigmoid sinuses; *Crista occipitalis interna* — internal occipital crest. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: The anterior part of the **external cranial base** (*basis cranii externa*) is formed by the hard palate and the alveolar arch of the maxilla, the middle part by the sphenoid bone and the inferior surfaces of the petrous parts of the temporal bones, and the posterior part by the occipital bone. **In the anterior part**: the hard palate (median and transverse sutures, incisive foramen, greater and lesser palatine foramina), behind it the posterior openings of the nasal cavity — the **choanae**, separated by the vomer; beside the choanae are the pterygoid processes of the sphenoid bone.

**In the middle part**: the foramen ovale and foramen spinosum, the spine of the sphenoid, the **foramen lacerum** (*foramen lacerum* — between the apex of the petrous part, the body of the sphenoid and the basilar part of the occipital bone), the external opening of the carotid canal, the jugular foramen, the styloid process and stylomastoid foramen, the mandibular fossa and articular tubercle, the external acoustic opening and the mastoid process. **In the posterior part**: the foramen magnum, the occipital condyles, the hypoglossal and condylar canals, the external occipital crest and protuberance, and the nuchal lines.

blocks.label: Figure 8.5
blocks.caption: External cranial base (bones colored): *Processus palatinus maxillae, lamina horizontalis ossis palatini* — hard palate; *Sutura palatina mediana, transversa* — palatine sutures; *Choanae* — choanae; *Vomer* — vomer; *Lamina medialis et lateralis processus pterygoidei* — plates of the pterygoid process; *Fossa infratemporalis* — infratemporal fossa; *Arcus zygomaticus* — zygomatic arch; *Foramen ovale, spinosum, lacerum* — foramen ovale, spinosum and lacerum; *Tuberculum articulare, fossa mandibularis* — articular tubercle, mandibular fossa; *Processus styloideus, foramen stylomastoideum* — styloid process, stylomastoid foramen; *Canalis caroticus* — carotid canal; *Foramen jugulare* — jugular foramen; *Processus mastoideus* — mastoid process; *Condylus occipitalis* — occipital condyle; *Foramen magnum* — foramen magnum; *Protuberantia occipitalis externa, linea nuchae superior et inferior* — external occipital protuberance, nuchal lines. blocks.text: The **orbit** (*orbita*) is a paired cavity shaped like a four-sided pyramid; its **base** — the **orbital opening** (*aditus orbitae*) — faces forward, and its **apex** faces backward and medially, toward the optic canal. The orbit contains the eyeball, its muscles, the lacrimal gland, vessels and nerves, and fatty tissue.

parts.text: When a blunt blow (a ball, a fist) strikes the eye region, pressure inside the orbit rises sharply and the thinnest walls break — the **inferior wall** (into the maxillary sinus) or the **medial wall** (into the ethmoidal cells) — a **"blow-out" fracture** (*blow-out*). Orbital tissue and the inferior rectus muscle become trapped in the fracture, causing inability to look upward and double vision; injury to the infraorbital nerve causes numbness of the cheek and upper lip.

blocks.text: The **nasal cavity** (*cavitas nasi*) opens anteriorly by the **piriform aperture** (*apertura piriformis*) and communicates posteriorly through the **choanae** with the nasal part of the pharynx; the **nasal septum** (*septum nasi osseum* — perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone and vomer) divides it into two halves. The **roof** is formed by the nasal bones, the nasal part of the frontal bone, the cribriform plate and the body of the sphenoid; the **floor** by the hard palate; the **lateral wall**, the most complex, by the maxilla (nasal surface and frontal process), the lacrimal bone, the ethmoidal labyrinth, the inferior nasal concha, the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone and the medial plate of the pterygoid process.

Three **nasal conchae** hang from the lateral wall: the **superior** and **middle** (parts of the ethmoid bone) and the **inferior** (an independent bone). Below them lie three **nasal meatuses**; the narrow space between the conchae and the septum is the **common nasal meatus**. Posterosuperior to the superior concha is the **sphenoethmoidal recess**. In the posterior part of the lateral wall the **sphenopalatine foramen** (*foramen sphenopalatinum*) connects the nasal cavity with the pterygopalatine fossa.

parts.text: The middle nasal meatus is the "crossroads" of the paranasal sinuses: **three** sinuses open into it — the frontal, maxillary, and anterior and middle ethmoidal cells. So swelling of the mucosa in this meatus (rhinitis) can block the outflow of several sinuses at once and cause **sinusitis**.

blocks.text: The **infratemporal fossa** (*fossa infratemporalis*) lies medial to the zygomatic arch and the ramus of the mandible; its **medial wall** is the lateral plate of the pterygoid process, its **anterior wall** the maxillary tuberosity, and its **roof** the infratemporal surface of the greater wing of the sphenoid; there is no bony wall below and laterally. It contains the pterygoid muscles, the maxillary artery, the pterygoid venous plexus and branches of the mandibular nerve. The fossa continues above into the temporal fossa, in front through the inferior orbital fissure into the orbit, and medially through the pterygomaxillary fissure into the pterygopalatine fossa; it communicates with the middle cranial fossa through the foramen ovale and foramen spinosum.

The **pterygopalatine fossa** (*fossa pterygopalatina*) is a narrow slit-like space, the medial continuation of the infratemporal fossa. Its **anterior wall** is the maxillary tuberosity, its **posterior wall** the base of the pterygoid process of the sphenoid, and its **medial wall** the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone. The fossa contains the **maxillary nerve**, the **pterygopalatine ganglion** and the terminal branches of the **maxillary artery**. It is an important "crossroads" communicating with most of the cavities of the skull.

blocks.title: Table 8.4. Communications of the pterygopalatine fossa
head: Foramen / canal
Where it leads
rows: To the region of the foramen lacerum (external cranial base)
To the oral cavity (through the greater and lesser palatine foramina)
To the nasal part of the pharynx

parts.text: Remember the **7** routes of the pterygopalatine fossa as "**C-O-N-M-I-P and L**": **C**ranial cavity (foramen rotundum), **O**rbit (inferior orbital fissure), **N**asal cavity (sphenopalatine foramen), **M**outh (greater palatine canal), **I**nfratemporal fossa (pterygomaxillary fissure), **P**harynx (pharyngeal canal) and the foramen **L**acerum region (pterygoid canal).

Because of the many communications of the pterygopalatine fossa, infections and tumors in this region (for example, juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma in young people) can spread into the nasal cavity, orbit, infratemporal fossa and cranial cavity. Block of the pterygopalatine ganglion is used in some types of headache; maxillary nerve block is performed through the greater palatine canal in operations on the maxilla.

sections.title: 8. Age and sex changes of the skull, and craniometry

blocks.title: Table 8.5. Age periods of the skull
head: Period
Features
rows: The neurocranium is ≈8 times larger than the facial skeleton; fontanelles and wide sutures; the frontal and parietal eminences are prominent; no paranasal sinuses, mastoid process, teeth or alveolar processes; the mandible consists of two halves
The skull grows rapidly (especially in the 1st year); the fontanelles close; the deciduous teeth erupt and the jaws grow; parts of the occipital and sphenoid bones fuse
Growth slows, mainly the cranial base and face grow; the permanent teeth erupt and the paranasal sinuses enlarge
The face and paranasal sinuses grow intensively; sex differences appear; the spheno-occipital synchondrosis ossifies
The sutures ossify (synostosis), the bones become thin and brittle; teeth are lost, the alveolar processes are resorbed, and the lower part of the face shortens

blocks.text: **Sex differences:** the male skull is usually larger and more massive, with distinct prominences (superciliary arches, glabella, occipital protuberance, mastoid processes), a sloping forehead, a blunt superior orbital margin and a well-marked mandibular angle; the female skull has a more vertical forehead, well-defined frontal and parietal eminences, weak prominences and a sharp orbital margin.

**Craniometry.** To assess the shape of the skull, the **cranial (cephalic) index** is calculated: the greatest transverse diameter (between the two parietal eminences) is divided by the greatest longitudinal diameter (glabella — most prominent point of the occiput) and multiplied by 100. An index **below 75** is **dolichocephalic** (long head), **75–80** **mesocephalic** (medium), and **above 80** **brachycephalic** (short, broad head).

parts.text: The shape of a newborn's head may change during delivery (the skull bones overlap one another — **molding**, caput succedaneum) — this resolves within a few days. In a child who always lies on the back, the occiput flattens (positional deformity); it must be distinguished from **craniosynostosis** (premature closure of sutures) — in craniosynostosis the head shape changes characteristically along a particular suture, and surgery is required.

skills.title: Practical skill: determining the cranial index

items: With calipers measure the **longitudinal** diameter from the glabella to the most prominent point of the occiput and the greatest **transverse** diameter between the two parietal eminences.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A soccer player was hit in the eye by a ball. The area around the eye is swollen, the patient cannot look upward and sees double; there is numbness of the cheek and upper lip on the same side. CT showed orbital tissue herniating into the cavity below.
cases.ask: Which wall of the orbit is fractured? How do you explain the numbness and the disturbed eye movement?
cases.answer: This is a **"blow-out" fracture of the orbital floor**. With the blow, pressure inside the orbit rose and one of the thinnest walls — the **inferior wall** (orbital surface of the maxilla) — broke, and tissue herniated into the **maxillary sinus**. Because the **inferior rectus muscle** is trapped in the fracture line, the eye does not move upward (double vision). The infraorbital nerve, lying in the **infraorbital groove and canal** of the inferior wall, is injured — it supplies the skin of the cheek, the side of the nose and the upper lip.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: After a fall onto the back of the head, a patient complains of inability to swallow, a hoarse voice, and deviation of the tongue to one side when it is protruded. There is bruising of the skin of the occiput and neck.
cases.ask: Which fossa of the cranial base is injured? Which foramina and nerves are damaged?
cases.answer: This is a fracture of the **posterior cranial fossa**. The disturbed swallowing and hoarse voice result from injury to the **glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X)** nerves passing through the **jugular foramen**; deviation of the tongue to one side results from injury to **CN XII**, passing through the **hypoglossal canal** (the tongue deviates toward the injured side). Fractures of the posterior fossa are the most dangerous because of proximity to the medulla oblongata.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient with chronic rhinitis has pain in the forehead and cheek regions and purulent nasal discharge; the pain increases when bending the head forward. Radiographs show opacification of the frontal and maxillary sinuses.
cases.ask: Why are these two sinuses inflamed together? Where do they open?
cases.answer: The frontal and maxillary sinuses (as well as the anterior and middle ethmoidal cells) open into the **middle nasal meatus**. In rhinitis the mucosa of this meatus swells and blocks the outflow openings of several sinuses at once — secretions accumulate, and **frontal and maxillary sinusitis** develop. Because the outflow opening of the maxillary sinus is in its upper part, pus does not drain well.

topics.title: Joints of bones. Joints of the bones of the trunk and their features in children. Joints of the skull bones. The temporomandibular joint

goals.text: To acquaint the student with the types of bone joints, the general structure of a joint, the classification of joints and their axes of movement; to teach the joints of the vertebral column, thoracic cage and skull bones, the temporomandibular joint and their age-related features.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the classification of bone joints: continuous (fibrous, cartilaginous, bony), symphyses and synovial joints;
the main and accessory elements of a joint;
the classification of joints by the number and shape of articular surfaces and by the axes of movement;
the intervertebral disc, the ligaments and joints of the vertebral column; the atlanto-occipital and atlanto-axial joints;
the physiological curvatures of the vertebral column and when they form;
the joints of the ribs with the vertebrae and the sternum;
the sutures and synchondroses of the skull and the structure and movements of the temporomandibular joint.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify and show the types of joints on the skeleton and on specimens;
classify a joint and state its axes and types of movement;
show the ligaments and curvatures of the vertebral column;
observe the movements of the temporomandibular joint by palpation in a living person.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The types of movement depend on the axes: around the **frontal axis** — flexion (*flexio*) and extension (*extensio*); around the **sagittal axis** — abduction (*abductio*) and adduction (*adductio*); around the **vertical axis** — medial and lateral rotation (*rotatio*); in the forearm bones — pronation and supination. In joints with two or more axes there is also **circular movement** (*circumductio*) — a movement describing a cone.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: With age the disc loses water and fissures appear in the anulus fibrosus — **osteochondrosis**. When lifting a heavy load, the nucleus pulposus may protrude through a tear in the anulus — **disc herniation**. Because the posterior longitudinal ligament is thick in the midline and thin at the sides, the herniation usually protrudes **posterolaterally** and compresses the **spinal nerve root** next to the intervertebral foramen (low back pain, pain radiating to the leg — radiculopathy). It occurs most often at the L~IV~–L~V~ and L~V~–S~I~ discs.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The transverse ligament of the atlas separates the dens from the spinal cord. If this ligament becomes lax or ruptures in rheumatoid arthritis, Down syndrome or injury, the dens may shift backward and **compress the upper part of the spinal cord** — this is life-threatening (respiratory center and segments of the phrenic nerve). Therefore, in children with Down syndrome, sports involving sharp flexion of the neck are restricted.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Pathological curvatures of the vertebral column: **scoliosis** — lateral curvature in the frontal plane (often at school age because of poor sitting posture, one-sided loads or uneven growth); **hyperkyphosis** ("hunchback") and **hyperlordosis**. For early detection the child is examined while bending forward (Adams forward bend test) — a rib hump on one side indicates scoliosis.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: When the mouth is opened excessively wide (yawning, vomiting, dental procedures), the head of the mandible may slide forward over the articular tubercle and remain in the infratemporal fossa — **dislocation of the mandible**: the mouth is locked open and the patient cannot close it. To reduce it, the physician places the thumbs on the patient's lower molars and presses the jaw first **downward**, then **backward**. In the newborn the articular tubercle is not apparent and the fossa is flat — so the forward-backward gliding movements needed for suckling are free.

blocks.text: **Arthrology** (Greek *arthron* — joint) is the study of the joints of bones. By the way they are connected, bone joints are divided into three groups: **continuous joints** (*synarthroses*) — there is no cavity between the bones, which are joined solidly by tissue; **symphyses (hemiarthroses)** (*hemiarthroses, symphyses*) — there is a small cleft within the cartilage; **discontinuous joints — synovial joints** (*diarthroses, articulationes synoviales*) — there is a joint cavity between the bones.

blocks.title: Table 9.1. Continuous joints
head: Type
Tissue
Examples
rows: **Ligaments** (the ligamenta flava — elastic); **membranes** (interosseous membranes of the forearm and leg); **sutures** — serrate (between the parietal bones), squamous (temporal and parietal), plane (facial bones); **gomphosis** — attachment of a tooth in its socket
**Permanent**: intervertebral discs, attachment of the 1st rib to the sternum; **temporary**: epiphyseal growth cartilage, spheno-occipital synchondrosis, cartilage between the parts of the hip bone
Ossification of temporary synchondroses: sacral vertebrae, hip bone, sutures in old age

blocks.label: Figure 9.1
blocks.caption: Types of continuous joints: interosseous membrane (syndesmosis), ligamenta flava, intervertebral discs (synchondrosis), sutures — serrate, squamous and plane sutures. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: **Symphyses (hemiarthroses)** — within a cartilaginous or fibrocartilaginous joint there is a narrow slit-like cavity, but there is no true joint capsule or synovial membrane. Examples: the **pubic symphysis** (*symphysis pubica*), the symphysis between the manubrium and body of the sternum, and sometimes the intervertebral discs.

Every joint has three **main elements**: 1) **articular surfaces** (*facies articulares*) — covered by **articular cartilage** (*cartilago articularis*, usually hyaline); 2) the **joint capsule** (*capsula articularis*) — consisting of a strong outer **fibrous membrane** and an inner **synovial membrane**; the synovial membrane covers all the structures inside the joint except the articular cartilage and is rich in blood vessels and nerves; 3) the **joint cavity** (*cavitas articularis*) — a hermetically closed slit-like space filled with a small amount of **synovial fluid**; the fluid moistens the articular surfaces, reduces friction and nourishes the cartilage.

blocks.label: Figure 9.2
blocks.caption: Diagram of the structure of a joint: 1 — synovial membrane; 2 — joint space; 3 — joint cavity; 4 — bone; 5 — articular cartilage; 6 — periosteum. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

blocks.text: **Accessory elements**: **ligaments** (extracapsular, intracapsular and capsular); **articular discs** (temporomandibular and sternoclavicular joints) and **menisci** (knee joint) — they make the articular surfaces congruent and absorb shock; the **articular labrum** (*labrum articulare* — deepens the articular fossa in the shoulder and hip joints); **synovial folds** and **synovial bursae** (*bursae synoviales*).
