blocks.text: By the number of articular surfaces, joints are classified as **simple** (two surfaces — the shoulder joint), **compound** (three or more surfaces — the elbow joint), **complex** (with a disc or meniscus inside — the knee joint) and **combined** (two separate joints moving together — the two temporomandibular joints).

parts.text: The types of movement depend on the axes: around the **frontal axis** — flexion (*flexio*) and extension (*extensio*); around the **sagittal axis** — abduction (*abductio*) and adduction (*adductio*); around the **vertical axis** — medial and lateral rotation (*rotatio*); in the forearm bones — pronation and supination. In joints with two or more axes there is also **circular movement** (*circumductio*) — a movement describing a cone.

blocks.text: The vertebrae are joined by their **bodies**, **arches** and **processes**. Between the bodies of adjacent vertebrae lies the **intervertebral disc** (*discus intervertebralis*) of fibrocartilage; there are 23 discs in all (there is no disc between the atlas and axis). At the periphery of the disc is the strong **anulus fibrosus** (*anulus fibrosus*) of concentric layers, and in the center the elastic, water-rich **nucleus pulposus** (*nucleus pulposus*); the nucleus acts as a shock absorber. The discs are ≈5–6 mm high in the cervical region and ≈10–12 mm in the lumbar region; they make up ≈1/4 of the length of the vertebral column.

blocks.label: Figure 9.5
blocks.caption: Intervertebral disc and vertebral joints, superior view: *Anulus fibrosus* — anulus fibrosus; *Nucleus pulposus* — nucleus pulposus; *Lig. longitudinale anterius, posterius* — anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments; *Lig. flavum* — ligamentum flavum; *Articulatio zygapophysialis* — zygapophysial (facet) joint; *Canalis vertebralis* — vertebral canal. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: The articular processes of adjacent vertebrae form the **zygapophysial (facet) joints** (*articulationes zygapophysiales*) — these are plane joints; their surfaces are oriented differently in each region (see topic 1) and determine the direction of movement. The 5th lumbar vertebra forms the **lumbosacral joint** with the sacrum, and the sacrum forms the **sacrococcygeal joint** with the coccyx.

blocks.label: Figure 9.7
blocks.caption: Sagittal section of the lumbar and sacral parts of the vertebral column: *Lig. longitudinale anterius, posterius* — anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments; *Lig. flavum* — ligamentum flavum; *Lig. interspinale, supraspinale* — interspinous and supraspinous ligaments; *Discus intervertebralis* — intervertebral disc; *Articulatio lumbosacralis* — lumbosacral joint; *Promontorium* — promontory; *Canalis sacralis* — sacral canal; *Lig. sacrospinale, sacrotuberale* — sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments; *Articulatio sacrococcygea* — sacrococcygeal joint. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: With age the disc loses water and fissures appear in the anulus fibrosus — **osteochondrosis**. When lifting a heavy load, the nucleus pulposus may protrude through a tear in the anulus — **disc herniation**. Because the posterior longitudinal ligament is thick in the midline and thin at the sides, the herniation usually protrudes **posterolaterally** and compresses the **spinal nerve root** next to the intervertebral foramen (low back pain, pain radiating to the leg — radiculopathy). It occurs most often at the L~IV~–L~V~ and L~V~–S~I~ discs.

blocks.text: Joints of the vertebral column with the skull

The **atlanto-occipital joint** (*articulatio atlantooccipitalis*) lies between the occipital condyles and the superior articular facets of the atlas; it is a paired, **ellipsoid**, combined joint: around the frontal axis the head can be nodded forward and backward (the "yes" movement), and around the sagittal axis tilted slightly to the side. It is reinforced by the **anterior and posterior atlanto-occipital membranes**.

**Atlanto-axial joints**: the unpaired **median** joint — between the dens of the axis and the anterior arch of the atlas and the **transverse ligament of the atlas** — is a **pivot** joint; the paired **lateral** joints — between the inferior articular facets of the atlas and the superior facets of the axis — are plane joints. Together they allow the head, with the atlas, to turn right and left around the vertical axis (the "no" movement, ≈30–40° to each side). The dens is held by the **cruciform ligament** (transverse ligament + longitudinal bands), the **apical ligament of the dens** and the **alar ligaments**; they are covered from behind by the **tectorial membrane** (continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament).

blocks.label: Figure 9.8
blocks.caption: Median atlanto-axial joint, superior view: *Dens axis* — dens of the axis; *Articulatio atlantoaxialis mediana* — median atlanto-axial joint; *Lig. transversum atlantis* — transverse ligament of the atlas; *Cavum articulare* — joint cavity; *Membrana tectoria* — tectorial membrane; *Lig. longitudinale posterius* — posterior longitudinal ligament. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.label: Figure 9.9
blocks.caption: Joints of the occipital bone, atlas and axis, posterior view (vertebral canal opened): *Lig. cruciforme atlantis* — cruciform ligament of the atlas (transverse ligament and longitudinal bands); *Ligg. alaria* — alar ligaments; *Lig. apicis dentis* — apical ligament of the dens; *Capsula articularis atlantooccipitalis, atlantoaxialis lateralis* — capsules of the atlanto-occipital and lateral atlanto-axial joints; *Os occipitale* — occipital bone. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: The transverse ligament of the atlas separates the dens from the spinal cord. If this ligament becomes lax or ruptures in rheumatoid arthritis, Down syndrome or injury, the dens may shift backward and **compress the upper part of the spinal cord** — this is life-threatening (respiratory center and segments of the phrenic nerve). Therefore, in children with Down syndrome, sports involving sharp flexion of the neck are restricted.

blocks.text: The vertebral column as a whole

In adults the vertebral column is not straight; in the sagittal plane it forms four **physiological curvatures**: convex forward — the **lordoses** (cervical and lumbar) and convex backward — the **kyphoses** (thoracic and sacral). The curvatures are related to upright walking: like a spring they soften shocks during walking and jumping and help maintain balance. The vertebral column performs flexion and extension (most in the cervical and lumbar regions), lateral bending, rotation (in the cervical and thoracic regions) and circumduction.

blocks.title: Table 9.4. Formation of the curvatures of the vertebral column
head: Curvature
Time of appearance
Cause
rows: The child begins to hold the head up (posterior neck muscles)
The child begins to stand and walk
During childhood, as the sacrum forms
Cervical and thoracic — by 7 years, lumbar — at 12–14 years; completely — at 18–20 years

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** In the newborn the vertebral column is almost straight (only a mild general kyphosis), ≈20 cm long, with a relatively long cervical part and short thoracic and lumbar parts. The discs are thick — making up **45–48%** of the length of the column (≈25–30% in adults) — and rich in blood vessels; the ligaments are poorly developed and mature by 12 years. Up to 20 years the height of the discs gradually decreases and the anulus fibrosus thickens. In old age the vertebral column shortens by up to 5 cm because of thinning of the discs and increased curvatures.

blocks.label: Figure 9.10
blocks.caption: Thoracic and lumbar parts of the vertebral column, MRI (sagittal section): 1 — spinal cord; 2 — ligaments between the spinous processes; 3 — spinous processes; 4 — intervertebral discs (bright bands); 5 — bodies of the thoracic vertebrae. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

parts.text: Pathological curvatures of the vertebral column: **scoliosis** — lateral curvature in the frontal plane (often at school age because of poor sitting posture, one-sided loads or uneven growth); **hyperkyphosis** ("hunchback") and **hyperlordosis**. For early detection the child is examined while bending forward (Adams forward bend test) — a rib hump on one side indicates scoliosis.

blocks.text: The ribs form two joints with the thoracic vertebrae. The **joint of the head of the rib** (*articulatio capitis costae*) lies between the head of the rib and the costal facets of two adjacent vertebrae; in ribs II–X there is an **intra-articular ligament** inside the joint running from the crest of the head to the disc; the capsule is reinforced by the **radiate ligament**. The **costotransverse joint** (*articulatio costotransversaria*) lies between the tubercle of the rib and the costal facet of the transverse process (absent in ribs XI–XII). The two joints together act as a **combined** joint that raises and lowers the rib around the axis of the rib neck — the basis of the respiratory movements.

blocks.label: Figure 9.11
blocks.caption: Joints of the ribs with the vertebrae: *Articulatio capitis costae* — joint of the head of the rib; *Lig. capitis costae radiatum* — radiate ligament; *Lig. capitis costae intraarticulare* — intra-articular ligament; *Articulatio costotransversaria* — costotransverse joint; *Lig. costotransversarium superius, laterale* — costotransverse ligaments; *Discus intervertebralis* — intervertebral disc. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: Anteriorly the ribs join the sternum: the cartilage of the **1st rib** forms a **synchondrosis** with the manubrium; the cartilages of **ribs II–VII** form the **sternocostal joints** (*articulationes sternocostales*) with the costal notches of the sternum — these are plane joints whose capsule is formed by the perichondrium, reinforced by the anterior and posterior **radiate sternocostal ligaments**; the ligaments blend with the periosteum of the sternum to form the **sternal membrane**. The cartilages of ribs VIII–X join one another by **interchondral joints**. Between the parts of the sternum there are **sternal synchondroses** (the one between the manubrium and body sometimes in the form of a symphysis).

blocks.label: Figure 9.12
blocks.caption: Joints of the ribs with the sternum (anterior view): *Articulationes sternocostales* — sternocostal joints; *Ligg. sternocostalia radiata* — radiate sternocostal ligaments; *Membrana sterni* — sternal membrane; *Synchondrosis costae primae* — synchondrosis of the 1st rib; *Articulationes interchondrales* — interchondral joints; *Membrana intercostalis externa* — external intercostal membrane. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

sections.title: 5. Joints of the skull bones and the temporomandibular joint

blocks.text: The bones of the calvaria are joined mainly by **sutures**: **serrate** (sagittal, coronal, lambdoid), **squamous** (between the temporal squama and the parietal bone) and **plane** (between facial bones, for example between the nasal bones). Between the bones of the cranial base there are **synchondroses**: permanent — petro-occipital, sphenopetrosal (cartilage in the region of the foramen lacerum); temporary — spheno-occipital, between the parts of the sphenoid bone, and others. In the newborn the bones of the calvaria do not form sutures — between them there are connective tissue membranes and fontanelles; the spaces between the bones of the cranial base are filled with cartilage. The sutures gradually ossify in old age (synostosis). Except for the mandible and hyoid bone, the skull bones are joined immovably.

The **temporomandibular joint** (*articulatio temporomandibularis*) is a paired, **combined** (the joints of both sides move together), **complex** (contains a disc) joint, **ellipsoid (condylar)** in shape. It is formed by the head of the mandible and the **mandibular fossa** and **articular tubercle** of the temporal bone; the articular surfaces are covered with fibrocartilage. Inside the joint lies the biconcave fibrocartilaginous **articular disc** (*discus articularis*) — fused at its edges to the capsule, it divides the joint cavity into **upper and lower compartments**; part of the tendon of the lateral pterygoid muscle attaches to the disc.

blocks.label: Figure 9.13
blocks.caption: Sagittal section of the temporomandibular joint: the mandibular fossa and articular tubercle (above), the head of the mandible, the articular disc between them, the upper and lower compartments of the joint cavity, the joint capsule and the lateral pterygoid muscle. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

blocks.text: The joint capsule is wide and loose, and thin in front. It is reinforced on the outer side by the **lateral ligament** (*lig. laterale*), running from the base of the zygomatic process to the neck of the mandible; outside the capsule lie the **sphenomandibular** (*lig. sphenomandibulare* — from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible) and **stylomandibular** (*lig. stylomandibulare*) ligaments.

blocks.label: Figure 9.14
blocks.caption: Temporomandibular joint, lateral view: *Lig. laterale* — lateral ligament; *Capsula articularis* — joint capsule; *Arcus zygomaticus* — zygomatic arch; *Processus styloideus* — styloid process; *Lig. stylomandibulare* — stylomandibular ligament. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.label: Figure 9.15
blocks.caption: Ligaments of the temporomandibular joint, medial view: *Lig. sphenomandibulare* — sphenomandibular ligament; *Lig. stylomandibulare* — stylomandibular ligament; *Lig. pterygospinale* — pterygospinous ligament; *Capsula articulationis temporomandibularis* — joint capsule; *Processus pterygoideus (lamina lateralis)* — lateral plate of the pterygoid process; *Hamulus pterygoideus* — pterygoid hamulus. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.title: Table 9.5. Movements at the temporomandibular joint
head: Movement
Axis
In which compartment of the joint
rows: Opening and closing the mouth (depression and elevation of the mandible)

In slight opening — in the **lower** compartment (the head rotates under the disc); in wide opening the head, together with the disc, **glides forward** onto the articular tubercle (upper compartment)
Protrusion and retraction of the mandible
In the **upper** compartment — the head, together with the disc, moves onto the tubercle

parts.text: When the mouth is opened excessively wide (yawning, vomiting, dental procedures), the head of the mandible may slide forward over the articular tubercle and remain in the infratemporal fossa — **dislocation of the mandible**: the mouth is locked open and the patient cannot close it. To reduce it, the physician places the thumbs on the patient's lower molars and presses the jaw first **downward**, then **backward**. In the newborn the articular tubercle is not apparent and the fossa is flat — so the forward-backward gliding movements needed for suckling are free.

blocks.text: **Age-related features of joints.** In the newborn all parts of the joints are anatomically formed, but the articular ends are cartilaginous, and ossification centers appear in them from 1–2 years up to adolescence. The joint capsule is tight and the ligaments are poorly developed; the folds and villi of the synovial membrane increase after birth and become more complex at 6–10 years. Joint growth accelerates at 2–3 years, when the child begins to move actively; full maturation of the joints is completed at **21–25 years**. In children the joints are more mobile and the ligaments more elastic.

skills.title: Practical skill: identifying and classifying joints

items: On the skeleton show examples of continuous joints: sutures (serrate, squamous, plane), interosseous membranes, synchondroses (discs, 1st rib), synostoses (sacrum).
For any joint: name the bones and surfaces forming it; classify the joint by the number and shape of its surfaces; show its axes and types of movement.
On a specimen of the vertebral column (or a figure) show the disc, the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments, the ligamenta flava, and the interspinous and supraspinous ligaments.
Demonstrate the movements at the atlanto-occipital and atlanto-axial joints (the "yes" and "no" movements) and name the ligaments that secure them.
Show the costovertebral and sternocostal joints; explain the axis of rib movement during inspiration.

skills.title: Practical skill: examining the temporomandibular joint

items: Place your index fingers in front of the auricles on both sides and ask the patient to open and close the mouth slowly: feel the head move forward and return.
Insert your little fingers into the external acoustic meatuses and feel the posterior surface of the head touch your finger when the mouth closes.
Measure the mouth opening (normally ≈4–5 cm between the incisors, i.e., the width of three fingers); note any pain, clicking or deviation of the jaw to one side.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 42-year-old porter felt sudden low back pain while lifting a heavy box; the pain radiates along the left buttock and the back of the thigh down to the heel, and there is numbness on the lateral side of the left foot. MRI showed protrusion of the L~V~–S~I~ disc posteriorly and to the left.
cases.ask: What is this condition? How is the disc built, and why did it protrude precisely in the posterolateral direction?
cases.answer: This is an **intervertebral disc herniation**. The disc consists of a peripheral **anulus fibrosus** and a central **nucleus pulposus**; under a heavy load the nucleus is pushed out under pressure through a tear in the anulus. Posteriorly in the midline the **posterior longitudinal ligament** is thick and blocks the herniation, but at the sides it is thin — so the herniation protrudes **posterolaterally** and compresses the **S~I~ nerve root** next to the intervertebral foramen (pain radiating to the buttock, back of the thigh, leg and heel — sciatica). The L~IV~–L~V~ and L~V~–S~I~ discs are affected most often, because load and movement are greatest in the lumbar region.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: While laughing, a patient yawned widely and afterward could not close the mouth; the mouth is locked open, the area in front of the ear is depressed, and speech and swallowing are difficult.
cases.ask: What injury has occurred, and at which joint? How should it be reduced?
cases.answer: This is a **dislocation of the temporomandibular joint** (anterior dislocation). When the mouth opens wide, the head of the mandible, together with the disc, moves onto the **articular tubercle**; with excessive opening it slips forward over the tubercle and becomes locked there by muscle contraction (in front of the ear the empty mandibular fossa forms a depression). Reduction: the thumbs (wrapped in gauze) are placed on the lower molars, the jaw is first pressed **downward** to bring it below the tubercle and then pushed **backward**.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A pediatrician is examining a 4-month-old infant. The baby holds the head well but does not yet sit. The mother is worried that the baby's spine "is not straight — there is a curve in the neck."
cases.ask: Is this normal? In what order do the curvatures of the vertebral column form?
cases.answer: Yes, it is **normal**. In the newborn the vertebral column is almost straight; once the child begins to hold the head upright (≈3 months), the **cervical lordosis** forms under the action of the posterior neck muscles. Later, when the child begins to sit (≈6 months), the **thoracic kyphosis** appears, and when the child begins to stand and walk (≈1 year), the **lumbar lordosis**; the sacral kyphosis forms during childhood. The curvatures become fixed by 7 years (cervical and thoracic) and at 12–14 years (lumbar).

topics.title: Joints of the bones of the shoulder girdle and free upper limb. Joints of the bones of the pelvic girdle and free lower limb: formation, structure, axes of movement. Appearance of joints on radiographs, CT and MRI

goals.text: To acquaint the student with the structure of the joints of the upper and lower limbs, their reinforcing ligaments, axes and types of movement, age-related features, and their appearance on radiographs, arthrography, CT and MRI; to explain the anatomical basis of typical dislocations and ligament injuries.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the structure of the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints;
the shoulder and elbow joints, the joints between the forearm bones, the radiocarpal (wrist) joint and the joints of the hand;
the sacroiliac joint, the pubic symphysis and the intrinsic ligaments of the pelvis;
the hip, knee and ankle joints, the menisci and the cruciate ligaments;
the joints of the foot (subtalar, talocalcaneonavicular, Chopart's and Lisfranc's joints);
the shape, axes and movements of each joint;
the age-related features of the joints and their appearance in imaging studies.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: show the bones and articular surfaces forming a joint on the skeleton and on specimens;
classify a joint and demonstrate its axes and movements on a living person;
name the main ligaments in Latin and explain their functions;
identify the joint space and bony structures on radiographs of the shoulder, elbow and knee joints.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Dislocation of the shoulder joint is the most common dislocation (≈50% of all dislocations). The weakest part of the capsule is its **anteroinferior** part, which is not covered by muscles, so the head usually dislocates **forward and downward** (below the coracoid process). The rounded contour of the shoulder is lost (a hollow below the acromion), and the arm is fixed in slight abduction. The **axillary nerve**, which passes below the head, may be injured — so sensation over the lateral surface of the shoulder is checked before and after reduction.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Subluxation of the radial head** ("nursemaid's elbow") occurs in children aged 1–4 years when the child's arm is pulled sharply (catching a falling child, "swinging" the child): in children the **anular ligament** is wide, while the head is small and hardly wider than the neck, so the head partly slips out of the ligament. The child does not move the arm, and the forearm hangs in pronation. It is easily reduced by flexing the elbow while supinating.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The most important **saddle** joint of the hand is the joint between the trapezium and the 1st metacarpal. Thanks to it, the thumb can be **opposed** to the other fingers (opposition) — the basis of the grasping function of the human hand. Osteoarthritis of this joint (rhizarthrosis) sharply impairs grasping in elderly people.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: At the end of pregnancy, under the action of hormones (relaxin), the ligaments of the sacroiliac joints and symphysis soften and the cleft in the symphysis widens — the pelvis can widen slightly during delivery. With excessive laxity, **symphysitis** develops (pain in the symphysis region, a "waddling gait"). In the newborn the **pubic symphysis** has the form of a synchondrosis; its cavity appears at 1–2 years and is clearly defined at 5–7 years.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In the newborn the **acetabulum is shallow and oval**, most of the femoral head lies outside the socket, the capsule is thin and tight, and the ligaments are weak. That is why **developmental dysplasia and congenital dislocation of the hip** occur at this age (more often in girls and in those born in breech presentation). Signs: asymmetry of the thigh skin folds, shortening of the leg, limited abduction of the thigh, the "clunk" (Ortolani) sign. Ultrasound screening is performed in newborns; on radiographs a break in Shenton's line indicates dislocation.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Three structures** may be injured together in a knee injury — the **"unhappy triad"**: the anterior cruciate ligament, the medial collateral (tibial collateral) ligament and the **medial meniscus** (because the medial meniscus is attached to the medial collateral ligament). This injury occurs when a blow strikes the knee from the lateral side while it is flexed and the leg is rotated outward (soccer, skiing).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: When the **anterior cruciate ligament** is torn, the leg can be pulled forward — the **"anterior drawer" sign** (with a torn posterior ligament — the "posterior drawer"). A **meniscal tear** presents with pain along the joint line and "locking" of the joint (the torn fragment is caught in the joint). When fluid or blood accumulates in the joint, the patella "floats" (ballottement), and the **suprapatellar bursa** swells and bulges above the patella; joint aspiration is performed precisely in the region of this bursa. The best method for visualizing the menisci and ligaments is **MRI**; they are treated arthroscopically.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: When the foot turns inward (a fall, walking on uneven ground), the **lateral ligaments** are injured most often, especially the anterior talofibular ligament ("ankle sprain"). With a stronger injury the malleoli fracture. Congenital **clubfoot** (*pes equinovarus*) is a position of the foot that is plantarflexed, turned inward (supinated) and adducted; it is treated from the first weeks of life with serial casting (the Ponseti method).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: On radiographs of children's joints most of the bone ends are **cartilaginous** and invisible, so the joint space appears **much wider** than in adults, and the epiphyses look like small "islands." To avoid misjudging this as a dislocation or joint effusion, one must know the age-specific norms and compare with the healthy side.

blocks.text: The shoulder girdle is attached to the axial skeleton by only one joint — the **sternoclavicular joint**. The **sternoclavicular joint** (*articulatio sternoclavicularis*) is formed between the sternal end of the clavicle and the clavicular notch of the sternum; it is saddle-shaped, but because of the **articular disc** inside it, it moves (to a limited extent) around three axes like a ball-and-socket joint: elevation and depression of the clavicle, forward and backward movement, and circumduction. It is reinforced by the **anterior and posterior sternoclavicular**, **interclavicular** and **costoclavicular** ligaments.

blocks.label: Figure 10.1
blocks.caption: Sternoclavicular joint (right side opened): *Discus articularis* — articular disc; *Lig. interclaviculare* — interclavicular ligament; *Lig. sternoclaviculare anterius* — anterior sternoclavicular ligament; *Lig. costoclaviculare* — costoclavicular ligament; *Clavicula* — clavicle; *Costa I* — 1st rib; *Manubrium sterni* — manubrium of the sternum. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: The **acromioclavicular joint** (*articulatio acromioclavicularis*) is a plane joint between the acromial end of the clavicle and the acromion. It is reinforced by the **acromioclavicular ligament** and the very strong **coracoclavicular ligament** (*lig. coracoclaviculare*: conoid and trapezoid parts). Intrinsic ligaments of the scapula: the **coracoacromial ligament** (forms a "vault" over the shoulder joint) and the **superior transverse scapular ligament** over the scapular notch.
**Age-related feature.** In the newborn the sternoclavicular joint is ball-shaped, and the articular disc is twice as large as the articular surfaces of the clavicle and sternum.

The **shoulder joint** (*articulatio humeri*) is formed by the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula. The surface of the head is 3–4 times larger than that of the cavity; this mismatch is partly made up by the fibrocartilaginous **glenoid labrum** (*labrum glenoidale*) at the rim of the cavity. The joint capsule is wide, loose and thin; it attaches on the scapula along the labrum and on the humerus along the **anatomical neck**, and below (with the arm lowered) it forms a fold — the **axillary recess**. The tendon of the long head of the biceps passes through the capsular cavity; the synovial membrane forms the **intertubercular synovial sheath** around the tendon and communicates with the bursa under the subscapularis tendon.

The capsule is reinforced by the **coracohumeral ligament** (*lig. coracohumerale*) and three **glenohumeral ligaments** in the capsular wall (*ligg. glenohumeralia*); but the joint is held mainly by the surrounding muscles — the tendons of the subscapularis, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor (the **rotator cuff**). From above, the joint is protected by the **coracoacromial arch** (the "vault" of the shoulder joint), consisting of the acromion, the coracoid process and the coracoacromial ligament; it limits raising the arm above shoulder level — raising it higher is done by movement of the scapula.

The shoulder joint is **ball-and-socket, multiaxial** — the most mobile joint in the body: flexion and extension around the frontal axis, abduction and adduction around the sagittal axis, medial and lateral rotation around the vertical axis, and circumduction.

blocks.label: Figure 10.2
blocks.caption: Frontal section of the shoulder joint: *Capsula articularis* — joint capsule (*membrana fibrosa* — fibrous membrane, *membrana synovialis* — synovial membrane); *Cavum articulare* — joint cavity; *Tendo m. bicipitis brachii (caput longum)* — tendon of the long head of the biceps; *Acromion* — acromion; *Scapula* — scapula; *Humerus* — humerus. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.label: Figure 10.3
blocks.caption: Shoulder joint opened (humerus removed), lateral view: the glenoid cavity of the scapula (*cavitas glenoidalis*), the glenoid labrum (*labrum glenoidale*), the glenohumeral ligaments (*ligg. glenohumeralia*), the coracoacromial ligament (*lig. coracoacromiale*) and the muscle tendons around the joint. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: Dislocation of the shoulder joint is the most common dislocation (≈50% of all dislocations). The weakest part of the capsule is its **anteroinferior** part, which is not covered by muscles, so the head usually dislocates **forward and downward** (below the coracoid process). The rounded contour of the shoulder is lost (a hollow below the acromion), and the arm is fixed in slight abduction. The **axillary nerve**, which passes below the head, may be injured — so sensation over the lateral surface of the shoulder is checked before and after reduction.

blocks.text: **Radiographic anatomy.** On an AP radiograph the glenoid cavity of the scapula appears as an oval with two convex lines, with the head of the humerus partly superimposed on it; above the head the acromion and acromioclavicular joint are seen, and medially the coracoid process. The joint space is a lucent band between the inner rim of the cavity and the head, on average **4 mm** wide.

blocks.label: Figure 10.4
blocks.caption: Radiograph of the right shoulder joint (arm abducted): 1 — acromion; 2 — coracoid process; 3 — clavicle; 4 — 1st rib; 5 — spine of the scapula; 6 — medial border of the scapula; 7 — scapula; 8 — lateral border of the scapula; 9 — glenoid cavity of the scapula; 10 — head of the humerus; 11 — humerus; 12 — greater tubercle. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** In the newborn the articular surfaces are cartilaginous, the articular surface of the scapula is flat and oval, the labrum is thin and low, the capsule is tight (forming folds below), and the ligaments are poorly developed. Formation of the joint and the increase in its range of motion accelerate when the child begins to use the arm actively.

sections.title: 3. The elbow joint and the joints of the forearm bones

blocks.text: The **elbow joint** (*articulatio cubiti*) is a **compound** joint: there are three joints within one capsule. 1) The **humeroulnar joint** (*articulatio humeroulnaris*) — between the trochlea of the humerus and the trochlear notch of the ulna; **hinge (helical)**, uniaxial. 2) The **humeroradial joint** (*articulatio humeroradialis*) — between the capitulum and the fovea on the head of the radius; ball-shaped, but movement occurs only around the frontal and vertical axes. 3) The **proximal radioulnar joint** (*articulatio radioulnaris proximalis*) — between the articular circumference of the radial head and the radial notch of the ulna; **pivot**.

The capsule is thin in front and behind and is reinforced at the sides by the **ulnar collateral ligament** (*lig. collaterale ulnare*) and the **radial collateral ligament** (*lig. collaterale radiale*); the epicondyles remain outside the capsule. The head of the radius is encircled by the **anular ligament** (*lig. anulare radii*), which attaches to the edges of the radial notch of the ulna. At the elbow joint **flexion and extension** occur around the frontal axis, and at the radioulnar joints **pronation and supination** around the vertical axis.

blocks.label: Figure 10.5
blocks.caption: Elbow joint, anterior view (capsule opened): *Trochlea humeri* — trochlea of the humerus; *Capitulum humeri* — capitulum; *Articulatio humeroulnaris, humeroradialis, radioulnaris* — humeroulnar, humeroradial and radioulnar joints; *Processus coronoideus* — coronoid process; *Circumferentia articularis* — articular circumference; *Lig. collaterale ulnare, radiale* — ulnar and radial collateral ligaments; *Lig. anulare radii* — anular ligament; *Capsula articularis* — joint capsule. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: The forearm bones are joined along their entire length by the **interosseous membrane of the forearm** (*membrana interossea antebrachii*, a syndesmosis), and at their distal ends by the **distal radioulnar joint** (pivot); in the latter a triangular **articular disc** lies below the head of the ulna. The proximal and distal radioulnar joints work as a **combined** joint: in pronation the radius rotates around the ulna and crosses it, and in supination the two lie parallel.

parts.text: **Subluxation of the radial head** ("nursemaid's elbow") occurs in children aged 1–4 years when the child's arm is pulled sharply (catching a falling child, "swinging" the child): in children the **anular ligament** is wide, while the head is small and hardly wider than the neck, so the head partly slips out of the ligament. The child does not move the arm, and the forearm hangs in pronation. It is easily reduced by flexing the elbow while supinating.

blocks.text: **Radiographic anatomy.** On an AP radiograph the spaces of the humeroulnar and humeroradial joints appear as a sharply outlined wavy band ≈3 mm wide; the olecranon is superimposed on the shadow of the medial edge of the humerus. On a lateral radiograph the trochlea, capitulum, olecranon and coronoid process are seen. **In children** 6 ossification centers appear one after another in the elbow region (capitulum ≈1 year, radial head ≈5, medial epicondyle ≈7, trochlea ≈10, olecranon ≈10, lateral epicondyle ≈11 years) — they are compared with the healthy side so as not to confuse them with fracture fragments.

**Age-related features.** In the newborn the ends of the bones forming the elbow joint are cartilaginous; the capsule encloses the joint leaving the epicondyles outside, and the ligaments are poorly developed.

sections.title: 4. The radiocarpal (wrist) joint and the joints of the hand

blocks.text: The **radiocarpal (wrist) joint** (*articulatio radiocarpalis*) is formed between the carpal articular surface of the radius and the articular disc (proximally) and the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum of the proximal row (distally); the ulna does not take part directly. It is **ellipsoid** and biaxial: flexion and extension around the frontal axis, radial and ulnar abduction (deviation) around the sagittal axis, and circumduction. It is reinforced by the **radial and ulnar collateral ligaments** and the **palmar and dorsal radiocarpal ligaments**.

Other joints of the hand: the **midcarpal joint** (*articulatio mediocarpalis*) — between the proximal and distal rows, with an S-shaped joint space, moving together with the radiocarpal joint; the **intercarpal joints**; the **carpometacarpal joints** — plane and of little mobility for fingers II–V, **saddle-shaped for the thumb** (opposition of the thumb); the **metacarpophalangeal joints** — ball-shaped (but in practice biaxial: flexion-extension, abduction-adduction); the **interphalangeal joints** — hinge, uniaxial (flexion-extension), reinforced by collateral ligaments.

blocks.label: Figure 10.6
blocks.caption: Frontal section of the joints of the hand (joint cavities colored): *Articulatio radioulnaris distalis* — distal radioulnar joint; *Discus articularis* — articular disc; *Articulatio radiocarpalis* — radiocarpal joint; *Articulatio mediocarpalis* — midcarpal joint; *Articulationes intercarpales* — intercarpal joints; *Articulationes carpometacarpales* — carpometacarpal joints; *Articulatio carpometacarpea pollicis* — carpometacarpal joint of the thumb; *Lig. collaterale carpi radiale, ulnare* — collateral ligaments of the wrist; *Ligg. intercarpalia interossea* — interosseous ligaments; *Os scaphoideum, lunatum, triquetrum, trapezium, trapezoideum, capitatum, hamatum* — carpal bones. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: **Radiographic anatomy.** The space of the radiocarpal joint appears as an arched lucent band between the radius and the proximal row; the space of the midcarpal joint between the two rows is S-shaped, 1.5–2 mm wide; the spaces of carpometacarpal joints II–V are ≈1.5 mm and irregular. **Age-related:** in the newborn the radiocarpal joint is formed between the radius, scaphoid and lunate; because the ulna is shorter, its head does not reach the triquetrum. The capsule is tight on the palmar side — extension of the hand is somewhat limited.

parts.text: The most important **saddle** joint of the hand is the joint between the trapezium and the 1st metacarpal. Thanks to it, the thumb can be **opposed** to the other fingers (opposition) — the basis of the grasping function of the human hand. Osteoarthritis of this joint (rhizarthrosis) sharply impairs grasping in elderly people.

blocks.text: The **sacroiliac joint** (*articulatio sacroiliaca*) is formed between the auricular surfaces of the sacrum and ilium; it is **plane**, with very little movement (amphiarthrosis). The capsule is thick and tight; it is reinforced by the **anterior**, **posterior** and very strong **interosseous sacroiliac ligaments** (between the tuberosities). With age the joint often partly ossifies. The **pubic symphysis** (*symphysis pubica*) is formed by the **interpubic disc** between the symphyseal surfaces of the two pubic bones; the disc contains a slit-like cavity. It is reinforced above by the **superior pubic ligament** and below by the **arcuate pubic ligament**.

Intrinsic ligaments of the pelvis: the **sacrotuberous ligament** (*lig. sacrotuberale*) and the **sacrospinous ligament** (*lig. sacrospinale*) — they convert the sciatic notches into the **greater** and **lesser sciatic foramina** (*foramen ischiadicum majus et minus*); through the greater sciatic foramen pass the piriformis muscle, the sciatic nerve and the gluteal vessels, and through the lesser the obturator internus muscle and the pudendal vessels and nerve. The **obturator membrane** (*membrana obturatoria*) closes the obturator foramen, leaving only the obturator canal above. The **iliolumbar ligament** connects the 5th lumbar vertebra to the iliac crest.

blocks.label: Figure 10.7
blocks.caption: Joints and ligaments of the pelvis, anterior view: *Lig. iliolumbale* — iliolumbar ligament; *Ligg. sacroiliaca anteriora* — anterior sacroiliac ligaments; *Lig. sacrospinale, sacrotuberale* — sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments; *Symphysis pubica, lig. pubicum superius, lig. arcuatum pubis* — pubic symphysis and its ligaments; *Membrana obturatoria, canalis obturatorius* — obturator membrane and canal; *Lig. inguinale* — inguinal ligament. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

parts.text: At the end of pregnancy, under the action of hormones (relaxin), the ligaments of the sacroiliac joints and symphysis soften and the cleft in the symphysis widens — the pelvis can widen slightly during delivery. With excessive laxity, **symphysitis** develops (pain in the symphysis region, a "waddling gait"). In the newborn the **pubic symphysis** has the form of a synchondrosis; its cavity appears at 1–2 years and is clearly defined at 5–7 years.

blocks.text: The **hip joint** (*articulatio coxae*) is formed between the head of the femur and the acetabulum of the hip bone (its **lunate surface**). The fibrocartilaginous **acetabular labrum** (*labrum acetabuli*) is attached to the rim of the acetabulum; it deepens the socket and embraces more than half of the head; the **transverse acetabular ligament** bridges the acetabular notch. That is why the joint is **cotyloid** (*articulatio cotylica*) — a variety of ball-and-socket joint, multiaxial, but with a smaller range of motion than the shoulder joint and much greater stability.

The capsule is very strong; on the hip bone it attaches to the rim of the acetabulum, and on the femur in front to the **intertrochanteric line** and behind ≈1.5 cm medial to the intertrochanteric crest — so most of the femoral neck lies **inside** the capsule. The capsule is reinforced by three capsular ligaments: the strongest ligament in the body, the **iliofemoral ligament** (*lig. iliofemorale*, Bertin's ligament; withstands loads up to 300 kg, limits hyperextension of the femur and keeps the body from falling backward when standing), and the **pubofemoral** (*lig. pubofemorale*) and **ischiofemoral ligaments** (*lig. ischiofemorale*). Inside the capsule is the **ligament of the head of the femur** (*lig. capitis femoris*) — running from the fovea of the head to the acetabular fossa; it carries an artery that nourishes the head (especially important in children). Circular fibers in the layers of the capsule form the **zona orbicularis** around the neck.

blocks.label: Figure 10.8
blocks.caption: Hip joint, anterior view: *Lig. iliofemorale* — iliofemoral ligament; *Lig. pubofemorale* — pubofemoral ligament; *Capsula articularis* — joint capsule; *Trochanter major, minor* — greater and lesser trochanters; *Spina iliaca anterior inferior* — anterior inferior iliac spine. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.label: Figure 10.9
blocks.caption: Hip joint opened (femoral head removed from the acetabulum): *Facies lunata* — lunate surface; *Labrum acetabuli* — acetabular labrum; *Fossa acetabuli* — acetabular fossa; *Lig. capitis femoris* — ligament of the head of the femur; *Lig. transversum acetabuli* — transverse acetabular ligament; *Caput ossis femoris* — head of the femur; *Membrana obturatoria* — obturator membrane; *Capsula articularis (cut)* — cut joint capsule. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: Movements: flexion around the frontal axis (≈120° with the knee flexed) and extension (limited by the iliofemoral ligament, ≈15°), abduction and adduction around the sagittal axis, medial and lateral rotation around the vertical axis, and circumduction. **Radiographic anatomy:** on an AP radiograph the acetabulum appears as a socket ≈3×5 cm in size; between the head and the socket there is an arched lucent joint space; in the inferomedial part of the acetabulum is the "teardrop" shadow; Shenton's line (a continuous arc along the upper margin of the obturator foramen and the lower margin of the femoral neck) is normally unbroken.

parts.text: In the newborn the **acetabulum is shallow and oval**, most of the femoral head lies outside the socket, the capsule is thin and tight, and the ligaments are weak. That is why **developmental dysplasia and congenital dislocation of the hip** occur at this age (more often in girls and in those born in breech presentation). Signs: asymmetry of the thigh skin folds, shortening of the leg, limited abduction of the thigh, the "clunk" (Ortolani) sign. Ultrasound screening is performed in newborns; on radiographs a break in Shenton's line indicates dislocation.

blocks.text: The **knee joint** (*articulatio genus*) is the largest and most complex joint in the human body. It is formed by the femoral condyles, the superior articular surfaces of the tibia and the posterior surface of the patella (the fibula does not take part). It is a **compound** (three bones), **complex** (with menisci) joint, **bicondylar** in shape. The main movement is **flexion and extension** around the frontal axis; in the flexed position slight **rotation** around the vertical axis is also possible.

The **menisci** are crescent-shaped fibrocartilaginous plates between the incongruent surfaces of the femur and tibia; they are triangular in section, with a thick outer edge attached to the capsule and a thin inner edge. The **medial meniscus** (*meniscus medialis*) is **C**-shaped and attached to the medial collateral ligament, so it is less mobile and **tears more often**; the **lateral meniscus** is **O**-shaped and more mobile. Anteriorly the menisci are joined by the **transverse ligament of the knee**. The menisci distribute load, absorb shock and stabilize the joint.

The **cruciate ligaments** (*ligg. cruciata genus*) lie inside the joint but outside the synovial membrane: the **anterior cruciate ligament** runs from the inner surface of the lateral femoral condyle to the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia — it limits **forward** displacement of the tibia; the **posterior cruciate ligament** runs from the inner surface of the medial condyle to the posterior intercondylar area — it limits **backward** displacement of the tibia. Extracapsular ligaments: the **tibial collateral ligament** (medial; blended with the capsule and the medial meniscus), the **fibular collateral ligament** (lateral; separate from the capsule), in front — the **patellar ligament** (*lig. patellae*), a continuation of the quadriceps tendon, and behind — the **oblique** and **arcuate popliteal ligaments**.

blocks.label: Figure 10.10
blocks.caption: Right knee joint, anterior view (capsule removed, patella pulled down, joint flexed): *Facies patellaris* — patellar surface; *Lig. cruciatum anterius, posterius* — anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments; *Meniscus medialis, lateralis* — medial and lateral menisci; *Lig. transversum genus* — transverse ligament of the knee; *Lig. collaterale tibiale, fibulare* — tibial and fibular collateral ligaments; *Lig. patellae* — patellar ligament; *Facies articularis patellae* — articular surface of the patella; *Articulatio tibiofibularis* — tibiofibular joint; *Caput fibulae* — head of the fibula. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.label: Figure 10.11
blocks.caption: Right knee joint, superior view of the tibia (cruciate ligaments cut): *Meniscus medialis* — medial meniscus (C-shaped); *Meniscus lateralis* — lateral meniscus (O-shaped); *Lig. transversum genus* — transverse ligament; *Lig. cruciatum anterius, posterius* — cruciate ligaments; *Lig. meniscofemorale posterius* — posterior meniscofemoral ligament; *Lig. patellae* — patellar ligament; *Tuberositas tibiae* — tibial tuberosity. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: In the knee joint the synovial membrane forms many folds (the fat-containing **alar folds**) and **bursae**; the largest is the **suprapatellar bursa** (*bursa suprapatellaris*), which communicates with the joint cavity and extends 5–6 cm above the patella. There are many other synovial bursae around the joint (prepatellar, infrapatellar and others).

parts.text: **Three structures** may be injured together in a knee injury — the **"unhappy triad"**: the anterior cruciate ligament, the medial collateral (tibial collateral) ligament and the **medial meniscus** (because the medial meniscus is attached to the medial collateral ligament). This injury occurs when a blow strikes the knee from the lateral side while it is flexed and the leg is rotated outward (soccer, skiing).

When the **anterior cruciate ligament** is torn, the leg can be pulled forward — the **"anterior drawer" sign** (with a torn posterior ligament — the "posterior drawer"). A **meniscal tear** presents with pain along the joint line and "locking" of the joint (the torn fragment is caught in the joint). When fluid or blood accumulates in the joint, the patella "floats" (ballottement), and the **suprapatellar bursa** swells and bulges above the patella; joint aspiration is performed precisely in the region of this bursa. The best method for visualizing the menisci and ligaments is **MRI**; they are treated arthroscopically.

blocks.text: **Radiographic anatomy.** On an AP radiograph the joint space between the femoral and tibial condyles appears as a clear, slightly curved lucent band **6–8 mm** wide — this corresponds to the thickness of the cartilages and menisci between the femur and tibia (the menisci are not visible on radiographs). The patella is superimposed on the shadow of the femur. On a lateral radiograph the patella, the oval shadow of the femoral condyles and the intercondylar eminence are seen.

blocks.label: Figure 10.12
blocks.caption: Radiograph of the right knee joint (AP projection): 1 — femur; 2 — intercondylar fossa; 3 — medial condyle of the tibia; 4 — lateral condyle; 5 — head of the fibula; 6 — fibula; 7 — tibia; 8 — tibial tuberosity; 9 — lateral condyle of the femur; 10 — medial condyle; 11 — patella. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: **Age-related features.** In the newborn the articular surfaces are cartilaginous, and there are ossification centers in the distal epiphysis of the femur and the proximal epiphysis of the tibia (a sign of maturity). The patella is cartilaginous; the menisci are relatively thick and rich in blood vessels (in adults only their outer edges are supplied with blood — so a tear of the inner part does not heal). Development of the joint continues **until 18 years**.

sections.title: 8. Joints of the leg bones and joints of the foot

blocks.text: The leg bones are joined proximally by the **tibiofibular joint** (*articulatio tibiofibularis* — plane, of little mobility), along their entire length by the **interosseous membrane of the leg**, and distally by the **tibiofibular syndesmosis** (*syndesmosis tibiofibularis*); the syndesmosis firmly holds the "mortise" of the ankle joint.

The **ankle (talocrural) joint** (*articulatio talocruralis*) is formed between the inferior articular surface and medial malleolus of the tibia and the lateral malleolus of the fibula (together the **"mortise"**) and the **trochlea** of the talus. It is a **hinge** joint, uniaxial: around the frontal axis — **flexion** (toward the sole, plantar flexion) and **extension** (raising the foot, dorsiflexion). The trochlea of the talus is wider in front — when the foot is plantarflexed it sits more loosely in the mortise, so in this position slight sideways movement and **sprain injuries** occur more often.

Ligaments: on the medial side the strong, four-part **medial (deltoid) ligament** (*lig. mediale, deltoideum*); on the lateral side three separate ligaments — the **anterior and posterior talofibular** and the **calcaneofibular ligaments**. The lateral ligaments are weaker, so when the foot turns inward (supination injury) the **anterior talofibular ligament** is most often stretched or torn.

blocks.label: Figure 10.13
blocks.caption: Right ankle joint, posterior view: *Tibia, fibula* — tibia and fibula; *Lig. tibiofibulare posterius* — posterior tibiofibular ligament; *Lig. talofibulare posterius* — posterior talofibular ligament; *Lig. calcaneofibulare* — calcaneofibular ligament; *Lig. mediale (deltoideum): pars tibiotalaris posterior, pars tibiocalcanea* — parts of the medial (deltoid) ligament; *Lig. talocalcaneum mediale, posterius* — talocalcaneal ligaments; *Articulatio subtalaris* — subtalar joint; *Sustentaculum tali* — sustentaculum tali; *Tuber calcanei* — calcaneal tuberosity. Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

Source: R.D. Sinelnikov. Atlas of Human Anatomy, vol. I (Uzbek edition).

blocks.text: The arches of the foot are held **passively** by the long plantar ligament (*lig. plantare longum*), the **plantar calcaneonavicular ligament** (*lig. calcaneonaviculare plantare* — the "spring" ligament, which supports the head of the talus) and the **plantar aponeurosis**, and **actively** by the muscles of the leg and foot.

**Radiographic anatomy.** On an AP radiograph the space of the ankle joint has the shape of an **inverted letter "U"**; the lateral malleolus is larger and lower than the medial one. On a lateral radiograph the talus forms three joints: its trochlea with the leg, its inferior surface with the calcaneus and its head with the navicular; the space of the posterior talocalcaneal joint is arched or S-shaped, 2–3 mm wide. **Age-related:** in the newborn the bones forming the ankle joint are mainly cartilaginous; because the lateral malleolus lies more posteriorly, the foot is in slight **supination** — in the first year the child walks on the outer edge of the foot. The arch of the foot appears in the first two years of life and is fully formed by 14–16 years.

parts.text: When the foot turns inward (a fall, walking on uneven ground), the **lateral ligaments** are injured most often, especially the anterior talofibular ligament ("ankle sprain"). With a stronger injury the malleoli fracture. Congenital **clubfoot** (*pes equinovarus*) is a position of the foot that is plantarflexed, turned inward (supinated) and adducted; it is treated from the first weeks of life with serial casting (the Ponseti method).

parts.text: On radiographs of children's joints most of the bone ends are **cartilaginous** and invisible, so the joint space appears **much wider** than in adults, and the epiphyses look like small "islands." To avoid misjudging this as a dislocation or joint effusion, one must know the age-specific norms and compare with the healthy side.

skills.title: Practical skill: studying joints on the skeleton and on specimens

items: For each joint, answer according to this algorithm: 1) which bones and which articular surfaces form it; 2) simple/compound/complex/combined; 3) shape; 4) axes and movements; 5) reinforcing ligaments; 6) age-related features.
At the shoulder joint show the glenoid labrum, the line of capsular attachment, the tendon in the intertubercular groove and the coracoacromial arch.
At the elbow joint show the three joints, the collateral ligaments and the anular ligament; demonstrate pronation and supination on the skeleton.
At the hip joint show the acetabular labrum, the ligament of the head and the iliofemoral ligament; at the knee joint show the menisci and the cruciate and collateral ligaments.
On the foot show the lines of Chopart's and Lisfranc's joints and their "key" ligaments.

skills.title: Practical skill: examining joint movements in a living person

items: Have the subject perform active and passive movements at the shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee and ankle joints; state around which axis each movement takes place.
Test pronation and supination with the elbow flexed at 90° and the arm held against the trunk (to exclude rotation at the shoulder joint).
Demonstrate the "anterior drawer" test at the knee: the patient lies supine, the knee is flexed to 90°, and the proximal part of the leg is pulled forward — normally there is almost no displacement.
Palpate the patella and show the region of the suprapatellar bursa.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: While catching the ball with his arm raised high, a basketball player collided with an opponent; there is sharp pain in the shoulder, the shoulder contour has become "angular" (a hollow below the acromion), he cannot move the arm, and sensation over the lateral surface of the shoulder is reduced.
cases.ask: What is the injury? Why this particular joint and this direction? Which nerve is injured?
cases.answer: This is an **anteroinferior dislocation of the shoulder joint**. The shoulder joint is ball-and-socket, with a small, shallow glenoid cavity (3–4 times smaller than the head) and a wide, loose capsule — the most mobile but the least stable joint. The **anteroinferior part** of the capsule is not covered by muscle tendons and is the weakest spot; with the arm abducted and laterally rotated, a blow drives the head out in this direction. Numbness over the lateral surface of the shoulder indicates injury to the **axillary nerve** (which passes below the head, around the surgical neck).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: During a game, a soccer player received a blow to the lateral side of the knee while the knee was flexed and the leg rotated outward. The knee is swollen and "gives way" when walking; on examination the "anterior drawer" sign is positive, and there is pain on the medial side of the joint.
cases.ask: Which structures are injured? What is this injury called, and how is the diagnosis confirmed?
cases.answer: This is the **"unhappy triad"**: the **anterior cruciate ligament** (anterior drawer sign — the tibia shifts forward), the **tibial (medial) collateral ligament** and the **medial meniscus** attached to it. With a lateral blow the knee bends inward (valgus) — the medial collateral ligament is stretched and torn, while the rotation leads to tears of the anterior cruciate ligament and the meniscus. The menisci and ligaments are not visible on radiographs — the diagnosis is confirmed by **MRI** or arthroscopy.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A mother sharply pulled her 2-year-old child by the hand so that the child would not fall on the street. The child is crying, holding the arm hanging at the side with the forearm in pronation, and does not use the elbow; there is no swelling.
cases.ask: What has happened? Explain the anatomical basis and how help is given.
cases.answer: This is a **subluxation of the radial head** ("nursemaid's elbow"). In small children the radial head is small and hardly wider than the neck, while the encircling **anular ligament** is wide and loose; when the arm is pulled, the head partly slips out of the ligament and the ligament becomes caught in the joint. Help: **supinate** the forearm while **flexing** the elbow at the same time — a click is felt as the head returns to its place, and the child soon begins to use the arm.

Ball-and-socket, multiaxial; glenoid labrum, wide capsule; usually dislocates forward and downward
Compound: humeroulnar (hinge), humeroradial (ball-shaped), proximal radioulnar (pivot)
Ellipsoid: radius + disc and the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum
Cotyloid; acetabular labrum; iliofemoral ligament (the strongest); artery in the ligament of the head
Compound, complex, bicondylar; menisci (medial C, lateral O), anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments

topics.title: General information on muscles. The superficial and deep muscles of the back of the trunk and their age-related changes

goals.text: To acquaint the student with the structure of skeletal muscle as an organ, the classification of muscles, their accessory apparatus and the principles of their action (levers, synergists and antagonists); to teach the structure, function, innervation and age-related features of the superficial and deep muscles of the back, the fasciae of the back and its regions.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the parts of a skeletal muscle (belly, head, tail, tendon, aponeurosis) and its sheaths;
the classification of muscles by shape, fiber direction, relation to joints and function;
the accessory apparatus of muscles: fasciae, tendon sheaths, synovial bursae, trochleae, sesamoid bones;
the types of levers and the concept of the anatomical and physiological cross-section of a muscle;
the origin, insertion and function of the superficial muscles of the back (trapezius, latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, levator scapulae, serratus posterior muscles);
the structure and function of the deep muscles of the back (splenius, erector spinae, transversospinalis and short muscles);
the thoracolumbar fascia, the lumbar triangle and the triangle of auscultation;
age-related changes of the muscles.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the muscles of the back in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
state the origin, insertion and function of each muscle;
observe the trapezius, latissimus dorsi and erector spinae in a living person and demonstrate their functions;
show the boundaries of the lumbar triangle and the triangle of auscultation.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The **strength** of a muscle depends on its physiological cross-section (pennate muscles are strong), its **range of motion** on the length of its fibers (long parallel-fibered muscles), and its **effective force** on the arms of the lever. At most joints muscles work as speed levers: they lose force but gain speed and range of movement.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Rule of innervation: the **superficial** muscles of the back (those going to the upper limb and ribs) are supplied by the **anterior (ventral)** rami of the spinal nerves (brachial plexus, intercostal nerves) or by the **accessory nerve** (trapezius), whereas the **deep — intrinsic** muscles of the back are supplied by the **posterior (dorsal)** rami of the spinal nerves.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: When the accessory nerve is injured (for example, during an operation in the lateral triangle of the neck), **paralysis of the trapezius** develops: the shoulder droops and raising the arm above the horizontal becomes difficult. When the dorsal scapular nerve is injured, the rhomboid muscles are paralyzed and the medial border of the scapula stands away from the thoracic cage. Because the **latissimus dorsi** is wide and has many blood vessels, it is used in plastic surgery to close tissue defects (musculocutaneous flap) and in operations supporting the heart (cardiomyoplasty).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: One of the most common causes of **low back pain** is strain and spasm of the erector spinae and multifidus muscles (improper lifting, prolonged sitting). Loads should be lifted not by bending over but **with the knees bent and the back straight** — then the load falls mainly on the leg muscles, and the discs and back muscles are not overstrained. Exercises that strengthen the multifidus muscles are used in the treatment of chronic low back pain.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: When studying the back muscles topographically, do not mix up the order of the layers: **trapezius and latissimus → rhomboids and levator scapulae → serratus posterior muscles → splenius → erector spinae → transversospinalis → short segmental and suboccipital muscles**. The three superficial layers are "migrated" muscles (of the upper limb and ribs); the rest are the intrinsic muscles of the back.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In school-age children, uneven development of the back muscles and poor sitting posture lead to **postural disorders** and **scoliosis**. Physical exercises that strengthen the back and abdominal muscles in a balanced way, swimming, a properly chosen desk and chair, and carrying a backpack on both shoulders are the basis of prevention.

blocks.text: **Myology** (Greek *mys* — muscle) is the study of muscles. Skeletal muscles are built of striated muscle tissue and contract voluntarily; together with the bones and their joints they form the **active part of the locomotor apparatus**. A human has more than 400 (according to some authors nearly 600) skeletal muscles; in adults their mass makes up ≈36–45% of body weight in men and ≈28–35% in women; about half of the muscle mass is in the lower limbs, 30% in the upper limbs, and the rest in the trunk and head.

Each muscle consists of a **belly** (*venter*) — the contractile part — and non-contractile **tendons** (*tendines*) of dense connective tissue. The proximal end of a muscle (nearer the trunk) is the **head** (*caput*), and the distal end the **tail** (*cauda*). A muscle usually **arises** from one bone (*origo* — usually the fixed point, *punctum fixum*) and **inserts** on another (*insertio* — the mobile point, *punctum mobile*); depending on the situation these points may swap. Broad flat tendons are called **aponeuroses** (for example, those of the broad abdominal muscles). Some muscles have **tendinous intersections** (*intersectiones tendineae*) dividing the belly into parts (the rectus abdominis).

Each muscle fiber is surrounded by the **endomysium**, each bundle of fibers by the **perimysium**, and the whole muscle by the **epimysium**; blood vessels and nerves enter along these connective tissue layers, which continue into the tendons. Muscles are rich in blood vessels; their contraction "pumps" the blood in the veins toward the heart (the **muscle pump**) — with inactivity (hypokinesia) this pump weakens, and the risk of venous stasis and thrombosis increases. A nerve usually enters a muscle at one place — the **neurovascular hilum**; the nerve contains motor (efferent) and sensory (afferent, from proprioceptors) fibers.

blocks.text: The strength of a muscle depends on its **physiological cross-section** — the area of a section cutting across all its fibers. In fusiform and strap-like muscles the anatomical and physiological cross-sections are the same; in **pennate muscles** the fibers are short and numerous, so the physiological cross-section is large — they are **strong**, but their range of contraction is small. Long parallel-fibered muscles are weaker but contract **over a large range and quickly**.

sections.title: 3. The accessory apparatus of muscles and their action

blocks.text: The work of muscles is supported by the **accessory apparatus**: **fasciae** — connective tissue sheaths surrounding a muscle or group of muscles; they form intermuscular septa that separate muscles, reduce friction during contraction and form sheaths for neurovascular bundles. **Tendon sheaths** — sheaths with fibrous and synovial parts where tendons pass over bone (hand, foot); the synovial sheath has two layers with fluid between them. **Synovial bursae** — flat sacs filled with fluid, located where tendons and muscles rub against bone. **Muscle trochleae** — bony prominences or fibrous rings around which a tendon turns (the trochlea of the superior oblique muscle of the eye). **Sesamoid bones** — bones within a tendon (the patella, the pisiform); they lengthen the lever arm of the muscle's pull.

blocks.text: Muscles performing the same movement are called **synergists**, and those performing opposite movements **antagonists** (for example, at the elbow the biceps, a flexor, and the triceps, an extensor). During movement the antagonists do not relax completely; rather, they make the movement smooth and precise. Muscle work may be **overcoming** (concentric: the muscle shortens and overcomes resistance), **yielding** (eccentric: the muscle lengthens and gradually gives way to resistance — e.g., slowly lowering a load) and **holding (static)** — keeping the body or a part of it in a certain position.

parts.text: The **strength** of a muscle depends on its physiological cross-section (pennate muscles are strong), its **range of motion** on the length of its fibers (long parallel-fibered muscles), and its **effective force** on the arms of the lever. At most joints muscles work as speed levers: they lose force but gain speed and range of movement.

sections.title: 4. Muscles of the back: general information

blocks.text: The back muscles form two layers. The **superficial muscles** are flat, broad muscles; developmentally they are related to the upper limb and the ribs; they arise from the vertebral column and insert on the shoulder girdle, the humerus or the ribs. The **deep (intrinsic) muscles** are the back's own (autochthonous) muscles; they lie on both sides of the vertebral column from the sacrum to the occipital bone, are supplied mainly by the **posterior (dorsal) rami** of the spinal nerves, and hold the vertebral column upright, extend it and rotate it.

parts.text: Rule of innervation: the **superficial** muscles of the back (those going to the upper limb and ribs) are supplied by the **anterior (ventral)** rami of the spinal nerves (brachial plexus, intercostal nerves) or by the **accessory nerve** (trapezius), whereas the **deep — intrinsic** muscles of the back are supplied by the **posterior (dorsal)** rami of the spinal nerves.

blocks.text: The first layer is formed by the **trapezius** and the **latissimus dorsi**, the second by the **rhomboid muscles** and the **levator scapulae**, and the third by the **serratus posterior superior and inferior**.

parts.text: When the accessory nerve is injured (for example, during an operation in the lateral triangle of the neck), **paralysis of the trapezius** develops: the shoulder droops and raising the arm above the horizontal becomes difficult. When the dorsal scapular nerve is injured, the rhomboid muscles are paralyzed and the medial border of the scapula stands away from the thoracic cage. Because the **latissimus dorsi** is wide and has many blood vessels, it is used in plastic surgery to close tissue defects (musculocutaneous flap) and in operations supporting the heart (cardiomyoplasty).

blocks.text: The deep muscles also form layers. The **superficial layer** is formed by the **splenius capitis and splenius cervicis** (*m. splenius capitis et cervicis*): they arise from the nuchal ligament and the spinous processes of the upper thoracic vertebrae and insert on the mastoid process and superior nuchal line (capitis) and on the transverse processes of the upper cervical vertebrae (cervicis); contracting bilaterally they extend the head and neck, unilaterally they turn them to the same side.

The **erector spinae** (*m. erector spinae*) is the strongest muscle of the back; it arises from the sacrum, the iliac crest, the spinous processes of the lumbar vertebrae and the thoracolumbar fascia, and above it divides into three parts: lateral — the **iliocostalis** (*m. iliocostalis*, to the angles of the ribs and the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae), middle — the **longissimus** (*m. longissimus*, to the transverse processes, ribs and mastoid process), medial — the **spinalis** (*m. spinalis*, between the spinous processes). Contracting bilaterally it **extends** the vertebral column and holds the trunk upright; unilaterally it bends it to the side.

blocks.text: Deeper still lie the **transversospinalis muscles** (*m. transversospinalis*): their fibers run obliquely from the transverse processes to the spinous processes of higher vertebrae. From superficial to deep: the **semispinalis** (*m. semispinalis* — spans 5–6 vertebrae; the semispinalis capitis inserts on the occipital bone), the **multifidus muscles** (*mm. multifidi* — span 2–4 vertebrae, best developed in the lumbar region) and the **rotatores** (*mm. rotatores* — 1–2 vertebrae). They extend the vertebral column and rotate it to the opposite side. Deepest of all are the short **interspinales** (*mm. interspinales*) and **intertransversarii** (*mm. intertransversarii*), the **levatores costarum**, and below the occiput the **suboccipital muscles** (*mm. suboccipitales* — rectus capitis posterior major and minor, obliquus capitis superior and inferior; they move the head at the atlanto-occipital and atlanto-axial joints).

parts.text: One of the most common causes of **low back pain** is strain and spasm of the erector spinae and multifidus muscles (improper lifting, prolonged sitting). Loads should be lifted not by bending over but **with the knees bent and the back straight** — then the load falls mainly on the leg muscles, and the discs and back muscles are not overstrained. Exercises that strengthen the multifidus muscles are used in the treatment of chronic low back pain.

sections.title: 7. Fasciae and regions of the back

blocks.text: The **thoracolumbar fascia** (*fascia thoracolumbalis*) surrounds the intrinsic muscles of the back and consists of two layers: the **superficial (posterior) layer** attaches to the spinous processes, the supraspinous ligament and the median sacral crest and is thick in the lumbar region (fused with the aponeurosis of the latissimus dorsi); the **deep (anterior) layer** stretches between the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae, the 12th rib and the iliac crest, separating the erector spinae from the quadratus lumborum. The two layers fuse at the lateral edge of the erector spinae and give origin to the transversus abdominis.

There are two triangles of practical importance on the back. The **lumbar triangle** (Petit's triangle, *trigonum lumbale inferius*) is bounded below by the iliac crest, medially by the latissimus dorsi and laterally by the external oblique muscle of the abdomen; its floor is formed by the internal oblique — this is a weak spot in the abdominal wall (**lumbar hernias** may occur). The **triangle of auscultation** lies between the trapezius, the latissimus dorsi and the medial border of the scapula (rhomboid major); it widens when the arms are crossed in front and the scapulae are drawn apart, and here breath sounds are heard well because the muscle layer is thin.

parts.text: When studying the back muscles topographically, do not mix up the order of the layers: **trapezius and latissimus → rhomboids and levator scapulae → serratus posterior muscles → splenius → erector spinae → transversospinalis → short segmental and suboccipital muscles**. The three superficial layers are "migrated" muscles (of the upper limb and ribs); the rest are the intrinsic muscles of the back.

blocks.text: In the newborn all skeletal muscles are formed but relatively poorly developed, making up **20–22%** of body weight; at 1–2 years this falls to ≈16–17%, and once the child begins to move actively it rises to ≈22% at 6 years and ≈27% at 8 years, reaching ≈36% in men and ≈33% in women in adulthood. The newborn's muscle fibers are thin (4–22 µm) with distinct cross-striation; fiber thickness increases to ≈90 µm by 18–20 years. In the newborn's muscles the vascular and nerve apparatus is well developed and connective tissue is scanty; after birth the tendinous part grows rapidly. The fasciae are thin and loose in the newborn and easily separated from the muscles; from the first month they develop according to muscle function.

The limbs of newborns and young children are cylindrical; as the muscles grow and subcutaneous fat decreases they become fusiform or conical. At **2–4 years** the long muscles of the back and the gluteus maximus grow rapidly (the child walks upright); the muscles holding the trunk upright develop intensively **after 7 years**, especially during adolescence.

**Age-related features of the back muscles.** In the newborn, of the superficial back muscles the trapezius is well developed; the latissimus dorsi is broad and thin, its aponeurosis passing into the muscular part without a clear boundary; the boundary between the muscular and tendinous parts of the rhomboids is not discernible; the serratus posterior muscles are thin, with poorly developed digitations. Of the deep muscles, the splenius capitis is well developed. In the erector spinae the middle part — the longissimus — is well developed, while the spinalis is poorly developed; the other deep muscles are weak, with thin tendons. The back muscles gradually strengthen as the child begins to hold the head up, sit and walk — in parallel with the formation of the curvatures of the vertebral column (see topic 9).

parts.text: In school-age children, uneven development of the back muscles and poor sitting posture lead to **postural disorders** and **scoliosis**. Physical exercises that strengthen the back and abdominal muscles in a balanced way, swimming, a properly chosen desk and chair, and carrying a backpack on both shoulders are the basis of prevention.
