cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After an operation to remove a lymph node in the lateral region of the neck, a patient reports that the shoulder has drooped, that he cannot raise the arm above the head, and that he has difficulty shrugging the shoulder.
cases.ask: Which nerve and which muscle are injured? Explain the function of this muscle.
cases.answer: The **accessory nerve (XI)**, which runs superficially across the lateral triangle of the neck, has been injured, resulting in paralysis of the **trapezius**. The upper part of this muscle elevates the scapula and shoulder, the middle part retracts the scapula toward the spine, and the lower part depresses it; the upper and lower parts together rotate the scapula, turning the glenoid cavity upward — this is what makes it possible to raise the arm above the horizontal. With paralysis these movements are impaired.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A warehouse worker lifted a heavy box from the floor with straight legs, bending at the waist, and felt sudden pain in the lower back. In the lumbar region, rigidly tense muscle ridges are palpable on both sides of the vertebral column, and bending is sharply limited.
cases.ask: Which muscle is strained? What are its parts and function? What is the correct way to lift a load?
cases.answer: This is a strain and reflex spasm of the **erector spinae** (*m. erector spinae*). It consists of three parts: lateral — iliocostalis, middle — longissimus, medial — spinalis; contracting bilaterally it extends the vertebral column and holds the trunk upright. When a load is lifted while bent over, the lever arm in the lumbar region is very long, and a large load falls on the muscle and the discs. The correct method is to lift **with the knees bent**, the back straight and the load held close to the body.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: While listening to the lungs, a physician asked the patient to cross the arms over the chest and lean slightly forward, and placed the stethoscope near the inferior angle of the scapula, between the scapula and the vertebral column.
cases.ask: Over which region was the stethoscope placed? What bounds it, and why is listening easy here?
cases.answer: This is the **triangle of auscultation**: bounded by the lower edge of the trapezius, the upper edge of the latissimus dorsi and the medial border of the scapula (rhomboid major). In this region there are no thick muscles over the chest wall, only a thin layer, so breath sounds are heard well. When the arms are crossed, the scapulae shift laterally and the triangle widens.

topics.title: Muscles of the thorax and the diaphragm. Muscles and fasciae of the abdomen and the inguinal canal

goals.text: To teach the student the structure, function and innervation of the muscles of the thoracic cage and abdominal wall, the parts and openings of the diaphragm, the mechanics of inspiration and expiration, the abdominal fasciae, the linea alba, the rectus sheath and the structure of the inguinal canal; to explain the clinical significance of the weak spots of the abdominal wall (sites of hernias).
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the superficial (going to the upper limb) and intrinsic (autochthonous) muscles of the thorax, their origin, insertion and function;
the parts, crura, openings and muscle-free triangles of the diaphragm;
the main and accessory muscles taking part in inspiration and expiration;
the muscles of the lateral, anterior and posterior walls of the abdomen;
the abdominal fasciae, the linea alba and the structure of the rectus sheath above and below the umbilicus;
the walls, rings and contents of the inguinal canal;
the age-related features of the thoracic and abdominal muscles.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the thoracic and abdominal muscles in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
show the openings of the diaphragm and the structures passing through them;
explain a cross-section of the rectus sheath without a diagram;
show the four walls and two rings of the inguinal canal and distinguish direct and indirect inguinal hernias.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The long thoracic nerve lies superficially on the surface of the serratus anterior in the axillary region and may be injured in breast operations (removal of axillary lymph nodes). The result is a **"winged scapula"** (*scapula alata*): when the patient pushes against a wall, the medial border and inferior angle of the scapula protrude backward, and raising the arm above the horizontal becomes difficult.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Pleural puncture** (thoracentesis) and chest drainage are performed in the intercostal space **along the upper border of the lower rib** — because the intercostal neurovascular bundle lies in the groove on the lower border of the upper rib. Puncture is usually performed in the 7th–8th intercostal space along the midaxillary or scapular line.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Because the phrenic nerve arises from the cervical segments (C~III~–C~V~), in diseases of the organs below the diaphragm (liver, gallbladder, spleen) or when blood accumulates in the abdominal cavity, pain is referred **to the shoulder region** (C~IV~ dermatome) — **referred pain** (for example, to the right shoulder in acute cholecystitis, to the left shoulder when the spleen ruptures — Kehr's sign). In a **hiatal hernia** part of the stomach slides into the thoracic cavity, and heartburn occurs. In newborns a **congenital diaphragmatic hernia** often occurs through the left lumbocostal triangle — the intestines move into the chest and the lung fails to develop.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: During an attack of bronchial asthma or in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, the patient sits **bracing the arms on a table or the knees** (the "orthopnea position"): once the shoulder girdle is fixed, the pectoralis major and minor and the serratus anterior swap their punctum fixum and punctum mobile, raise the ribs and assist inspiration. In forced expiration the contraction of the abdominal muscles is visible.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Umbilical hernia is common in infants and usually closes spontaneously by 3–5 years as the umbilical ring strengthens. Indirect inguinal hernia and hydrocele of the testis, by contrast, are related to failure of the **processus vaginalis** of the peritoneum to close — this is a congenital defect, usually treated surgically.

sections.title: 1. Muscles of the thorax: general information

blocks.text: By origin and function the thoracic muscles are divided into two groups. The **first group** consists of muscles that arise from the thoracic cage and insert on the bones of the shoulder girdle and the humerus: the **pectoralis major**, **pectoralis minor**, **subclavius** and **serratus anterior**. In development they have "migrated" to the chest from the limb bud; they mainly move the upper limb and shoulder girdle, and when the limb is fixed they act as accessory respiratory muscles. The **second group** consists of the intrinsic (autochthonous) muscles of the thoracic cage: the **external and internal intercostals**, the **innermost intercostals**, the **subcostals** and the **transversus thoracis**; they move the ribs and take part in inspiration and expiration. The **diaphragm** lies between the thoracic and abdominal cavities.

parts.text: The long thoracic nerve lies superficially on the surface of the serratus anterior in the axillary region and may be injured in breast operations (removal of axillary lymph nodes). The result is a **"winged scapula"** (*scapula alata*): when the patient pushes against a wall, the medial border and inferior angle of the scapula protrude backward, and raising the arm above the horizontal becomes difficult.

sections.title: 3. Intrinsic muscles of the thoracic cage

blocks.text: The **external intercostal muscles** (*mm. intercostales externi*), 11 on each side, arise from the lower border of the upper rib; their fibers run **downward and forward** (obliquely, in the "hands in pockets" direction) and insert on the upper border of the lower rib. They extend from the tubercle of the rib to the cartilage; between the cartilages the space is covered by the **external intercostal membrane**. Function — raising the ribs for **inspiration**.

The **internal intercostal muscles** (*mm. intercostales interni*) lie deep to the external ones; they arise from the upper border of the lower rib, their fibers run **upward and forward** (perpendicular to the external ones) and insert on the lower border of the upper rib, internal to the costal groove. They extend from the sternum to the angle of the rib; from the angle to the vertebra they are continued by the **internal intercostal membrane**. Function — lowering the ribs for **expiration** (their interchondral part, however, assists inspiration). Their deepest part is distinguished as the **innermost intercostal muscles**; the intercostal **neurovascular bundle** (vein, artery, nerve — from above downward) lies in the costal groove between the internal and innermost muscles.

blocks.label: Figure 12.4
blocks.caption: Intercostal muscles (Figure No. 305): A — general view; B — arrangement of the muscles in the intercostal space. 1 — external intercostal membrane; 2 — external intercostal muscles; 3 — internal intercostal muscles; 4 — 1st rib; 5 — manubrium of the sternum; 6 — body of the sternum; 7 — xiphoid process; 8 — costal cartilage; 9 — innermost intercostal muscles; 10 — supreme intercostal vein; 11 — supreme intercostal artery; 12 — intercostal nerves; 13 — collateral branch; 14 — parietal pleura; 15 — endothoracic fascia; 16 — costal groove. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev et al. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 1.

blocks.text: The **subcostal muscles** (*mm. subcostales*) lie on the posteroinferior inner surface of the thoracic cage near the angles of ribs X–XII and span one or two ribs; the **transversus thoracis** (*m. transversus thoracis*) lies on the posterior surface of the anterior chest wall — it arises from the lower part of the body of the sternum and the xiphoid process and inserts on costal cartilages II–VI. Both lower the ribs and take part in expiration. All the intrinsic muscles are supplied by the **intercostal nerves**.

parts.text: **Pleural puncture** (thoracentesis) and chest drainage are performed in the intercostal space **along the upper border of the lower rib** — because the intercostal neurovascular bundle lies in the groove on the lower border of the upper rib. Puncture is usually performed in the 7th–8th intercostal space along the midaxillary or scapular line.

blocks.text: The **diaphragm** (*diaphragma*) is a flat musculotendinous partition, domed upward, separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities; it is the main respiratory muscle. It arises from the bones surrounding the inferior thoracic aperture and is divided into three parts according to its origin; its fibers run radially and form the **central tendon** (*centrum tendineum*) in the middle.

items: The **lumbar part** (*pars lumbalis*) arises by the right and left **crura** from the bodies of the lumbar vertebrae: the right crus is stronger, from L~I~–L~IV~, and the left crus from L~I~–L~III~. This part also includes the **medial and lateral arcuate ligaments** (stretched over the psoas major and quadratus lumborum) and the **median arcuate ligament** (over the aorta).
The **costal part** (*pars costalis*) arises from the inner surface of the lower six ribs, interdigitating with the slips of the transversus abdominis.
The **sternal part** (*pars sternalis*), the smallest part, arises from the posterior surface of the xiphoid process.

blocks.text: Between the parts of the diaphragm there are weak spots without muscle fibers: the **lumbocostal triangle** (Bochdalek's triangle — between the lumbar and costal parts) and the **sternocostal triangle** (Larrey's triangle — between the sternal and costal parts). They are covered above by the pleura and endothoracic fascia and below by the peritoneum and endoabdominal fascia; **diaphragmatic hernias** may occur through them. The diaphragm is supplied by the **phrenic nerve** (*n. phrenicus*, C~III~–C~V~).

parts.text: Because the phrenic nerve arises from the cervical segments (C~III~–C~V~), in diseases of the organs below the diaphragm (liver, gallbladder, spleen) or when blood accumulates in the abdominal cavity, pain is referred **to the shoulder region** (C~IV~ dermatome) — **referred pain** (for example, to the right shoulder in acute cholecystitis, to the left shoulder when the spleen ruptures — Kehr's sign). In a **hiatal hernia** part of the stomach slides into the thoracic cavity, and heartburn occurs. In newborns a **congenital diaphragmatic hernia** often occurs through the left lumbocostal triangle — the intestines move into the chest and the lung fails to develop.

blocks.text: In quiet **inspiration** the diaphragm contracts, and its dome descends and flattens — the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity increases (in quiet breathing the diaphragm provides ≈2/3 of ventilation); the external intercostal muscles raise the ribs, increasing the anteroposterior and transverse dimensions of the thoracic cage. Quiet **expiration** is mainly **passive** — due to the elastic recoil of the lungs, the elasticity of the costal cartilages and the pressure of the abdominal organs. In deep (forced) breathing the **accessory muscles** join in.

parts.text: During an attack of bronchial asthma or in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, the patient sits **bracing the arms on a table or the knees** (the "orthopnea position"): once the shoulder girdle is fixed, the pectoralis major and minor and the serratus anterior swap their punctum fixum and punctum mobile, raise the ribs and assist inspiration. In forced expiration the contraction of the abdominal muscles is visible.

blocks.text: In the thoracic region the superficial fascia is poorly developed; it encloses the mammary gland and sends septa into it (the suspensory ligaments of the breast). The **pectoral fascia** (*fascia pectoralis*), with its superficial layer, encloses the pectoralis major (attaching above to the clavicle and medially to the sternum, continuing laterally into the deltoid and axillary fasciae); its deep layer — the **clavipectoral fascia** — encloses the pectoralis minor and subclavius. The **proper fascia of the thorax** covers the external intercostal muscles from outside; the **endothoracic fascia** (*fascia endothoracica*) lines the thoracic cage from inside, bordering the parietal pleura.

The abdominal muscles form the walls of the abdominal cavity and, by topography, are divided into muscles of the **lateral wall** (three broad muscles), the **anterior wall** (rectus and pyramidalis) and the **posterior wall** (quadratus lumborum). The three broad muscles of the lateral wall — the **external oblique**, **internal oblique** and **transversus** — have fibers running in three different directions (the external downward and medially, the internal mainly upward and medially, the transversus horizontally); this "three-ply plywood" gives strength to the abdominal wall. Their aponeuroses form the sheath of the rectus abdominis and, in the midline, the **linea alba**.

The rectus abdominis is divided into bellies by **3–4 tendinous intersections** (*intersectiones tendineae*); the intersections fuse with the anterior layer of the sheath — which is why athletes show a "six-pack."

sections.title: 8. Abdominal fasciae, the linea alba and the rectus sheath

blocks.text: The **superficial fascia of the abdomen** lies between the subcutaneous fat and the muscles. Layers of the **proper fascia** enclose each broad muscle; in the region of the superficial inguinal ring the fascia of the external oblique forms the **intercrural fibers** and continues onto the spermatic cord as the **external spermatic fascia**. The **transversalis fascia** (*fascia transversalis*) lines the abdominal wall from inside — it is part of the endoabdominal fascia; internal to it lie the preperitoneal fat and the parietal peritoneum.

The **linea alba** (*linea alba*) is a fibrous band stretched from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis, formed by the crossing and interweaving of the fibers of the aponeuroses of the three broad muscles. Above the umbilicus it is wide (≈2–2.5 cm) and thin; below it is narrow and thick. Because it has few blood vessels, the **midline laparotomy** incision is made along this line in surgery. The **umbilical ring** lies in the middle of the linea alba.
The **rectus sheath** (*vagina m. recti abdominis*) is formed by the aponeuroses of the three broad muscles, and its structure differs above and below the umbilicus:

blocks.text: The **inguinal canal** (*canalis inguinalis*) is a slit **4–5 cm** long lying obliquely (from above and laterally, downward and medially) between the broad abdominal muscles above the medial half of the inguinal ligament. In males the **spermatic cord** passes through it (ductus deferens, testicular artery and veins, nerves), and in females the **round ligament of the uterus**; in both sexes the **ilioinguinal nerve** passes through the canal. In males the canal is wider and shorter.

These fossae are the sites where inguinal hernias emerge.

sections.title: 10. Weak spots of the abdominal wall

blocks.text: Places in the abdominal wall where muscles are absent or thin are sites where **hernias** (*herniae*) occur: the **inguinal canal** (inguinal hernias), the **umbilical ring** (umbilical hernia — especially in infants), the **linea alba** (epigastric hernia — above the umbilicus, because there the linea alba is wide and thin), the **femoral canal** (femoral hernia — topic 14), the **lumbar triangle** (lumbar hernia), the muscle-free triangles of the diaphragm and the esophageal hiatus (diaphragmatic hernias). Increased intra-abdominal pressure (heavy lifting, chronic cough, constipation, pregnancy) causes hernias to appear.

items: In the newborn the pectoralis major is well defined; the tendinous part of the pectoralis minor is poorly developed; the serratus anterior is developed, but its digitations are not well separated.

Because the newborn's breathing is mainly of the **abdominal (diaphragmatic) type**, the intercostal muscles are weak; once thoracic breathing begins they thicken — the transverse dimension of some muscles increases 5–6 times by 12 years.

The newborn's diaphragm is relatively well developed: its mass makes up **5.3%** of the mass of all muscles (1–1.3% in adults); the dome is high, the central tendon small (12–15% of its area), and the sternocostal and lumbocostal triangles relatively large. Until 5 years the ribs lie horizontally, so the diaphragm stands high; at 7 years it resembles that of the adult.

The abdominal muscles and aponeuroses are weak in the newborn, and the abdomen protrudes; they grow rapidly after the child begins to walk. The tendinous intersections of the rectus lie higher in children; the posterior layer of the sheath is poorly developed.

In the newborn the width of the linea alba is 5–8 mm at the xiphoid process and 12–16 mm at the umbilicus; there are thin areas in its upper part and at the umbilicus. The transversalis fascia is thin; the preperitoneal fat appears from 2 years.

In the newborn the inguinal canal is short, wide and almost straight; at 1 year its length is 0.5–2.5 cm, and with age it lengthens and becomes oblique; the superficial ring lies higher and its crura are poorly developed. The structure of the canal is fully formed by 3 years.

parts.text: Umbilical hernia is common in infants and usually closes spontaneously by 3–5 years as the umbilical ring strengthens. Indirect inguinal hernia and hydrocele of the testis, by contrast, are related to failure of the **processus vaginalis** of the peritoneum to close — this is a congenital defect, usually treated surgically.

skills.title: Practical skill: observing the thoracic and abdominal muscles in a living person

items: Have your partner place the hands on the hips and press hard — palpate the contraction of the pectoralis major and the anterior axillary fold.
Have the subject push against a wall — see the digitations of the serratus anterior on the lateral surface of the chest; check that the scapula stays applied to the thoracic cage.
Lying supine, have the subject raise the head and shoulders — see the rectus and its tendinous intersections, and check for a bulge between the recti along the linea alba (diastasis).
Find the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic tubercle, and draw the projection of the inguinal ligament and, above its medial half, the projection of the inguinal canal.

skills.title: Practical skill: demonstrating the inguinal canal on a specimen

items: Find the aponeurosis of the external oblique and the inguinal ligament — the anterior and inferior walls of the canal.
Above the pubic tubercle show the superficial inguinal ring, its medial and lateral crura and the intercrural fibers.
Cut the aponeurosis and show the lower borders of the internal oblique and transversus (roof) and the transversalis fascia (posterior wall).
Trace the spermatic cord (or round ligament of the uterus) to the deep ring; show that the inferior epigastric vessels lie medial to the deep ring.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After removal of the axillary lymph nodes for cancer of the left breast, a woman reports that she cannot raise her arm above her head. On examination, when the patient pushes against a wall, the medial border and inferior angle of the left scapula protrude backward.
cases.ask: Which nerve and muscle are injured? Why has raising the arm become difficult?
cases.answer: The **long thoracic nerve**, lying on the surface of the serratus anterior in the axillary region, has been injured, resulting in paralysis of the **serratus anterior** — a "winged scapula." This muscle presses the scapula against the thoracic cage and, together with the trapezius, rotates the inferior angle of the scapula laterally, turning the glenoid cavity upward; this is what allows the arm to be raised above the horizontal. When the muscle is paralyzed this rotation is impaired.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A newborn shows severe respiratory distress and cyanosis after birth; the abdomen is "sunken," no breath sounds are heard over the left half of the chest, but bowel sounds are heard there. A radiograph shows intestinal loops in the left thoracic cavity.
cases.ask: What defect should be suspected? Through which weak spot of the diaphragm did the intestines pass into the chest?
cases.answer: This is a **congenital diaphragmatic hernia**. Most often, owing to failure to close of the muscle-free **lumbocostal triangle** (Bochdalek's triangle) between the lumbar and costal parts of the diaphragm, mainly on the left side, abdominal organs pass into the thoracic cavity, compress the lung and prevent its development (hypoplasia). In the newborn these triangles are relatively large. It is treated surgically.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 45-year-old porter notices a swelling in the right groin that enlarges on coughing and straining and disappears when he lies down. The swelling descends into the scrotum. At operation the hernial sac was found inside the coverings of the spermatic cord, emerging from the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric artery.
cases.ask: What type of hernia is this? Name the walls and rings of the inguinal canal.
cases.answer: This is an **indirect inguinal hernia**: the hernia enters from the lateral inguinal fossa through the deep inguinal ring, passes along the whole canal and emerges from the superficial ring into the scrotum; it lies lateral to the inferior epigastric artery (a direct hernia lies medially, emerging from the medial inguinal fossa). Walls of the inguinal canal: anterior — aponeurosis of the external oblique, posterior — transversalis fascia, roof — lower borders of the internal oblique and transversus, floor — inguinal ligament; rings — superficial (between the crura of the aponeurosis) and deep (in the transversalis fascia).

topics.title: Muscles and fasciae of the upper limb. Topography of the upper limb

goals.text: To teach the student the structure, function and innervation of the muscles of the shoulder girdle, arm, forearm and hand, the fasciae of the upper limb, the retinacula and synovial tendon sheaths, and the topographic structures of the upper limb (axillary fossa, spaces, canals, grooves), and to explain their clinical significance.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the muscles of the shoulder girdle and the composition of the "rotator cuff";
the anterior (flexor) and posterior (extensor) groups of arm muscles;
the anterior group of forearm muscles by layers and the posterior group;
the muscles of the hand: thenar, hypothenar and middle groups;
the fasciae of the upper limb, the retinacula, the carpal tunnel and the synovial sheaths;
the axillary fossa, the triangular and quadrangular spaces, the humeromuscular (radial) canal, the cubital fossa and the forearm grooves;
the nerve supply of each muscle group and the changes in the position of the hand when the nerves are injured;
the age-related features of the upper limb muscles.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the muscles of the upper limb in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
palpate the main muscles, tendons and grooves in a living person;
demonstrate and test the function of each muscle by movement;
name the structures passing through the axillary spaces, the humeromuscular canal and the carpal tunnel.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The basic rule of innervation of the upper limb muscles: the **anterior group of the arm** — musculocutaneous nerve; **all posterior (extensor) muscles of the arm and forearm** — radial nerve; the **anterior group of the forearm** — median nerve (except the flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of the flexor digitorum profundus — ulnar nerve); the **muscles of the hand** — mainly the ulnar nerve (most of the thenar and lumbricals I–II — median nerve).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The **rotator cuff** is the "cuff" formed by the tendons of the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis blending with the capsule of the shoulder joint; it holds the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity of the scapula (the main active stabilizer of the shoulder joint). The most frequently injured is the **supraspinatus tendon**: it passes under the acromion and is compressed when the arm is raised between 60° and 120° (**"painful arc" syndrome**, impingement). Tendon tears occur in elderly people and in athletes who often raise the arm overhead. Because the **axillary nerve** runs around the surgical neck of the humerus, it is injured in fractures in this region and in shoulder dislocation, leading to paralysis and atrophy of the deltoid.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Tendon reflexes**: tapping the biceps tendon with a reflex hammer flexes the forearm (biceps reflex, segments C~V~–C~VI~), and tapping the triceps tendon extends it (triceps reflex, C~VII~–C~VIII~). Changes in the reflexes are used for localizing diagnosis in injuries of spinal cord segments and nerves. In elderly people the tendon of the long head of the biceps may rupture in the intertubercular groove — on flexion a "Popeye sign" (bulging of the muscle belly) appears in the lower part of the arm.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Lateral epicondylitis** ("tennis elbow") is chronic strain of the common tendon of the extensor muscles arising from the lateral epicondyle (especially the extensor carpi radialis brevis); pain increases when the hand is extended against resistance. **Medial epicondylitis** ("golfer's elbow") is strain of the common flexor tendon. The **radial nerve** is injured in the radial groove in fractures of the shaft of the humerus — all the extensor muscles are paralyzed, and **"wrist drop"** appears (the hand and fingers cannot be extended).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Interosseous muscles: the **palmar** interossei **adduct** and the **dorsal** interossei **abduct** (mnemonic "PAD–DAB"); the axis line is the **3rd (middle) finger**. When the ulnar nerve is injured, the patient cannot hold a sheet of paper between the fingers (paralysis of the interossei), and when gripping paper between the thumb and index finger flexes the thumb (because the adductor does not work, the long flexor compensates — Froment's sign).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Carpal tunnel syndrome** is compression of the median nerve in the tunnel (pregnancy, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, prolonged computer work): numbness of fingers I–III and pain that worsens at night, and in late stages atrophy of the thenar and weakness of thumb opposition. Treatment involves dividing the flexor retinaculum. **The structure of the synovial sheaths** determines the spread of purulent tenosynovitis: pus in the sheath of the little finger or thumb can spread into the common sheath and the forearm (Pirogov's/Parona's space), forming a **V-shaped phlegmon**; in fingers II–IV, by contrast, the process is usually confined to the finger. **De Quervain's disease** is stenosing inflammation of the sheath of the tendons in the first extensor compartment (abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In the radial groove of the forearm, above the styloid process, the radial artery lies superficially and can be pressed against the bone, so the **pulse** is taken here. If pressure in the "anatomical snuffbox" is painful, a **fracture of the scaphoid** is suspected (this fracture may not be visible on initial radiographs and may have complications).

sections.title: 1. Muscles of the upper limb: general information

blocks.text: The muscles of the upper limb are divided into **muscles of the shoulder girdle** and **muscles of the free upper limb** — those of the arm, forearm and hand. The upper limb is an organ of labor, so its muscles are numerous and finely differentiated; muscles providing precise finger movements are especially well developed in the forearm and hand. The muscles of the arm and forearm are separated by fascial septa into **anterior (flexor)** and **posterior (extensor)** groups; each group is supplied mainly by one nerve — knowing this rule is the key to understanding nerve injuries.

parts.text: The basic rule of innervation of the upper limb muscles: the **anterior group of the arm** — musculocutaneous nerve; **all posterior (extensor) muscles of the arm and forearm** — radial nerve; the **anterior group of the forearm** — median nerve (except the flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of the flexor digitorum profundus — ulnar nerve); the **muscles of the hand** — mainly the ulnar nerve (most of the thenar and lumbricals I–II — median nerve).

blocks.text: The muscles of the arm are divided into two groups by the **medial and lateral intermuscular septa** running from the brachial fascia to the humerus. The **anterior group** (flexors) — the **biceps brachii**, **coracobrachialis** and **brachialis** — are all supplied by the **musculocutaneous nerve**. The **posterior group** (extensors) — the **triceps brachii** and **anconeus** — are supplied by the **radial nerve**.

blocks.text: The forearm muscles are multiarticular — they act on the elbow, radioulnar, radiocarpal and finger joints. They are divided into an **anterior group** (flexors of the hand and fingers, pronators; arising mainly from the **medial epicondyle**) and a **posterior group** (extensors and the supinator; arising mainly from the **lateral epicondyle**). The anterior group lies in **four layers**, the posterior group in **two layers**.

sections.title: 6. Fasciae, retinacula and tendon sheaths of the upper limb

blocks.text: By region, the fasciae of the upper limb are divided into the **deltoid**, **supraspinous and infraspinous**, **brachial** and **antebrachial** fasciae. The **brachial fascia** sends the medial and lateral **intermuscular septa** to the humerus. The **antebrachial fascia** is even stronger; in the wrist region it thickens to form the **retinacula**. In the palm the fascia forms the strong triangular **palmar aponeurosis** (*aponeurosis palmaris*) — its apex faces the flexor retinaculum and the tendon of the palmaris longus, and its base faces the fingers.

The **flexor retinaculum** (*retinaculum musculorum flexorum*) bridges the carpal groove to form the **carpal tunnel** (*canalis carpi*); through it pass the **median nerve** and nine tendons — the 8 tendons of the flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus (in a common synovial sheath) and the tendon of the flexor pollicis longus (in a separate sheath). On the medial side of the retinaculum is the **ulnar canal** (Guyon's canal), through which the ulnar nerve and vessels pass, and on the lateral side the **radial canal**, through which the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis passes.

The space under the **extensor retinaculum** (*retinaculum musculorum extensorum*) is divided into **six osteofibrous compartments** (from the radial side): 1) abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis; 2) extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis; 3) extensor pollicis longus; 4) extensor digitorum and extensor indicis; 5) extensor digiti minimi; 6) the tendon of the extensor carpi ulnaris. The tendons in each compartment are surrounded by a synovial sheath.

Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev et al. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 1.

blocks.text: On the palmar side the **common flexor synovial sheath** begins 1–2 cm above the retinaculum, descends to the middle of the palm and usually continues into the sheath of the **little finger**, reaching its distal phalanx; the sheath of the flexor pollicis longus also continues to the distal phalanx of the thumb. The synovial sheaths of **fingers II–IV**, by contrast, are separate and lie only from the metacarpophalangeal joint to the distal phalanx.

parts.text: **Carpal tunnel syndrome** is compression of the median nerve in the tunnel (pregnancy, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, prolonged computer work): numbness of fingers I–III and pain that worsens at night, and in late stages atrophy of the thenar and weakness of thumb opposition. Treatment involves dividing the flexor retinaculum. **The structure of the synovial sheaths** determines the spread of purulent tenosynovitis: pus in the sheath of the little finger or thumb can spread into the common sheath and the forearm (Pirogov's/Parona's space), forming a **V-shaped phlegmon**; in fingers II–IV, by contrast, the process is usually confined to the finger. **De Quervain's disease** is stenosing inflammation of the sheath of the tendons in the first extensor compartment (abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis).

blocks.text: The **axillary fossa** (*fossa axillaris*) is bounded in front by the skin fold corresponding to the lower border of the pectoralis major and behind by the fold corresponding to the lower border of the latissimus dorsi; through it pass the **axillary artery and vein**, the cords of the **brachial plexus** and lymph nodes. Three triangles are distinguished in the **anterior wall** of the axillary cavity: the **clavipectoral** (between the clavicle and the upper border of the pectoralis minor), the **pectoral** (the region of the pectoralis minor) and the **subpectoral** (between the lower borders of the pectoralis minor and major).

blocks.text: The **cubital fossa** (*fossa cubitalis*) is a triangular depression on the front of the elbow, bounded above by the brachialis (its floor), laterally by the brachioradialis and medially by the pronator teres; it contains the brachial artery (which divides here into the radial and ulnar arteries), the median nerve and the biceps tendon; on its surface lies the **median cubital vein**, used for drawing blood. On the **anterior surface of the forearm** there are three grooves: the **radial groove** (between the brachioradialis and flexor carpi radialis — the radial artery and the superficial branch of the radial nerve), the **median groove** (between the flexor carpi radialis and flexor digitorum superficialis — the median nerve) and the **ulnar groove** (between the flexor digitorum superficialis and flexor carpi ulnaris — the ulnar artery and nerve). On the posterolateral side of the wrist, when the thumb is extended, the **"anatomical snuffbox"** forms between the tendons of the first and third compartments; the scaphoid and the radial artery lie in its floor.

parts.text: In the radial groove of the forearm, above the styloid process, the radial artery lies superficially and can be pressed against the bone, so the **pulse** is taken here. If pressure in the "anatomical snuffbox" is painful, a **fracture of the scaphoid** is suspected (this fracture may not be visible on initial radiographs and may have complications).

items: In the newborn the muscles of the shoulder girdle are well defined, but their tendons are short and thin.
The anterior and posterior groups of arm muscles are well developed; all three heads of the triceps are well formed, and their tendinous parts are clearly visible, though thin.

The anterior group of forearm muscles is sufficiently developed, with well-defined tendons; of the posterior group, the extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis have long bellies and short tendons; the proximal part of the extensor digitorum is broad; the supinator is flat and broad.

In the newborn the tone of the flexors exceeds that of the extensors — the arms are flexed and the fingers clenched into a fist (physiological hypertonia), which decreases during the first months of life.

The palmar muscles are poorly developed in the newborn and consist of fine muscle fibers; they grow considerably in the first year of life — in parallel with grasping objects and, later, learning fine finger movements.

skills.title: Practical skill: testing the upper limb muscles in a living person

items: Deltoid: abduction of the arm to the horizontal against resistance; palpate the muscle contracting over the shoulder.
Rotator cuff: with the elbow flexed, rotate the arm laterally (infraspinatus and teres minor) and medially (subscapularis) against resistance.
Biceps: flexion of the supinated forearm against resistance; palpate its tendon in the cubital fossa.
Triceps: extension of the flexed elbow against resistance.
Flex the hand and see the tendons of the palmaris longus and flexor carpi radialis at the wrist; find the pulse on the radial artery.
Extend the thumb and show the "anatomical snuffbox" and the tendons bounding it.
Spread and close the fingers (interossei); touch the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger (opposition).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 35-year-old woman has complained for 4 months of numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers of the right hand and pain that wakes her at night; she works at a computer all day. On examination the thenar eminence is slightly flattened and opposition of the thumb to the little finger is weak; holding the wrist flexed intensifies the symptoms.
cases.ask: Which nerve is compressed, and where? What forms the canal, and what else passes through it?
cases.answer: **Carpal tunnel syndrome** — the **median nerve** is compressed in the carpal tunnel. The tunnel is formed by the groove of the carpal bones and the **flexor retinaculum** stretched over it. Besides the median nerve, the 8 tendons of the flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus (in a common synovial sheath) and the tendon of the flexor pollicis longus pass through it. The median nerve supplies the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens, superficial head of the flexor brevis) — hence the thenar atrophy and weak opposition.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A young man fractured the middle third of the humerus. Since then he cannot extend his hand and fingers — when he stretches the arm forward, the hand hangs down; sensation is reduced on the back of the thumb, between metacarpals I and II.
cases.ask: Which nerve is injured, and why precisely in this fracture? Which muscles are paralyzed?
cases.answer: The **radial nerve** is injured: it lies directly on the bone in the **radial groove** on the posterior surface of the humerus (in the humeromuscular canal), so it is easily injured in fractures of the middle third. As a result, the **posterior group of forearm muscles** — the radial and ulnar extensors of the wrist, extensor digitorum, extensor pollicis and abductor pollicis longus, and the supinator — is paralyzed: **"wrist drop."** The triceps is usually spared, because its branches arise above the groove.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A cook pricked the palmar surface of her right little finger with a fish bone. 3 days later the whole little finger is swollen and held flexed, and any attempt to extend it is acutely painful; the swelling is spreading to the medial part of the palm and the wrist, and pain has also appeared in the thenar eminence.
cases.ask: How is the purulent process spreading? Which anatomical structure is responsible?
cases.answer: This is **purulent tenosynovitis** of the little finger. The synovial sheath of the little finger usually continues into the **common flexor synovial sheath**, which passes through the carpal tunnel into the forearm; often the common sheath communicates in the forearm region with the sheath of the flexor pollicis longus. Therefore pus can spread from the little finger to the palm and forearm (Pirogov's/Parona's space), and then into the sheath of the thumb, forming a **V-shaped phlegmon**. Because the sheaths of fingers II–IV are separate, the process in them is usually confined to the finger. Urgent surgical opening and drainage of the sheath are required.

topics.title: Muscles of the lower limb: muscles of the pelvis, thigh, leg and foot. Fasciae and topography of the lower limb

goals.text: To teach the student the structure, function and innervation of the muscles of the pelvic girdle, thigh, leg and foot, the fasciae of the lower limb, the retinacula and synovial sheaths, and the topographic structures of the lower limb (muscular and vascular lacunae, femoral triangle, femoral and adductor canals, popliteal fossa, canals of the leg), and to explain their significance in standing and walking.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the internal and external muscles of the pelvis, their origin, insertion, function and innervation;
the anterior, medial and posterior groups of thigh muscles;
the anterior, lateral and posterior groups of leg muscles;
the dorsal and plantar muscles of the foot;
the fascia lata, the retinacula and the canals under them;
the muscular and vascular lacunae, the femoral triangle, the femoral canal, the adductor canal, the popliteal fossa and the cruropopliteal canal;
the age-related features of the lower limb muscles.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the muscles of the lower limb in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
palpate the main muscles, tendons, the femoral triangle and the popliteal fossa in a living person;
demonstrate the function of each muscle group by movement;
explain the walls and ring of the femoral canal and the path of a femoral hernia.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Intramuscular injections** into the buttock are given into the **upper outer quadrant** of the buttock — the sciatic nerve and gluteal vessels emerge through the infrapiriform and suprapiriform foramina into the inferomedial part of the buttock. When the gluteus medius and minimus (or the superior gluteal nerve) are paralyzed, the pelvis **drops toward the opposite side** when the patient stands on the affected leg — **Trendelenburg's sign** (a "waddling gait" with bilateral injury). In spasm of the piriformis the sciatic nerve is compressed, causing pain in the buttock and back of the thigh (piriformis syndrome).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Knee jerk** — when the patellar ligament is tapped, the quadriceps contracts and the leg extends (segments L~II~–L~IV~, femoral nerve). The **posterior thigh muscles** ("hamstrings") are the muscles most often strained and torn in athletes — being biarticular, during sprinting they are stretched and contract at the same time. Strain of the adductor muscles ("groin strain") is common in soccer players.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The order of structures passing behind the medial malleolus from front to back: tendon of the **tibialis posterior** → tendon of the **flexor digitorum longus** → **posterior tibial artery and veins** → **tibial nerve** → tendon of the **flexor hallucis longus**. An English mnemonic based on the initial letters: "**T**om, **D**ick **A**nd **V**ery **N**ervous **H**arry" (*tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, arteria, vena, nervus, flexor hallucis longus*).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The **calcaneal (Achilles) tendon** is the strongest tendon in the body; its rupture (often during jumping or a sudden start) presents as inability to stand on tiptoe. Tapping the calcaneal tendon plantarflexes the foot — the **Achilles reflex** (S~I~–S~II~). The **common fibular nerve** lies superficially around the neck of the fibula and is injured by fractures, tight casts or prolonged sitting with crossed legs: the anterior and lateral groups are paralyzed, producing **"foot drop"** and a "steppage gait" (walking with the leg lifted high so that the toes do not catch the ground).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Femoral hernia** occurs more often in women (the pelvis is wider, and the vascular lacuna and femoral ring are larger) and presents as a bulge **below** the inguinal ligament, medial to the femoral vein (an inguinal hernia bulges above the inguinal ligament, superomedial to the pubic tubercle). Because the femoral ring is narrow and rigidly bounded, femoral hernias are frequently **strangulated**. In the femoral triangle, slightly medial to the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, the pulse of the femoral artery is felt; here **arterial puncture** (coronary angiography, angiography) and catheterization of the femoral vein (medial to the artery) are performed.

sections.title: 1. Muscles of the lower limb: general information

blocks.text: The muscles of the lower limb are divided into **muscles of the pelvic girdle** and muscles of the free lower limb — those of the **thigh**, **leg** and **foot**. Unlike the upper limb, the lower limb is an organ of **support and locomotion**, so its muscles are large and strong, often multi-headed (quadriceps, triceps), and insert by short, strong tendons; they are adapted to carrying body weight, maintaining the upright posture and walking. The lower limb muscles make up **more than half** of the total muscle mass.

The pelvic muscles arise from the pelvic bones and the vertebral column, insert on the proximal end of the femur and move the **hip joint** around all three axes. They are divided into **internal** (arising from the pelvic cavity) and **external** groups.

blocks.text: The thigh muscles surround the femur on all sides, act on the hip and knee joints and are divided into three groups: **anterior** (mainly knee extensors; **femoral nerve**), **medial** (adductors; **obturator nerve**) and **posterior** (thigh extensors and knee flexors; **sciatic nerve**). The groups are separated by the intermuscular septa of the fascia lata running to the femur.

sections.title: 6. Fasciae and retinacula of the lower limb

blocks.text: The **iliac fascia** covers the iliopsoas; its thickened part between the inguinal ligament and the iliopubic eminence — the **iliopectineal arch** — divides the space under the inguinal ligament into the **muscular lacuna** and the **vascular lacuna**. The **fascia lata** (*fascia lata*) is the strongest fascia in the body; laterally it thickens to form the **iliotibial tract** (the tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus insert into it). In the upper third of the thigh the fascia lata splits into two layers; its superficial layer contains the **saphenous opening** (*hiatus saphenus*, fossa ovalis) — bounded by the **falciform margin**, closed by the cribriform fascia — through which the **great saphenous vein** drains into the femoral vein.

The **crural fascia** forms the anterior and posterior intermuscular septa; posteriorly it splits into superficial and deep layers, separating the triceps surae from the deep group. In the region of the malleoli the fascia thickens to form the **retinacula**: the **superior and inferior extensor retinacula** (Y-shaped; for the tendons of the anterior group), the **flexor retinaculum** (between the medial malleolus and the calcaneus — forming the **medial malleolar canal**, through which the tendons of the deep posterior group and the tibial neurovascular bundle pass), and the **superior and inferior fibular retinacula** (behind the lateral malleolus). On the sole the fascia forms the thick **plantar aponeurosis** — it holds the longitudinal arch like a "tie-rod."

blocks.text: The **femoral canal** (*canalis femoralis*) does not exist in a healthy person — it forms only when a **femoral hernia** develops. Normally, in the medial angle of the vascular lacuna there is the **femoral ring** (*anulus femoralis*): in front — the inguinal ligament, behind — the pectineal ligament (fascia), medially — the lacunar ligament, laterally — the femoral vein; from the abdominal side it is closed by the transversalis fascia and peritoneum. The hernia enters through the femoral ring (internal opening), passes between the layers of the fascia lata and emerges under the skin through the **saphenous opening** (external opening). Walls of the canal: anterior — superficial layer of the fascia lata (superior horn of the falciform margin), lateral — sheath of the femoral vein, posterior — deep layer of the fascia lata (pectineal fascia).

parts.text: **Femoral hernia** occurs more often in women (the pelvis is wider, and the vascular lacuna and femoral ring are larger) and presents as a bulge **below** the inguinal ligament, medial to the femoral vein (an inguinal hernia bulges above the inguinal ligament, superomedial to the pubic tubercle). Because the femoral ring is narrow and rigidly bounded, femoral hernias are frequently **strangulated**. In the femoral triangle, slightly medial to the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, the pulse of the femoral artery is felt; here **arterial puncture** (coronary angiography, angiography) and catheterization of the femoral vein (medial to the artery) are performed.

items: In the newborn the lower limb muscles are less developed than those of the upper limb; they grow rapidly in the first year of life — as the child crawls, stands and begins to walk. In the newborn the lower limb muscles make up ≈38% of the total muscle mass (in adults — more than half); intensive growth is observed up to 5–6 years and during puberty.

In the newborn the gluteus maximus and medius are well developed and the gluteus minimus poorly; the tensor fasciae latae is short and flat, and the iliotibial tract thin. The gluteus maximus grows intensively once the child begins to walk upright (2–4 years) and forms the prominence of the buttock.

In the newborn the sartorius is relatively broad and runs straight; the quadriceps and its heads are well developed. The semitendinosus has few tendinous fibers, and the semimembranosus is relatively large.
Because the contractile part of the leg muscles is long, the newborn's leg is of the same girth in its upper and lower parts (cylindrical); the deep-layer muscles are not fully mature.
The plantar muscles are poorly developed; when the child begins to walk they mature first and take part in forming the arch of the foot.
In the newborn the femoral triangle is relatively large (occupying ≈1/3 of the thigh), the muscular and vascular lacunae are narrow and vertically placed, and the popliteal fossa is shallow.

items: Lying supine, flex the thigh against resistance — iliopsoas; extend the knee — quadriceps; test the knee jerk.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 65-year-old woman noticed a painful walnut-sized bulge in the groin, below the inguinal ligament and medial to the femoral vein; for 6 hours she has had severe pain, vomiting and no bowel movement. The bulge does not return to the abdominal cavity.
cases.ask: What hernia and what complication should be suspected? By what route did the hernia emerge, and why is it prone to strangulation?
cases.answer: This is a **strangulated femoral hernia**. The hernia entered through the **femoral ring** (in front — inguinal ligament, behind — pectineal ligament, medially — lacunar ligament, laterally — femoral vein), passed between the layers of the fascia lata and emerged under the skin through the **saphenous opening** (hiatus saphenus) — which is why the bulge lies below the inguinal ligament (an inguinal hernia lies above it). The femoral ring is narrow and its walls, especially the lacunar ligament, are rigid and do not stretch — so femoral hernias are frequently strangulated. It is common in women because of the width of the pelvis. Emergency surgery is required.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: After a nurse gave an intramuscular injection into a patient's buttock, the patient felt an "electric shock" pain running down the leg; later weakness developed in the posterior thigh group and all the muscles of the leg and foot.
cases.ask: Which nerve is injured? Where is the correct injection site, and why?
cases.answer: The **sciatic nerve** is injured: it leaves the pelvis through the **infrapiriform foramen**, descends under the gluteus maximus in the inferomedial part of the buttock and supplies the posterior thigh group and all the muscles of the leg and foot. The correct injection site is the **upper outer quadrant** of the buttock (or the region of the gluteus medius and minimus — the "ventrogluteal" site between the anterior superior iliac spine and the iliac crest), because there are no large nerves or vessels there.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: While playing volleyball, a 40-year-old man felt a blow above the heel "as if someone had kicked him" as he tried to jump, and fell. On examination a gap is palpable 3–4 cm above the calcaneal tuberosity, and the patient cannot stand on tiptoe; lying prone, squeezing the calf does not plantarflex the foot.
cases.ask: Which structure is injured? Which muscles form it, and which reflex, carried by which nerve, is lost?
cases.answer: The **calcaneal (Achilles) tendon is ruptured**. It is formed by the union of the tendons of the **triceps surae** — the two-headed **gastrocnemius** (arising from the femoral condyles) and the **soleus** (from the tibia and fibula) — and inserts on the calcaneal tuberosity; it plantarflexes the foot (standing on tiptoe, jumping, push-off in walking). It is supplied by the tibial nerve; the **Achilles reflex** (S~I~–S~II~) is lost. Failure of the foot to plantarflex when the calf is squeezed is the classic sign of tendon rupture (Thompson test).

topics.title: Muscles and fasciae of the neck and head. Topography of the neck

goals.text: To teach the student the structure, function, innervation and age-related features of the neck muscles (superficial, hyoid and deep), the cervical fasciae and triangles, the muscles of the head — muscles of facial expression and muscles of mastication — and the fasciae of the head; to explain their clinical significance.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the structure and function of the superficial muscles of the neck (platysma, sternocleidomastoid);
the muscles above and below the hyoid bone;
the deep lateral (scalene) and medial (prevertebral) muscles of the neck;
the layers of the cervical fascia and the spaces they form;
the regions and triangles of the neck, the interscalene and antescalene spaces;
the features and main groups of the muscles of facial expression;
the muscles of mastication and their role in movements of the mandible;
the age-related features of the head and neck muscles.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the neck and head muscles in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
palpate the sternocleidomastoid, masseter and temporalis in a living person;
outline the triangles of the neck and name the main structures in them;
test the function of the muscles of facial expression (assessment of facial nerve function).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Wry neck** (*torticollis*) is tilting of the head to one side with the face turned to the opposite side. In the **congenital** form, the sternocleidomastoid becomes fibrotic and shortened because of birth trauma or a developmental defect — a firm "lump" is palpable on one side of the infant's neck. Early massage and special (stretching) exercises often give results without surgery; untreated, facial asymmetry develops.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: During swallowing and speech the hyoid bone is "suspended" between the muscles above and below it: the upper muscles raise it and the larynx (in swallowing the larynx rises and the epiglottis closes its inlet), and the lower ones lower it. When both groups contract together, the hyoid bone is fixed and serves as a fixed point for the muscles that depress the mandible.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Scalenus anterior syndrome** (or when a cervical rib is present) — the brachial plexus and subclavian artery are compressed in the interscalene space: pain, numbness, coldness of the hand and a weakened pulse are observed. The subclavian vein, which passes in front of the anterior scalene, is not compressed — it is convenient for **catheterization** (infraclavicular or supraclavicular puncture).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Purulent processes (neck **phlegmons**) spread along the fascial spaces of the neck. From the retropharyngeal and pretracheal (visceral) spaces pus can descend into the **mediastinum**, causing a serious complication — **mediastinitis**. Therefore neck phlegmons arising from dental and throat infections are opened as surgical emergencies.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In the **carotid triangle** the common carotid artery can be pressed against the **carotid tubercle** on the transverse process of the 6th cervical vertebra — the pulse is taken here, and it is pressed here to stop bleeding temporarily. At the bifurcation of the carotid artery lies the carotid sinus — firm pressure on it can cause reflex bradycardia and fainting.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Peripheral facial nerve palsy** (Bell's palsy) — all the muscles of facial expression on one side are paralyzed: the forehead wrinkles disappear, the eye does not close (on attempting to close the eye the eyeball turns upward and the sclera is visible — "hare's eye"), the nasolabial fold flattens, the corner of the mouth droops, and food collects between the cheek and teeth (paralysis of the buccinator). In **central** palsy (stroke), by contrast, only the **lower** part of the face is affected — the forehead muscles are spared owing to bilateral cortical innervation.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Trismus** is inability to open the mouth owing to tonic spasm of the muscles of mastication; it is an early sign of tetanus and also occurs with inflammation of the lower wisdom tooth and abscesses around the masticatory muscles. When the mouth is opened excessively wide (yawning, dental procedures), the pull of the lateral pterygoid moves the head of the mandible forward past the articular tubercle, causing **dislocation of the mandible** — the mouth is locked open.

sections.title: 1. Muscles of the neck: general information

blocks.text: Because the neck muscles differ in origin and function, their topography is complex. By topography they are divided into three groups: **superficial muscles** (platysma, sternocleidomastoid), **muscles attached to the hyoid bone** (suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles) and **deep muscles** (lateral — scalene muscles; medial — prevertebral muscles).

The **platysma** (*platysma*) is a thin, broad muscular sheet lying under the skin; it arises from the fascia of the upper chest (at the level of the 2nd rib) and inserts on the border of the mandible, the masseteric fascia and the skin at the corner of the mouth. It tenses the skin of the neck, protecting the subcutaneous veins from compression, and draws the corner of the mouth down. By origin and innervation it is close to the **muscles of facial expression** — it is supplied by the **facial nerve**.

blocks.label: Figure 15.1
blocks.caption: Platysma, left lateral view (Figure No. 261). Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev et al. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 1.

blocks.text: The **sternocleidomastoid** (*m. sternocleidomastoideus*) arises by two heads — from the anterior surface of the manubrium and from the sternal end of the clavicle — and inserts on the mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral part of the superior nuchal line. Contracting **unilaterally**, it tilts the head to its own side and turns the face to the **opposite** side; contracting **bilaterally**, it throws the head back (or flexes the neck), and with the head fixed it raises the sternum and clavicle, acting as an accessory respiratory muscle. It is supplied by the **accessory nerve** (XI) and branches of the cervical plexus. This muscle is an important landmark of the neck — it divides the neck into the medial and lateral triangles.

parts.text: During swallowing and speech the hyoid bone is "suspended" between the muscles above and below it: the upper muscles raise it and the larynx (in swallowing the larynx rises and the epiglottis closes its inlet), and the lower ones lower it. When both groups contract together, the hyoid bone is fixed and serves as a fixed point for the muscles that depress the mandible.

blocks.text: **Lateral group** — the **anterior, middle and posterior scalene muscles** (*mm. scaleni*): they arise from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae; the anterior and middle insert on the 1st rib and the posterior on the 2nd rib. They raise the ribs (accessory muscles of inspiration), and with the ribs fixed bend the neck to the side. **Medial (prevertebral) group** — the **longus colli**, **longus capitis**, and **rectus capitis anterior and lateralis**: lying on the anterior surface of the vertebral column, they flex the neck and head forward and bend them to the side. The deep muscles are supplied by branches of the cervical and brachial plexuses.

Source: Sh.J. Teshaev et al. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 1.

blocks.text: There are two spaces among the scalene muscles: the **interscalene space** (*spatium interscalenum*) — between the anterior and middle scalenes and the 1st rib; the **subclavian artery** and the trunks of the **brachial plexus** pass through it. The **antescalene space** (*spatium antescalenum*) — in front of the anterior scalene (bounded anteriorly by the sternohyoid and sternothyroid); the **subclavian vein** passes through it.

parts.text: **Scalenus anterior syndrome** (or when a cervical rib is present) — the brachial plexus and subclavian artery are compressed in the interscalene space: pain, numbness, coldness of the hand and a weakened pulse are observed. The subclavian vein, which passes in front of the anterior scalene, is not compressed — it is convenient for **catheterization** (infraclavicular or supraclavicular puncture).

blocks.text: According to the international anatomical nomenclature, the cervical fascia consists of three layers:

items: The **superficial (investing) layer** (*lamina superficialis*) encircles the neck like a collar, forming sheaths for the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius and a capsule for the submandibular gland; below it attaches to the manubrium and clavicle, and above to the base of the mandible, continuing into the masseteric fascia.

The **pretracheal layer** (*lamina pretrachealis*) stretches between the hyoid bone, the manubrium and the clavicles, forming sheaths for the infrahyoid muscles; laterally it attaches to the omohyoid; it also encloses the cervical viscera (larynx, trachea, thyroid gland).

The **prevertebral layer** (*lamina prevertebralis*) covers the prevertebral and scalene muscles behind the pharynx and esophagus; together with the brachial plexus and subclavian artery it continues into the axilla.

blocks.text: In addition, the **carotid sheath** (*vagina carotica*) is distinguished, enclosing the common carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus nerve. Between the layers there are spaces filled with loose tissue: the **suprasternal interfascial space** (between the superficial and pretracheal layers, above the sternum), the **pretracheal (visceral) space** and the **retropharyngeal space** (in front of the prevertebral layer) — the last continues below into the mediastinum.

parts.text: Purulent processes (neck **phlegmons**) spread along the fascial spaces of the neck. From the retropharyngeal and pretracheal (visceral) spaces pus can descend into the **mediastinum**, causing a serious complication — **mediastinitis**. Therefore neck phlegmons arising from dental and throat infections are opened as surgical emergencies.

blocks.text: The neck is bounded above by the border of the mandible, the external acoustic opening and the mastoid process, and below by the jugular notch of the manubrium, the clavicle and the acromion; the posterior (nuchal) region lies behind the lateral border of the trapezius. On each side the sternocleidomastoid divides the neck into the **medial (anterior)** and **lateral** triangles; the omohyoid and digastric divide them into smaller triangles.

sections.title: 7. Muscles of the head: muscles of facial expression

blocks.text: The muscles of the head are divided into muscles of **facial expression** and muscles of **mastication**. The **muscles of facial expression** develop from the second branchial arch and are supplied by the **facial nerve** (VII). Their characteristic features: 1) they are not covered by fascia; 2) they arise from bone and insert into the **skin** (some lie entirely within the skin); 3) they are arranged mainly around the natural openings (palpebral fissure, mouth, nostrils, ear) in a circular (constricting) or radial (dilating) direction; 4) on contraction they form skin folds and change the expression of the face — the **facial expression** — and they also take part in speech, eating and vision.

**Orbicularis oculi** (*m. orbicularis oculi*) — palpebral, orbital and lacrimal parts; closes the eye (palpebral part — gently, orbital part — tight squeezing), dilates the lacrimal sac and aids tear drainage. **Corrugator supercilii** and **procerus** — vertical and transverse wrinkles between the eyebrows (frowning)

blocks.text: The **temporal fascia** arises from the superior temporal line and the epicranial aponeurosis, covers the temporalis and near the zygomatic arch splits into superficial and deep layers (attaching to the lateral and medial surfaces of the zygomatic arch, with fat between them). The **masseteric fascia** covers the masseter and continues posteriorly into the capsule of the **parotid gland**. The **buccopharyngeal fascia** covers the buccinator and passes onto the lateral wall of the pharynx. Between the buccinator and masseter lies the **buccal fat pad** (Bichat's fat pad).

items: In the newborn the mandible is small and the hyoid bone lies high, so the suprahyoid muscles are relatively long and the infrahyoid muscles short.

The neck muscles are thin in the newborn; the sternocleidomastoid, digastric and scalene muscles are relatively well developed. At 5–7 years all the neck muscles are well formed, resembling those of adults by 10–14 years; their development is completed at 20–25 years.
The cervical fasciae are very thin and loose in the newborn, and there is little loose tissue in the interfascial spaces; their volume increases considerably at 6–7 years and further during puberty.
In newborns and children aged 2–3 years the boundaries of the neck lie high, so the triangles also lie higher; they reach their adult position after 15 years.

In the newborn the muscles of facial expression, except the orbicularis oris and buccinator, are thin and weak; the **orbicularis oris** and **buccinator**, which take part in suckling, are well developed. The epicranial aponeurosis of the occipitofrontalis is poorly developed.

The muscles of mastication are poorly developed in the newborn; they thicken and strengthen as the deciduous teeth, especially the molars, erupt. During this period much fat accumulates in the temporal and buccal regions, giving the child's face its round shape. At 5–8 years the muscles and fasciae of the head are well developed.

skills.title: Practical skill: testing the muscles of facial expression and mastication (facial and trigeminal nerves)

items: Ask the patient to raise the eyebrows (occipitofrontalis), frown (corrugator supercilii) and close the eyes tightly (orbicularis oculi); compare the two sides.
Ask the patient to show the teeth, smile (zygomatic muscles and risorius), puff out the cheeks (buccinator and orbicularis oris) and whistle.
Tensing the neck (pulling the lower lip down) — observe the platysma.
Ask the patient to clench the teeth and palpate the contraction of the masseter and temporalis on both sides (motor branch of the trigeminal nerve).
Check for deviation of the jaw to the side when the mouth opens — with unilateral paralysis of the lateral pterygoid the jaw deviates toward the paralyzed side.
Turning the head to the side against resistance and shrugging the shoulders — test the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (accessory nerve).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: The mother of a 3-week-old infant says that the baby's head is always tilted to the right with the face turned to the left. On examination a firm, painless, bean-sized mass is palpable on the right side of the neck along the sternocleidomastoid. The delivery was difficult, in breech presentation.
cases.ask: What is the disease? Which muscle is affected, and why is the head held in exactly this position?
cases.answer: **Congenital muscular torticollis** (*torticollis*). As a result of birth trauma, hemorrhage occurred into the **right sternocleidomastoid**, which became fibrotic and shortened. Contracting unilaterally, this muscle **tilts the head to its own side** and **turns the face to the opposite side** — which is why the head is tilted to the right and the face turned to the left. Early positional treatment, massage and stretching exercises are effective; if they fail, the muscle is lengthened surgically after 1 year of age.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: On waking in the morning, a 40-year-old man noticed that the left half of his face had become "crooked": he cannot close his left eye or raise his left eyebrow, food collects in his left cheek when he eats, and the left corner of his mouth droops. There is no disturbance of limb movement.
cases.ask: Which nerve is injured? Explain the signs in terms of muscle function. How is this distinguished from central palsy?
cases.answer: **Peripheral palsy of the left facial nerve** (Bell's palsy) — all the **muscles of facial expression** on the left are paralyzed: the **occipitofrontalis** (the eyebrow cannot be raised, no forehead wrinkles), the **orbicularis oculi** (the eye does not close), the **buccinator** (food collects between the cheek and teeth), and the **levator anguli oris and zygomatic muscles** (the corner of the mouth droops). In central palsy (stroke) only the lower half of the face is affected and the forehead muscles are spared, because the upper part of the facial nucleus receives bilateral cortical innervation.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: After sitting in the dentist's chair with the mouth wide open, a 25-year-old patient was unable to close the mouth: the mouth is half open, the mandible protrudes, a depression is palpable in front of the ear, and speaking and swallowing are difficult.
cases.ask: What has happened? Which muscles are involved in producing it?
cases.answer: This is an **anterior dislocation of the mandible** (at the temporomandibular joint). When the mouth opens wide, the **lateral pterygoid** pulls the head of the mandible and the disc forward; with excessive opening the head passes forward over the articular tubercle, and spasm of the elevators of the jaw — the **masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid** — locks it in this position. That is why a depression is felt in front of the ear (in place of the articular fossa). Treatment — reduction by pressing the jaw downward and backward (the Hippocratic method).

topics.title: The oral cavity, teeth, tongue, salivary glands, soft palate. The pharynx, Pirogov's ring. Their age-related changes

goals.text: To teach the student general concepts about the internal organs, the principles of structure of the wall of the alimentary canal, the structure, topography, development and age-related features of the oral cavity and its organs — the lips, cheeks, palate, teeth, tongue and salivary glands — and of the pharynx; to explain the significance of the lymphoepithelial ring.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the classification of the internal organs and the layers of the wall of the alimentary canal;
the boundaries and parts of the oral cavity and the structure of the lips and cheeks;
the hard and soft palate, the palatine muscles and the palatine arches (fauces);
the parts and tissues of a tooth, the types of teeth, dental formulas, and the eruption times of deciduous and permanent teeth;
the parts and papillae of the tongue and its intrinsic and extrinsic muscles;
the major and minor salivary glands, their ducts and the sites where they open;
the parts, wall and muscles of the pharynx and the Pirogov–Waldeyer lymphoepithelial ring;
the age-related features of the oral organs and the pharynx.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: show the structures of the oral cavity in a living person (frenula, palatine arches, tonsils, lingual papillae, papillae of the salivary ducts);
write the dental formula and estimate a child's age from the teeth;
find the structures of the tongue, salivary glands and pharynx on specimens and in an atlas and name them in Latin.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Cleft palate** ("wolf's mouth," *palatoschisis*) is failure of the palatine processes to fuse during fetal life; it often occurs together with **cleft lip** ("harelip"). In the infant, sucking is impaired and milk passes into the nose, and later speech is disturbed; it is corrected surgically. When the **vagus nerve** is injured, the soft palate droops on that side, and on saying "ah" the uvula deviates **toward the healthy side**.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Tooth eruption is an indicator of a child's **biological age** and development: in a child under 1 year, the number of deciduous teeth can be roughly estimated by the formula **(age in months − 4)**. Late eruption is seen in rickets, hypothyroidism and other diseases. **Caries** is demineralization of the enamel and dentin; if the process reaches the pulp — **pulpitis** (severe pain); if it extends beyond the root apex — **periodontitis**; and because the roots of the upper molars lie close to the maxillary sinus, **odontogenic maxillary sinusitis** may develop.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Innervation of the tongue: **motor** — hypoglossal nerve (XII); **general sensation** — anterior 2/3 by the lingual nerve (V~3~), posterior 1/3 by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX); **taste** — anterior 2/3 by the chorda tympani of the facial nerve (VII), posterior 1/3 by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX), the most posterior part of the root and the epiglottis by the vagus nerve (X). With unilateral injury of the hypoglossal nerve, the protruded tongue deviates **toward the injured side** (the healthy genioglossus pushes the tongue from its own side).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Epidemic parotitis** (mumps) is a viral infection with painful swelling of the parotid glands; because the gland lies within a dense fascial capsule, the swelling is very painful; complications — orchitis, pancreatitis, meningitis. **Sialolithiasis** (salivary stone disease) occurs most often in the duct of the **submandibular gland** (the duct is long and ascending, and its secretion thicker): the gland swells and hurts during meals. In operations on the parotid gland there is a risk of injuring the **facial nerve**, which passes through the gland.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Enlargement of the pharyngeal tonsil in children — **adenoids** — makes nasal breathing difficult (mouth open, "adenoid face") and, by blocking the opening of the auditory tube, causes frequent **otitis**. **Tonsillitis** (angina) is inflammation of the palatine tonsils; its complications are **peritonsillar abscess** and **retropharyngeal abscess**; from the latter pus can descend into the mediastinum. Foreign bodies such as fish bones become lodged in the piriform recesses.

sections.title: 1. General information on the internal organs

blocks.text: **Splanchnology** is the study of the internal organs. The internal organs include the **digestive**, **respiratory** and **urogenital** organs (in the broad sense also the endocrine glands and the cardiovascular system); they lie mainly in the body cavities — thoracic, abdominal and pelvic — as well as in the head and neck, and provide metabolism and reproduction. By structure the internal organs are divided into **tubular (hollow)** organs — esophagus, stomach, intestines, trachea, urinary bladder, etc. — and **parenchymatous** organs — liver, lungs, kidneys, salivary glands, etc.

The **digestive system** begins with the oral cavity and ends at the anus; it includes the oral cavity (teeth, tongue, salivary glands), pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small and large intestines, and the liver and pancreas. The total length of the alimentary canal is 8–10 m. In development the gut tube is divided into the **head gut** (mouth and pharynx), the **foregut** (esophagus, stomach, initial part of the duodenum, liver, pancreas), the **midgut** (small intestine, cecum, ascending colon and part of the transverse colon) and the **hindgut** (the rest of the large intestine). Most of it develops from **endoderm**; the epithelium of the oral cavity and the lower part of the rectum derive from **ectoderm**.
