blocks.text: The **oral cavity** (*cavitas oris*) is the initial part of the digestive system. It is bounded below by the **oral diaphragm** (mylohyoid muscles), above by the **hard and soft palate**, at the sides by the **cheeks** and in front by the **lips**; behind, it communicates with the pharynx through the **fauces** (*fauces*). The teeth and the alveolar processes of the jaws divide it into two parts: the **oral vestibule** (*vestibulum oris*) — the slit between the lips and cheeks and the teeth and gums — and the **oral cavity proper** (*cavitas oris propria*) — internal to the teeth, filled by the tongue when the mouth is closed.

blocks.label: Figure 16.1
blocks.caption: The oral cavity, anterior view (Figure No. 3): 1 — lower lip; 2 — gum; 3 — teeth; 4 — palatine tonsil; 5 — palatoglossal arch; 6 — soft palate; 7 — upper lip; 8 — frenulum of the upper lip; 9 — hard palate; 10 — uvula; 11 — palatopharyngeal arch; 12 — dorsum of the tongue; 13 — body of the tongue; 14 — tip of the tongue; 15 — frenulum of the lower lip. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The basis of the **lips** (*labia oris*) is the orbicularis oris; they are covered outside by skin and inside by mucosa, with the red **intermediate part** (vermilion) between them. In the midline the mucosa passes onto the gum, forming the **frenula of the upper and lower lips**; the skin of the upper lip bears the **philtrum** (*philtrum*). Small **labial glands** lie in the submucosa of the lips. The basis of the **cheek** (*bucca*) is the buccinator; the **buccal fat pad** lies between the skin and the muscle. On the mucosa of the cheek, opposite the upper **second molar**, is the **papilla of the parotid duct**. The **gums** (*gingivae*) are thick mucosa covering the alveolar processes and firmly attached to the periosteum; they encircle the necks of the teeth.

The **hard palate** (*palatum durum*) is the anterior 2/3 of the palate; its basis is formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones. Its mucosa is firmly attached to the periosteum; in the middle is the **palatine raphe**, from which the **transverse palatine folds** run to both sides; in front, behind the incisors, is the **incisive papilla**.

The **soft palate** (*palatum molle*) is the posterior 1/3 of the palate; its basis is formed by the **palatine aponeurosis** and muscles, covered on both sides by mucosa. Its posterior part hangs down to form the **velum palatinum** (*velum palatinum*), with the **uvula** (*uvula*) in the middle. From the edges of the velum two pairs of arches descend: the anterior — the **palatoglossal arch** (to the root of the tongue), and the posterior — the **palatopharyngeal arch** (to the lateral wall of the pharynx). The **palatine tonsil** lies in the **tonsillar fossa** between the arches. The velum, the palatoglossal arches and the root of the tongue bound the **isthmus of the fauces** (*isthmus faucium*).

parts.text: **Cleft palate** ("wolf's mouth," *palatoschisis*) is failure of the palatine processes to fuse during fetal life; it often occurs together with **cleft lip** ("harelip"). In the infant, sucking is impaired and milk passes into the nose, and later speech is disturbed; it is corrected surgically. When the **vagus nerve** is injured, the soft palate droops on that side, and on saying "ah" the uvula deviates **toward the healthy side**.

blocks.text: The **teeth** (*dentes*) lie in the dental sockets (alveoli) of the maxilla and mandible and take part in biting and grinding food and in producing speech sounds. A tooth is attached to its alveolus by a **gomphosis** (dentoalveolar joint) by means of the **periodontium**. Each tooth has a **crown** (*corona dentis*) — the part visible in the oral cavity, a **neck** (*cervix dentis*) — the narrowing surrounded by the gum, and a **root** (*radix dentis*, 1–3). Inside the crown is the **pulp cavity**, which continues into the **root canal** and opens by a foramen at the root apex; the cavity is filled by the **pulp**, rich in blood vessels and nerves.

The main substance of a tooth is **dentin**; the dentin of the crown is covered by **enamel** (the hardest tissue in the body, ≈96% mineral), and that of the root by **cementum**. The crown has **lingual**, **vestibular** (labial or buccal), **contact** (facing neighboring teeth) and **occlusal (masticatory)** surfaces.

Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: Adults have **32 permanent teeth**. Their arrangement is expressed by the **dental formula** — the teeth in one half of a jaw from the midline: **2 · 1 · 2 · 3** (incisors, canine, premolars, molars). Children have **20 deciduous teeth**, with no premolars: the formula is **2 · 1 · 0 · 2**. Deciduous teeth resemble permanent ones but are smaller, with bluish-white enamel and short roots spread widely to the sides (the bud of the permanent tooth lies between them). The third molar — the **wisdom tooth** — erupts last (at 16–25 years) or may not erupt at all.

blocks.text: **Development.** The teeth develop from **ectoderm** (enamel) and **mesenchyme** (dentin, pulp, cementum, periodontium). In the 7th week of fetal life the epithelium of the jaw processes thickens to form the **dental lamina**, from which the **enamel organs** grow out; the mesenchyme forms the **dental papilla** (the source of dentin and pulp). The buds of the deciduous teeth and most permanent teeth appear during fetal life; the crowns of the deciduous teeth begin to calcify in the second half of fetal life. Deciduous teeth begin to erupt at **6–8 months** and number 20 by **2–2.5 years**; from **6–7 years** permanent teeth begin to replace them. The first permanent tooth is the **first molar** (at 6 years, behind the deciduous teeth, not in place of any deciduous tooth).

parts.text: Tooth eruption is an indicator of a child's **biological age** and development: in a child under 1 year, the number of deciduous teeth can be roughly estimated by the formula **(age in months − 4)**. Late eruption is seen in rickets, hypothyroidism and other diseases. **Caries** is demineralization of the enamel and dentin; if the process reaches the pulp — **pulpitis** (severe pain); if it extends beyond the root apex — **periodontitis**; and because the roots of the upper molars lie close to the maxillary sinus, **odontogenic maxillary sinusitis** may develop.

blocks.text: The **tongue** (*lingua*, Greek *glossa*) is a mobile organ built of striated muscles and covered by mucosa; it takes part in mixing and swallowing food, taste and speech. The tongue has a **tip** (*apex*), **body** (*corpus*) and **root** (*radix*), an upper surface — the **dorsum of the tongue** (*dorsum linguae*), an inferior surface and **margins**. Along the dorsum runs the **median sulcus**, and at the junction of the body and root the V-shaped **terminal sulcus** (*sulcus terminalis*); at its apex lies the **foramen cecum of the tongue** (*foramen caecum*) — a remnant of the embryonic thyroglossal duct.

blocks.text: The mucosa of the root of the tongue has no papillae — there lies an aggregation of lymphoid nodules, the **lingual tonsil**. From the root of the tongue the **median and lateral glossoepiglottic folds** pass to the epiglottis; between them are the epiglottic valleculae. On the inferior surface of the tongue, in the midline, is the **frenulum of the tongue** (*frenulum linguae*), on either side of it the **sublingual papillae** (where the ducts of the submandibular and sublingual glands open) and the backward-running **sublingual folds**.

Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **lingual septum** divides the tongue along the midline into two symmetrical halves. The muscles of the tongue are divided into two groups. The **intrinsic muscles** (arising and ending within the tongue) — the **superior and inferior longitudinal**, **transverse** and **vertical** muscles — change the shape of the tongue (shorten, narrow and flatten it, raise or lower its tip). The **extrinsic muscles** (arising from bone) change the position of the tongue: the **genioglossus** (*m. genioglossus*) draws the tongue forward and downward (protrudes it), the **hyoglossus** (*m. hyoglossus*) backward and downward, and the **styloglossus** (*m. styloglossus*) backward and upward. All the muscles of the tongue (except the palatoglossus) are supplied by the **hypoglossal nerve** (XII).

blocks.label: Figure 16.8
blocks.caption: Muscles of the tongue (A — inferior view; B — lateral view; Figure No. 13): genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus, palatoglossus, inferior longitudinal muscle, hyoid bone and mandible. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: Innervation of the tongue: **motor** — hypoglossal nerve (XII); **general sensation** — anterior 2/3 by the lingual nerve (V~3~), posterior 1/3 by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX); **taste** — anterior 2/3 by the chorda tympani of the facial nerve (VII), posterior 1/3 by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX), the most posterior part of the root and the epiglottis by the vagus nerve (X). With unilateral injury of the hypoglossal nerve, the protruded tongue deviates **toward the injured side** (the healthy genioglossus pushes the tongue from its own side).

blocks.text: The **minor salivary glands** (1–5 mm) lie in the mucosa and submucosa: the **labial**, **buccal**, **palatine** and **lingual** glands. By the nature of their secretion the glands are **serous** (protein-rich fluid), **mucous** and **mixed**. The **major salivary glands** — three pairs — lie outside the oral cavity, but their ducts open into the mouth. 1–1.5 L of saliva is secreted per day.

parts.text: **Epidemic parotitis** (mumps) is a viral infection with painful swelling of the parotid glands; because the gland lies within a dense fascial capsule, the swelling is very painful; complications — orchitis, pancreatitis, meningitis. **Sialolithiasis** (salivary stone disease) occurs most often in the duct of the **submandibular gland** (the duct is long and ascending, and its secretion thicker): the gland swells and hurts during meals. In operations on the parotid gland there is a risk of injuring the **facial nerve**, which passes through the gland.

blocks.text: The **pharynx** (*pharynx*) is an unpaired funnel-shaped organ **12–14 cm** long where the digestive and respiratory tracts cross. Above it is attached to the cranial base (the **vault of the pharynx**), and below, at the level of the **6th–7th cervical vertebrae**, it passes into the esophagus. Behind it lie the prevertebral muscles and fascia (with the **retropharyngeal space** between them), and at the sides the neurovascular bundle of the neck. According to the organs in front of it, it has three parts:

items: The **nasal part** (*pars nasalis*, nasopharynx) — between the vault and the soft palate; in front it communicates with the nasal cavity through the choanae; on its lateral walls lie the **pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube** (connecting it with the middle ear) and the **torus tubarius** above it; at the junction of the vault and posterior wall — the **pharyngeal tonsil** (adenoids), around the tubal opening — the **tubal tonsils**.

The **oral part** (*pars oralis*, oropharynx) — between the soft palate and the laryngeal inlet; it opens into the oral cavity through the isthmus of the fauces; here the respiratory and digestive tracts cross.

The **laryngeal part** (*pars laryngea*, laryngopharynx) — from the laryngeal inlet to the esophagus; in its anterior wall is the laryngeal inlet, and on either side of it the **piriform recesses** (where foreign bodies can become lodged).

blocks.label: Figure 16.10
blocks.caption: Parts of the pharynx, posterior wall opened (Figure No. 24): pharyngeal tonsil, torus tubarius, pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube, salpingopharyngeal fold, soft palate and uvula, palatopharyngeal arch, epiglottis, laryngeal inlet, piriform recesses, esophagus. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **wall of the pharynx** consists of a mucosa (pseudostratified ciliated epithelium in the nasal part, stratified squamous in the lower parts), the dense **pharyngobasilar fascia** in place of the submucosa (which above anchors the pharynx to the cranial base), a muscular coat and an adventitia. The **muscles** are striated: the **constrictors** — superior, middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictors (meeting at the pharyngeal raphe in the posterior wall; contracting in sequence from above downward, they push the bolus into the esophagus) — and the **elevators** — the stylopharyngeus and palatopharyngeus (raise the pharynx during swallowing). The pharyngeal muscles are supplied mainly by the **pharyngeal plexus** (IX, X).

blocks.label: Figure 16.11
blocks.caption: Muscles of the pharynx, posterior view (Figure No. 25): 1 — pharyngeal raphe; 2 — greater horn of the hyoid bone; 3 — stylopharyngeus; 4 — stylohyoid; 5 — posterior belly of the digastric; 6 — superior pharyngeal constrictor; 7 — pharyngobasilar fascia; 8 — accessory muscle bundle; 9 — deep part of the masseter; 10 — superficial part of the masseter; 11 — medial pterygoid; 12 — middle constrictor; 13 — inferior constrictor. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: In the **act of swallowing** the tongue pushes the bolus through the isthmus of the fauces into the pharynx; the soft palate rises, separating off the nasal part of the pharynx; the pharynx and larynx rise, and the **epiglottis** closes the laryngeal inlet; the constrictor muscles pass the bolus into the esophagus.

The **Pirogov–Waldeyer lymphoepithelial ring** consists of aggregations of lymphoid tissue encircling, like a ring, the entrance into the pharynx from the oral and nasal cavities: **two paired** — the **palatine tonsils** and **tubal tonsils**, and **two unpaired** — the **pharyngeal tonsil** and **lingual tonsil**. They act as the first immune barrier against antigens entering the respiratory and digestive tracts.

parts.text: Enlargement of the pharyngeal tonsil in children — **adenoids** — makes nasal breathing difficult (mouth open, "adenoid face") and, by blocking the opening of the auditory tube, causes frequent **otitis**. **Tonsillitis** (angina) is inflammation of the palatine tonsils; its complications are **peritonsillar abscess** and **retropharyngeal abscess**; from the latter pus can descend into the mediastinum. Foreign bodies such as fish bones become lodged in the piriform recesses.

items: In the newborn there are no teeth and the alveolar processes are poorly developed, so the oral cavity is small and its vestibule is a narrow slit; after the teeth erupt (infancy and early childhood) the oral cavity enlarges considerably. The gums bear ridges at the sites of the future teeth.

The newborn's lips are thick, with transverse ridges on their inner surface and a tubercle in the middle of the upper lip — adaptations for suckling; the orbicularis oris is well developed. The **buccal fat pad** is well developed in the newborn — it stiffens the cheek and prevents the oral wall from being sucked inward during suckling.

In the newborn the hard palate is broad and flat, without a noticeable vault; the soft palate lies horizontally and does not touch the posterior wall of the pharynx — the baby can breathe freely while suckling. The length of the palate is 3.9 cm in the newborn, 5.2 cm at 5 months and 7.9 cm at 20 years.

The newborn's tongue is short, broad and thick, filling the oral cavity; the fungiform, foliate and vallate papillae and taste buds are well developed, the filiform papillae few; the frenulum is short. The tongue muscles are well developed because they take an active part in suckling.

In the newborn the parotid gland is relatively large (≈1.8 g); salivation increases from 2–3 months ("physiological drooling" — the baby cannot yet swallow saliva); the gland grows rapidly from 4 months to 2 years (≈9 g) and reaches 30 g by 20 years. The sublingual gland weighs ≈0.4 g in the newborn.

The newborn's pharynx is wide and short (≈3 cm long), funnel-shaped, with a thin wall; its lower border lies at the level of the 3rd–4th cervical vertebrae (6th–7th in adults). The vault is not apparent. The pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube is slit-like, patent and close to the hard palate, and the torus tubarius is undeveloped — infection passes easily into the middle ear; by 12–14 years the opening becomes round.

In the newborn the oral part of the pharynx is very short (≈0.5 cm) and the laryngeal part relatively long; the epiglottis stands high — this allows the baby to suckle (swallow) and breathe at the same time.
The tonsils are poorly developed in the newborn; they enlarge from 1–2 years, are largest at 4–7 years (adenoids are common at this age), and gradually involute after puberty.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: The mother of a 9-month-old baby is worried that not a single tooth has erupted yet. The baby has softness of the skull bones, a widely open anterior fontanelle, a "rachitic rosary" on the ribs and excessive sweating.
cases.ask: When and in what order do the deciduous teeth normally begin to erupt? With what disease may this condition be associated?
cases.answer: Normally the deciduous teeth erupt from **6–8 months**, beginning with the **lower central incisors**, then the upper central and lateral incisors (7–10 months), first molars (12–21 months), canines (15–20 months) and second molars (21–30 months); by **2–2.5 years** there are 20 deciduous teeth (formula 2·1·0·2). The absence of teeth at 9 months and the bone changes noted are signs of **rickets** (vitamin D deficiency); late tooth eruption is also seen in hypothyroidism. The child should be examined by a pediatrician.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: An 8-year-old child always keeps the mouth open, snores at night, has difficulty breathing through the nose, and often complains of earache and reduced hearing. On examination the face is elongated and the upper lip short.
cases.ask: Which lymphoid structure is enlarged? Why are ear diseases common? Which ring does this structure belong to?
cases.answer: The **pharyngeal tonsil** (adenoids) is enlarged. It lies in the **nasal part** of the pharynx, at the junction of the vault and posterior wall; when enlarged it blocks the choanae, making nasal breathing difficult, and covers the **pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube** on the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, impairing ventilation of the middle ear — resulting in otitis and reduced hearing. The pharyngeal tonsil is part of the **Pirogov–Waldeyer lymphoepithelial ring** (the paired palatine and tubal tonsils and the unpaired pharyngeal and lingual tonsils).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 35-year-old patient complains that every time he eats, a painful swelling appears under the left side of the mandible and gradually subsides after the meal. A hard mass is palpable in the floor of the mouth in the region of the left sublingual papilla.
cases.ask: Which gland and duct are affected? Why does this disease occur so often in precisely this gland?
cases.answer: This is a **stone in the duct of the left submandibular gland** (sialolithiasis). The gland lies in the submandibular triangle; its **Wharton's duct** runs forward along the floor of the mouth and opens on the **sublingual papilla**. During meals salivation increases, and because the stone blocks the duct, the gland swells and becomes painful. Sialolithiasis occurs mainly in this gland because its duct is long and ascending (saliva flows against gravity), and its secretion is mixed — thicker and rich in calcium.

topics.title: The esophagus. General information on the abdominal organs. The stomach. The small and large intestines: structure, differences, age-related changes

goals.text: To teach the student the structure, parts, topography, features of the wall layers, development and age-related changes of the esophagus, stomach, small and large intestines; to explain the regions of the abdominal cavity and the projection of its organs, the features distinguishing the small and large intestines, and their clinical significance.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the boundaries of the abdominal cavity and the regions of the anterior abdominal wall;
the parts, constrictions, topography and wall structure of the esophagus;
the parts, wall, glands, shapes, skeletotopy and syntopy of the stomach;
the parts of the duodenum and the ducts opening into it;
the differences between the jejunum and ileum and the structure of the small intestinal mucosa;
the parts of the large intestine and the external features distinguishing it from the small intestine;
the structure of the cecum, vermiform appendix and rectum;
the development and age-related features of these organs.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: draw the regions on the anterior abdominal wall and show the projection of the organs;
distinguish the small and large intestines on a specimen by their external features;
find the parts of the stomach, duodenum and large intestine in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
show the projection of the base of the appendix onto the abdominal wall (McBurney's point).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The constrictions of the esophagus are the sites where **foreign bodies become lodged**, **cicatricial strictures after chemical burns** and **cancer** occur most often; they are also taken into account when passing an endoscope (esophagoscope) (the distance from the incisors to the cardia is ≈40 cm). In its lower part the **esophageal veins** anastomose with the portal vein through the gastric veins — in cirrhosis of the liver they become varicose and are a source of dangerous bleeding (see topic 30).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Gastric ulcers** are most often located on the **lesser curvature** and in the pyloric part; when an ulcer of the posterior wall perforates it may penetrate into the pancreas (penetration), and an ulcer of the lesser curvature may be complicated by bleeding from the left gastric artery. **Pyloric stenosis** is congenital thickening of the muscle of the pyloric sphincter in infants (most often boys aged 2–6 weeks): "projectile" vomiting after feeds, and an "olive"-like mass is palpable in the epigastric region; it is treated surgically (pyloromyotomy).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Meckel's diverticulum** is a remnant of the embryonic **vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct** (connecting the umbilicus with the gut); it occurs in ≈2% of people, in the ileum ≈60–100 cm above the cecum, on the antimesenteric wall. Its inflammation (diverticulitis) mimics appendicitis; if it contains gastric mucosa it causes ulceration and bleeding. Therefore, at an operation for appendicitis, if the appendix is found unchanged, the ileum is examined. **Duodenal ulcers** are located in the **duodenal bulb** in ≈95% of cases.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Acute appendicitis** is the most common surgical emergency. The base of the appendix projects onto the anterior abdominal wall at **McBurney's point** — at the junction of the lateral and middle thirds of the line joining the umbilicus with the right anterior superior iliac spine. Depending on the position of the appendix, the pain is felt in different places: with a retrocecal position — in the lower back; with a pelvic position — above the pubis (with disturbed urination); in pregnant women — higher up. In children the greater omentum is short and thin, so the inflammation is not walled off and **peritonitis** develops rapidly.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The **rectal venous plexus** lies in the submucosa of the anal canal; its varicose dilation is **hemorrhoids**. Above the pectinate line sensation is visceral (painless), below it somatic (very painful) — so internal hemorrhoids and intestinal cancer are painless, while anal fissures are very painful. **Digital rectal examination** (per rectum) allows assessment of the prostate, the cervix of the uterus and the lower part of the ampulla. In children the rectal mucosa is loosely attached, so **rectal prolapse** is common.

sections.title: 1. The abdominal cavity and the abdominal regions

blocks.text: The **abdominal cavity** (*cavitas abdominis*) is bounded above by the diaphragm, behind by the lumbar part of the vertebral column, the quadratus lumborum and psoas major, and in front and at the sides by the abdominal muscles; below it continues into the cavity of the lesser pelvis. The walls of the cavity are lined internally by the **endoabdominal fascia** and the **parietal peritoneum**. The relation of the organs to the peritoneum is considered in later topics (topic 19).

The anterior abdominal wall is divided by two horizontal lines — the **subcostal (intercostal) line** (joining the lowest points of the 10th ribs) and the **interspinous line** (joining the anterior superior iliac spines) — into three tiers, and by two vertical lines (along the lateral borders of the recti) into **9 regions**.

blocks.text: The **esophagus** (*oesophagus*) is a muscular tube flattened anteroposteriorly, **25–30 cm** long; it carries the bolus from the pharynx to the stomach. It begins as the continuation of the pharynx at the level of the **6th–7th cervical vertebrae** and passes into the stomach at the level of the **10th–11th thoracic vertebrae** (on the left). It has three parts: the **cervical part** (C~VI~–T~II~; in front — the trachea, at the sides — the recurrent laryngeal nerves and common carotid arteries), the **thoracic part** (the longest; in the posterior mediastinum, in front of the vertebral column, behind the trachea down to the 4th thoracic vertebra, then crossed by the aortic arch and the left main bronchus; in its lower part the vagus nerves lie — the left in front, the right behind) and the **abdominal part** (1–3 cm; passing through the diaphragm, it enters the stomach behind the left lobe of the liver).

blocks.text: **Wall**: the mucosa is covered by **stratified squamous epithelium**, with a well-developed muscularis mucosae and esophageal glands; because of the well-developed submucosa it forms **longitudinal folds** (the lumen is star-shaped in cross-section); the **muscular coat** has inner circular and outer longitudinal layers — striated in the upper 1/3, mixed in the middle 1/3 and smooth in the lower 1/3; the outer layer is an **adventitia** (only the abdominal part is covered by peritoneum).

blocks.label: Figure 17.1
blocks.caption: Cross-section of the esophagus: 1 — adventitia; 2 — longitudinal layer of the muscular coat; 3 — circular layer; 4 — submucosa; 5 — mucosa; 6 — epithelium; 7 — lumen of the esophagus; 8 — mucosal folds. Source: A. Ahmedov et al. Anatomy, vol. I, 2018.

parts.text: The constrictions of the esophagus are the sites where **foreign bodies become lodged**, **cicatricial strictures after chemical burns** and **cancer** occur most often; they are also taken into account when passing an endoscope (esophagoscope) (the distance from the incisors to the cardia is ≈40 cm). In its lower part the **esophageal veins** anastomose with the portal vein through the gastric veins — in cirrhosis of the liver they become varicose and are a source of dangerous bleeding (see topic 30).

blocks.text: The **stomach** (*gaster, ventriculus*) is the widest part of the alimentary canal; it lies in the upper part of the abdominal cavity below the diaphragm and liver: **3/4 in the left hypochondrium** and **1/4 in the epigastric region**. It has **anterior and posterior walls**, a **lesser curvature** facing upward and to the right, and a **greater curvature** facing downward and to the left. On the lesser curvature, at the junction of the body and the pyloric part, is the **angular notch**.

items: The **cardiac part** (*pars cardiaca*) — the area around the **cardiac orifice**, where the esophagus opens (T~XI~ on the left).

The **fundus of the stomach** (*fundus gastricus*) — the part rising as a dome to the left of the cardia; in the upright position air collects in it (the "gas bubble" on radiographs); between it and the esophagus is the **cardiac notch**.
The **body of the stomach** (*corpus gastricum*) — the largest part, between the fundus and the pyloric part.

The **pyloric part** (*pars pylorica*) — consisting of the wide **pyloric antrum** and the narrow **pyloric canal**; it opens into the duodenum through the orifice of the **pylorus** (L~I~ on the right).

blocks.label: Figure 17.2
blocks.caption: Parts of the stomach, anterior view (Figure No. 27): 1 — pyloric antrum; 2 — duodenum; 3 — pyloric canal; 4 — angular notch; 5 — lesser curvature; 6 — cardiac part; 7 — esophagus; 8 — fundus; 9 — greater curvature; 10 — body of the stomach. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The capacity of the stomach averages **1.5–3 L**; its length (when empty) is 18–20 cm, and the distance between the curvatures 7–8 cm. **Syntopy**: the anterior wall is in contact with the diaphragm, the left lobe of the liver and the anterior abdominal wall; the posterior wall — through the omental bursa — with the pancreas, the left kidney and suprarenal gland, and the spleen; the greater curvature with the transverse colon. From the lesser curvature the **hepatogastric ligament** passes to the liver, and from the greater curvature the **gastrosplenic** ligament to the spleen and the **gastrocolic ligament** to the transverse colon (greater omentum).

blocks.label: Figure 17.3
blocks.caption: Topography of the stomach (Figure No. 29): the relation of the stomach to the liver, spleen, diaphragm, transverse colon and omenta; the hepatogastric ligament, greater omentum and gastric vessels. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: **Wall of the stomach**: the **mucosa** has simple columnar epithelium; numerous **gastric folds** (the longitudinal folds along the lesser curvature form the **gastric canal** — liquids pass quickly along it), **gastric areas** (1–6 mm) and the **gastric pits** in them, into which the gastric glands open. The glands (≈35 million) are **cardiac**, **proper (fundic)** (in the fundus and body; **chief cells** — pepsinogen; **parietal (oxyntic) cells** — hydrochloric acid and Castle's intrinsic factor, necessary for absorption of vitamin B~12~) and **pyloric** glands (mucus; G cells — gastrin). The **muscular coat** consists of three layers of smooth muscle: outer **longitudinal**, middle **circular** (the strongest; at the pylorus it forms the **pyloric sphincter**) and inner **oblique fibers**. Outside is the **serosa** (the stomach is covered by peritoneum on all sides — intraperitoneal).

blocks.label: Figure 17.4
blocks.caption: The stomach (A — external structure, anterior view; B — muscular coat; Figure No. 30): cardiac part, anterior wall, lesser and greater curvatures, angular notch, pylorus and pyloric canal; in B — the oblique fibers, circular and longitudinal layers. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **shapes of the stomach** (on radiographs) depend on body build: **J-shaped (fishhook)** (the most common, ≈80%, normosthenic), **horn-shaped** (wide and high-lying; hypersthenic, in children and the elderly), **elongated hook (stocking-shaped)** (low-lying; asthenic, more often in women).

parts.text: **Gastric ulcers** are most often located on the **lesser curvature** and in the pyloric part; when an ulcer of the posterior wall perforates it may penetrate into the pancreas (penetration), and an ulcer of the lesser curvature may be complicated by bleeding from the left gastric artery. **Pyloric stenosis** is congenital thickening of the muscle of the pyloric sphincter in infants (most often boys aged 2–6 weeks): "projectile" vomiting after feeds, and an "olive"-like mass is palpable in the epigastric region; it is treated surgically (pyloromyotomy).

blocks.text: The **small intestine** (*intestinum tenue*) is the longest part of the alimentary canal (**2.2–4.4 m** in the living, 5–6 m in the cadaver); it extends from the pylorus to the ileocecal valve. Here food undergoes final digestion under the action of intestinal juice, pancreatic juice and bile, and nutrients are absorbed into the blood and lymph. It has three parts: the **duodenum**, the **jejunum** and the **ileum** (the last two, having a mesentery, are called the **mesenteric part of the small intestine**).

The **duodenum** (*duodenum*) is **25–30 cm** long and lies in a horseshoe shape around the **head of the pancreas** at the level of L~I~–L~III~. Its parts: the **superior part** (4–5 cm; its initial dilated part — the **bulb (ampulla)** — is covered by peritoneum and mobile), the **descending part** (8–10 cm; to the right of L~I~–L~III~), the **horizontal (inferior) part** and the **ascending part** (to the left of L~II~ it forms the **duodenojejunal flexure** and passes into the jejunum; the flexure is suspended from the diaphragm by the **suspensory muscle (ligament) of Treitz**). Except for the bulb, the duodenum is **retroperitoneal**.

On the medial wall of the descending part is a **longitudinal fold**; at its lower end, on the **major papilla** (papilla of Vater), the **common bile duct** and the **main pancreatic duct** open together (surrounded by the sphincter of Oddi); 2–3 cm above it, on the **minor papilla**, the **accessory pancreatic duct** opens. The **duodenal (Brunner's) glands** lie in the submucosa.

blocks.label: Figure 17.5
blocks.caption: The duodenum, opened, internal view (Figure No. 35): circular folds, major and minor papillae, common bile duct, main and accessory pancreatic ducts, pyloric sphincter, head and body of the pancreas, superior mesenteric artery and vein, duodenojejunal flexure. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **jejunum** (*jejunum*, ≈2/5) forms horizontal loops in the upper left part of the abdominal cavity; the **ileum** (*ileum*, ≈3/5) forms vertical loops in the lower right part and enters the cecum in the right iliac fossa. They are suspended from the posterior abdominal wall by the **mesentery** (*mesenterium*); the root of the mesentery (≈15 cm) runs obliquely from the left side of L~II~ to the right sacroiliac joint.

blocks.text: **Wall of the small intestine.** The mucosa has ≈650 **circular folds (of Kerckring)** (up to 8 mm high), ≈4 million **intestinal villi** (0.2–1.2 mm; each containing a central lymphatic capillary — the **lacteal**) and the **intestinal glands (crypts of Lieberkühn)** opening between them; the epithelium is simple columnar, with **brush-border** (microvillous) cells and goblet cells. The folds, villi and microvilli increase the absorptive surface ≈600 times (to ≈200 m²). The mucosa contains **solitary lymphoid nodules** (≈15,000) and **aggregated lymphoid nodules** — **Peyer's patches** (20–30, 2–3 cm, mainly in the ileum, on the antimesenteric wall). The muscular coat has inner circular and outer longitudinal layers; serosa.

blocks.label: Figure 17.6
blocks.caption: The small intestine (A — layers of the wall, reconstruction; B — cross-section; Figure No. 38): mucosa, villi, circular folds, submucosa and its nerve plexus, circular and longitudinal layers of the muscular coat and the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus between them, serosa, mesentery and its blood vessels. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.label: Figure 17.7
blocks.caption: Meckel's diverticulum of the ileum (Figure No. 41): 1 — mesentery of the small intestine; 2 — ileum; 3 — mesentery of the diverticulum; 4 — ileal diverticulum. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: **Meckel's diverticulum** is a remnant of the embryonic **vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct** (connecting the umbilicus with the gut); it occurs in ≈2% of people, in the ileum ≈60–100 cm above the cecum, on the antimesenteric wall. Its inflammation (diverticulitis) mimics appendicitis; if it contains gastric mucosa it causes ulceration and bleeding. Therefore, at an operation for appendicitis, if the appendix is found unchanged, the ileum is examined. **Duodenal ulcers** are located in the **duodenal bulb** in ≈95% of cases.

blocks.text: The **large intestine** (*intestinum crassum*) is the continuation of the small intestine, **1–1.5 m** long, with a diameter ≈2 times that of the small intestine (4–8 cm); it extends from the cecum to the anus. Water and electrolytes are absorbed here and feces are formed; the microflora takes part in the synthesis of vitamins (K, B group). Its parts: the **cecum** (with the vermiform appendix), the **colon** — **ascending**, **transverse**, **descending** and **sigmoid** — and the **rectum**. The large intestine surrounds the loops of the small intestine like a "frame."

No villi; crypts deep, many goblet cells; semilunar folds

blocks.label: Figure 17.8
blocks.caption: The large intestine, anterior view (Figure No. 43): cecum and vermiform appendix, ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, right (hepatic) and left (splenic) colic flexures, teniae, haustra, omental appendices, rectum. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **cecum** (*caecum*) is the initial, widest (7–7.5 cm) and shortest (6–8 cm) part of the large intestine; it lies in the right iliac fossa below the entry of the ileum; it is covered by peritoneum on all sides but has no mesentery. The ileum opens into the cecum through the **ileal orifice**; around the orifice is the **ileocecal valve (Bauhin's valve)**, consisting of upper and lower lips — it prevents the contents of the large intestine from returning into the small intestine. From the posteromedial wall of the cecum, where the teniae converge, arises the **vermiform appendix** (*appendix vermiformis*): 2–20 cm long (on average 8–9 cm), 0.5–1 cm in diameter, with a mesentery (*mesoappendix*); its mucosa contains a great deal of lymphoid tissue (the "intestinal tonsil"). Its position varies: descending (into the pelvis), lateral, medial, anterior and behind the cecum (retrocecal).

blocks.label: Figure 17.9
blocks.caption: Cecum and vermiform appendix, anterior wall of the cecum opened (Figure No. 46): ileal orifice and the upper and lower lips of the ileocecal valve, frenula of the valve, orifice of the appendix, haustra and semilunar folds, teniae, mesoappendix. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: **Acute appendicitis** is the most common surgical emergency. The base of the appendix projects onto the anterior abdominal wall at **McBurney's point** — at the junction of the lateral and middle thirds of the line joining the umbilicus with the right anterior superior iliac spine. Depending on the position of the appendix, the pain is felt in different places: with a retrocecal position — in the lower back; with a pelvic position — above the pubis (with disturbed urination); in pregnant women — higher up. In children the greater omentum is short and thin, so the inflammation is not walled off and **peritonitis** develops rapidly.

blocks.text: The **ascending colon** (15–20 cm) rises in the right lateral region of the abdomen and below the liver forms the **right (hepatic) flexure**; the **transverse colon** (on average 50 cm) is mobile owing to its long mesentery, forms a downward-facing arch and, beside the spleen, passes by the **left (splenic) flexure** into the **descending colon** (10–15 cm); this continues in the left iliac fossa as the **sigmoid colon** (15–67 cm, with a mesentery, mobile), which passes into the rectum at the level of the 3rd sacral vertebra. The ascending and descending colon are **mesoperitoneal** (the posterior wall lacks peritoneum), the transverse and sigmoid colon **intraperitoneal**.

The **rectum** (*rectum*) is the last part of the alimentary canal, **14–18 cm** long; it begins in the lesser pelvis at the 3rd sacral vertebra and ends in the perineum with the **anus**. In the sagittal plane it forms two curves: the **sacral flexure** (convex backward) and the **perineal flexure** (convex forward). Its parts: the wide **ampulla** (pelvic part) and the narrow **anal canal** (perineal part, ≈4 cm). There are no teniae, haustra or omental appendices — the longitudinal muscle layer is continuous. The ampulla has 2–3 **transverse folds** (the largest on the right, ≈6–7 cm above the anus — Kohlrausch's fold), and the anal canal has 6–10 **anal columns** with **anal sinuses** between them; their lower boundary is the **anorectal (pectinate) line**. The circular layer forms the **internal (involuntary) sphincter**; the **external (voluntary) sphincter** is striated and belongs to the perineal muscles. The upper part of the rectum is covered by peritoneum on all sides, the middle part on three sides, and the lower part lies outside the peritoneum.

blocks.label: Figure 17.10
blocks.caption: The rectum (A — its position in the lesser pelvis; B — distal part of the rectum, frontal section; Figure No. 49): ampulla, transverse folds, anal canal, anal columns and sinuses, internal and external sphincters, levator ani, anorectal line. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: The **rectal venous plexus** lies in the submucosa of the anal canal; its varicose dilation is **hemorrhoids**. Above the pectinate line sensation is visceral (painless), below it somatic (very painful) — so internal hemorrhoids and intestinal cancer are painless, while anal fissures are very painful. **Digital rectal examination** (per rectum) allows assessment of the prostate, the cervix of the uterus and the lower part of the ampulla. In children the rectal mucosa is loosely attached, so **rectal prolapse** is common.

blocks.text: In the 4th week of fetal life the primitive gut tube extends from the stomach to the cloaca and has dorsal and ventral mesenteries. The stomach appears as a fusiform dilation and in the **2nd month** rotates **90°** around its longitudinal axis (the left surface faces forward, the right backward), then rotates around an anteroposterior axis to take an oblique position; this is why the left vagus nerve comes to lie on the anterior wall and the right on the posterior wall. In the **5th week** the midgut lengthens rapidly, forming the **intestinal loop** toward the umbilicus; its apex is connected to the yolk sac by the **vitelline duct**. In weeks 6–10 the loop passes into the umbilical cord (**physiological umbilical herniation**), rotates **270°** (counterclockwise) around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery and returns to the abdominal cavity: the cecum lies first below the liver and then descends into the right iliac fossa. Failure of the cecum to descend or a disturbance of rotation causes intestinal obstruction and an unusual position of the appendix.

items: In the newborn the **esophagus** is 10–12 cm long, funnel-shaped, with a lumen of 4–9 mm; its constrictions are not apparent; it begins at the level of the 3rd–4th cervical vertebrae (4th–5th at 2 years, 6th–7th at 15 years). The mucosa is delicate, the glands poorly developed and the muscle layer thin; longitudinal folds appear at 2–3 years; it grows rapidly up to 12–15 years. The cardiac sphincter is poorly developed in the newborn — which is why **regurgitation** is common in infants.

In the newborn the **stomach** lies vertically to the left of the vertebral column; the fundus, cardiac and pyloric parts are poorly defined; it is ≈5 cm long with a capacity of **≈30–50 mL**, ≈80 mL at 10 days, **250–300 mL** at 1 year and 1300–1500 mL at 10–12 years. At 5 months it becomes horizontal; the pyloric part becomes apparent at 4–6 months and the fundus at 10 months; the cardiac part forms by 8 years.

The mucosa of the newborn's stomach is relatively thick with few folds; there are ≈200 thousand gastric pits (≈4 million at 15 years) and ≈0.5 million glands (35 million in adults). Because the glands are immature, little hydrochloric acid and pepsin are secreted. The muscle layer, especially the oblique fibers, is poorly developed; the pyloric sphincter is stronger than the cardiac sphincter.

The **small intestine** is relatively long in the newborn (1.5–3 m): the ratio of intestinal length to body length is **8.3:1** in the newborn, 6:1 at 1 year and 5.4:1 in adults. Periods of rapid growth are 1–3 and 10–15 years. The mucosa is thin and rich in blood vessels, with incompletely developed folds, villi and glands; its permeability is high (antibodies, but also toxins, are easily absorbed). The duodenum is ring-shaped, 7.5–10 cm long, at the level of L~I~; by 12 years its position resembles that of adults.

The **large intestine** is ≈63 cm long in the newborn (83 cm at 1 year, 118 cm at 10 years); the teniae are poorly developed, and haustra (appearing at 6 months) and omental appendices (at 2 years) are absent; they are fully formed by 6–7 years.

In the newborn the **cecum** lies above the iliac wing (it descends into the right iliac fossa by 14 years); the appendix is ≈4–5 cm long and opens by a wide funnel-shaped orifice (hence appendicitis is rare in infants), and its lymphoid tissue is greatest in childhood. The ileocecal valve is poorly developed, and the orifice is round until 1 year.

The **sigmoid colon** is relatively long in the newborn (≈20 cm), with a long mesentery, and lies in the upper part of the abdominal cavity (hence constipation and volvulus are more common in children); at 7 years it descends into the lesser pelvis. The **rectum** in the newborn is cylindrical, 5–6 cm long, with no ampulla or flexures; the ampulla forms in early childhood and the flexures after 8 years.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 19-year-old man presented with pain that began around the umbilicus and after 6 hours shifted to the lower right abdomen, with nausea and a temperature of 37.8 °C. Pressure at the lateral third of the line joining the umbilicus and the right anterior superior iliac spine causes sharp pain.
cases.ask: What disease should be suspected? Why was the pain at first around the umbilicus? Name the positional variants of this organ.
cases.answer: **Acute appendicitis**. The point of tenderness is **McBurney's point**, the projection of the base of the appendix. The initial pain is **visceral** — because the appendix is a midgut derivative, its visceral afferents go to segment T~X~ (the umbilical dermatome); once the inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, the pain becomes **somatic** and is clearly localized in the right iliac region. The appendix arises from the posteromedial wall of the cecum where the teniae converge and may be directed downward (into the pelvis), laterally, medially, anteriorly or behind the cecum (retrocecal) — this changes the clinical picture.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 3-week-old boy has begun "projectile" vomiting after every feed; the vomit contains no bile, and he is losing weight. After feeding, wave-like peristalsis is seen moving from left to right in the epigastric region, and a firm olive-sized mass is palpable below the right costal margin.
cases.ask: Which part of which organ is affected? Why is there no bile in the vomit?
cases.answer: This is **pyloric stenosis** — congenital hypertrophy of the circular muscle layer (pyloric sphincter) in the **pyloric part** of the stomach; the "olive" is the thickened pylorus. Because the obstruction is **at the level of the pylorus**, i.e., **above the major duodenal papilla** where the bile duct opens, there is no bile in the vomit. The strong gastric contractions (peristalsis) are an attempt to overcome the obstruction. Treatment is surgical (pyloromyotomy).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A barium radiographic study showed a wide intestinal shadow forming a "frame" around the edge of the abdominal cavity, with semicircular bulges along its sides; there are flexures at the upper right and left corners; in the center lie narrow loops with serrated edges.
cases.ask: Which intestines are seen on the radiograph? What are the semicircular bulges, and how are they formed?
cases.answer: The wide shadow around the edge is the **large intestine** (cecum, ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon; the flexures are the **right (hepatic)** and **left (splenic)** flexures), and the narrow serrated loops in the center are the **small intestine** (the serrated appearance is given by the circular folds of Kerckring). The semicircular bulges are **haustra**: the longitudinal muscle layer of the large intestine is gathered into three **teniae**, and because the teniae are shorter than the intestine itself, the wall forms sacculations; the grooves between them correspond internally to the semilunar folds.

topics.title: The liver, gallbladder and bile ducts, pancreas: structure, topography, age-related changes

goals.text: To teach the student the external and internal structure, lobes and segments, blood circulation and topography of the large glands of the digestive system — the liver and pancreas — and the structure, development and age-related features of the gallbladder and bile ducts; to explain their clinical significance.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the surfaces, borders, fissures, lobes and ligaments of the liver;
the structures entering and leaving the porta hepatis;
the segmental structure of the liver (8 segments according to Couinaud) and the structure of the lobule;
the skeletotopy and syntopy of the liver;
the parts of the gallbladder and the bile ducts and their sphincters;
the parts, duct, topography and exocrine and endocrine parts of the pancreas;
the development and age-related features of the liver and pancreas.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the structures of the liver, gallbladder, bile ducts and pancreas in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
show the borders of the liver and the projection of the fundus of the gallbladder on the body;
state the arrangement of the structures in the hepatoduodenal ligament.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Clinically, the borders of the liver are determined by **percussion** (Kurlov's method); its enlargement (hepatomegaly) is seen in hepatitis, heart failure and tumors. In **cirrhosis of the liver** the pressure in the portal vein rises (portal hypertension) — fluid accumulates in the abdominal cavity (ascites), the spleen enlarges and the portocaval anastomoses dilate (esophageal varices, "caput medusae") (topic 30). Because the liver tissue is soft and rich in blood, it tears in abdominal injuries, causing severe internal bleeding.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Projection of the fundus of the gallbladder** — the point where the right costal margin crosses the lateral border of the rectus (the tip of the 9th costal cartilage); in acute cholecystitis pressure at this point with deep inspiration is painful (Murphy's sign). In **gallstone disease** a stone may block the cystic duct or common bile duct, causing **jaundice**; lodged at the major papilla, it may make bile reflux into the pancreatic duct (because of the common ampulla), causing **acute pancreatitis**. In cholecystectomy the cystic artery is found in Calot's triangle (between the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the visceral surface of the liver).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: A **tumor of the head of the pancreas** compresses the common bile duct, causing painless, progressively increasing **obstructive jaundice** and an enlarged, painless gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign). Because the gland lies posteriorly, in **pancreatitis** the pain radiates to the back ("girdle pain"). The superior mesenteric vessels passing through the notch of the gland and the portal vein behind it are considered the most dangerous area in surgery (pancreaticoduodenectomy).

sections.title: 1. The liver: general information and external structure

blocks.text: The **liver** (*hepar*, Greek *hepar*) is the **largest gland** in the body: in adults it weighs **≈1.5 kg** (≈2–3% of body weight), is reddish-brown and of soft consistency. It is a multifunctional organ: it produces **bile** (0.5–1 L per day), takes part in the metabolism of proteins (albumin, clotting factors), glycogen and lipids, **detoxifies harmful substances** (barrier function), stores glycogen, vitamins and iron, and in the fetus **forms blood**.

The liver has two surfaces: the **diaphragmatic surface** — smooth, convex, facing forward and upward, matching the dome of the diaphragm; and the **visceral surface** (facing the viscera) — uneven, facing downward and backward, bearing impressions of neighboring organs. In front the surfaces are separated by the sharp **inferior border** (with the notch for the gallbladder and the notch for the round ligament). The sagittally running **falciform ligament** on the diaphragmatic surface divides the liver into the **right** (larger) and **left** lobes; in its free lower edge lies the obliterated umbilical vein — the **round ligament of the liver**. Behind, the peritoneum forms the frontally running **coronary ligament**, whose ends are the **right and left triangular ligaments**. The area between the layers of the coronary ligament not covered by peritoneum — the **bare area** (*area nuda*) — adheres directly to the diaphragm.

blocks.label: Figure 18.1
blocks.caption: The liver (A — diaphragmatic surface; B — visceral surface; Figure No. 52): right and left lobes, quadrate and caudate lobes, falciform, coronary, right and left triangular ligaments, bare area, round ligament and ligamentum venosum, groove for the inferior vena cava, porta hepatis with the portal vein, proper hepatic artery and bile ducts, gallbladder, fibrous appendix of the liver. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: On the **visceral surface** there are three grooves arranged in the shape of the letter "H". The **left sagittal groove** contains in its anterior part the **fissure for the round ligament** and in its posterior part the **fissure for the ligamentum venosum** (the remnant of the fetal ductus venosus of Arantius); it marks the border of the left lobe. The **right sagittal groove** forms in its anterior part the **fossa for the gallbladder** and in its posterior part the **groove for the inferior vena cava**. They are connected by the transverse groove — the **porta hepatis** (*porta hepatis*). The grooves separate two additional lobes from the right lobe: in front — the **quadrate lobe** (in front of the porta), behind — the **caudate lobe** (behind the porta, with its caudate and papillary processes).

blocks.title: Table 18.1. Structures passing through the porta hepatis
head: Enter
Leave
rows: **Portal vein** (*v. portae hepatis*) — venous blood rich in nutrients from the unpaired abdominal organs (≈75% of the blood reaching the liver)
**Common hepatic duct** (formed by the union of the right and left hepatic ducts)
**Proper hepatic artery** (*a. hepatica propria*) — oxygen-rich blood (≈25%)

blocks.text: These structures lie between the layers of the **hepatoduodenal ligament**: on the right — the **common bile duct**, on the left — the **proper hepatic artery**, and between and behind them — the **portal vein** (mnemonic from the Latin initials: **D**uctus — right, **A**rteria — left, **V**ena — behind, "DAV"). The **hepatic veins** (3–4 large ones), by contrast, do not leave through the porta but drain directly from the posterior surface of the liver into the **inferior vena cava**.

blocks.label: Figure 18.2
blocks.caption: Visceral surface of the liver (A — blood vessels and gallbladder preserved; B — blood vessels and gallbladder removed; Figure No. 53): gastric, esophageal, duodenal, colic, renal and suprarenal impressions; omental tuberosity, caudate and papillary processes, inferior vena cava, hepatic veins. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

sections.title: 2. Internal structure and blood circulation of the liver

blocks.text: The liver is covered externally by peritoneum (serosa; except for the bare area — it is a **mesoperitoneal** organ) and beneath it by a thin, strong **fibrous capsule** (Glisson's capsule). At the porta the fibrous capsule enters the liver together with the vessels and bile ducts, dividing it into lobes, segments and lobules.

**Segmental structure.** According to the branching of the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile ducts (C. Couinaud, 1957), the liver has **2 lobes**, **5 sectors** and **8 segments**. Each segment is supplied by a 3rd-order branch of the portal vein and the corresponding branches of the artery and bile duct, and is relatively independent — this allows **segmental resection** (removal of only the affected segment of the liver). The border between the functional right and left lobes does not run along the falciform ligament but along a plane passing through the **gallbladder fossa and the inferior vena cava** (Cantlie's line).

Segments

V — right anterior medial; VI — right anterior lateral; VII — right posterior lateral; VIII — right posterior medial

blocks.label: Figure 18.3
blocks.caption: Arrangement of the lobes and segments of the liver on the diaphragmatic (A) and visceral (B) surfaces (Figure No. 54). The segments are marked with Roman numerals; labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **hepatic lobule** (*lobulus hepatis*) is the structural-functional unit of the liver: a hexagonal prism 1–2.5 mm in diameter; there are ≈500 thousand in the liver. In the center of the lobule lies the **central vein**, from which the **hepatic plates (cords)** — double rows of **hepatocytes** — radiate. Between the cords are **sinusoidal capillaries** (with Kupffer cells — macrophages — in their walls). At the boundaries of the lobules, where their edges meet, lie the **portal areas (triads)**: the **interlobular vein** (a branch of the portal vein), the **interlobular artery** and the **interlobular bile duct**. The **bile canaliculi** between the rows of hepatocytes carry bile to the periphery of the lobule — to the interlobular bile ducts.

blocks.label: Figure 18.4
blocks.caption: Structure of the liver, diagram (Figure No. 57): the hepatic lobule surrounded by portal areas; the portal areas are occupied by the artery, vein and bile ducts; in the center of the lobule — the central vein, sinusoidal capillaries, sublobular vein (after L.C. Junqueira, J. Carneiro). Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **blood circulation of the liver** is peculiar: blood reaches the liver from two sources and leaves by one route. Portal vein → segmental veins → interlobular veins → perilobular veins → **sinusoidal capillaries** (into which blood from the interlobular arteries also flows — mixed blood) → **central vein** → sublobular (collecting) veins → **hepatic veins** → inferior vena cava. Because the portal system has two capillary networks (in the intestinal wall and in the hepatic sinusoids), it is called the **wonderful venous network (rete mirabile) of the liver**. Bile flows in the direction opposite to the blood — from the center of the lobule to its periphery.

blocks.label: Figure 18.5
blocks.caption: Blood supply of the hepatic lobule (Figure No. 60): 1 — segmental vein and artery; 2 — portal vein; 3 — hepatic artery; 4 — interlobular vein and artery; 5 — perilobular vein and artery; 6 — sinusoidal capillary; 7 — central vein; 8 — hepatic lobule; 9 — sublobular (collecting) vein; 10 — hepatic vein. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The liver lies mainly in the **right hypochondrium** and **epigastric** regions, and partly in the left hypochondrium; normally it does not project below the costal margin. **Skeletotopy**: its upper border is at the **4th intercostal space** (or 5th rib) in the right midclavicular line and at the 10th intercostal space in the right midaxillary line; on the left, at the 5th intercostal space in the parasternal line. Its lower border is at the 10th rib in the right midaxillary line, then runs along the **right costal margin**, leaves the margin at the junction of the 9th and 10th costal cartilages, crosses the epigastric region obliquely (in the midline, halfway between the xiphoid process and the umbilicus) and returns to the margin on the left at the junction of the 7th and 8th costal cartilages.

**Syntopy**: the diaphragmatic surface is in contact with the diaphragm (and through it with the right lung and pleura and the heart); the visceral surface with the **stomach** (left lobe), the **duodenum**, the **right kidney** and **suprarenal gland**, the **right colic flexure** (right lobe) and the **abdominal part of the esophagus**. From the liver arise the **hepatogastric** and **hepatoduodenal** ligaments (together — the **lesser omentum**) and the **hepatorenal ligament**.

parts.text: Clinically, the borders of the liver are determined by **percussion** (Kurlov's method); its enlargement (hepatomegaly) is seen in hepatitis, heart failure and tumors. In **cirrhosis of the liver** the pressure in the portal vein rises (portal hypertension) — fluid accumulates in the abdominal cavity (ascites), the spleen enlarges and the portocaval anastomoses dilate (esophageal varices, "caput medusae") (topic 30). Because the liver tissue is soft and rich in blood, it tears in abdominal injuries, causing severe internal bleeding.

blocks.text: The **gallbladder** (*vesica biliaris (fellea)*) is a pear-shaped organ in which bile collects and is concentrated; it lies in the gallbladder fossa on the visceral surface of the liver. It is **8–12 cm** long, 4–5 cm wide and has a capacity of **40–70 mL**. Its parts: the **fundus** (projecting below the inferior border of the liver and touching the anterior abdominal wall), the **body** and the **neck** (facing the porta, through the infundibulum), which continues into the **cystic duct**. Its wall consists of a mucosa (folds; in the neck and cystic duct a **spiral fold** — Heister's valve), a smooth muscle coat and a serosa (on its inferior surface) or adventitia.

**Bile ducts**: bile canaliculi → interlobular bile ducts → **right and left hepatic ducts** → (uniting at the porta) **common hepatic duct** (4–5 cm) + **cystic duct** (3–4 cm) → **common bile duct** (*ductus choledochus*, 6–8 cm, 5–8 mm in diameter). The common bile duct descends in the hepatoduodenal ligament, behind the superior part of the duodenum and behind (or within) the head of the pancreas, joins the **pancreatic duct**, forming the **hepatopancreatic ampulla**, and opens on the **major papilla** in the descending part of the duodenum.

blocks.label: Figure 18.6
blocks.caption: Gallbladder and duodenum (Figure No. 61): 1 — descending part of the duodenum; 2 — major papilla; 3 — fundus of the gallbladder; 4 — minor papilla; 5 — body of the gallbladder; 6 — infundibulum of the gallbladder; 7 — neck of the gallbladder; 8 — cystic duct; 9 — right hepatic duct; 10 — left hepatic duct; 11 — common hepatic duct; 12 — superior part of the duodenum; 13 — common bile duct; 14 — accessory pancreatic duct; 15 — pancreatic duct; 16 — horizontal part of the duodenum. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: Bile flow is regulated by **sphincters**: the **sphincter of the common bile duct** (Boyden's), the **sphincter of the pancreatic duct** and the **sphincter of the ampulla** (the **sphincter of Oddi**). Between meals they are closed, and the bile continuously produced by the liver collects in the gallbladder through the cystic duct; when food (especially fatty food) enters the duodenum, the gallbladder contracts under the action of cholecystokinin, the sphincters open and bile flows into the intestine.

blocks.label: Figure 18.7

parts.text: **Projection of the fundus of the gallbladder** — the point where the right costal margin crosses the lateral border of the rectus (the tip of the 9th costal cartilage); in acute cholecystitis pressure at this point with deep inspiration is painful (Murphy's sign). In **gallstone disease** a stone may block the cystic duct or common bile duct, causing **jaundice**; lodged at the major papilla, it may make bile reflux into the pancreatic duct (because of the common ampulla), causing **acute pancreatitis**. In cholecystectomy the cystic artery is found in Calot's triangle (between the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the visceral surface of the liver).

blocks.text: The **pancreas** (*pancreas*) is the second largest of the digestive glands; it is grayish-pink and lobulated, **14–18 cm** long and weighs **≈70–80 g**. It is a **mixed gland**: its **exocrine** part produces 1.5–2 L of **pancreatic juice** per day (trypsin, lipase, amylase and other enzymes, bicarbonates); its **endocrine** part — ≈1 million **islets of Langerhans** — secretes insulin, glucagon and somatostatin (topic 24).

The gland lies transversely behind the stomach on the posterior wall of the abdominal cavity at the level of **L~I~–L~II~**; the peritoneum covers only its anterior and partly its inferior surface (a **retroperitoneal** organ). Its parts: the **head** (L~I~–L~III~, within the "horseshoe" of the duodenum; below it the **uncinate process**), the **neck** (the junction of the head and body; behind it the superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein unite to form the **portal vein**; at its lower edge is the **notch** — through which the superior mesenteric artery and vein pass), the **body** (three-sided; anterosuperior, posterior and anteroinferior surfaces; on the anterosuperior surface the **omental tuberosity**) and the **tail** (reaching the hilum of the spleen).

blocks.text: **Syntopy**: in front — the **stomach** (through the omental bursa); behind — the **inferior vena cava**, **aorta**, **celiac plexus**, left kidney and suprarenal gland, and left renal vein; along its upper border runs the **splenic artery**, and on its posterior surface the **splenic vein**; the duodenum embraces its head; its tail touches the spleen. The **main pancreatic duct** (duct of Wirsung) runs through the whole gland from the tail to the head, joins the common bile duct and opens on the **major papilla**; the **accessory duct** (duct of Santorini), arising from the upper part of the head, opens on the **minor papilla**.

Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: A **tumor of the head of the pancreas** compresses the common bile duct, causing painless, progressively increasing **obstructive jaundice** and an enlarged, painless gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign). Because the gland lies posteriorly, in **pancreatitis** the pain radiates to the back ("girdle pain"). The superior mesenteric vessels passing through the notch of the gland and the portal vein behind it are considered the most dangerous area in surgery (pancreaticoduodenectomy).

blocks.text: The **liver** appears in the 3rd–4th week of fetal life as an endodermal outgrowth from the ventral wall of the foregut (the future duodenum) — the **hepatic diverticulum**. From its cranial part develop the **hepatic cords** and hepatic ducts, from its caudal part the **gallbladder** and cystic duct, and from the base of the common outgrowth the **common bile duct**. The liver bud grows into the mesenchyme of the ventral mesentery and the septum transversum; the ventral mesentery remains as the **lesser omentum** and the **falciform ligament**. The hepatic cords surround the vitelline and umbilical veins, and sinusoids form. Because in the fetus the liver is a **hematopoietic organ** (from the 6th week), it is very large (≈10% of body weight at 3 months).

The **pancreas** develops in the 4th week from the **dorsal** and **ventral** buds of the duodenum. Owing to rotation of the duodenum, the ventral bud moves backward and fuses with the dorsal bud: the ventral bud forms the lower part of the head and the uncinate process, and the dorsal bud forms the upper part of the head, the body and the tail. The main duct forms from the duct of the ventral bud and the distal part of the dorsal duct, and the accessory duct from the proximal part of the dorsal duct. If the buds fail to fuse completely, a gland with two ducts develops (pancreas divisum); if the ventral bud rotates abnormally, an **annular pancreas** encircling the duodenum develops (a cause of intestinal obstruction).

items: In the newborn the liver is **relatively very large**: it weighs ≈135–150 g (**4–4.5%** of body weight, vs. 2–3% in adults) and occupies the upper half of the abdominal cavity; its four lobes are clearly visible; it is full of blood and soft, and the boundaries of the lobules are indistinct.

In the newborn the **left lobe** is equal to or larger than the right — in the fetus the left lobe received the oxygen-rich blood of the umbilical vein. After birth, because the circulation changes, the growth of the left lobe slows.

In the newborn the inferior border of the liver lies **2.5–4 cm** below the costal margin in the right midclavicular line and 3.5–4 cm below the xiphoid process in the midline; in early childhood it projects 1.5–2 cm below the margin; **after 7 years** it hides behind the costal margin. Palpation of the liver in children is a normal finding.

The mass of the liver increases 2 times by 1 year, 3 times by 2–3 years, increases 6 times by 9 years and 10 times by puberty; its maximum mass is reached at 21–30 years. The boundaries of the lobules become distinct at 1 year, and their structure resembles that of adults by 8 years.

In the newborn the gallbladder is cylindrical or fusiform, ≈3 cm long, deeply embedded in the liver tissue; at 6–7 months it becomes pear-shaped and at 2 years reaches the border of the liver; by 13–14 years it resembles that of adults. Its capacity is ≈3 mL at 3 months, ≈8.5 mL at 3 years and ≈34 mL at 9 years.

In the newborn the pancreas is very small — it weighs **2–3 g**, is 4–6 cm long and lies at the level of T~XII~ (higher); it is mobile because there is no retroperitoneal fat. There is much connective tissue and little glandular tissue; most of the gland is the head. Its mass increases 2 times by 6 months, is ≈10 g at 1 year, ≈20 g at 3 years, 30–35 g at 10 years and reaches 65–90 g by 14–16 years.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In a man injured in a road traffic accident, severe bleeding into the abdominal cavity was found; at operation a tear of the liver was discovered. To stop the bleeding temporarily, the surgeon inserted his fingers into the omental (epiploic) foramen and compressed the hepatoduodenal ligament (the Pringle maneuver).
cases.ask: Which structures lie in this ligament, and how are they arranged? Why does compressing the ligament reduce, but not completely stop, bleeding from the liver?
cases.answer: In the **hepatoduodenal ligament** (the right part of the lesser omentum; the anterior wall of the omental foramen) lie the structures carrying blood to the liver: **on the right — the common bile duct**, **on the left — the proper hepatic artery**, **behind — the portal vein**. When the ligament is compressed, **both** inflows of blood to the liver — the portal vein (≈75%) and the hepatic artery (≈25%) — stop. Yet the bleeding does not stop completely, because the **hepatic veins**, which carry blood away from the liver, do not pass through the porta but drain directly from the posterior surface of the liver into the **inferior vena cava** and are not compressed.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: An overweight 45-year-old woman presented with severe colicky pain below the right costal margin and nausea after a fatty meal. Two days later her skin and the whites of her eyes turned yellow, her urine darkened and her stools became pale. Ultrasound showed stones in the gallbladder and dilation of the common bile duct.
cases.ask: By what route does bile flow? Where may the stone be lodged, and why did jaundice appear? What complication is a risk?
cases.answer: Bile is formed in the liver: right and left hepatic ducts → **common hepatic duct** → (collecting in the gallbladder via the cystic duct and returning) → **common bile duct** → **hepatopancreatic ampulla** → **major papilla** (sphincter of Oddi) → duodenum. Jaundice and dilation of the common bile duct indicate that the stone is lodged in the **common bile duct** or at the **major papilla** (choledocholithiasis): bile does not reach the intestine (pale stools), and bilirubin returns to the blood (yellow skin, dark urine). If the stone lodges in the ampulla, bile may reflux into the pancreatic duct through the common channel, and **acute pancreatitis** may develop.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: On examining a healthy 2-year-old child, a pediatrician palpated the inferior border of the liver 1.5–2 cm below the costal margin in the right midclavicular line; the border is soft, smooth and painless. The mother is worried.
cases.ask: Is this normal? Explain the age-related features of the liver.
cases.answer: This is **normal**. In children the liver is relatively large: in the newborn it makes up 4–4.5% of body weight (2–3% in adults), and its inferior border lies 2.5–4 cm below the costal margin in the right midclavicular line; in early childhood it projects 1.5–2 cm; **after 7 years** it hides behind the costal margin. In the newborn the left lobe is also relatively large. If the border becomes firm, painful or excessively enlarged for age, further investigation is needed.
