topics.title: The peritoneum: its structure and relation to the abdominal organs. Sinuses, bursae, recesses and their significance in surgical practice

goals.text: To teach the student the layers of the peritoneum and the peritoneal cavity, the relation of organs to the peritoneum, the peritoneal ligaments, omenta and mesenteries, the compartments, bursae, canals (paracolic gutters), sinuses and recesses of the peritoneal cavity, their development, age-related features and significance in surgery.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the layers of the peritoneum, the peritoneal cavity and the retroperitoneal space;
the intra-, meso- and extraperitoneal position of organs;
the peritoneal ligaments around the liver, stomach and intestines, the lesser and greater omenta and the mesenteries;
the upper, middle and lower compartments (storeys) of the peritoneal cavity;
the hepatic, pregastric and omental bursae and the boundaries of the omental foramen;
the paracolic gutters, the mesenteric sinuses and the peritoneal recesses;
the folds and fossae on the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall and the peritoneal pouches in the lesser pelvis;
the development and age-related features of the peritoneum.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: show the peritoneal ligaments, omenta, mesenteries and bursae on specimens and in an atlas;
state and show the boundaries of the omental foramen;
explain the routes by which fluid (blood, pus) spreads in the peritoneal cavity.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Intraperitoneal organs cannot be reached surgically **without opening the peritoneal cavity**; extraperitoneal organs (kidney, ureter), by contrast, can be approached through the lumbar region without opening the peritoneal cavity — this reduces the risk of peritoneal infection (peritonitis).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The **greater omentum** is the "policeman of the abdomen": being mobile, it adheres to a focus of inflammation (for example, an inflamed appendix or a perforated ulcer) and walls off the process (forming an inflammatory mass). In children the greater omentum is short and thin, so this protection is weak — appendicitis rapidly progresses to **generalized peritonitis**. In surgery the omentum is used as "natural material" to close defects.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In bleeding from the liver, the surgeon inserts the index finger into the **omental foramen** and compresses the hepatoduodenal ligament with the thumb (the **Pringle maneuver**) — the vessels bringing blood to the liver are temporarily occluded. When an **ulcer of the posterior wall of the stomach** perforates, the gastric contents pour into the omental bursa and may remain confined there for a time; pancreatic pseudocysts and fluid in acute pancreatitis also collect in the omental bursa.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Peritoneal recesses are sites where **internal hernias** can form: if an intestinal loop enters a recess and becomes trapped, intestinal obstruction occurs (most often at the duodenojejunal flexure — **Treitz's hernia**). In a supine patient, fluid in the abdominal cavity collects in the lowest places — the **hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch)** and the pelvis; on ultrasound fluid is looked for here first (the FAST examination).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Blood from the abdominal cavity (in a ruptured ectopic pregnancy) and pus (from appendicitis or adnexitis) collect in the **pouch of Douglas**; it is **punctured** through the posterior fornix of the vagina (culdocentesis) or examined digitally through the rectum (bulging and tenderness). In men the rectovesical pouch is examined through the rectum.

sections.title: 1. The peritoneum and the peritoneal cavity

blocks.text: The **peritoneum** (*peritoneum*) is the serous membrane lining the walls of the abdominal cavity and covering the organs within it. Its total area is **≈1.7 m²**; its surface is covered by **mesothelium**, beneath which lie a basement membrane and connective tissue layers. The peritoneum consists of two layers: the **parietal peritoneum** (*peritoneum parietale*), lining the abdominal walls, and the **visceral peritoneum** (*peritoneum viscerale*), covering the organs; they are continuous with each other. Between the parietal layer and the abdominal wall lies the **subperitoneal (subserous) layer** — fatty tissue; on the posterior wall it is well developed and fills the **retroperitoneal space** (*spatium retroperitoneale*) — where the kidneys, suprarenal glands, ureters, aorta, inferior vena cava and other structures lie.

The narrow slit between the layers is the **peritoneal cavity** (*cavitas peritonealis*); it contains a small amount (20–30 mL) of serous fluid that allows the organs to glide. In males the cavity is closed; in females it communicates through the openings of the uterine tubes with the uterus and through the vagina with the exterior. The peritoneum **produces and absorbs serous fluid** (its diaphragmatic part is especially active in absorption), **fixes** the organs, and performs protective (phagocytosis, walling off inflammation by forming adhesions) and **fat-storage** functions.

parts.text: Intraperitoneal organs cannot be reached surgically **without opening the peritoneal cavity**; extraperitoneal organs (kidney, ureter), by contrast, can be approached through the lumbar region without opening the peritoneal cavity — this reduces the risk of peritoneal infection (peritonitis).

blocks.text: Where the peritoneum passes from the wall to an organ or from one organ to another, it forms two-layered folds — **ligaments**, **omenta** and **mesenteries**; blood vessels, nerves and lymphatics reach the organ between their layers.

items: **Ligaments of the liver**: from the diaphragm and anterior abdominal wall to the liver — the **falciform**, **coronary**, **right and left triangular** ligaments; from the liver to neighboring organs — the **hepatorenal**, **hepatogastric** and **hepatoduodenal** ligaments.

The **lesser omentum** (*omentum minus*) is a peritoneal duplication passing from the porta hepatis to the lesser curvature of the stomach (**hepatogastric ligament**) and the superior part of the duodenum (**hepatoduodenal ligament**). The common bile duct, proper hepatic artery and portal vein lie in the hepatoduodenal ligament (topic 18).

The **greater omentum** (*omentum majus*) is a **four-layered** peritoneal fold hanging like an apron from the greater curvature of the stomach and covering the loops of the small intestine in front (the two anterior layers descend, then turn back and ascend, fusing with the transverse colon and its mesentery). Its initial part is the **gastrocolic ligament**. Between its layers lie fat and lymphoid aggregates ("milky spots").
**Ligaments of the stomach**: the gastrophrenic, gastrosplenic and gastrocolic ligaments; from the spleen — the phrenicosplenic and splenorenal ligaments.

**Mesenteries**: the **mesentery of the small intestine** (root ≈15–18 cm, running obliquely from the left side of L~II~ to the right sacroiliac joint), the **transverse mesocolon** (dividing the peritoneal cavity into upper and lower compartments), the **sigmoid mesocolon** and the **mesoappendix**.

In children the greater omentum is short and thin, so this protection is weak — appendicitis rapidly progresses to **generalized peritonitis**. In surgery the omentum is used as "natural material" to close defects.

sections.title: 4. Compartments and bursae of the peritoneal cavity

blocks.text: The transverse colon and its mesentery divide the peritoneal cavity into **upper (supracolic)** and **lower (infracolic)** compartments (in some textbooks the lower compartment is divided into a **middle** compartment — from the mesentery to the pelvic inlet — and a **lower (pelvic)** compartment).

The **upper compartment** lies between the diaphragm and the transverse mesocolon; it contains the liver, gallbladder, stomach, spleen, superior part of the duodenum and the pancreas. It is divided into three bursae:

blocks.text: The **omental foramen** (*foramen omentale*, epiploic foramen of Winslow; 2–3 cm) lies in the right wall of the omental bursa and connects the bursa (through its vestibule) with the hepatic bursa. Its boundaries: **in front** — the hepatoduodenal ligament (the right free edge of the lesser omentum), **behind** — the parietal peritoneum covering the inferior vena cava, **above** — the caudate lobe of the liver, **below** — the superior part of the duodenum.

sections.title: 5. The lower compartment: gutters, sinuses and recesses

blocks.text: The **lower compartment** lies below the transverse mesocolon and continues into the cavity of the lesser pelvis; it contains most of the small and large intestines and the urinary and genital organs (in the pelvis). The ascending and descending colon and the root of the mesentery of the small intestine divide it into four parts:

items: The **right paracolic gutter** (right paracolic sulcus) — between the right lateral abdominal wall and the ascending colon; above it **communicates freely** with the hepatic bursa (the right subhepatic and subphrenic spaces), and below with the right iliac fossa and the lesser pelvis.

The **left paracolic gutter** (left paracolic sulcus) — between the descending colon and the left lateral abdominal wall; above it is bounded by the **phrenicocolic ligament** (it barely communicates with the upper compartment), and below it communicates with the lesser pelvis.

The **right mesenteric (infracolic) sinus** — between the root of the mesentery of the small intestine, the ascending colon and the transverse mesocolon; triangular in shape and relatively **closed**.
The **left mesenteric (infracolic) sinus** — between the root of the mesentery and the descending and sigmoid colon; below it is **open to the cavity of the lesser pelvis**.

Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: **Peritoneal recesses (fossae)** form where organs pass into one another or into the wall: the **superior and inferior duodenal** recesses (at the duodenojejunal flexure), the **superior and inferior ileocecal** recesses, the **retrocecal** recess and the **intersigmoid** recess (at the root of the sigmoid mesocolon). In the upper compartment — the **subhepatic**, **subphrenic** and **hepatorenal** recesses.

Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: Peritoneal recesses are sites where **internal hernias** can form: if an intestinal loop enters a recess and becomes trapped, intestinal obstruction occurs (most often at the duodenojejunal flexure — **Treitz's hernia**). In a supine patient, fluid in the abdominal cavity collects in the lowest places — the **hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch)** and the pelvis; on ultrasound fluid is looked for here first (the FAST examination).

sections.title: 6. The peritoneum of the anterior abdominal wall and the lesser pelvis

blocks.text: On the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall, below the umbilicus, the parietal peritoneum forms **5 folds**: the unpaired **median umbilical fold** (containing the obliterated urinary duct — the **urachus**), the paired **medial umbilical folds** (the obliterated **umbilical arteries**) and the paired **lateral umbilical folds** (the **inferior epigastric** artery and veins). Between the folds there are fossae: between the median and medial folds — the **supravesical fossae**, between the medial and lateral folds — the **medial inguinal fossae** (site of direct inguinal hernia), and lateral to the lateral fold — the **lateral inguinal fossae** (deep inguinal ring; site of indirect inguinal hernia) (topic 12).

blocks.label: Figure 19.8
blocks.caption: Peritoneum of the anterior abdominal wall, internal view (Figure No. 74): median, medial and lateral umbilical folds, supravesical, medial and lateral inguinal fossae, round ligament of the liver, falciform ligament, deep inguinal ring, urinary bladder. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: **In the lesser pelvis** the peritoneum covers the organs and forms pouches. **In males**: between the rectum and bladder — the **rectovesical pouch**. **In females**: between the bladder and uterus — the **vesicouterine pouch**, and between the uterus and rectum — the **rectouterine pouch** (**pouch of Douglas**) — the lowest point of the female peritoneal cavity; its floor is in contact with the posterior fornix of the vagina.

blocks.label: Figure 19.9
blocks.caption: The peritoneum in the region of the urinary and genital organs (A — in males; B — in females; Figure No. 91): rectovesical, vesicouterine and rectouterine pouches, rectum, urinary bladder, uterus, vagina, prostate, sigmoid mesocolon. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: Blood from the abdominal cavity (in a ruptured ectopic pregnancy) and pus (from appendicitis or adnexitis) collect in the **pouch of Douglas**; it is **punctured** through the posterior fornix of the vagina (culdocentesis) or examined digitally through the rectum (bulging and tenderness). In men the rectovesical pouch is examined through the rectum.

sections.title: 7. Spread of fluids in the peritoneal cavity

blocks.text: The parts of the peritoneal cavity communicate with one another, and fluid (blood, pus, intestinal contents) spreads by definite routes. For example, in appendicitis pus may ascend along the **right paracolic gutter** to the right subhepatic and **subphrenic space**, forming a **subphrenic abscess**, or descend into the **lesser pelvis**. When a gastric or duodenal ulcer perforates, the contents may run down the right paracolic gutter into the right iliac fossa, causing pain resembling appendicitis. Because the left paracolic gutter is closed above by the phrenicocolic ligament, on the left side processes spread upward less. Placing the patient in the semi-sitting (Fowler's) position directs pus into the pelvis and reduces the risk of a subphrenic abscess.

blocks.label: Figure 19.10
blocks.caption: Organs in the abdominal cavity, transverse section between the 2nd and 3rd lumbar vertebrae (diagram; Figure No. 87): 1 — small intestine; 2 — visceral peritoneum; 3 — aorta; 4 — inferior vena cava; 5 — duodenum; 6 — psoas major; 7 — retroperitoneal space; 8 — kidney; 9 — colon; 10 — peritoneal cavity; 11 — parietal peritoneum; 12 — mesentery of the small intestine; 13 — rectus abdominis. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The peritoneal cavity develops from the **coelom** (body cavity). The primitive gut tube is attached to the posterior abdominal wall by the **dorsal mesentery**, and the stomach and the initial part of the duodenum to the anterior wall by the **ventral mesentery**. After the liver grows into the ventral mesentery, it gives rise to the **lesser omentum** (the part between the liver and stomach) and the **falciform ligament** (the part between the liver and anterior abdominal wall). When the stomach rotates 90°, its dorsal mesentery (the **dorsal mesogastrium**) is drawn to the left and downward and hangs down as a double layer — this is how the **greater omentum** and **omental bursa** form; the posterior layers of the greater omentum fuse with the transverse colon and its mesentery by 3–4 months of postnatal life. After the gut rotates, the mesenteries of the ascending and descending colon and the duodenum adhere to the posterior abdominal wall (**fusion of the primary mesentery**), and these organs become meso- or retroperitoneal.

items: In the newborn the abdominal cavity is relatively large and the organs lie high; once the child begins to walk, the diaphragm descends, and because the thoracic organs grow rapidly, the abdominal cavity becomes relatively smaller.

In the newborn the peritoneum is **thin and transparent** — blood and lymph vessels show through it; there is **no fat** in the subperitoneal layer, mesenteries, ligaments or omenta. Fat appears at 2 years and increases considerably from 7 years; at 16–18 years the fat in the retroperitoneal space, omenta and mesenteries increases and the organs become more firmly fixed.

In the newborn the **greater omentum** is very short and thin and does not cover the loops of the small intestine; it is almost undeveloped until 2 years, and by 7 years it covers the anterior surface of the intestines. This is why inflammatory processes in young children are not walled off by the omentum.

In the newborn the root of the mesentery of the small intestine is almost **vertical**; with age it lengthens and becomes oblique. Because the ascending colon is undeveloped and the cecum lies high, the peritoneal recesses have a different shape — they are poorly developed and shallow.
The absorptive capacity of the peritoneum is high in children — toxins are absorbed rapidly, which is why peritonitis is severe in children.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 6-year-old child was brought to hospital 2 days after the onset of abdominal pain. At operation the vermiform appendix was found perforated and pus had spread throughout the abdominal cavity (generalized peritonitis).
cases.ask: Why does appendicitis progress rapidly to generalized peritonitis in children? Which features of the peritoneum and omentum are responsible?
cases.answer: In children the **greater omentum is short and thin** (almost undeveloped until 2 years, covering the intestines only by 7 years) — it cannot reach the focus of inflammation and wall it off with adhesions. In addition, in children the peritoneum is **thin** and **highly absorptive** (toxins are absorbed rapidly), the mesenteries and omenta contain little fat, and the peritoneal recesses are shallow — there are no barriers to confine the infection. Because the right paracolic gutter communicates freely above with the hepatic bursa and below with the lesser pelvis, pus spreads rapidly.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient with a gastric ulcer suddenly developed "dagger-like" pain in the epigastric region. A few hours later the pain was also felt in the lower right abdomen, and the abdominal wall was board-like. A radiograph showed free air under the diaphragm.
cases.ask: What complication has occurred? By what anatomical route did the gastric contents reach the right iliac region? Why has the free air collected under the diaphragm?
cases.answer: **Perforation of the ulcer into the abdominal cavity**. The gastric (or duodenal) contents flow from the **hepatic bursa** of the upper compartment (the right subhepatic space) down along the **right paracolic gutter** (the groove between the ascending colon and the right lateral abdominal wall) into the **right iliac fossa** — which is why pain resembling appendicitis appears. In an upright patient, free air rises to the highest point of the peritoneal cavity — **under the diaphragm** — and is seen on the radiograph as a "crescent" of lucency.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 26-year-old woman was brought in with sharp lower abdominal pain, dizziness and fainting; her period is late and her blood pressure is low. The physician performed a puncture through the posterior fornix of the vagina and obtained blood from the abdominal cavity.
cases.ask: In which part of the peritoneal cavity has the blood collected, and why was the puncture made precisely from this site?
cases.answer: The probable diagnosis is a **ruptured ectopic (tubal) pregnancy** with intra-abdominal bleeding. In women the **lowest point** of the peritoneal cavity is the **rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas)** between the uterus and rectum; blood in the abdominal cavity collects here in both the upright and supine positions. The floor of this pouch is in direct contact with the **posterior fornix of the vagina** (separated only by the vaginal wall and peritoneum), so the presence of blood can be quickly established by puncture through the vagina (culdocentesis).

topics.title: General information on the respiratory organs. Structure of the nasal cavity. The larynx. Their age-related changes

goals.text: To teach the student the general structure and development of the respiratory system, the structure of the external nose, nasal cavity, nasal meatuses and paranasal sinuses, and the topography, cartilages, joints, muscles and cavity of the larynx, with their age-related features and clinical significance.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the organs of the respiratory system and the upper and lower respiratory tracts;
the parts and cartilages of the external nose;
the walls of the nasal cavity, the nasal conchae and meatuses, and the sinuses and ducts opening into them;
the paranasal sinuses and the sites where they open;
the skeletotopy and syntopy of the larynx;
the cartilages, joints and ligaments of the larynx;
the groups of laryngeal muscles by function;
the parts of the laryngeal cavity and the rima glottidis;
the development and age-related features of the nose and larynx.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: show the nasal conchae, meatuses and the openings of the paranasal sinuses in an atlas and on specimens;
find the laryngeal cartilages and muscles and name them in Latin;
palpate the laryngeal prominence, the thyroid and cricoid cartilages and the cricothyroid ligament in a living person.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Nosebleed** (epistaxis) most often comes from **Kiesselbach's area** — the vascular region in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum — which is close to the nasal vestibule, so pinching the alae of the nose or anterior packing is effective. Deviation of the nasal septum makes breathing difficult (septoplasty). The roof of the nasal cavity — the **cribriform plate** — is thin: in fractures of the cranial base, **CSF leak** (rhinorrhea) and loss of smell occur through it.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The opening of the **maxillary sinus** lies **high** above the floor of the sinus (into the middle nasal meatus, in the superomedial wall of the sinus), so in the upright position fluid drains poorly from it — **maxillary sinusitis** is common and tends to become chronic. The floor of the sinus is very close to the roots of the upper molars (odontogenic sinusitis). Puncture of the maxillary sinus is performed through the inferior nasal meatus. Inflammation of the frontal sinus is **frontal sinusitis**, and of the ethmoidal cells **ethmoiditis** (which may spread into the orbit).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Cricothyrotomy (coniotomy)** is emergency opening of the larynx through the **median cricothyroid (conus elasticus) ligament** when the upper airway is suddenly obstructed (foreign body, laryngeal edema). This ligament lies superficially under the skin and is easily palpated between the lower border of the thyroid cartilage and the arch of the cricoid cartilage; because it lies above the large vessels and the isthmus of the thyroid gland, the procedure can be performed quickly and relatively safely.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: All the intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the **inferior laryngeal nerve** (the continuation of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, X), except the **cricothyroid** — supplied by the **external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve**. The **only** muscle that opens the rima glottidis is the posterior cricoarytenoid; if it is paralyzed bilaterally, the rima glottidis remains closed and there is a risk of **asphyxia**.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The **recurrent laryngeal nerve** is injured in thyroid operations, aneurysm of the aortic arch or mediastinal tumors (the left nerve, which loops around the aortic arch, is longer and more often affected): unilateral injury causes **hoarseness**; bilateral injury fixes the vocal folds in the median position, and severe respiratory failure develops. Sensation of the laryngeal mucosa: above the vocal folds — the superior laryngeal nerve (internal branch); below — the inferior laryngeal nerve.

blocks.text: The **respiratory system** (*systema respiratorium*) provides **gas exchange** between the organism and the environment — saturating the blood with oxygen and removing carbon dioxide. It consists of the **airways** and the organ of gas exchange — the paired **lungs**. The airways are divided into **upper** (nasal cavity, nasal and oral parts of the pharynx) and **lower** (larynx, trachea, bronchi) tracts. Because the walls of the airways contain a bony or cartilaginous skeleton, they do not collapse; their inner surface is lined mainly by **pseudostratified ciliated epithelium** — the cilia sweep mucus and the dust stuck to it outward. In the airways air is **cleaned, moistened and warmed**; smell and voice production also take place here.

blocks.label: Figure 20.1
blocks.caption: The respiratory system (sagittal section through the nasal cavity, mouth and larynx, slightly lateral to the midline; Figure No. 92): nasal conchae and meatuses, paranasal sinuses, pharynx, larynx and its parts, trachea and its bifurcation, main, lobar and segmental bronchi, right and left lungs, pulmonary arteries and veins. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: **Development.** The external nose and nasal cavity develop together with the skull bones and the olfactory organ. The **lower airways** appear in the **3rd–4th week** of fetal life as an outgrowth of the ventral wall of the foregut — the **laryngotracheal (respiratory) diverticulum**; its endoderm gives rise to the epithelium and glands of the airways, and the surrounding mesenchyme to the cartilages, muscles and connective tissue. The diverticulum is separated from the foregut by the **tracheoesophageal septum** — a defect in it causes anomalies such as **tracheoesophageal fistula**. Its distal end divides into two **lung buds** (3 lobar buds on the right, 2 on the left). The **laryngeal cartilages** develop from the mesenchyme of the 4th–6th branchial arches (the cricoid first, the thyroid last); the laryngeal muscles arise from the 4th and 6th branchial arches and are supplied by branches of the vagus nerve.

The **external nose** (*nasus externus*) has a **root** (between the eyebrows, separated from the forehead by a notch), a **dorsum**, a **tip (apex)** and **alae**; the lower borders of the alae bound the **nostrils** (*nares*). Its skeleton is formed above by the **nasal bones** and the frontal processes of the maxillae, and below by **hyaline cartilages**: the paired **lateral cartilage** (the lateral wall of the nose), the paired **major alar cartilage** (whose medial and lateral crura bound the nostril), the **minor alar cartilages** and **accessory cartilages**, and the unpaired quadrangular **septal cartilage**.

blocks.label: Figure 20.2
blocks.caption: The external nose (A — anterior view; B — nasal cartilages, inferior view; Figure No. 93): 1 — septal cartilage; 2 — accessory alar cartilages; 3 — lateral process (lateral cartilage); 4 — nasal bone; 5 — lateral crus of the major alar cartilage; 6 — medial crus of the major alar cartilage; 7 — nostrils; 8 — alae of the nose. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **nasal cavity** (*cavitas nasi*) opens in front to the exterior through the nostrils and behind into the nasal part of the pharynx through the **choanae**. The **nasal septum** (*septum nasi*) divides it into right and left halves; the posterior **bony part** of the septum is formed by the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone and the vomer, and the anterior part by **cartilage** and a **membranous part** (mobile). The walls of the cavity: **roof** — the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone (in front the nasal and frontal bones, behind the body of the sphenoid); **floor** — the hard palate; **medial** — the nasal septum; **lateral** — the most complex wall (maxilla, lacrimal, ethmoid, palatine and sphenoid bones and the inferior nasal concha).

blocks.label: Figure 20.3
blocks.caption: The nasal septum (nasal mucosa removed; Figure No. 97): perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone, vomer, septal cartilage, medial crus of the major alar cartilage, cribriform plate, frontal and sphenoidal sinuses, hard palate, incisive canal. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: In the front of each half, under the ala of the nose, is the **nasal vestibule**, lined by skin with hairs and sebaceous and sweat glands. Three **nasal conchae** hang from the lateral wall — the **superior** and **middle** (parts of the ethmoid bone) and the **inferior** (an independent bone); between them lie the **superior**, **middle** and **inferior nasal meatuses**. Between the conchae and the septum is the slit-like **common nasal meatus**; behind the conchae the **nasopharyngeal meatus** leads to the choanae. Behind the superior concha is the **sphenoethmoidal recess**.

blocks.label: Figure 20.4
blocks.caption: Lateral wall of the nasal cavity (Figure No. 98): 1 — inferior nasal meatus; 2 — salpingopharyngeal fold; 3 — pharyngeal tonsil; 4 — middle nasal concha; 5 — superior nasal concha; 6 — sphenoidal sinus; 7 — sphenoethmoidal recess; 8 — superior nasal meatus; 9 — middle nasal meatus; 10 — inferior nasal concha; 11 — limen nasi; 12 — nasal vestibule. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **mucosa of the nasal cavity** is divided into two regions. The **olfactory region** covers the superior concha, part of the middle concha and the upper part of the septum; it contains the **olfactory cells** (primary sensory neurons) — their axons pass through the foramina of the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb (the olfactory nerves, CN I). The **respiratory region** is the rest; it has pseudostratified ciliated epithelium and mucous glands, and in the submucosa, especially of the middle and inferior conchae, **cavernous venous plexuses** — these warm the air but also cause swelling of the mucosa.

parts.text: **Nosebleed** (epistaxis) most often comes from **Kiesselbach's area** — the vascular region in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum — which is close to the nasal vestibule, so pinching the alae of the nose or anterior packing is effective. Deviation of the nasal septum makes breathing difficult (septoplasty). The roof of the nasal cavity — the **cribriform plate** — is thin: in fractures of the cranial base, **CSF leak** (rhinorrhea) and loss of smell occur through it.

blocks.text: The **paranasal sinuses** (*sinus paranasales*) are air-filled cavities in the skull bones; they communicate with the nasal cavity and are lined by its mucosa. They lighten the skull, give resonance to the voice, and warm and moisten the air. They are: the **maxillary sinus (antrum of Highmore)** (the largest, ≈15–20 mL), the **frontal sinus**, the **sphenoidal sinus** and the **ethmoidal cells (labyrinth)**.

blocks.label: Figure 20.6
blocks.caption: Cavities of the pneumatic skull bones (paranasal sinuses), shown in color (A — anterior view; B — left lateral view; Figure No. 103): 1 — frontal sinus; 2 — ethmoidal labyrinth; 3 — maxillary sinus; 4 — sphenoidal sinus. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: The opening of the **maxillary sinus** lies **high** above the floor of the sinus (into the middle nasal meatus, in the superomedial wall of the sinus), so in the upright position fluid drains poorly from it — **maxillary sinusitis** is common and tends to become chronic. The floor of the sinus is very close to the roots of the upper molars (odontogenic sinusitis). Puncture of the maxillary sinus is performed through the inferior nasal meatus. Inflammation of the frontal sinus is **frontal sinusitis**, and of the ethmoidal cells **ethmoiditis** (which may spread into the orbit).

blocks.text: The **larynx** (*larynx*) is part of the airway, an organ that produces the voice and protects the lower airways from foreign bodies. It lies in the anterior region of the neck below the hyoid bone and forms the **laryngeal prominence** (*prominentia laryngea*, "Adam's apple," well marked in men). In adults it lies at the level of the **4th–6th (7th) cervical vertebrae** (slightly higher in women). Above it is suspended from the hyoid bone, and below it continues into the trachea. **In front** — the infrahyoid muscles and cervical fascia; **at the sides** — the lobes of the thyroid gland and the neurovascular bundle of the neck; **behind** — the laryngeal part of the pharynx. In swallowing and phonation the larynx moves up and down.

sections.title: 6. Cartilages, joints and ligaments of the larynx

blocks.text: **Joints**: the **cricothyroid joint** (paired, combined) — around the frontal axis the thyroid cartilage tilts forward and returns: the vocal ligaments **tense** or relax; the **cricoarytenoid joint** (paired) — around the vertical axis the arytenoid cartilages rotate inward and outward, and they also glide toward and away from each other: the rima glottidis **narrows** or **widens**. **Ligaments and membranes**: the **thyrohyoid membrane** (with the median and lateral thyrohyoid ligaments), the **median cricothyroid ligament** (conical ligament; between the cricoid arch and the thyroid cartilage), the **cricotracheal ligament**, and the **hyoepiglottic** and **thyroepiglottic** ligaments.

blocks.label: Figure 20.7
blocks.caption: Joints and ligaments of the laryngeal cartilages (A — anterior view; B — posterior view; Figure No. 109): thyroid, cricoid and arytenoid cartilages and the epiglottis, hyoid bone, thyrohyoid membrane, median cricothyroid ligament, cricothyroid and cricoarytenoid joints, tracheal cartilages. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: **Cricothyrotomy (coniotomy)** is emergency opening of the larynx through the **median cricothyroid (conus elasticus) ligament** when the upper airway is suddenly obstructed (foreign body, laryngeal edema). This ligament lies superficially under the skin and is easily palpated between the lower border of the thyroid cartilage and the arch of the cricoid cartilage; because it lies above the large vessels and the isthmus of the thyroid gland, the procedure can be performed quickly and relatively safely.

blocks.text: The laryngeal muscles are striated and are divided into **extrinsic** (moving the larynx as a whole — the muscles attached to the hyoid bone, topic 15) and **intrinsic** muscles. The intrinsic muscles change the position of the cartilages, the width of the rima glottidis and the tension of the vocal ligaments.

parts.text: All the intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the **inferior laryngeal nerve** (the continuation of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, X), except the **cricothyroid** — supplied by the **external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve**. The **only** muscle that opens the rima glottidis is the posterior cricoarytenoid; if it is paralyzed bilaterally, the rima glottidis remains closed and there is a risk of **asphyxia**.

The **recurrent laryngeal nerve** is injured in thyroid operations, aneurysm of the aortic arch or mediastinal tumors (the left nerve, which loops around the aortic arch, is longer and more often affected): unilateral injury causes **hoarseness**; bilateral injury fixes the vocal folds in the median position, and severe respiratory failure develops. Sensation of the laryngeal mucosa: above the vocal folds — the superior laryngeal nerve (internal branch); below — the inferior laryngeal nerve.

blocks.text: The **laryngeal cavity** (*cavitas laryngis*) is hourglass-shaped: its upper and lower parts are wide and its middle narrow. It is entered from the pharynx through the **laryngeal inlet**, bounded in front by the epiglottis, at the sides by the **aryepiglottic folds** and behind by the arytenoid cartilages and the fold between them. On the lateral wall of the cavity there are two pairs of folds: above — the **vestibular folds** (false vocal cords), below — the **vocal folds** (containing the **vocal ligament** and the **vocalis muscle**). Between them lies the **laryngeal ventricle**, extending laterally.

items: The **laryngeal vestibule** — from the inlet to the vestibular folds; between the vestibular folds is the **rima vestibuli**.

The **intermediate (middle) part** — the shortest part, between the vestibular and vocal folds; between the right and left vocal folds is the **narrowest point** of the larynx — the **rima glottidis** (*rima glottidis*): the anterior **intermembranous** part (between the vocal ligaments, ≈2/3) and the posterior **intercartilaginous** part (between the bases of the arytenoid cartilages). Its length is 20–24 mm in men and 16–19 mm in women; its width is ≈5 mm in quiet breathing and up to ≈15 mm in deep breathing.
The **infraglottic cavity** (*cavitas infraglottica*) — below the vocal folds; it widens downward and passes into the trachea.

blocks.text: The laryngeal mucosa is lined mainly by **pseudostratified ciliated epithelium**, but the **vocal folds** and part of the epiglottis by **stratified squamous epithelium**; the vocal fold has no glands, and the mucosa adheres firmly to the ligament (it is whitish). Beneath the mucosa is the **fibroelastic membrane**: its upper part is the **quadrangular membrane** (its lower edge — the vestibular ligament), and its lower part is the **conus elasticus** (its upper free edge — the **vocal ligament**; in front it thickens to form the median cricothyroid ligament).

Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.caption: Functions of the laryngeal muscles (diagram; Figures No. 121 and No. 122): the effect of contraction of the cricothyroid, oblique and transverse arytenoids, lateral and posterior cricoarytenoids, thyroarytenoid and vocalis on the shape of the rima glottidis and the tension of the vocal ligaments. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: **Voice production.** During expiration the rima glottidis narrows and the vocal ligaments tense; air leaving the lungs makes them vibrate. The **pitch** of the voice depends on the tension, length and thickness of the ligaments, its **loudness** on the pressure of the airflow, and its **timbre** on the resonators (pharynx, mouth, nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses); speech sounds are shaped by the tongue, lips, palate and teeth (articulation).

items: The newborn's nose is short, flat and broad; its root is narrow, the dorsum and tip are not defined, and the cartilages are poorly developed; the nostrils are oval and horizontal, becoming round by 5 years.

In the newborn the nasal cavity is low (≈17.5 mm) and narrow; the conchae are relatively thick and do not reach the septum. **The inferior nasal meatus is almost absent** (the inferior concha touches the floor of the cavity), the middle meatus is poorly developed, and the superior meatus is present in only ≈30% of cases — the baby breathes mainly through the **common nasal meatus**. If the mucosa swells, nasal breathing easily stops — the baby has difficulty suckling. The nasal cavity enlarges 1.5 times by 10 years and 2 times by 20 years.

In the newborn, of the paranasal sinuses only the **maxillary sinus** (small, ≈5×10×3.5 mm) and the buds of the ethmoidal cells are present; the maxillary sinus occupies the body of the bone by 8–9 years. The **frontal sinus** begins to develop in the 2nd year (pea-sized at 5 years); the **sphenoidal sinus** develops from 3–4 years and is formed by 12–15 years; the ethmoidal cells resemble those of adults by 14 years. This is why frontal sinusitis is almost never seen in young children.

In the newborn the larynx is relatively large, funnel-shaped and **high** — at the level of the 2nd–4th cervical vertebrae; the epiglottis stands high and touches the root of the tongue — this allows the baby to breathe while suckling. The larynx gradually descends.

The cartilages of the newborn's larynx are thin and flexible; the laminae of the thyroid cartilage form an obtuse angle (there is no laryngeal prominence); the rima glottidis is ≈6.5 mm and the vocal ligaments are short. The mucosa is delicate and rich in blood and lymph vessels, and the submucosa of the infraglottic cavity is loose — in inflammation it swells rapidly, narrowing the laryngeal cavity (**false croup**).

The larynx grows rapidly at 1–3 years and during puberty. From 10–12 years in boys the angle between the laminae of the thyroid cartilage decreases (≈90°), the laryngeal prominence appears and the vocal ligaments lengthen — the **voice breaks (mutation)**; in girls the change is barely noticeable. In old age the laryngeal cartilages calcify (in men the thyroid and cricoid cartilages from 20 years).

skills.title: Practical skill: palpating the larynx and examining the nasal cavity

items: Along the anterior midline of the neck, from above downward, palpate: body of the hyoid bone → thyrohyoid membrane → laryngeal prominence and superior thyroid notch → lower border of the thyroid cartilage → **median cricothyroid ligament** (a soft depression) → arch of the cricoid cartilage → tracheal rings.
Ask the patient to swallow — observe the larynx rising.
Using a nasal speculum (rhinoscope) or an atlas, show the nasal vestibule, the anterior part of the septum (Kiesselbach's area) and the anterior ends of the inferior and middle conchae.
Demonstrate how to test for tenderness by pressing over the projections of the frontal and maxillary sinuses (above the eyebrow and over the cheek).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After a thyroidectomy the patient's voice became hoarse. On laryngoscopy the left vocal fold is motionless in the median position, while the right fold moves normally.
cases.ask: Which nerve is injured? Which muscles does it supply, and why has the voice changed? What happens with bilateral injury?
cases.answer: The **left recurrent laryngeal nerve** (inferior laryngeal nerve) is injured — it runs in the tracheoesophageal groove behind the lobes of the thyroid gland and may be damaged during operation. It supplies **all the intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid**. The vocal fold on the injured side remains motionless, and the rima glottidis does not close completely — the voice becomes hoarse. With bilateral injury the **only dilators — the posterior cricoarytenoid muscles** — are paralyzed, the vocal folds become fixed in the median position and the rima glottidis narrows — severe respiratory failure develops, and a tracheostomy may be needed.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: At night a 2-year-old child suddenly woke with a "barking" cough, a hoarse voice and noisy, labored breathing (inspiratory stridor); during the day the child had had a runny nose.
cases.ask: What condition (false croup) has developed? Which age-related features of the larynx predispose to it?
cases.answer: This is **acute stenosing laryngotracheitis (false croup)** — swelling of the laryngeal mucosa, especially of the **infraglottic cavity**, in a viral infection. In young children the laryngeal cavity and rima glottidis are **narrow**, the cartilages are soft, the mucosa is delicate and **rich in blood and lymph vessels**, and there is much **loose submucosa** below the vocal folds — even 1 mm of swelling narrows the lumen considerably and makes breathing difficult. At night, when the child is lying down, the swelling increases.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: For 10 days a 30-year-old woman has complained of purulent nasal discharge, heaviness and pain in the cheek below the eye that increases when she bends over, and toothache. A month ago an upper molar was treated.
cases.ask: Which paranasal sinus is inflamed? Where does it open, and why is the inflammation prone to become chronic? What is the connection with the tooth?
cases.answer: The **maxillary sinus (antrum of Highmore)** is inflamed — **maxillary sinusitis**. The sinus opens into the **middle nasal meatus** through the semilunar hiatus; because the opening lies in the **superomedial** part of the sinus, high above its floor, pus drains poorly in the upright position and the process becomes chronic. The floor of the sinus is very close to the **roots of the upper molars and premolars** (sometimes separated only by a thin bony plate or mucosa), so a dental infection can pass into the sinus (**odontogenic maxillary sinusitis**).

topics.title: The trachea, bronchi and lungs. The pleura. The mediastinum. Their age-related changes

goals.text: To teach the student the external and internal (segmental, acinar) structure of the trachea, bronchial tree and lungs, the borders of the lungs and pleura, the layers, cavity and recesses of the pleura, and the parts and contents of the mediastinum, with their development, age-related features and clinical significance.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the topography, parts and wall structure of the trachea;
the differences between the main bronchi and the branching of the bronchial tree;
the surfaces, borders, fissures and lobes of the lungs and the contents of the root of the lung;
the bronchopulmonary segments and the structure of the pulmonary lobule and acinus;
the layers of the pleura, the pleural cavity and its recesses;
the projection of the borders of the lungs and pleura onto the body surface;
the parts of the mediastinum and the organs in each;
the age-related features of the respiratory organs.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the trachea, bronchi, lobes of the lungs and the elements of the root of the lung in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
show the borders of the lungs and pleura on the thoracic cage along the topographic lines;
state the order of arrangement of the components of the right and left lung roots.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Foreign bodies** most often enter the **right main bronchus** (and the right lower lobe bronchus) — it is wide, short and almost a straight continuation of the trachea. Widening and immobility of the carina (on bronchoscopy) may be a sign of enlarged bifurcation lymph nodes — for example, metastasis of lung cancer.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The lungs have two blood circulations: **functional** — pulmonary artery (venous blood) → alveolar capillaries → pulmonary veins (arterial blood) — the pulmonary circulation; **nutritive** — the **bronchial arteries**, arising from the thoracic aorta, nourish the bronchi, pleura and lung tissue.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Fluid (**pleurisy**, **hydrothorax**), blood (**hemothorax**) or air (**pneumothorax**) may accumulate in the pleural cavity. Fluid collects first in the **costodiaphragmatic recess**; **pleural puncture** is performed in the 7th–8th intercostal space along the midaxillary or posterior axillary line, **along the upper border of the lower rib** (to avoid injuring the neurovascular bundle). In pneumothorax the negative pressure is lost and the lung collapses. Because the cupula of the pleura lies above the clavicle, it may be injured in neck wounds and during subclavian vein catheterization.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Because the mediastinal tissue communicates with the fascial spaces of the neck, in neck phlegmons and perforation of the esophagus pus enters it, and severe **mediastinitis** develops. Mediastinal tumors (for example, thymoma, lymphoma) compress neighboring organs, causing signs such as shortness of breath, difficulty swallowing, **superior vena cava syndrome** (swelling of the face and neck) and hoarseness (recurrent nerve).

blocks.text: The **trachea** (*trachea*) is the air-conducting tube that continues the larynx; it begins at the level of the **6th cervical vertebra** (at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage) and at the level of the **4th–5th thoracic vertebrae** (the level of the sternal angle) forms the **tracheal bifurcation** (*bifurcatio tracheae*), dividing into the right and left main bronchi. It is **9–11 cm** long and 15–18 mm in diameter. At the bifurcation the **carina** (*carina*) projects internally — an important landmark at bronchoscopy.

items: **Cervical part** — in front: the isthmus of the thyroid gland (over rings II–IV), the infrahyoid muscles and cervical fascia; behind: the esophagus; at the sides: the lobes of the thyroid gland and the neurovascular bundle of the neck.

**Thoracic part** — in the superior mediastinum; in front: the thymus (in children), the left brachiocephalic vein, the aortic arch and the brachiocephalic trunk; behind: the esophagus; at the sides: the mediastinal pleura, on the right the azygos vein, on the left the aortic arch and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.

blocks.text: **Wall**: the basis of the trachea consists of **16–20 hyaline cartilaginous half-rings** joined by **anular ligaments**; they are open behind, where the ends of the cartilages are joined by smooth muscle bundles and connective tissue — the **membranous wall** (allowing food to pass through the esophagus). Inside is a **mucosa** with pseudostratified ciliated epithelium (mucous glands, lymphoid nodules), a **submucosa** (tracheal glands), a **fibrocartilaginous membrane** and on the outside an **adventitia**.

blocks.caption: The trachea (A — cross-section; B — region of the tracheal bifurcation, the carina, internal view; V — reconstructed segment of the trachea; G — wall of the trachea, sagittal section; Figure No. 130): cartilaginous half-rings, anular ligaments, membranous wall, mucosa, tracheal glands, adventitia. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

sections.title: 2. The bronchi and the bronchial tree

parts.text: **Foreign bodies** most often enter the **right main bronchus** (and the right lower lobe bronchus) — it is wide, short and almost a straight continuation of the trachea. Widening and immobility of the carina (on bronchoscopy) may be a sign of enlarged bifurcation lymph nodes — for example, metastasis of lung cancer.

blocks.text: The **bronchial tree** (*arbor bronchialis*): main bronchi (1st order) → **lobar bronchi** (2nd; 3 on the right, 2 on the left) → **segmental bronchi** (3rd; 10 in each lung) → subsegmental and small bronchi (dividing in two 9–10 times) → **lobular bronchus** (≈1 mm in diameter) → **terminal bronchioles** (≈0.5 mm in diameter, ≈20,000 in both lungs; their wall has no cartilage or glands and relatively much smooth muscle). As the caliber decreases, the cartilage in the bronchial wall changes from rings to plates and disappears in the bronchioles.

blocks.label: Figure 21.2
blocks.caption: Trachea and bronchi, anterior view (Figure No. 128): right and left main bronchi, lobar bronchi, all segmental bronchi (B I–B X), tracheal cartilages and anular ligaments, cricothyroid ligament. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **lung** (*pulmo*, Greek *pneumon*) is the organ of gas exchange; the right and left lungs lie in the lateral parts of the thoracic cavity within the pleural sacs, with the **mediastinum** between them. They are irregularly conical; the right lung is shorter and wider (the right dome of the diaphragm is higher), the left lung longer and narrower (the heart is displaced to the left). Each adult lung weighs ≈0.5–0.6 kg, and the total alveolar surface is ≈70–100 m².

items: **Surfaces**: the **costal surface** (convex), the **diaphragmatic surface (base)** (concave), the **medial surface** — the anterior **mediastinal part** (cardiac impression, deeper in the left lung) and the posterior **vertebral part**; between the lobes — the **interlobar surfaces**.

**Borders**: the **anterior border** (sharp; in the left lung the **cardiac notch** and below it the **lingula of the left lung**), the **inferior border** (sharp), and the posterior border (blunt, rounded).
**Apex** — 2–3 cm above the clavicle and 3–4 cm above the 1st rib (behind, at the level of the spinous process of the 7th cervical vertebra).

blocks.text: **Fissures and lobes**: in the right lung the **oblique fissure** and the **horizontal fissure** divide it into **superior, middle and inferior** lobes; in the left lung only the **oblique fissure** divides it into **superior and inferior** lobes. Posteriorly the oblique fissure begins at the level of the spinous process of the 3rd thoracic vertebra and runs forward and downward along the 6th rib; the horizontal fissure branches off the oblique fissure in the midaxillary line and runs along the 4th rib to the sternum.

Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **hilum of the lung** (*hilum pulmonis*) is a depression on the medial surface; through it pass the structures making up the **root of the lung** (*radix pulmonis*): **entering** — the main bronchus, pulmonary artery, bronchial arteries and nerves (pulmonary plexus); **leaving** — the pulmonary veins (2 from each lung), bronchial veins and lymphatic vessels. Bronchopulmonary lymph nodes lie at the hilum.

sections.title: 4. Internal structure of the lung: segments, lobule, acinus

blocks.text: A **bronchopulmonary segment** is a cone-shaped part of the lung supplied by a segmental bronchus and a segmental branch of the pulmonary artery and separated by connective tissue septa (its apex faces the hilum and its base the lung surface). The segmental veins lie in the septa between the segments — a landmark for the segment boundaries. According to the international nomenclature each lung has **10 segments** (in the left lung the apical and posterior, and the medial basal and anterior basal segments often fuse, giving 8–9). The segmental structure allows **segmentectomy** (removal of a single lung segment) and precise localization of a lesion on radiographs.

blocks.text: The **pulmonary lobule** is a pyramidal part 1–1.5 cm in diameter supplied by a lobular bronchus (≈800 in each lung). Within the lobule the bronchus divides into 12–18 **terminal bronchioles**. The **acinus** (*acinus*) is the **structural-functional unit** of the lung: the branches of one terminal bronchiole — **respiratory bronchioles** (orders I–III, with alveoli in their walls) → **alveolar ducts** → **alveolar sacs** → **alveoli**. The two lungs contain ≈300–700 million alveoli; the alveolar wall is lined by **alveolocytes** (type I — gas exchange, type II — produce **surfactant**) and a network of capillaries. The thickness of the **air–blood barrier** is ≈0.5 µm. The aggregate of acini is called the **respiratory portion** (gas exchange), and the bronchial tree above it the **conducting portion**.

blocks.label: Figure 21.7
blocks.caption: A segmental bronchus and its branches (A — general view; B — branching of the respiratory bronchioles; Figure No. 142): segmental bronchus, terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, alveoli, interalveolar septa, pulmonary acinus. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: The lungs have two blood circulations: **functional** — pulmonary artery (venous blood) → alveolar capillaries → pulmonary veins (arterial blood) — the pulmonary circulation; **nutritive** — the **bronchial arteries**, arising from the thoracic aorta, nourish the bronchi, pleura and lung tissue.

blocks.text: The **pleura** (*pleura*) is the serous membrane enveloping the lungs and lining the walls of the thoracic cavity. The **visceral (pulmonary) pleura** adheres firmly to the lung tissue and also enters the fissures; at the **root of the lung** it passes into the **parietal pleura**, and below the root it forms the two-layered **pulmonary ligament**, which descends to the diaphragm. Parts of the **parietal pleura**: the **costal**, **diaphragmatic** and **mediastinal** pleura; above, over the apex of the lung, it forms the **cupula of the pleura**. Between the layers is the narrow **pleural cavity** (*cavitas pleuralis*) — it contains ≈1–2 mL of serous fluid, and its pressure is below atmospheric (**negative pressure**) — which is why the lung is stretched behind the wall of the thoracic cage.

Where the parts of the parietal pleura pass into one another, **pleural recesses (sinuses)** form — reserve spaces that the lung does not fully enter even in inspiration: the **costodiaphragmatic recess** (the largest and deepest, ≈6–8 cm in the midaxillary line; the lowest point), the **costomediastinal recess** (in front, larger on the left in the region of the cardiac notch) and the **phrenicomediastinal recess**.

blocks.label: Figure 21.8
blocks.caption: The lungs in the pleural cavity, anterior view (Figure No. 153): lobes of the right and left lungs, cupula of the pleura, costal and diaphragmatic pleura, right and left costodiaphragmatic recesses, costomediastinal recess, lumbar part and crura of the diaphragm, esophageal hiatus. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: Fluid (**pleurisy**, **hydrothorax**), blood (**hemothorax**) or air (**pneumothorax**) may accumulate in the pleural cavity. Fluid collects first in the **costodiaphragmatic recess**; **pleural puncture** is performed in the 7th–8th intercostal space along the midaxillary or posterior axillary line, **along the upper border of the lower rib** (to avoid injuring the neurovascular bundle). In pneumothorax the negative pressure is lost and the lung collapses. Because the cupula of the pleura lies above the clavicle, it may be injured in neck wounds and during subclavian vein catheterization.

sections.title: 6. Borders of the lungs and pleura

blocks.text: The inferior border of the left lung runs half a rib to one rib lower than that of the right. The inferior border of the pleura lies on average **one to two ribs below** that of the lung — the difference corresponds to the costodiaphragmatic recess. **Anterior borders**: the right lung and pleura descend from behind the sternoclavicular joint along the sternum to the 6th costal cartilage; the anterior border of the left lung deviates laterally along the cardiac notch at the level of the **4th costal cartilage** and passes into the inferior border at the 6th costal cartilage. Behind the sternum two **interpleural areas** remain between the two pleurae: above — the **thymic area** (above the 2nd rib), below — the **pericardial area** (below the 4th rib, on the left) — here the heart can be reached without injuring the pleura (pericardiocentesis). The **posterior border** descends along the vertebral column from the cupula of the pleura to the head of the 12th rib.

blocks.label: Figure 21.9
blocks.caption: Borders of the lungs and pleura, anterior view (Figure No. 155): cupula of the pleura and apex of the lung, anterior and inferior borders of the pleura and lungs, cardiac notch of the left lung, interpleural areas, topographic lines (anterior median, sternal, parasternal, midclavicular lines). Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **mediastinum** (*mediastinum*) is the complex of organs between the right and left mediastinal pleurae, together with the tissue between them. Its boundaries: **in front** — the sternum, **behind** — the thoracic vertebrae, **at the sides** — the mediastinal pleura, **below** — the diaphragm, **above** — the superior thoracic aperture. According to the international nomenclature, the mediastinum is divided by a conventional horizontal plane passing through the sternal angle (angle of Louis) and the disc between the 4th and 5th thoracic vertebrae into **superior** and **inferior** parts, and the inferior part, by the pericardium, into **anterior**, **middle** and **posterior** parts.

blocks.title: Table 21.5. Parts and contents of the mediastinum

blocks.text: In practice the mediastinum is also divided by a frontal plane passing through the trachea and main bronchi into the **anterior** (thymus, heart and pericardium, great vessels, phrenic nerves, trachea, bronchi) and **posterior** (esophagus, aorta, azygos and hemiazygos veins, thoracic duct, vagus nerves, sympathetic trunks) mediastinum.

parts.text: Because the mediastinal tissue communicates with the fascial spaces of the neck, in neck phlegmons and perforation of the esophagus pus enters it, and severe **mediastinitis** develops. Mediastinal tumors (for example, thymoma, lymphoma) compress neighboring organs, causing signs such as shortness of breath, difficulty swallowing, **superior vena cava syndrome** (swelling of the face and neck) and hoarseness (recurrent nerve).

items: In the newborn the **trachea** begins at the level of the 3rd–4th cervical vertebrae and divides at the level of the **2nd–3rd thoracic vertebrae**; it is 3.2–4.5 cm long, funnel-shaped, ≈8–10 mm in diameter; its cartilages are soft and flexible, its membranous wall relatively wide, and its mucosa delicate, with few glands and rich in blood vessels. It grows rapidly in the first 6 months and during puberty; the bifurcation descends to the level of the 4th–5th thoracic vertebrae at 7 years and later to the 5th.

In the newborn the **main bronchi** are short (≈1.2 cm); the right bronchus diverges at ≈26° and the left at ≈49°; their cartilages are poorly developed. The branching of the bronchial tree at birth resembles that of adults; the bronchi grow rapidly in the 1st year and during puberty.

In the newborn the **lungs** are large relative to the thoracic cage and weigh ≈50–57 g (both); the upper lobes are small and the lower lobes large; the upper and middle lobes of the right lung are of equal size. There is much connective tissue and few elastic fibers — in children the lung tissue is less airy and swells easily (predisposition to pneumonia).

At birth the number of alveoli is ≈1/6–1/3 of that of adults; **up to 7–8 years** maturation of the bronchial tree and an increase in the number of alveoli continue; new alveoli form up to 12–15 years, after which they mainly grow in volume. The structure of the lung is completed at 15–25 years; the vital capacity increases 4 times by 1 year, 8 times by 8 years, 10 times by 12 years and 20 times by 20 years.

In the newborn the apex of the lung is at the level of the 1st rib, and the inferior border is one rib higher than in adults; with age they gradually descend. In the elderly the elasticity of the lungs decreases (age-related emphysema), and the apex descends lower.

In the newborn the **pleura** is very thin and mobile (little loose tissue) — which is why in children the mediastinal organs shift easily when fluid or air accumulates in the pleural cavity. The pleura resembles that of adults by 7 years.

In the newborn the **mediastinum** is wide and short (the diaphragm is high, the heart horizontal and the thymus large), occupying ≈1/2 of the thoracic cavity, and ≈1/3 at 1 month; by 3 years it resembles that of adults.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: While playing, a 3-year-old child swallowed (inhaled) a nut; after a violent coughing fit the cough lessened somewhat, but shortness of breath persists. On auscultation breath sounds are diminished over the lower part of the right lung.
cases.ask: Where may the foreign body have gone, and why precisely there? What examination and treatment are required?
cases.answer: A foreign body most often enters the **right main bronchus**, and then the **right lower lobe bronchus**: the right main bronchus is **short and wide** and almost a **vertical continuation** of the trachea (deviating ≈20–25° from the tracheal axis), whereas the left bronchus is longer, narrower and diverges at ≈45°. If the bronchus is blocked, the part of the lung beyond it collapses (atelectasis) or becomes overinflated — breath sounds are diminished. Diagnosis and treatment — removal of the foreign body by **bronchoscopy**.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: After a road traffic accident a patient has severe shortness of breath, lagging of the left side of the chest during breathing, a hyperresonant (box-like) percussion note and absent breath sounds; the trachea is displaced to the right.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? Which property of the pleura keeps the lung stretched, and why has the lung collapsed here? Why is the mediastinum displaced?
cases.answer: This is a **left-sided (tension) pneumothorax** — air has entered the pleural cavity. Normally, between the parietal and visceral pleura, **the pressure in the closed pleural cavity is below atmospheric (negative)**, and the lung is held stretched behind the wall of the thoracic cage. When air enters, the negative pressure is lost and the lung, owing to its own elasticity, **collapses**. In a valvular (tension) pneumothorax air accumulates and the pressure rises, and the **mediastinal** organs (heart, trachea) shift to the healthy side — this impairs the circulation. Emergency treatment — needle decompression in the 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line, followed by drainage.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a patient with heart failure, fluid was found in the right pleural cavity. The physician performed pleural puncture in the 8th intercostal space along the posterior axillary line.
cases.ask: In which part of the pleural cavity does the fluid collect? Why is the puncture performed precisely at this site, and along which border of the rib?
cases.answer: Fluid collects first in the lowest and deepest part of the pleural cavity — the **costodiaphragmatic recess**; it is deepest (6–8 cm) in the region of the midaxillary and posterior axillary lines. Here the inferior border of the lung (9th rib in the posterior axillary line) lies above the border of the pleura (10th rib), so the needle enters the recess without injuring the lung; if the puncture is made too low, the diaphragm and liver may be injured. The needle is inserted **along the upper border of the lower rib** — the intercostal neurovascular bundle lies in the groove on the lower border of the upper rib.
