topics.title: The kidney. The ureter, urinary bladder and urethra. Their age-related changes

goals.text: To teach the student the composition and development of the urinary system, the external and internal structure, coverings, topography and segments of the kidney, the nephron and the renal circulation, and the structure and topography of the urinary passages — the renal calyces and pelvis, the ureter, the urinary bladder and the urethra — with their age-related features and clinical significance.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the composition of the urinary system and the three-stage development of the kidney;
the external structure, skeletotopy, syntopy and coverings of the kidney;
the cortex and medulla, lobes and segments of the kidney;
the structure of the nephron and the features of the renal circulation;
the parts and constrictions of the renal calyces, pelvis and ureter;
the parts, wall, trigone and topography of the urinary bladder;
the parts of the male and female urethra and their differences;
the age-related features of the urinary organs.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the structures of the kidney, calyces, pelvis, ureter and bladder in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
show the projection of the kidney on the body and its relation to the 12th rib;
name the constrictions of the ureter and the parts of the male urethra.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Developmental anomalies: failure of the kidney to ascend — **ectopia** (lumbar, iliac or pelvic kidney); fusion of the lower poles of the two kidneys — **horseshoe kidney** (during ascent it is caught on the inferior mesenteric artery); **duplication** of the kidney and ureter; unilateral **agenesis**; if the urachus remains patent — leakage of urine from the umbilicus (urachal fistula). If the pubic bones and anterior abdominal wall fail to fuse — **bladder exstrophy**.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: When the fatty capsule is sharply reduced (rapid weight loss) and the abdominal muscles weaken, **descent of the kidney (nephroptosis)** develops — because the fascia is open below, the kidney slides downward; the ureter kinks and urine flow is impaired. Because the kidney lies behind the peritoneum, it can be reached surgically **through the lumbar region** (without opening the peritoneal cavity). In kidney diseases pain is referred to the lumbar region, and along the ureter to the groin.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In **urolithiasis** stones most often lodge in the **three constrictions** of the ureter and cause severe colicky pain — **renal colic**: the pain radiates from the loin along the side of the abdomen to the groin, the testis (labium majus) and the inner surface of the thigh (segments T~XI~–L~II~). In women, during hysterectomy the ureter may be ligated, because it lies **beneath the uterine artery** ("water under the bridge").

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Bladder catheterization** is the passage of a catheter through the urethra into the bladder; in men it is more difficult because of the curves and constrictions of the canal. In urinary retention (for example, in prostatic hyperplasia) the full bladder bulges above the pubis and is not covered by peritoneum — so **suprapubic puncture** (cystostomy) is performed without injuring the peritoneal cavity. On **cystoscopy** the trigone of the bladder and the ureteric orifices are seen.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In women the urethra is short, wide and straight, and its external orifice is close to the vagina and anus — which is why **ascending urinary tract infections** (cystitis, pyelonephritis) are much more common in women than in men. In men, by contrast, the urethra is long and curved — care is needed during catheterization and cystoscopy (risk of injury to the membranous part).

sections.title: 1. The urinary system and its development

blocks.text: The **urinary system** (*systema urinarium*) removes metabolic waste products (urea, creatinine, uric acid, etc.), excess water and salts from the blood, forms urine and excretes it; in this way it regulates water-salt and acid-base balance, arterial pressure (renin) and hematopoiesis (erythropoietin). Its components: the **kidneys**, which form urine; the **calyces, pelvis and ureters**, which carry it away; the **urinary bladder**, where urine collects; and the **urethra**, which discharges it.

The **kidney** develops from the intermediate mesoderm (nephrotomes and the nephrogenic cord) **in three stages**: 1) the **pronephros** (*pronephros*) — appears in the cervical segments in the 3rd week and soon disappears, leaving only its duct; 2) the **mesonephros** (*mesonephros*, Wolffian body) — in the 4th week in the thoracolumbar segments; its duct (the **mesonephric, Wolffian duct**) becomes the seminal (genital) ducts in males; 3) the **metanephros** (*metanephros*) — from the 5th week: the **ureteric bud**, growing out of the mesonephric duct, gives rise to the ureter, pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts, and the **metanephrogenic tissue** to the nephrons. The definitive kidney first appears in the pelvis, then **ascends to the lumbar region** and rotates around its axis (the hilum turning from an anterior to a medial position). The **bladder** develops from the anterior part of the cloaca — the urogenital sinus; its apex is connected with the allantois (later the **urachus** — the median umbilical ligament).

parts.text: Developmental anomalies: failure of the kidney to ascend — **ectopia** (lumbar, iliac or pelvic kidney); fusion of the lower poles of the two kidneys — **horseshoe kidney** (during ascent it is caught on the inferior mesenteric artery); **duplication** of the kidney and ureter; unilateral **agenesis**; if the urachus remains patent — leakage of urine from the umbilicus (urachal fistula). If the pubic bones and anterior abdominal wall fail to fuse — **bladder exstrophy**.

sections.title: 2. External structure and topography of the kidney

blocks.text: The **kidney** (*ren*, Greek *nephros*) is a paired, bean-shaped, dark red organ; it is **10–12 cm** long, 5–6 cm wide, ≈4 cm thick, and weighs **120–200 g**. It has **anterior** (more convex) and **posterior** (flatter) **surfaces**, **superior** and **inferior poles (extremities)**, and a convex **lateral** and a concave **medial border**. In the middle of the medial border is the **renal hilum**, which continues internally into the **renal sinus**. The **renal artery** and nerves enter through the hilum, and the **renal vein**, the **pelvis (ureter)** and lymphatics leave; the structures from front to back are: **vein, artery, pelvis** ("VAP").

blocks.label: Figure 22.1
blocks.caption: Right kidney, external structure (A — anterior view; B — posterior view; Figure No. 164): superior and inferior poles, anterior and posterior surfaces, lateral and medial borders, renal hilum, renal artery and vein, renal pelvis, ureter, suprarenal gland, fibrous capsule. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: **Skeletotopy**: the kidneys lie on the posterior wall of the abdominal cavity, **behind the peritoneum** (retroperitoneal), on both sides of the vertebral column at the level of T~XI~–L~III~; their upper poles are close together and the lower poles farther apart. Because of the liver, the **right kidney** lies **≈2 cm lower** than the left. The upper pole of the left kidney is at the middle of T~XI~ and its lower pole at the upper border of L~III~; those of the right kidney are at the lower border of T~XI~ and the middle of L~III~. The **12th rib** crosses the left kidney across the middle of its posterior surface and the right kidney in the region of its upper pole. The hila are at the level of L~I~–L~II~.

**Syntopy**: through its coverings the posterior surface is in contact with the diaphragm, quadratus lumborum, psoas major and transversus abdominis; the **suprarenal gland** lies on the upper pole. In front of the **right kidney** are the liver (upper 2/3), the right colic flexure (below) and the descending part of the duodenum (at the medial border). In front of the **left kidney** are the stomach (above), the tail of the pancreas (in the middle) and loops of the jejunum (below), and at its lateral border the spleen and the left colic flexure.

blocks.label: Figure 22.2
blocks.caption: The kidneys (Figure No. 169, B — syntopy of the right and left kidneys; the boundaries of the contact areas of the adjacent organs): liver, duodenum, right colic flexure, stomach, spleen, pancreas, descending colon, jejunum, suprarenal glands. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: **Coverings of the kidney** (from inside outward): 1) the **fibrous capsule** — thin and strong, easily stripped from a healthy kidney; 2) the **fatty capsule** — adipose tissue, especially thick on the posterior surface and at the hilum (the **perirenal fat body**); 3) the **renal fascia** — consisting of anterior and posterior layers; they unite at the lateral border and the upper pole, but are open below and medially (along the ureter and vessels). The **fixing apparatus** holding the kidney in place: the coverings (especially the fatty capsule and fascia), the renal vessels, intra-abdominal pressure and the tone of the abdominal muscles, and the renal bed (a depression formed by the muscles).

blocks.label: Figure 22.3
blocks.caption: Fasciae and coverings of the kidney (diagram, transverse section at the level of the 1st lumbar vertebra; Figure No. 165): anterior and posterior layers of the renal fascia, fatty capsule, kidney, parietal peritoneum, aorta, inferior vena cava, liver, lumbar vertebra. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: When the fatty capsule is sharply reduced (rapid weight loss) and the abdominal muscles weaken, **descent of the kidney (nephroptosis)** develops — because the fascia is open below, the kidney slides downward; the ureter kinks and urine flow is impaired. Because the kidney lies behind the peritoneum, it can be reached surgically **through the lumbar region** (without opening the peritoneal cavity). In kidney diseases pain is referred to the lumbar region, and along the ureter to the groin.

blocks.text: On a frontal section of the kidney two substances are distinguished. The **cortex** (*cortex renalis*) is the outer layer, 4–7 mm thick and reddish; it comprises the **convoluted part**, containing the **renal corpuscles** and convoluted tubules, and the **medullary rays** (radiate part) entering from the medulla; the cortex extends between the pyramids to form the **renal columns**. The **medulla** (*medulla renalis*) consists of **10–15 renal pyramids**: their bases face the cortex and their apices — the **renal papillae** — face the renal sinus; 15–20 papillary ducts open on each papilla, forming the **area cribrosa**.

blocks.label: Figure 22.4
blocks.caption: Cortex and medulla of the kidney, frontal section of the kidney (Figure No. 175): cortex, renal columns, pyramids and medullary rays, renal papillae, minor and major calyces, renal pelvis, renal sinus, segmental artery and vein, fibrous capsule, ureter. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: A **renal lobe** is one pyramid with the cortex surrounding it; each lobe contains ≈600 **cortical lobules** in the cortex. According to the distribution of the blood vessels, the kidney has **5 segments**: **superior**, **anterior superior**, **anterior inferior**, **inferior** and **posterior**; at the hilum the renal artery divides into anterior (4 segments) and posterior (the posterior segment) branches; the segmental arteries are **without anastomoses** (end arteries) — this allows segmental resection.

The **nephron** is the structural-functional unit of the kidney; each kidney contains **≈1 million** nephrons. Its parts: the **renal corpuscle** — the vascular **glomerulus** and the two-layered **glomerular capsule** surrounding it (Shumlyansky–Bowman capsule); the **proximal convoluted tubule**; the **nephron loop** (loop of Henle) — descending and ascending limbs; the **distal convoluted tubule**; this opens through a **connecting tubule** into a **collecting duct** (the collecting ducts are not part of the nephron). About 80% of the nephrons are **cortical** (with a short loop) and ≈20% **juxtamedullary** (the glomerulus at the corticomedullary junction, the loop extending deep into the medulla — important for concentrating urine).

**Renal circulation**: renal artery → segmental arteries → **interlobar** (between the pyramids) → **arcuate** (at the bases of the pyramids) → **interlobular** arteries → **afferent arteriole** → glomerular capillaries → **efferent arteriole** (narrower — hence the high pressure in the glomerulus) → peritubular capillaries → veins (of the same names) → renal vein. Because the glomerular capillaries lie between two arterioles, they are called the **wonderful vascular network (rete mirabile) of the kidney**. Each day **1500–1800 L** of blood pass through the kidneys, **150–180 L of primary urine** are filtered, and as a result of reabsorption in the tubules **1–1.5 L of secondary (final) urine** are formed.

blocks.label: Figure 22.5
blocks.caption: Structure and blood supply of the renal cortex and medulla (Figure No. 181): glomerular capsule, renal corpuscles, proximal and distal convoluted tubules, straight tubules, collecting ducts, papillary ducts, afferent and efferent vessels, interlobar, arcuate and interlobular arteries and veins, vasa recta, calyces, renal artery and vein, ureter. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

sections.title: 4. The renal calyces, pelvis and ureter

blocks.text: Each renal papilla (or 2–3 of them) is embraced by a **minor calyx** (8–9 in all); 2–3 minor calyces unite to form a **major calyx** (superior, middle, inferior); the major calyces unite to form the funnel-shaped **renal pelvis** (*pelvis renalis*); the pelvis leaves the hilum, narrows and passes into the **ureter**. By shape the pelvis may be **ampullary** (embryonic), **branched** (mature) or intermediate (fetal). In the wall of the fornix of the minor calyces there is a ring of smooth muscle — the **fornical apparatus**; it regulates the outflow of urine and prevents its backflow (pyelorenal reflux).

blocks.label: Figure 22.6
blocks.caption: Variants of the structure of the renal calyces and pelvis (A — mature (branched) form; B — fetal form; V — embryonic (ampullary) form; Figure No. 174): 1 — ureter; 2 — renal pelvis; 3 — major calyces; 4 — minor calyces. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **ureter** (*ureter*) is the tube carrying urine from the pelvis to the bladder; it is **30–35 cm** long and 6–8 mm in diameter, and lies retroperitoneally. Its parts: the **abdominal part** — lies in front of the psoas major and is crossed anteriorly by the testicular (ovarian) vessels; the **pelvic part** — at the pelvic brim the right ureter passes in front of the external iliac vessels and the left in front of the common iliac vessels, then it descends along the pelvic wall (crossing the ductus deferens in males and passing **beneath the uterine artery** in females); the **intramural part** (1.5–2 cm) — pierces the bladder wall obliquely (acting as a valve against reflux). Its wall: mucosa (transitional epithelium, longitudinal folds), muscular coat (2 layers above, 3 below) and adventitia.

head: Constriction
Location
rows: Where the pelvis passes into the ureter (the ureteropelvic junction)
At the entrance into the lesser pelvis — where it crosses the iliac vessels (pelvic brim)

blocks.label: Figure 22.7
blocks.caption: Topography and constrictions of the ureter (Figure No. 188): kidneys, suprarenal glands, psoas major, ureters, their narrowing at the exit from the renal pelvis, where they cross the iliac vessels and within the bladder wall, their crossing with the testicular (ovarian) vessels, bladder, aorta and inferior vena cava. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: In **urolithiasis** stones most often lodge in the **three constrictions** of the ureter and cause severe colicky pain — **renal colic**: the pain radiates from the loin along the side of the abdomen to the groin, the testis (labium majus) and the inner surface of the thigh (segments T~XI~–L~II~). In women, during hysterectomy the ureter may be ligated, because it lies **beneath the uterine artery** ("water under the bridge").

blocks.text: The **urinary bladder** (*vesica urinaria*) is an unpaired muscular organ in which urine collects; its capacity averages **500–700 mL** (the urge to void appears at 250–300 mL). Its parts: the **apex**, facing forward and upward (from it the **median umbilical ligament** — the remnant of the urachus — runs to the umbilicus), the **body**, the posteroinferior **fundus** and the narrowed lower **neck**, which passes into the urethra. The bladder lies in the lesser pelvis **behind the pubic symphysis** (with the prevesical fat between them — the space of Retzius); when full it rises above the symphysis and contacts the anterior abdominal wall **without intervening peritoneum**. **In males** behind it are the rectum, the seminal vesicles and the ampullae of the ductus deferentes, and below it the **prostate**; **in females** behind it are the cervix of the uterus and the vagina, and below it the urogenital diaphragm. The empty bladder is extraperitoneal; the full bladder is mesoperitoneal.

blocks.label: Figure 22.8

Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: **Wall of the bladder**: **mucosa** — transitional epithelium (adapted to distension), forming folds in the empty bladder; **submucosa**; **muscular coat** — three layers of smooth muscle (outer and inner longitudinal, middle circular), together the **detrusor muscle** (*m. detrusor vesicae*), which expels urine; in the region of the neck the circular fibers form the **internal (involuntary) sphincter**; the outer layer is a serosa above and an adventitia elsewhere. In the fundus of the bladder is the **trigone of the bladder** (*trigonum vesicae*, Lieutaud's trigone) — at its angles lie the two **ureteric orifices** and the **internal urethral orifice**; here there is no submucosa and the mucosa adheres firmly to the muscle — no folds are formed. Between the ureteric orifices runs the **interureteric fold**.

parts.text: **Bladder catheterization** is the passage of a catheter through the urethra into the bladder; in men it is more difficult because of the curves and constrictions of the canal. In urinary retention (for example, in prostatic hyperplasia) the full bladder bulges above the pubis and is not covered by peritoneum — so **suprapubic puncture** (cystostomy) is performed without injuring the peritoneal cavity. On **cystoscopy** the trigone of the bladder and the ureteric orifices are seen.

blocks.text: The **male urethra** (*urethra masculina*) is an S-shaped tube **16–22 cm** long; it runs from the **internal orifice** in the bladder to the **external orifice** on the glans penis; besides urine it also conveys **seminal fluid**.

blocks.text: **Constrictions** of the canal: the internal orifice, the membranous part and the external orifice; **dilations**: the prostatic part, the bulb of the corpus spongiosum and the navicular fossa. **Curvatures**: the fixed **posterior (subpubic)** curvature and the mobile **anterior (prepubic)** curvature (straightened during erection).

The **female urethra** (*urethra feminina*) is short (**2.5–4 cm**), wide (8–12 mm) and almost straight, fused with the anterior wall of the vagina; it passes through the urogenital diaphragm and opens by its external orifice into the **vestibule of the vagina** between the clitoris and the vaginal orifice; where it passes through the diaphragm it is surrounded by the **external (voluntary) sphincter**.

parts.text: In women the urethra is short, wide and straight, and its external orifice is close to the vagina and anus — which is why **ascending urinary tract infections** (cystitis, pyelonephritis) are much more common in women than in men. In men, by contrast, the urethra is long and curved — care is needed during catheterization and cystoscopy (risk of injury to the membranous part).

items: The newborn's kidney is **relatively large**, rounded and **lobulated** (embryonic lobulation) — its surface is bumpy because the cortex is poorly developed; this disappears by 2–3 years. It is ≈4.2 cm long and weighs ≈12 g (both ≈25 g; ≈0.8% of body weight, vs. ≈0.5% in adults); the ratio of the thickness of the cortex to the medulla is 1:4 (1:2 in adults). The left kidney is larger than the right.

In the newborn the kidneys lie **lower**: the upper pole at the upper border of T~XII~ and the lower pole at the lower border of L~IV~; because the vertebral column grows rapidly, they rise relatively by 1 year and resemble those of adults after 7 years. In children the longitudinal axes of the kidneys are parallel; from 5–6 years the upper poles approach each other.

In the newborn the kidney **has no fatty capsule** — it appears in early childhood and is well defined by 7 years; the fascia is thin — the kidney is mobile and palpable in young children. The kidney grows rapidly in the 1st year and at 5–9 and 16–19 years, mainly through the cortex (the cortex thickens 4 times, the medulla 2 times). The number of nephrons at birth equals that of adults, but they are immature — the concentrating ability of the child's kidney is low.
In the newborn the renal pelvis is wide and ampullary and often lies **outside the kidney**; by 3 years it moves inside the kidney.

In the newborn the ureter is 5–7 cm long, tortuous and thin-walled, with poorly developed muscle and elastic fibers; it is ≈10 cm at 1 year, ≈15 cm at 4 years and 18–20 cm at puberty; its structure resembles that of adults by 8 years.

In the newborn the **bladder is fusiform and high** — it lies mainly in the **abdominal cavity** (its apex halfway between the umbilicus and the pubic symphysis) and is in contact with the peritoneum in front as well; its fundus is not formed, and its trigone lies frontally. Its capacity is **50–80 mL** in the newborn, 180–200 mL at 5 years and 500–700 mL at puberty; its shape is pear-like at 1.5–2 years, plum-like at 5 years, ovoid at 10 years and spherical in adolescence. With age the bladder descends into the lesser pelvis.

In the newborn boy the urethra is 5–6 cm long, in girls 1–3 cm; the muscle layer of the urethra and the **external (voluntary) sphincter are fully formed by 12–13 years**. Voluntary control of urination develops at 2–3 years.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 35-year-old man presented with sudden severe colicky pain in the right loin radiating along the right side of the abdomen to the groin and testis; he is restless and cannot find a comfortable position. There are red blood cells in the urine. Ultrasound showed dilation of the right renal pelvis and a 6 mm stone in the ureter at the pelvic brim.
cases.ask: What is the condition? In which constrictions of the ureter do stones lodge? Why does the pain radiate to the groin and testis?
cases.answer: This is **renal colic** — a stone is lodged in the ureter (urolithiasis). The ureter has **three constrictions**: the junction of the pelvis with the ureter, the **entrance into the lesser pelvis** (where it crosses the iliac vessels) and the **intramural part** in the bladder wall (the narrowest). Because the stone blocks the ureter, the outflow of urine is impaired and the pelvis is dilated. The sensory fibers of the kidney and ureter go to segments **T~XI~–L~II~** — pain is referred to the areas supplied by these segments: the loin, the lateral abdominal wall, the groin and the testis (ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 22-year-old woman has had frequent, painful urination and suprapubic pain for the third time this year (acute cystitis). Her husband has not had this disease.
cases.ask: Why is cystitis much more common in women than in men? State the differences between the female and male urethras.
cases.answer: The female urethra is **short (2.5–4 cm), wide and almost straight**, and its external orifice lies in the **vestibule of the vagina**, close to the vagina and anus — microbes easily ascend into the bladder (ascending infection). The male urethra is **long (16–22 cm) and S-shaped**, consists of prostatic, membranous and spongy parts, has three constrictions and opens on the glans penis — there are more barriers to ascending infection. In women the urethra is fused with the anterior wall of the vagina and conveys only urine; in men it also conveys seminal fluid.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A thin 30-year-old woman who has lost weight complains of right loin pain that increases on standing and decreases on lying down. Urography performed in the upright position showed that the right kidney had descended by two vertebrae and the ureter was kinked.
cases.ask: What is the condition (nephroptosis)? Name the factors that hold the kidney in place, and explain why it occurs especially in thin women and on the right side.
cases.answer: This is **nephroptosis** — descent of the kidney. The **fixing apparatus** of the kidney: its coverings — especially the **fatty capsule** and the **renal fascia** — the renal vessels (artery and vein), intra-abdominal pressure and the tone of the anterior abdominal wall muscles, and the **renal bed** formed by the muscles. With sharp weight loss the fatty capsule diminishes; because the renal fascia is **open below**, the kidney slides downward. Because the right kidney lies lower owing to the liver and the right renal bed is shallower, nephroptosis is more often right-sided; in women the abdominal wall is weaker (pregnancies). Kinking of the ureter impairs urine flow.

topics.title: The male and female genital organs and their age-related changes. Topography of the perineum: the pelvic and urogenital diaphragms and their sex differences

goals.text: To teach the student the development of the genital organs, the structure, topography and function of the male and female internal and external genital organs, the descent of the testis into the scrotum and the coverings of the testis, and the structure of the perineum and of the urogenital and pelvic diaphragms, with their sex differences, age-related features and clinical significance.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the development and congenital anomalies of the internal and external genital organs;
the structure of the testis, epididymis, seminal ducts, seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands;
the descent of the testis, the spermatic cord and the coverings of the testis;
the structure of the penis and scrotum;
the parts, wall, ligaments and topography of the ovary, uterine tube, uterus and vagina;
the female external genital organs;
the boundaries of the perineum and the muscles and fasciae of the urogenital and pelvic diaphragms;
the age-related features of the genital organs.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the parts of the male and female genital organs in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
describe in sequence the route of sperm from the testis to the urethra;
compare the coverings of the testis with the layers of the abdominal wall;
outline the urogenital and pelvic diaphragms in the perineal region.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Developmental anomalies: **hypospadias** (the external urethral orifice on the underside of the penis — the urethral folds have not fused), **epispadias** (on the upper surface), **cryptorchidism** (failure of the testis to descend into the scrotum — it remains in the abdominal cavity or the inguinal canal), **hermaphroditism** (pseudo- or true), and incomplete fusion of the Müllerian ducts — a **bicornuate**, **septate** or **double** uterus.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The route of sperm: **convoluted seminiferous tubules → straight tubules → rete testis → efferent ductules → duct of the epididymis → ductus deferens (ampulla) → ejaculatory duct → urethra (prostatic, membranous, spongy parts) → external orifice**. Composition of semen: spermatozoa (testis, ≈5%) + secretion of the seminal vesicles (≈60%) + prostatic secretion (≈30%) + secretion of the bulbourethral glands.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Prostatic adenoma (benign hyperplasia)** — in older men the middle and periurethral parts of the prostate enlarge and compress the urethra: urination becomes difficult, and urinary retention may occur. **Prostate cancer** usually develops in the posterior peripheral part of the gland — it is detected as a hard nodule on **digital rectal examination**. **Vasectomy** (male sterilization) is ligation/division of the ductus deferens in the scrotum or spermatic cord.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: For spermatogenesis the testis must be in the scrotum, at a temperature ≈2–3 °C below body temperature (the dartos and cremaster muscles and the pampiniform plexus — a "heat exchanger" — regulate the temperature). In **cryptorchidism** spermatogenesis is impaired and the risk of tumors increases — surgery (orchiopexy) before 1 year of age is recommended. If the processus vaginalis remains patent — **congenital indirect inguinal hernia** or **hydrocele of the testis**. Dilation of the veins of the pampiniform plexus is **varicocele** (more often on the left, because the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle). The **cremasteric reflex** — elevation of the testis on stroking the inner surface of the thigh (L~I~–L~II~).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Ectopic pregnancy** most often develops in the **ampulla** of the uterine tube; when the tube ruptures there is severe bleeding into the peritoneal cavity (the blood collects in the pouch of Douglas). Because the uterine tube opens into the peritoneal cavity, genital tract infections in women can lead to **pelvic peritonitis**. When the pelvic floor muscles weaken (multiple deliveries), **prolapse of the uterus and vaginal walls** occurs. The uterine artery crosses **in front of and above the ureter** in the parametrium — a risk of ureteric injury in hysterectomy.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: During childbirth the perineal tissues are stretched and may **tear**; to prevent this an **episiotomy** (controlled incision of the perineum) is performed — the incision is usually made in a mediolateral direction to avoid injuring the perineal body and the anal sphincter. When the pelvic floor muscles weaken, urinary incontinence and prolapse of organs occur; special exercises (Kegel exercises) are recommended to strengthen them.

blocks.text: In the early stages of development the genital organs are **the same in both sexes (indifferent)**. The **gonads** develop in the 4th–5th week from the epithelium and mesenchyme of the **genital ridge** on the medial surface of the mesonephros; the primordial germ cells migrate from the wall of the yolk sac. Two pairs of ducts form: the **mesonephric (Wolffian) duct** and the **paramesonephric (Müllerian) duct**. If a Y chromosome (SRY gene) is present, from the 7th week the gonad becomes a **testis**; the testis produces testosterone (for development of the Wolffian duct) and **anti-Müllerian hormone** (causing regression of the Müllerian ducts). If there is no Y chromosome, the gonad becomes an **ovary**, and the Wolffian duct regresses.

sections.title: 2. Male genital organs: the testis and epididymis

blocks.text: The **male internal genital organs** are the testis, epididymis, ductus deferens, seminal vesicles, ejaculatory duct, prostate and bulbourethral glands; the **external** organs are the penis and scrotum (the male urethra was considered in topic 22).

blocks.label: Figure 23.1
blocks.caption: Male genital organs, left lateral view (diagram; Figure No. 207): testis, epididymis, ductus deferens, seminal vesicle, prostate, bulbourethral gland, parts of the male urethra, corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum of the penis, scrotum, bladder, rectum, pelvic and perineal muscles. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **testis** (*testis*, Greek *orchis*) is a paired **mixed gland**: it produces **spermatozoa** and secretes **testosterone** (Leydig cells). It lies in the scrotum, the left testis slightly lower; it is oval, ≈4 cm long, ≈3 cm wide and ≈2 cm thick, and weighs 20–30 g. It has medial and lateral surfaces, anterior and posterior borders, and upper and lower poles; the epididymis is attached to its posterior border. It is covered externally by the strong **tunica albuginea**; at the posterior border this thickens to form the **mediastinum testis**, from which radial **septula** divide the testis into **250–300 lobules**. Each lobule contains 2–3 **convoluted seminiferous tubules** (70–80 cm long; their wall contains spermatogenic epithelium and Sertoli cells); they continue as the **straight tubules** → **rete testis** (in the mediastinum) → 12–15 **efferent ductules** into the epididymis.

The **epididymis** (*epididymis*) lies along the posterior border of the testis; it has a **head** (conical lobules formed by the efferent ductules), a **body** and a **tail**. Its single, highly coiled **duct** is **6–8 m** long; spermatozoa travel through it for ≈2 weeks, mature and acquire the ability to fertilize; they are stored in its tail. Rudiments are found on the testis and epididymis — the **appendix of the testis** (a remnant of the Müllerian duct) and the **appendix of the epididymis** (a remnant of the Wolffian duct).

Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

sections.title: 3. The seminal ducts and the accessory genital glands

blocks.text: The **ductus deferens** (*ductus deferens*) is the continuation of the duct of the epididymis; it is **40–50 cm** long, with a thick muscular wall (it feels like a firm cord on palpation) and a lumen of ≈0.5 mm. Its parts: the **scrotal part**, the **funicular part** (in the spermatic cord), the **inguinal part** (in the inguinal canal) and the **pelvic part** — leaving the deep inguinal ring, it descends along the lateral pelvic wall, **crosses in front of and above the ureter**, and at the fundus of the bladder widens to form the **ampulla**. The ampulla joins the duct of the **seminal vesicle** to form the **ejaculatory duct** (≈2 cm); this pierces the prostate and opens on the **seminal colliculus** in the prostatic part of the urethra.

The **seminal vesicles** (*glandulae vesiculosae*) are paired, coiled tubular glands (≈5 cm long) lying behind the fundus of the bladder, lateral to the ampullae; they produce most of the seminal fluid (rich in fructose). The **prostate** (*prostata*) is a chestnut-shaped glandular-muscular organ (weighing ≈20 g) lying below the bladder and surrounding the initial part of the urethra; its **base** faces the bladder and its **apex** the urogenital diaphragm; its **anterior surface** faces the pubic symphysis, and its **posterior surface** is in contact with the rectal ampulla (it is palpated through the rectum). It has **right and left lobes** and between them an **isthmus (middle lobe)**; the ducts of 30–50 glandules open around the seminal colliculus; its muscle tissue takes part in the involuntary sphincter of the urethra. The **bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands** are pea-sized, lying behind the membranous part of the urethra within the urogenital diaphragm; their ducts open into the spongy part of the urethra.

parts.text: The route of sperm: **convoluted seminiferous tubules → straight tubules → rete testis → efferent ductules → duct of the epididymis → ductus deferens (ampulla) → ejaculatory duct → urethra (prostatic, membranous, spongy parts) → external orifice**. Composition of semen: spermatozoa (testis, ≈5%) + secretion of the seminal vesicles (≈60%) + prostatic secretion (≈30%) + secretion of the bulbourethral glands.

**Prostatic adenoma (benign hyperplasia)** — in older men the middle and periurethral parts of the prostate enlarge and compress the urethra: urination becomes difficult, and urinary retention may occur. **Prostate cancer** usually develops in the posterior peripheral part of the gland — it is detected as a hard nodule on **digital rectal examination**. **Vasectomy** (male sterilization) is ligation/division of the ductus deferens in the scrotum or spermatic cord.

sections.title: 4. Descent of the testis, the spermatic cord and the coverings of the testis

blocks.text: The testis develops in the abdominal cavity, in the lumbar region, and descends under the influence of the **gubernaculum testis** (*gubernaculum testis*): at 3 months it lies beside the deep inguinal ring, at **7–8 months** it passes through the inguinal canal, and **by the time of birth** it descends into the scrotum. Ahead of the testis the peritoneum bulges out to form the **processus vaginalis of the peritoneum**; the testis takes all the layers of the abdominal wall with it. After birth the upper part of the processus vaginalis closes, and its lower part forms the **tunica vaginalis** around the testis.

The **spermatic cord** (*funiculus spermaticus*) is a round cord (15–20 cm) extending from the deep inguinal ring to the upper pole of the testis; its contents: the **ductus deferens**, the **testicular artery**, the artery of the ductus deferens, the cremasteric artery, the **pampiniform venous plexus**, lymphatic vessels, nerves (testicular plexus, genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve) and the remnant of the processus vaginalis.

parts.text: For spermatogenesis the testis must be in the scrotum, at a temperature ≈2–3 °C below body temperature (the dartos and cremaster muscles and the pampiniform plexus — a "heat exchanger" — regulate the temperature). In **cryptorchidism** spermatogenesis is impaired and the risk of tumors increases — surgery (orchiopexy) before 1 year of age is recommended. If the processus vaginalis remains patent — **congenital indirect inguinal hernia** or **hydrocele of the testis**. Dilation of the veins of the pampiniform plexus is **varicocele** (more often on the left, because the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle). The **cremasteric reflex** — elevation of the testis on stroking the inner surface of the thigh (L~I~–L~II~).

blocks.text: The **penis** (*penis*) is the organ of urination and ejaculation; it has a **root** (attached to the pubic and ischial bones), a **body** (its upper surface — the dorsum of the penis) and a **glans** (with its corona and neck; at its tip the external urethral orifice). The penis consists of **two corpora cavernosa** (above; their posterior ends — the **crura** — attach to the ischiopubic rami) and **one corpus spongiosum** (below; the urethra runs through it; it ends behind in the **bulb** and in front in the **glans**). Each body is enclosed in a **tunica albuginea**; inside are endothelium-lined **caverns** — when they fill with blood, **erection** occurs. The skin of the penis is thin and mobile; over the glans it forms the fold of the **prepuce** (*preputium*) and, below, its **frenulum**. The penis is supported by the superficial and deep fasciae and the **suspensory ligaments**.

The **scrotum** (*scrotum*) is a skin-muscle sac lying behind and below the root of the penis; it is divided into two compartments by the **scrotal septum** (corresponding externally to the **scrotal raphe**); each compartment contains a testis, the epididymis and the initial part of the spermatic cord.

The **female internal genital organs** are the **ovaries**, **uterine tubes**, **uterus** and **vagina**; the external organs make up the **female pudendum** (mons pubis, labia majora and minora, vestibule of the vagina, clitoris, vestibular glands and bulb).

blocks.label: Figure 23.6
blocks.caption: Female internal genital organs, anterior view (uterus not opened; Figure No. 250): fundus, body and cervix of the uterus, isthmus, ampulla, infundibulum and fimbriae of the uterine tubes, ovaries and their proper and suspensory ligaments, broad ligament of the uterus, mesosalpinx, epoophoron, vesicular appendices, ureter, rectouterine fold, vagina. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **ovary** (*ovarium*) is a paired **mixed gland**: the ova (oocytes) mature in it, and it secretes **estrogens** and **progesterone**. It lies on the lateral wall of the lesser pelvis, in the **ovarian fossa**; it is oval, 2.5–5 cm long and weighs 5–8 g. It has **medial** and **lateral surfaces**, a free and a **mesovarian border** (with the **hilum of the ovary**), and **tubal** and **uterine poles**. The ovary is held by its **mesovarium** (from the posterior layer of the broad ligament of the uterus), the **suspensory ligament of the ovary** (from the pelvic wall; containing the ovarian vessels) and the **proper ligament of the ovary** (to the angle of the uterus). It is not covered by peritoneum — its surface is covered by a simple "germinal" epithelium, beneath which lies the tunica albuginea; inside are the **cortex** (follicles) and **medulla** (vessels).

In the cortex there are **follicles** at different stages of maturity: **primordial**, **primary**, **secondary** and the mature **tertiary (Graafian follicle)**. Each month one Graafian follicle ruptures, and the ovum is released into the peritoneal cavity (**ovulation**); in place of the ruptured follicle the **corpus luteum** forms (if no pregnancy occurs, it becomes the **corpus albicans**). At birth the ovary contains ≈1–2 million primordial follicles, ≈300–400 thousand remain by puberty, and ≈400–500 ovulate during the entire reproductive period.

blocks.label: Figure 23.7
blocks.caption: Development of follicles in the ovary (diagram; Figure No. 257): A — primordial follicle; B — primary (growing) follicle; V — secondary (vesicular) follicle; G — corpus luteum; D — ovulation; E — preovulatory secondary (vesicular) follicle; ovarian stroma, blood vessels, atretic body, scar in place of the corpus luteum. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **uterine tube** (*tuba uterina*, Fallopian tube) is 10–12 cm long; it lies in the upper border of the broad ligament of the uterus (in the **mesosalpinx**). Its parts: the **uterine part** (intramural; opens by the **uterine orifice**), the **isthmus** (narrow), the **ampulla** — the longest part, where **fertilization usually takes place** — and the **infundibulum**, which opens into the peritoneal cavity by the **abdominal orifice**, surrounded by **fimbriae**. Its wall: a mucosa with ciliated epithelium (longitudinal folds), a smooth muscle layer (peristalsis) and a serosa. The ovum is moved toward the uterus by ciliary action and peristalsis.

The **uterus** (*uterus*, Greek *metra*) is a pear-shaped, muscular unpaired organ; the fetus develops in it, and it expels the fetus at delivery. It is 7–8 cm long, ≈4 cm wide and weighs 40–50 g (more in women who have given birth). Its parts: the **fundus** (above the entry of the tubes), the **body**, the **isthmus** (*isthmus*) and the **cervix** (*cervix*) — with **supravaginal** and **vaginal parts**; in the vaginal part of the cervix is the **external os** (round in nulliparous women, a transverse slit in parous women). Inside is the triangular **uterine cavity** and the **cervical canal**. Its wall: the **endometrium** (mucosa; changes during the menstrual cycle), the **myometrium** (a thick smooth muscle layer) and the **perimetrium** (serosa). The uterus lies in the lesser pelvis between the bladder and rectum; its normal position is **anteflexion** (the body bent forward relative to the cervix) and **anteversion** (the whole uterus tilted forward).

**Ligaments of the uterus**: the **broad ligament** — a peritoneal duplication passing from the lateral borders of the uterus to the pelvic walls (containing the tubes, ovaries, vessels and the **parametrium** connective tissue); the **round ligament** — from the angle of the uterus through the inguinal canal to the labium majus (maintains anteversion); the **cardinal (transverse cervical) ligaments** — between the cervix and the lateral pelvic walls; the **uterosacral** and **vesicouterine** ligaments. The **pelvic floor muscles** (especially the levator ani) play the main role in supporting the uterus.

The **vagina** (*vagina*) is a musculomembranous tube 8–10 cm long, flattened anteroposteriorly; above, around the cervix, it forms the **vaginal fornix** (anterior, posterior — the deepest — and lateral parts), and below it passes through the urogenital diaphragm and opens into the vestibule (in virgins partly closed by the **hymen**). In front are the bladder and urethra, behind — the rectum (and above, the pouch of Douglas). The mucosa has transverse **vaginal rugae** and longitudinal **columns**; there are no glands.

blocks.label: Figure 23.8
blocks.caption: Female genital organs, sagittal section, left lateral view (Figure No. 248): ovary, uterine tube, uterus and its broad and round ligaments, vagina, bladder, rectum, vesicouterine and rectouterine pouches, parametrium, ureter and uterine artery, clitoris, labia, bulb of the vestibule, pelvic diaphragm. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: **Ectopic pregnancy** most often develops in the **ampulla** of the uterine tube; when the tube ruptures there is severe bleeding into the peritoneal cavity (the blood collects in the pouch of Douglas). Because the uterine tube opens into the peritoneal cavity, genital tract infections in women can lead to **pelvic peritonitis**. When the pelvic floor muscles weaken (multiple deliveries), **prolapse of the uterus and vaginal walls** occurs. The uterine artery crosses **in front of and above the ureter** in the parametrium — a risk of ureteric injury in hysterectomy.

blocks.text: The **mons pubis** is an elevation over the pubic symphysis, rich in fat and covered with hair. The **labia majora** are paired skin folds (homologues of the scrotum); between them lies the **pudendal cleft**. The **labia minora** are thin skin folds inside the labia majora (without fat); in front they form the **prepuce** and **frenulum of the clitoris**; between them is the **vestibule of the vagina** — into which open the **external urethral orifice** (in front), the **vaginal orifice** (behind), the **greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands** (beside the vaginal orifice) and the lesser vestibular glands. The **clitoris** is the homologue of the penis: two corpora cavernosa, a body and a glans (there is no corpus spongiosum — it has become the **bulb of the vestibule**; the bulb lies around the vaginal orifice, at the base of the labia majora).

sections.title: 8. The perineum. The urogenital and pelvic diaphragms

blocks.text: The **perineum** (*perineum*), in the broad sense, is the complex of soft tissues closing the outlet of the lesser pelvis; it is a diamond-shaped region bounded in front by the lower border of the pubic symphysis, behind by the tip of the coccyx, and at the sides by the inferior rami of the pubic and ischial bones, the ischial tuberosities and the sacrotuberous ligaments. The line joining the ischial tuberosities divides the diamond into two triangles: the anterior — the **urogenital region** (urogenital diaphragm) — and the posterior — the **anal region** (pelvic diaphragm). In the narrow sense the perineum is the region between the external genitalia and the anus; deep within it lies the **perineal body (central tendon of the perineum)** — a fibromuscular node to which many muscles attach.

blocks.text: Through the **urogenital diaphragm** pass the urethra in men and the urethra and vagina in women; through the **pelvic diaphragm** passes the rectum. The diaphragms are covered by superior and inferior fasciae; the superficial perineal fascia covers the superficial muscles. Between the pelvic diaphragm and the ischial tuberosity lies the fat-filled **ischioanal (ischiorectal) fossa** (containing **Alcock's (pudendal) canal**, through which the internal pudendal vessels and nerve pass).

Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: During childbirth the perineal tissues are stretched and may **tear**; to prevent this an **episiotomy** (controlled incision of the perineum) is performed — the incision is usually made in a mediolateral direction to avoid injuring the perineal body and the anal sphincter. When the pelvic floor muscles weaken, urinary incontinence and prolapse of organs occur; special exercises (Kegel exercises) are recommended to strengthen them.

items: In the newborn boy the testes are usually in the scrotum; the testis is small (≈10 mm long, ≈0.2 g), and the seminiferous tubules have no lumen and are little coiled. By 1 year its mass increases ≈3 times, after which it grows slowly; at puberty it grows rapidly, reaching 20 g by 18–20 years. A lumen and spermatogenesis appear in the tubules **at puberty** (≈13–15 years). Cryptorchidism is common in premature infants.

In the newborn the epididymis is relatively large (≈20 mm); it grows slowly in the first 10 years, then rapidly. The ductus deferens is thin (≈0.6 mm); the seminal vesicles are very small and lie high (covered by peritoneum on all sides). The processus vaginalis closes in the first months of life.

In the newborn the prostate is round, lies high and weighs ≈0.8 g, consisting mainly of muscle and connective tissue; at puberty its glandular part develops and it comes to resemble that of adults; in old age it often undergoes hyperplasia. In the newborn the penis is 2–2.5 cm long, and the prepuce is long and covers the glans (physiological phimosis — normal up to 3–5 years); it grows slowly until puberty, then rapidly.

In the newborn girl the ovaries are relatively large, lie **above the pelvic inlet** (in the abdominal cavity), and are smooth and elongated; the number of follicles is greatest (≈1–2 million); later they descend into the lesser pelvis. At puberty, as a result of ovulations, the surface becomes uneven (scarred); after menopause they shrink.

In the newborn the uterus lies **high** (above the pubis, in the abdominal cavity), is cylindrical, 3–3.5 cm long and weighs 3–5 g; **its cervix is longer than its body** (2/3 of its length); under the influence of maternal hormones the endometrium is developed (sometimes in the first week of life there is a bloody vaginal discharge). After birth it shrinks somewhat, from 7 years it descends into the lesser pelvis, and at puberty its body becomes larger than the cervix and it takes on a pear shape.

In the newborn the uterine tubes are tortuous and relatively long (because the broad ligament is shorter than the tube); the vagina is short (≈2.5–3.5 cm), lies high and is arched. The labia majora do not completely cover the labia minora; the clitoris is relatively large. The external genitalia grow rapidly at puberty.
The perineal muscles and fasciae are poorly developed in children, with little fat; they develop strongly at puberty, especially in females.

skills.title: Practical skill: demonstrating the genital organs on specimens

items: On a male specimen show the testis and the head, body and tail of the epididymis; trace the spermatic cord to the inguinal canal and name its coverings.
In the lesser pelvis show the ductus deferens crossing the ureter, the ampulla, the seminal vesicle and the prostate.
On a female specimen show the parts of the uterus, the broad and round ligaments, the parts of the uterine tube (isthmus, ampulla, infundibulum, fimbriae), and the ovary and its ligaments.
In the perineum draw the line joining the ischial tuberosities and outline the urogenital and anal triangles; show the superficial muscles and the anal sphincter.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: The mother of a 1-year-old boy noticed that the right side of the scrotum is empty. On examination the right testis is not in the scrotum, and a small mobile mass is palpable in the region of the inguinal canal; the left testis is in place.
cases.ask: What is the condition? How and when does the testis normally descend into the scrotum? Why is treatment necessary?
cases.answer: This is right-sided **cryptorchidism** (undescended testis; here — in the inguinal canal). The testis develops in the lumbar region of the abdominal cavity and descends under the influence of the **gubernaculum**: at 3 months it lies beside the deep inguinal ring, **at 7–8 months it passes through the inguinal canal**, and by birth it descends into the scrotum, preceded by the **processus vaginalis of the peritoneum**. For spermatogenesis the testis must be at a temperature 2–3 °C below body temperature; in an undescended testis the spermatogenic epithelium is damaged and the **risk of tumors** increases; often there is also a hernia because of the patent processus vaginalis. Therefore surgery (orchiopexy) is recommended before 1 year of age.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 68-year-old man complains of frequent urination at night, a weak urinary stream and a feeling of incomplete bladder emptying. On digital rectal examination the gland is enlarged and soft-elastic, and the median groove is flattened.
cases.ask: Which organ is enlarged? Why is urination impaired, and why can this organ be examined through the rectum?
cases.answer: The **prostate** is enlarged — **prostatic hyperplasia (adenoma)**. The prostate lies below the bladder and surrounds the **prostatic part of the urethra**; when it enlarges (especially its middle lobe and periurethral part) it compresses the urethra and obstructs the outflow of urine from the bladder — the stream weakens, residual urine remains, and frequent urges to void appear. The **posterior surface of the prostate is in contact with the rectal ampulla** (separated only by a thin fascia — Denonvilliers' fascia), so its size, consistency and the groove between its right and left lobes are easily palpated through the rectum.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: During a first delivery, as the fetal head was emerging, the obstetrician saw that the perineal tissues were overstretched and at risk of tearing, and incised the perineum in a mediolateral direction (episiotomy).
cases.ask: Describe the structure of the female perineum and its sex differences. Why is the incision made obliquely to the side rather than along the midline toward the anus?
cases.answer: The perineum consists of the soft tissues closing the outlet of the lesser pelvis; the line between the ischial tuberosities divides it into the **urogenital** triangle (the urethra and vagina pass through it; the superficial and deep transverse perineal, ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus muscles, the urethral sphincter) and the **anal** triangle (pelvic diaphragm — the levator ani and coccygeus, the external anal sphincter). In women the perineum is wide and low, the perineum in the narrow sense is short (≈3 cm), and the **perineal body** is large and stretches greatly during childbirth. A midline incision or tear may extend **from the perineal body into the external anal sphincter and rectum** (fecal incontinence); a mediolateral incision bypasses the sphincter.

topics.title: The endocrine glands: pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroid and suprarenal glands, the endocrine parts of the pancreas and gonads. Their age-related changes

goals.text: To teach the student the general features and classification of the endocrine glands, the hypothalamic-pituitary system, and the structure, topography, blood supply, hormones, age-related features and clinical significance of the pineal, thyroid, parathyroid and suprarenal glands, the pancreatic islets and the endocrine parts of the gonads.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the general features of the endocrine glands and their classification by origin;
the parts, topography and hormones of the pituitary gland and its connection with the hypothalamus;
the structure and function of the pineal gland;
the parts, coverings, topography and blood supply of the thyroid gland;
the location and function of the parathyroid glands;
the cortex and medulla, zones and hormones of the suprarenal glands;
the endocrine cells of the pancreatic islets and the gonads;
the age-related features of the endocrine glands.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the endocrine glands in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
show the projection of the thyroid gland in a living person and the method of palpating it;
explain, on an anatomical basis, the signs of deficiency and excess of the hormones of each gland.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: A **pituitary adenoma** growing upward compresses the **optic chiasm** — loss of the temporal visual fields on both sides (**bitemporal hemianopia**) is observed; on radiographs the sella turcica is enlarged. Excess **growth hormone** causes **gigantism** in children and, in adults (after the growth plates have closed), **acromegaly** (enlargement of the facial bones, hands and feet); deficiency causes **pituitary dwarfism**. Deficiency of **vasopressin** causes **diabetes insipidus** (5–20 L of urine per day). The pituitary is reached by the **transsphenoidal** route — through the nasal cavity and sphenoidal sinus.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Tumors of the pineal gland (pinealomas) in children may present with **precocious puberty** owing to loss of its inhibitory effect; by compressing the tectal (quadrigeminal) plate they impair upward gaze (Parinaud's syndrome) and, by compressing the cerebral aqueduct, lead to **hydrocephalus**.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Enlargement of the thyroid gland is **goiter** (struma); endemic goiter is common in iodine-deficient regions. Congenital **hypothyroidism** causes **cretinism** (retarded mental and physical development; hence newborns are screened), and in adults **myxedema**. **Hyperthyroidism** (Graves' / Basedow's disease) causes tachycardia, weight loss, irritability and protrusion of the eyes (exophthalmos). In **thyroidectomy** the recurrent laryngeal nerve (beside the inferior thyroid artery) and the parathyroid glands must not be injured; when the superior thyroid artery is ligated, the **external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve**, which lies close to it, may be damaged.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: If the parathyroid glands are accidentally removed or their blood supply is disrupted during thyroidectomy, blood calcium falls sharply and **tetany** develops — painful muscle spasms (the "obstetrician's hand" position of the hand, laryngospasm); this is life-threatening. In parathyroid adenoma, by contrast, hypercalcemia, softening of the bones and kidney stones are observed.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Insufficiency of the suprarenal cortex is **Addison's disease** (weakness, low blood pressure, bronzing of the skin — owing to increased ACTH). Excess cortisol causes **Itsenko–Cushing syndrome** (obesity of the face and trunk, "moon face," hypertension, diabetes mellitus, red striae on the skin). A tumor of the medulla is a **pheochromocytoma** (paroxysmal severe hypertension). The right suprarenal vein is very short and drains directly into the inferior vena cava — the risk of bleeding in adrenalectomy is high.

blocks.text: **Endocrine glands (glands of internal secretion)** have no ducts and release the biologically active substances they produce — **hormones** — directly into the blood or lymph. Hormones act via the blood on distant **target organs**, regulating metabolism, growth, development, reproduction and adaptation; together with the nervous system they provide **neurohumoral regulation**. General features of the endocrine glands: **absence of ducts**, **rich blood supply** (the organs receiving the most blood per unit mass), **fenestrated (sinusoidal) capillaries**, small size and **close connection with the nervous system**.

Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: In addition, there are endocrine parts within mixed glands (pancreatic islets, Leydig cells of the testis, follicles and corpus luteum of the ovary) and the **diffuse endocrine system** — scattered endocrine cells in the intestine, airways and other organs (the APUD system).

The **pituitary gland** (*hypophysis, glandula pituitaria*) is the central endocrine gland: it regulates the activity of many peripheral glands. It is bean-shaped, ≈10–17 × 5–15 × 5–10 mm, and weighs **≈0.5–0.6 g** (larger in women, especially in pregnancy). It lies in the **hypophysial fossa of the sella turcica** of the sphenoid bone; above it is covered by the **diaphragma sellae** of the dura mater, and through its opening the **infundibulum** connects it with the tuber cinereum of the hypothalamus. At its sides lie the **cavernous venous sinuses** (internal carotid artery, nerves III, IV, V~1~, V~2~, VI), and above and in front the **optic chiasm**.

blocks.text: The **hypothalamus** controls the pituitary by two routes: 1) the **hypothalamohypophysial tract** — the axons of the magnocellular nuclei carry hormones to the neurohypophysis; 2) the **hypophysial portal system** — the parvocellular neurosecretory nuclei release **releasing hormones (liberins)** and **inhibiting hormones (statins)** into the **primary capillary network** in the infundibulum; via the **hypophysial portal veins** they reach the **secondary capillary network** in the adenohypophysis and stimulate or inhibit hormone secretion. The pituitary is supplied by the **superior and inferior hypophysial arteries** (from the internal carotid artery).

Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: A **pituitary adenoma** growing upward compresses the **optic chiasm** — loss of the temporal visual fields on both sides (**bitemporal hemianopia**) is observed; on radiographs the sella turcica is enlarged. Excess **growth hormone** causes **gigantism** in children and, in adults (after the growth plates have closed), **acromegaly** (enlargement of the facial bones, hands and feet); deficiency causes **pituitary dwarfism**. Deficiency of **vasopressin** causes **diabetes insipidus** (5–20 L of urine per day). The pituitary is reached by the **transsphenoidal** route — through the nasal cavity and sphenoidal sinus.

blocks.text: The **pineal gland** (*glandula pinealis, corpus pineale*) is a small gland resembling a pine cone (8–15 mm long, weighing ≈0.2 g), belonging to the epithalamus of the diencephalon. It lies in the groove between the superior colliculi of the tectal plate and is attached to the thalami by the **habenulae**. Its parenchyma consists of **pinealocytes** and glial cells; with age calcium salts accumulate in it, forming **brain sand** (a midline landmark on radiographs). Depending on light (retina → hypothalamus → sympathetic pathway), the pineal gland produces **melatonin** — it regulates **circadian rhythms** (sleep-wakefulness) and in childhood **inhibits sexual maturation**; it also secretes serotonin and other peptides.

blocks.label: Figure 24.4
blocks.caption: Position of the pineal gland in the brain (Figure No. 289): lateral ventricles and corpus callosum opened; 17 — pineal gland; third ventricle and its choroid plexus, columns of the fornix, thalami, caudate nucleus, internal cerebral veins and great cerebral vein, cerebellum. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: Tumors of the pineal gland (pinealomas) in children may present with **precocious puberty** owing to loss of its inhibitory effect; by compressing the tectal (quadrigeminal) plate they impair upward gaze (Parinaud's syndrome) and, by compressing the cerebral aqueduct, lead to **hydrocephalus**.

blocks.text: The **thyroid gland** (*glandula thyroidea*) is the largest endocrine gland (weighing **20–40 g**, larger in women); it lies in the anterior region of the neck, in front of and beside the larynx and trachea. It consists of **right and left lobes** and the **isthmus** joining them (over tracheal rings II–IV); in ≈30–50% of people there is a **pyramidal lobe** extending upward from the isthmus (a remnant of the thyroglossal duct). The upper poles of the lobes reach the laminae of the thyroid cartilage, and the lower poles the 5th–6th tracheal rings.

The gland is enclosed in a **fibrous capsule**, from which septa pass inward, dividing it into lobules; externally the pretracheal layer of the cervical fascia forms a **fascial sheath** (the gland is attached to the larynx by ligaments, which is why it **rises with the larynx during swallowing**). The structural-functional unit of the gland is the **follicle**: a vesicle lined by a single layer of **thyrocytes** and filled with **colloid** (thyroglobulin). The thyrocytes produce the iodine-containing **thyroxine (T~4~)** and **triiodothyronine (T~3~)**, and the **parafollicular (C) cells** between the follicles produce **calcitonin** (lowers blood calcium).

blocks.label: Figure 24.5
blocks.caption: The thyroid gland (A — anterior view; B — posterior view; Figure No. 278): 1 — isthmus of the thyroid gland; 2 — lobes of the thyroid gland; 3 — median cricothyroid ligament; 4 — thyroid cartilage; 5 — pyramidal lobe; 6 — cricothyroid muscle; 7 — trachea; 8 — superior parathyroid gland; 9 — superior thyroid artery; 10 — inferior parathyroid gland; 11 — inferior thyroid artery. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: **Topography**: in front — the infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, omohyoid), the cervical fasciae and skin; posteromedially — the larynx, trachea, pharynx and esophagus, with the **recurrent laryngeal nerve** in the groove between them; laterally — the **common carotid artery**, internal jugular vein and vagus nerve. **Blood supply**: the **superior thyroid artery** (from the external carotid artery) and the **inferior thyroid artery** (from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery), sometimes the unpaired **thyroid ima artery** (from the aortic arch or brachiocephalic trunk). Its veins drain into the internal jugular and brachiocephalic veins.

parts.text: Enlargement of the thyroid gland is **goiter** (struma); endemic goiter is common in iodine-deficient regions. Congenital **hypothyroidism** causes **cretinism** (retarded mental and physical development; hence newborns are screened), and in adults **myxedema**. **Hyperthyroidism** (Graves' / Basedow's disease) causes tachycardia, weight loss, irritability and protrusion of the eyes (exophthalmos). In **thyroidectomy** the recurrent laryngeal nerve (beside the inferior thyroid artery) and the parathyroid glands must not be injured; when the superior thyroid artery is ligated, the **external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve**, which lies close to it, may be damaged.

blocks.text: The **parathyroid glands** (*glandulae parathyroideae*) are usually **4** (2 superior and 2 inferior), pea-sized (4–8 × 3–4 × 2–3 mm), with a total mass of **0.1–0.35 g**; they lie on the **posterior surface** of the lobes of the thyroid gland, between its fibrous capsule and fascial sheath; their number and location vary (sometimes within the gland, in the mediastinum or beside the thymus). The superior glands develop from the 4th pharyngeal pouch and the inferior glands from the 3rd (together with the thymus) — which is why the inferior glands may be displaced lower. The chief cells produce **parathyroid hormone** — it increases the release of calcium from bone, its reabsorption in the kidney and its absorption in the intestine (via vitamin D), **raising blood calcium** (antagonist of calcitonin).

blocks.label: Figure 24.6
blocks.caption: Parathyroid glands and the blood vessels of the thyroid gland, right lateral view (Figure No. 280): superior and inferior parathyroid glands, thyroid gland, superior and inferior thyroid arteries, superior, middle and inferior thyroid veins, recurrent laryngeal nerve, pharynx, esophagus, trachea, common, internal and external carotid arteries, internal jugular vein. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: If the parathyroid glands are accidentally removed or their blood supply is disrupted during thyroidectomy, blood calcium falls sharply and **tetany** develops — painful muscle spasms (the "obstetrician's hand" position of the hand, laryngospasm); this is life-threatening. In parathyroid adenoma, by contrast, hypercalcemia, softening of the bones and kidney stones are observed.

blocks.text: The **suprarenal (adrenal) glands** (*glandulae suprarenales*) are paired glands on the upper poles of the kidneys, behind the peritoneum, within the renal fascia (but separated from the kidney by a layer of fat), at the level of T~XI~–T~XII~. The **right gland** is triangular (in front of it — the liver and inferior vena cava), the **left gland** crescentic (in front of it — the stomach, pancreas and splenic vessels). Each weighs **≈6–7 g** (both 12–13 g) and is 40–60 mm long. The suprarenal vein leaves through the **hilum** on the anterior surface. The gland is enclosed in a fibrous capsule and consists of two substances differing in origin and function.

**Glucocorticoids** (cortisol) — carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism, stress; suppress inflammation and immunity

Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **blood supply** is very rich: the **superior** (from the inferior phrenic artery), **middle** (from the abdominal aorta) and **inferior** (from the renal artery) suprarenal arteries. There is a single **vein**: the right drains into the **inferior vena cava** and the left into the **left renal vein**. The medulla is supplied by sympathetic preganglionic fibers (splanchnic nerves) — it is regarded as a modified sympathetic ganglion. **Paraganglia** (for example, the carotid body and the para-aortic paraganglia) also consist of chromaffin tissue.

parts.text: Insufficiency of the suprarenal cortex is **Addison's disease** (weakness, low blood pressure, bronzing of the skin — owing to increased ACTH). Excess cortisol causes **Itsenko–Cushing syndrome** (obesity of the face and trunk, "moon face," hypertension, diabetes mellitus, red striae on the skin). A tumor of the medulla is a **pheochromocytoma** (paroxysmal severe hypertension). The right suprarenal vein is very short and drains directly into the inferior vena cava — the risk of bleeding in adrenalectomy is high.

sections.title: 7. The pancreatic islets and the endocrine part of the gonads

blocks.text: The **pancreatic islets** (islets of Langerhans) are ≈1 million cell clusters scattered among the exocrine acini (0.1–0.3 mm in diameter; 1–2% of the mass of the gland), more numerous in the **tail** of the gland. Their cells: **β cells** (≈70%) — **insulin** (lowers blood glucose), **α cells** (≈20%) — **glucagon** (raises glucose), **δ cells** — **somatostatin**, **PP cells** — pancreatic polypeptide. The islets are densely surrounded by fenestrated capillaries. Insulin deficiency causes **diabetes mellitus**.

blocks.label: Figure 24.9
blocks.caption: Structure of a pancreatic islet (diagram; after V.G. Eliseev et al.; Figure No. 284): alpha, beta, delta and PP cells, blood capillaries. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: **Endocrine part of the gonads**: **in the testis** — the **interstitial (Leydig) cells** between the seminiferous tubules (produce testosterone under the action of LH) and the Sertoli cells (inhibin, anti-Müllerian hormone); **in the ovary** — the **granulosa** and **theca** cells of the follicular wall (estrogens) and, after ovulation, the **corpus luteum** (progesterone); in pregnancy the **placenta** also produces hormones. The sex hormones regulate the secondary sexual characteristics, the sexual cycle and reproductive function.

items: In the newborn the **pituitary** is pear-shaped and weighs ≈0.1–0.15 g; it grows rapidly in the 2nd year, at 4–5 years and at 11–12 years (onset of puberty); its mass increases 2 times by 10 years and 3 times by 15 years, and it is largest at 20 years (≈0.53–0.56 g); it is always larger in women. It grows together with the sella turcica.

In the newborn the **pineal gland** is round and small; it grows rapidly in the first year (≈100 mg) and reaches its definitive size (≈150 mg) **by 6 years**. It is active in childhood and involutes after puberty; brain sand begins to accumulate from 7–10 years.

In the newborn the **thyroid gland** is relatively large but structurally immature, weighing ≈1–3 g; it grows gradually until puberty to 10–14 g, grows rapidly at puberty to ≈25 g, and reaches 30–35 g after 20 years. In childhood the thyroid hormones are crucial for growth and **brain development**; in old age the gland shrinks.
In the newborn the **parathyroid glands** are very small (total mass 6–9 mg); they grow 3–4 times in infancy, then slowly, reaching 120–140 mg by 20 years; they are larger in women.

In the newborn the **suprarenal glands** are **relatively very large** (each ≈7–9 g — equal to those of adults; ≈1/3 of the mass of the kidney), mainly because of the fetal cortex. After birth the fetal zone rapidly involutes, and the gland shrinks ≈2 times during the 1st year; the cortical zones begin to re-form from 5 years and are completed at puberty; their mass is ≈4.6 g at 5 years, ≈6.6 g at 10 years, ≈8.6 g at 15 years and ≈13 g at 20 years (both). The medulla is poorly developed in the newborn.

In the newborn the **pancreatic islets** are relatively numerous (≈3.5% of the volume of the gland, ≈120 thousand); their number increases throughout life to 1 million, while their relative volume decreases to 1–2%.

The **endocrine activity of the gonads** increases during fetal life (in the testis — for sexual differentiation) and **at puberty** (activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis); in women the ovarian hormones decline at menopause.

skills.title: Practical skill: palpating the thyroid gland

items: Seat the patient; the physician stands behind the patient and places the 2nd–4th fingers of both hands between the anterior borders of the sternocleidomastoid muscles and the larynx.
Below the cricoid cartilage, in front of the trachea, palpate the isthmus of the gland, and on either side the lobes.
Ask the patient to swallow — the gland rises with the larynx (because of its fascial sheath and ligaments); this distinguishes it from other structures in the neck.
Assess the size and consistency of the gland and the presence of nodules; remember that the isthmus lies over tracheal rings II–IV and the lobes from the thyroid cartilage to rings V–VI.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: For a year a 45-year-old woman has complained of headache and deteriorating vision: she has lost her side vision (she does not notice cars coming from the side in the street). Her menstrual cycle is disturbed, and milk is being secreted from her breasts. MRI showed a tumor in the sella turcica growing upward.
cases.ask: Which gland is affected? What is the anatomical cause of the visual disturbance? Which hormone is being produced in excess?
cases.answer: A **pituitary adenoma** (prolactinoma). The pituitary lies in the hypophysial fossa of the sella turcica, above it is the diaphragma sellae, and in front of and above it lies the **optic chiasm**. The tumor, growing upward, compresses the middle part of the chiasm — the **crossing fibers coming from the medial (nasal) halves of the retinas of both eyes**; as a result the **temporal visual fields** of both eyes are lost — **bitemporal hemianopia**. The lactotroph cells of the adenohypophysis produce excess **prolactin**: milk secretion (galactorrhea) and disturbance of the menstrual cycle.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: One day after total thyroidectomy the patient developed numbness around the lips and in the fingers, followed by painful spasms of the hands (the fingers in the "obstetrician's hand" position). The voice is hoarse.
cases.ask: Which structures have been injured? Explain their location and function.
cases.answer: 1) The **parathyroid glands** have been removed or their blood supply disrupted — they lie on the **posterior surface** of the lobes of the thyroid gland, between the fibrous capsule and the fascial sheath (usually 4). They produce **parathyroid hormone**, raising blood calcium; when they are lost, **hypocalcemia** develops — neuromuscular excitability increases and **tetany** develops. 2) Hoarseness indicates injury to the **recurrent laryngeal nerve** — it runs in the groove between the trachea and esophagus, close to the inferior thyroid artery, in contact with the posteromedial surface of the lobes of the gland, and supplies the laryngeal muscles.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In recent months a 30-year-old patient has had paroxysmal headaches, palpitations, sweating and rises in arterial pressure up to 230/130 mmHg. CT showed a 4 cm tumor in the left suprarenal gland; urinary catecholamine metabolites are sharply elevated.
cases.ask: Which part of the suprarenal gland is affected? State the origin and hormones of this part. Explain the structure of the suprarenal gland.
cases.answer: This is a **pheochromocytoma** — a tumor of the chromaffin cells of the **suprarenal medulla**. The medulla develops from the **neural crest** (sympathetic neuroblasts) and is regarded as a modified sympathetic ganglion; it produces **epinephrine and norepinephrine** — their excess release causes paroxysmal hypertension, tachycardia and sweating. The suprarenal gland is enclosed externally by a fibrous capsule and consists of a **cortex** (mesodermal: zona glomerulosa — aldosterone, zona fasciculata — cortisol, zona reticularis — androgens) and a **medulla**. The left gland is crescentic, and its vein drains into the left renal vein.
