topics.title: The heart: external and internal structure, wall, conducting system, blood supply and innervation. The pericardium. The circulations. Age-related features of the heart

goals.text: To teach the student the general structure of the vascular system, the circulations, the external and internal structure of the heart, its chambers and valves, the layers of its wall, the conducting system, its blood supply and innervation, the pericardium, and the topography and age-related features of the heart.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the systemic, pulmonary and cardiac (coronary) circulations;
the shape, dimensions, surfaces, borders and grooves of the heart;
the internal structure and openings of the atria and ventricles;
the structure and mechanism of action of the heart valves;
the layers of the heart wall, the fibrous skeleton and the conducting system;
the coronary arteries, cardiac veins and cardiac nerves;
the parts and sinuses of the pericardium;
the borders of the heart, the projection of the valves and their auscultation points, and age-related features.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the chambers of the heart, the valves and the coronary vessels on specimens and in an atlas and name them in Latin;
show the borders of the heart and the auscultation points of the valves in a living person;
identify the arcs (bulges) of the cardiac shadow on a radiograph.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In the pulmonary circulation **venous blood flows in the arteries** and **arterial blood in the veins** — a vessel is named not by the composition of its blood but by the direction of flow (from the heart or to the heart). In the liver there is an additional **portal system**: blood from the unpaired abdominal organs passes first through the hepatic capillaries via the portal vein.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: When the conducting system is damaged, **heart blocks** develop: if the atrioventricular node or the bundle of His is affected (often in occlusion of the **right coronary artery** — it supplies both nodes), **AV block** results; in complete block the ventricles contract at their own rhythm (≈30–40/min), and fainting attacks (Morgagni–Adams–Stokes) occur; treatment — a **pacemaker** (its electrode is introduced into the right ventricle via the superior vena cava). Bundle branch block appears on the ECG as widening of the QRS complex.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Myocardial infarction** develops with thrombosis of a coronary artery: if the **anterior interventricular branch** (the "widow-maker artery") is occluded — the anterior wall of the left ventricle, the septum and the apex are affected; the **circumflex branch** — the lateral and posterior walls of the left ventricle; the **right coronary artery** — the inferior (diaphragmatic) wall, often with rhythm and conduction disturbances. Cardiac pain (angina pectoris) radiates to the **left shoulder, the inner surface of the arm, the neck and the mandible** — because these are also supplied by segments T~I~–T~V~ (and C~VIII~) (**referred pain**). Treatment: angioplasty and stenting, coronary artery bypass grafting.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In **pericarditis** a friction rub of the layers is heard. Fluid or blood accumulating rapidly in the pericardial cavity (cardiac wound, aortic rupture) compresses the heart and prevents it from filling — **cardiac tamponade**. Emergency **pericardiocentesis** (puncture) is usually performed at **Larrey's point** — from the angle between the xiphoid process and the left 7th costal cartilage, directed upward and backward into the anteroinferior sinus.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Enlargement of the chambers appears on radiographs as bulging of particular arcs: in mitral stenosis the left atrium enlarges and the waist of the heart is flattened ("mitral configuration"); in aortic valve disease and arterial hypertension the left ventricular arc enlarges and the waist deepens ("aortic configuration"). Because the left atrium is close to the esophagus, when enlarged it displaces the esophagus backward (seen on contrast radiography), and **transesophageal echocardiography** shows the left atrium well.

sections.title: 1. The vascular system and the circulations

blocks.text: The **cardiovascular system** consists of the heart, arteries, veins and the **microcirculatory bed** between them (arterioles, precapillaries, capillaries, postcapillaries, venules). **Arteries** carry blood from the heart to the organs (regardless of its composition), and **veins** bring it from the organs to the heart. Blood vessels are absent in the epidermis, hair, nails, cornea, lens and articular cartilage.

sections.title: 2. External structure and position of the heart

blocks.text: The **heart** (*cor*) is a hollow, four-chambered muscular organ; it is cone-shaped and roughly the size of its owner's fist. It is 12–13 cm long, 9–10.5 cm wide and 6–7 cm anteroposteriorly, and in adults weighs **≈250–350 g** (more in men). The heart lies in the **middle mediastinum**, within the pericardium: **2/3 to the left of the midline** and 1/3 to the right. Its longitudinal axis is oblique — running from above downward, from right to left and from back to front.

items: The **base** (*basis cordis*) faces upward, to the right and backward; the atria and the great vessels (aorta, pulmonary trunk, venae cavae and pulmonary veins) are here.
The **apex** (*apex cordis*) faces downward, to the left and forward; it lies in the left 5th intercostal space, 1–1.5 cm medial to the midclavicular line (the apex beat).

**Surfaces**: the anterior **sternocostal** (mainly the right ventricle), the inferior **diaphragmatic** (mainly the left ventricle) and the lateral **pulmonary** surfaces; the **right** (sharp) and **left** (blunt) borders.

**Grooves**: the **coronary sulcus** (the boundary between the atria and ventricles; the coronary arteries and coronary sinus lie in it), the **anterior** and **posterior interventricular sulci** (the projection of the interventricular septum); they meet to the right of the apex at the **notch of the cardiac apex**.
The **auricles** are anterior projections of the atria; the right auricle embraces the aorta and the left auricle the pulmonary trunk from the left.

blocks.text: The heart is divided by the **interatrial** and **interventricular septa** into right (venous blood) and left (arterial blood) halves; each half consists of an **atrium** and a **ventricle**, which communicate through the **atrioventricular orifices**.

blocks.text: The valves are **folds (duplications) of the endocardium** that ensure one-way blood flow. **Atrioventricular (cuspid) valves**: the **right — tricuspid** (anterior, posterior and septal cusps) and the **left — bicuspid, mitral** (anterior and posterior cusps). The bases of the cusps are attached to the **fibrous ring**, and their free edges are connected by **chordae tendineae** to the **papillary muscles** — when the ventricle contracts (systole) the cusps close, and the chordae prevent them from everting into the atrium.

**Semilunar valves** — at the orifices of the **pulmonary trunk** and **aorta**, each with **3** pocket-like cusps (in the pulmonary trunk — anterior, right, left; in the aorta — the **posterior (noncoronary)**, **right** and **left coronary** cusps). Each cusp has a **nodule** in the middle of its free edge and **lunules** at the sides; between the cusp and the vessel wall lies a **sinus**. The **right and left coronary arteries** arise from the aortic sinuses. When the ventricles relax (diastole), the returning blood fills the pockets and closes the valve.

Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

sections.title: 5. The heart wall and the fibrous skeleton

items: The **endocardium** is the inner layer: endothelium and connective tissue; it lines the chambers, valves and chordae tendineae.

The **myocardium** is the middle and thickest layer: **striated cardiac muscle tissue** (cardiomyocytes joined by intercalated discs form a functional syncytium; it contracts involuntarily). The **atrial** myocardium has 2 layers: superficial (common to both atria, transverse) and deep (separate for each, longitudinal and encircling the venous openings). The **ventricular** myocardium has 3 layers: outer oblique and inner longitudinal (common; at the apex they pass into each other forming the **vortex cordis**; the papillary muscles and trabeculae derive from the inner layer) and a middle circular layer (separate for each ventricle). The atrial and ventricular myocardium are separated by **fibrous rings** — they are connected only through the conducting system.
The **epicardium** is the outer layer: the visceral layer of the serous pericardium (mesothelium + connective tissue, beneath which lie fat and the coronary vessels).

The **cardiac skeleton** — the right and left **fibrous rings**, the aortic and pulmonary rings, the **right and left fibrous trigones** between them, and the membranous part of the interventricular septum; it supports the valves and myocardium and acts as an electrical insulator.

sections.title: 6. The conducting system of the heart

blocks.text: The **conducting system** consists of **atypical cardiomyocytes** (few myofibrils, much sarcoplasm) that generate impulses automatically in the heart and conduct them to the myocardium:

items: The **sinoatrial node** (Keith–Flack; *nodus sinuatrialis*) — in the wall of the right atrium, **between the opening of the superior vena cava and the right auricle** (the upper part of the sulcus terminalis, under the epicardium); the **1st-order pacemaker**, 60–80 impulses per minute.
The interatrial bundles (anterior — Bachmann's, middle, posterior) carry the impulse to the atria and to the lower node.

The **atrioventricular node** (Aschoff–Tawara; *nodus atrioventricularis*) — in the lower part of the interatrial septum, in front of the opening of the coronary sinus (Koch's triangle); it delays the impulse slightly (so that the atria contract before the ventricles); 40–60 impulses.

The **atrioventricular bundle** (bundle of His) — pierces the right fibrous trigone, runs along the membranous part of the interventricular septum and in its muscular part divides into the **right and left bundle branches** (the right branch reaches the anterior papillary muscle via the septomarginal trabecula).
The **Purkinje fibers** (subendocardial branches) spread into the ventricular myocardium, first to the papillary muscles.

blocks.label: Figure 25.9
blocks.caption: The conducting system of the heart (diagram; Figure No. 325): 1 — right ventricle; 2 — inferior vena cava; 3 — interventricular septum; 4 — right atrium; 5 — interatrial septum; 6 — sinoatrial node; 7 — superior vena cava; 8 — left atrium; 9 — atrioventricular node; 10 — atrioventricular bundle; 11 — right bundle branch; 12 — left bundle branch; 13 — left ventricle; 14 — subendocardial branches (Purkinje fibers). Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: When the conducting system is damaged, **heart blocks** develop: if the atrioventricular node or the bundle of His is affected (often in occlusion of the **right coronary artery** — it supplies both nodes), **AV block** results; in complete block the ventricles contract at their own rhythm (≈30–40/min), and fainting attacks (Morgagni–Adams–Stokes) occur; treatment — a **pacemaker** (its electrode is introduced into the right ventricle via the superior vena cava). Bundle branch block appears on the ECG as widening of the QRS complex.

sections.title: 7. Blood supply and innervation of the heart

blocks.text: The **right coronary artery** (*a. coronaria dextra*) arises from the right aortic sinus and runs under the right auricle along the coronary sulcus to the right and backward; its branches: the **conus branch**, the **sinoatrial nodal branch** (in ≈60% of cases), the **right marginal branch**, the **posterior interventricular branch** (along the posterior sulcus to the apex) and the atrioventricular nodal branch. It supplies the right atrium and ventricle, part of the posterior wall of the left ventricle, the posterior 1/3 of the interventricular septum and both nodes.

The **left coronary artery** (*a. coronaria sinistra*) arises from the left aortic sinus, passes between the pulmonary trunk and the left auricle and soon divides in two: the **anterior interventricular branch** (along the anterior sulcus to the apex; septal branches — the anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum; diagonal branches) and the **circumflex branch** (along the coronary sulcus to the left and backward; the left marginal branch). The left coronary artery supplies the left atrium, most of the left ventricle, the anterior part of the septum and part of the anterior wall of the right ventricle. The coronary arteries fill during diastole (in systole their openings are partly covered by the cusps and the myocardium compresses the vessels).

Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: **Cardiac veins**: the main ones drain into the **coronary sinus** (in the posterior part of the coronary sulcus, opening into the right atrium) — the **great cardiac vein** (in the anterior interventricular sulcus, then in the coronary sulcus), the **middle cardiac vein** (in the posterior interventricular sulcus), the **small cardiac vein** (in the right coronary sulcus), the **posterior veins of the left ventricle** and the **oblique vein of the left atrium**. The **anterior veins of the right ventricle** and the **smallest veins** (Thebesian) open directly into the chambers. Lymph flows from networks in the heart wall to the mediastinal nodes.

**Innervation**: **sympathetic** fibers — from the cervical ganglia of the sympathetic trunk (superior, middle and inferior cervical cardiac nerves) and from thoracic ganglia II–V (they accelerate and strengthen cardiac contraction and dilate the coronary arteries); **parasympathetic** — the cardiac branches of the **vagus nerve** (slow the rhythm). They form the **superficial cardiac plexus** below the aortic arch and the **deep cardiac plexus** between the aortic arch and the tracheal bifurcation; from these arise the coronary plexuses and the plexuses in the heart wall (with cardiac ganglia). **Sensory** fibers carry pain impulses via the sympathetic nerves to spinal cord segments T~I~–T~V~.

parts.text: **Myocardial infarction** develops with thrombosis of a coronary artery: if the **anterior interventricular branch** (the "widow-maker artery") is occluded — the anterior wall of the left ventricle, the septum and the apex are affected; the **circumflex branch** — the lateral and posterior walls of the left ventricle; the **right coronary artery** — the inferior (diaphragmatic) wall, often with rhythm and conduction disturbances. Cardiac pain (angina pectoris) radiates to the **left shoulder, the inner surface of the arm, the neck and the mandible** — because these are also supplied by segments T~I~–T~V~ (and C~VIII~) (**referred pain**). Treatment: angioplasty and stenting, coronary artery bypass grafting.

blocks.text: The **pericardium** (pericardial sac) is a closed sac surrounding the heart. The **fibrous pericardium** is the outer dense layer; at its base it blends with the adventitia of the great vessels, below it is attached to the central tendon of the diaphragm, and in front to the sternum by the **sternopericardial ligaments**. The **serous pericardium** — its **parietal layer** lines the fibrous pericardium internally, and its **visceral layer** is the epicardium; they pass into each other at the base of the great vessels, and between them is the **pericardial cavity**, containing a small amount (20–50 mL) of serous fluid. Its parts: the **sternocostal**, **diaphragmatic** and right and left **mediastinal** parts (at the sides run the phrenic nerves and the pericardiacophrenic vessels; behind are the esophagus, thoracic aorta, and azygos and hemiazygos veins).

items: The **transverse sinus** — between the aorta and pulmonary trunk in front and the superior vena cava, right atrium and pulmonary veins behind; in surgery it is used to separate the aorta and pulmonary trunk and apply a clamp.
The **oblique sinus** — on the posterior surface of the heart, between the right and left pulmonary veins and the inferior vena cava, behind the left atrium.
The **anteroinferior sinus** — the lowest part, at the junction of the sternocostal and diaphragmatic parts; fluid collects here first.

blocks.label: Figure 25.12
blocks.caption: The pericardial cavity and its sinuses, view of the posterior wall of the pericardium, heart removed (Figure No. 329): 1 — left lung; 2 — left pulmonary artery; 3 — left inferior pulmonary vein; 4 — pericardium; 9 — right superior pulmonary vein; 10 — transverse pericardial sinus; 11 — right pulmonary artery; 12 — aortic arch; 13 — superior vena cava; inferior vena cava, oblique sinus. Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: In **pericarditis** a friction rub of the layers is heard. Fluid or blood accumulating rapidly in the pericardial cavity (cardiac wound, aortic rupture) compresses the heart and prevents it from filling — **cardiac tamponade**. Emergency **pericardiocentesis** (puncture) is usually performed at **Larrey's point** — from the angle between the xiphoid process and the left 7th costal cartilage, directed upward and backward into the anteroinferior sinus.

sections.title: 9. Topography of the heart, projection of the valves and radiographic anatomy

items: **Upper border** — at the level of the upper border of the 3rd costal cartilages.
**Right border** — from the 3rd to the 5th costal cartilage, 1–2 cm to the right of the right border of the sternum (right atrium).
**Lower border** — from the right 5th costal cartilage to the apex (mainly the right ventricle).
**Left border** — along a convex arc from the left 3rd costal cartilage (midway between the sternal border and the midclavicular line) to the apex (left auricle and left ventricle).
**Apex** — left 5th intercostal space, 1–1.5 cm medial to the midclavicular line.

blocks.text: **Radiographic anatomy** (PA projection): along the border of the central cardiovascular shadow there are **2 arcs on the right** — above, the superior vena cava (ascending aorta), below, the right atrium; and **4 arcs on the left** — the aortic arch, the pulmonary trunk, the left auricle (atrium) and the left ventricle. The concavity between the arcs of the left auricle and the pulmonary trunk is the **waist of the heart**. The position of the heart depends on body build: **oblique** in normosthenics (axis ≈45° to the horizontal), **transverse** in hypersthenics (25–30°) and **vertical** in asthenics ("drop heart," 50–60°).

parts.text: Enlargement of the chambers appears on radiographs as bulging of particular arcs: in mitral stenosis the left atrium enlarges and the waist of the heart is flattened ("mitral configuration"); in aortic valve disease and arterial hypertension the left ventricular arc enlarges and the waist deepens ("aortic configuration"). Because the left atrium is close to the esophagus, when enlarged it displaces the esophagus backward (seen on contrast radiography), and **transesophageal echocardiography** shows the left atrium well.

items: The newborn's heart is **rounded** (the atria are large and the ventricles poorly developed), with a transverse dimension of 2.7–3.9 cm and a length of 3.0–3.5 cm; the right atrium is considerably larger than the left. The pectinate and papillary muscles are poorly defined, and the chordae tendineae are relatively thick and short.

Its mass in the newborn is **≈24 g** (≈0.8% of body weight, vs. ≈0.5% in adults); it increases 2 times by 1 year, 3 times by 4–5 years, increases 10 times by puberty and 15 times by 18–20 years. In the 1st year the atria grow faster; at 2–6 years the atria and ventricles grow equally; after 10 years the ventricles grow faster.

In the newborn the walls of both ventricles are almost equally thick (≈5 mm); after birth (once the pulmonary circulation starts working) the left ventricle thickens rapidly and by 2 years is 2 times as thick as the right; by 15 years the wall of the left ventricle thickens 2.5 times and that of the right only ≈0.3 times. From 2 years fat begins to accumulate under the epicardium.

The newborn's heart lies **high and transversely** (the diaphragm is high): the apex is in the left **4th intercostal space**, 1–2 cm **lateral** to the midclavicular line; until 1 year the upper border is in the 2nd intercostal space. At 2–3 years the heart takes an oblique position, and in adolescence it resembles that of adults. On radiographs the infant's cardiac shadow is spherical; in the elderly the heart is "lying," and the aortic shadow is distinct.

After birth the **foramen ovale** (within a few months; in ≈20–25% of adults it does not close completely) and the **ductus arteriosus (of Botallo)** close — the fetal circulation is considered in detail in topic 30.

In the newborn the pericardium is rounded, embraces the heart tightly, and its upper border reaches the level of the sternoclavicular joints; the heart rate in the newborn is ≈140/min and decreases with age.

skills.title: Practical skill: showing the borders of the heart and the auscultation points of the valves

items: On a patient or a model, find the sternal angle (angle of Louis), locate the 2nd rib and count the intercostal spaces below it.
Mark the apex in the left 5th intercostal space, 1–1.5 cm medial to the midclavicular line (the apex beat is palpated here).
Draw the upper (3rd costal cartilages), right (1–2 cm to the right of the right sternal border, cartilages III–V), lower and left borders with a marker.

Demonstrate the order of auscultation: 1) apex — mitral; 2) right 2nd intercostal space — aortic; 3) left 2nd intercostal space — pulmonary; 4) base of the xiphoid process — tricuspid; 5) Botkin–Erb point (left 3rd intercostal space) — aortic.
Explain the difference between the projection points (where the valves actually lie) and the auscultation points (where the sound is best transmitted along the blood flow).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 58-year-old man complains of severe crushing retrosternal pain lasting 40 minutes; the pain radiates to the inner surface of the left arm and to the mandible. The ECG shows ST elevation in leads V~1~–V~4~ (infarction of the anterior wall of the left ventricle and the interventricular septum).
cases.ask: Which artery is affected? State its origin and course. Why does the pain radiate to the arm and jaw?
cases.answer: The affected artery is the **anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery**. The left coronary artery arises from the left sinus of the aortic bulb, passes between the pulmonary trunk and the left auricle and divides into the **anterior interventricular** and **circumflex** branches; the anterior interventricular branch runs along the anterior interventricular sulcus to the apex and supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle, the anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum (with the bundle branches) and the apex. Sensory fibers from the heart enter spinal cord segments **T~I~–T~V~** via the sympathetic nerves; the same segments (and C~VIII~) supply the skin of the inner surface of the arm, which is why the pain is **referred** there.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A young man with a stab wound to the left side of the chest beside the sternum in the 4th intercostal space was brought to the emergency department. His arterial pressure is 70/40 mmHg, the neck veins are distended and the heart sounds are muffled.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? Which part of the heart is most likely to have been injured? What does emergency treatment consist of, and how is it performed?
cases.answer: This is **cardiac tamponade** — blood has accumulated in the pericardial cavity, compressing the heart and preventing it from filling in diastole (Beck's triad: hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds). The sternocostal surface is formed mainly by the **right ventricle**, so it is the part most often injured. Emergency treatment — **pericardiocentesis**: the needle is inserted from **Larrey's point** (the angle between the xiphoid process and the left 7th costal cartilage), directed upward and backward into the **anteroinferior sinus** of the pericardium (the lowest point, where blood collects first; the pleura and internal thoracic artery are not injured); then the wound is sutured surgically.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 65-year-old patient complains of dizziness and brief fainting attacks. The heart rate is 36/min. The ECG shows the atria and ventricles contracting independently of each other (complete AV block). He has a history of inferior wall myocardial infarction.
cases.ask: Which part of the conducting system is affected? Explain the structure of the conducting system and the blood supply of this part.
cases.answer: The affected part is the **atrioventricular node** (Aschoff–Tawara) and/or the **bundle of His**. The conducting system: **sinoatrial node** (in the wall of the right atrium between the opening of the superior vena cava and the right auricle; the pacemaker) → interatrial bundles → **atrioventricular node** (in the lower part of the interatrial septum, in front of the opening of the coronary sinus) → **bundle of His** (pierces the fibrous skeleton; in the muscular part of the septum divides into right and left branches) → **Purkinje fibers**. The atrial and ventricular myocardium are separated by **fibrous rings**, so the impulse passes only through this bundle; if it is damaged, the ventricles contract at their own slow rhythm. In most people the atrioventricular node receives blood from the **right coronary artery** (from the region of the posterior interventricular branch) — inferior wall infarction also results from occlusion of this artery. Treatment — a pacemaker.

topics.title: The aorta and its parts. Branches of the aortic arch. The common, external and internal carotid arteries. Blood supply of the brain

goals.text: To teach the student the parts and topography of the aorta, the branches arising from the aortic arch, the course, branches and areas of supply of the common, external and internal carotid arteries, the blood supply of the brain and the arterial circle (of Willis), with their age-related features and clinical significance.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the parts, boundaries and topography of the aorta;
the branches of the aortic arch and the topography of the common carotid artery;
the anterior, posterior, medial and terminal branches of the external carotid artery;
the parts and branches of the maxillary artery;
the parts and branches of the internal carotid artery, and the ophthalmic artery;
the intracranial branches of the vertebral and basilar arteries;
the arterial circle of the brain and the areas supplied by the cerebral arteries;
the anastomoses and age-related features of the arteries of the head and neck.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the aorta and the arteries of the head and neck in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
take the pulse of the common carotid, facial and superficial temporal arteries in a living person and show the points of compression for hemostasis;
identify the parts of the circle of Willis on an angiogram and a diagram.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Coarctation of the aorta** is a congenital narrowing, usually in the region of the aortic isthmus (near the ligamentum arteriosum): blood pressure is high in the arms and low in the legs, with weak pulses; blood reaches the lower body by **collateral routes** — subclavian → internal thoracic → intercostal arteries, and the dilated intercostal arteries produce **rib notching on the lower borders of the ribs** on radiographs. **Aortic aneurysm** and **dissecting aneurysm** most often affect the ascending aorta and the arch; an aneurysm of the arch compresses the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The **pulse** of the common carotid artery is felt at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid at the level of the thyroid cartilage; in bleeding the artery is pressed against the anterior tubercle of the transverse process of the 6th cervical vertebra — the **carotid tubercle** (Chassaignac's). Carotid sinus massage (vagal reflex) may stop an attack of tachycardia, but in the elderly may cause bradycardia and fainting. The **bifurcation** is the site where atherosclerotic plaques most often form (a cause of stroke); treatment — carotid endarterectomy.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The **middle meningeal artery** lies in a groove on the inner surface of the bone in the temporal region (the **pterion** — the thin area where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet); if a blow to this area fractures the bone, the artery tears and an **epidural hematoma** forms between the dura mater and the bone (loss of consciousness after a "lucid interval") — emergency trephination is needed. **Nosebleeds** most often come from **Kiesselbach's area** in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum, where the sphenopalatine, greater palatine, superior labial (from the facial artery) and anterior ethmoidal (from the internal carotid) arteries anastomose.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Ischemic stroke** most often occurs in the territory of the **middle cerebral artery**; its thin **lenticulostriate branches** ("arteries of stroke") rupture in hypertension, and blood is shed into the region of the **internal capsule** — **hemiplegia** and hemianesthesia on the opposite side. **Saccular (berry) aneurysms** form at the branching points of the circle of Willis (most often the anterior communicating artery); if they rupture, **subarachnoid hemorrhage** results (a sudden "worst headache of my life"). An aneurysm of the **posterior communicating artery** compresses the oculomotor nerve (III) passing beside it, causing ptosis and a dilated pupil.

blocks.text: The **aorta** is the largest unpaired arterial vessel of the systemic circulation; it begins from the left ventricle. It has three parts: the **ascending aorta**, the **aortic arch** and the **descending aorta** (which in turn is divided into the **thoracic** and **abdominal aorta**). Its wall is that of an **elastic-type** artery: the tunica media contains many elastic membranes, which stretch in systole and push the blood onward in diastole (the **compression chamber** function).

Passes from behind the 2nd costal cartilage to the left and backward, over the left bronchus, and becomes the descending aorta at the level of T~IV~; at the transition is the narrowed **aortic isthmus** (*isthmus*); below it are the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk and the **ligamentum arteriosum**; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the arch

blocks.text: The **brachiocephalic trunk** (*truncus brachiocephalicus*, ≈3–4 cm long) arises from the aortic arch behind the right 2nd costal cartilage, passes upward and to the right in front of the trachea, and behind the **right sternoclavicular joint** divides into the **right common carotid** and **right subclavian arteries**. Occasionally the **thyroid ima artery** to the thyroid gland arises from it.

parts.text: **Coarctation of the aorta** is a congenital narrowing, usually in the region of the aortic isthmus (near the ligamentum arteriosum): blood pressure is high in the arms and low in the legs, with weak pulses; blood reaches the lower body by **collateral routes** — subclavian → internal thoracic → intercostal arteries, and the dilated intercostal arteries produce **rib notching on the lower borders of the ribs** on radiographs. **Aortic aneurysm** and **dissecting aneurysm** most often affect the ascending aorta and the arch; an aneurysm of the arch compresses the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness.

blocks.text: The **common carotid artery** (*a. carotis communis*) arises on the right from the brachiocephalic trunk and on the left directly from the aortic arch (so the left one is 2–2.5 cm longer and has a thoracic part). In the neck it ascends beside the trachea and esophagus, in front of the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae, behind the sternocleidomastoid and omohyoid muscles, and **gives off no branches**. Lateral to it lies the **internal jugular vein**, with the **vagus nerve** behind and between them; all three are enclosed in the **carotid sheath** (cervical fascia) and form the main **neurovascular bundle** of the neck.

At the level of the **upper border of the thyroid cartilage** (C~IV~), in the **carotid triangle**, it divides into the **external** and **internal carotid arteries** (the **carotid bifurcation**). At the bifurcation the beginning of the internal carotid artery is dilated as the **carotid sinus** (baroreceptors — sense blood pressure; nerve IX), and behind the bifurcation lies the rice-grain-sized **carotid body** (glomus — chemoreceptors that sense O~2~ and CO~2~ in the blood).

parts.text: The **pulse** of the common carotid artery is felt at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid at the level of the thyroid cartilage; in bleeding the artery is pressed against the anterior tubercle of the transverse process of the 6th cervical vertebra — the **carotid tubercle** (Chassaignac's). Carotid sinus massage (vagal reflex) may stop an attack of tachycardia, but in the elderly may cause bradycardia and fainting. The **bifurcation** is the site where atherosclerotic plaques most often form (a cause of stroke); treatment — carotid endarterectomy.

blocks.text: The **external carotid artery** (*a. carotis externa*) at first ascends **medial and anterior** to the internal carotid artery after the bifurcation, then lateral to it; it passes under the posterior belly of the digastric and the stylohyoid muscle, enters the **parotid gland** and at the level of the **neck of the mandible** divides into its terminal branches — the **superficial temporal** and **maxillary arteries**. **The difference from the internal carotid artery** in the neck: the external carotid artery gives off branches in the neck, the internal one does not. Its branches (8–9 in all) are divided into four groups:

parts.text: The **middle meningeal artery** lies in a groove on the inner surface of the bone in the temporal region (the **pterion** — the thin area where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet); if a blow to this area fractures the bone, the artery tears and an **epidural hematoma** forms between the dura mater and the bone (loss of consciousness after a "lucid interval") — emergency trephination is needed. **Nosebleeds** most often come from **Kiesselbach's area** in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum, where the sphenopalatine, greater palatine, superior labial (from the facial artery) and anterior ethmoidal (from the internal carotid) arteries anastomose.

blocks.text: The **internal carotid artery** (*a. carotis interna*) is the main artery of the brain and the eyeball. In the neck it ascends vertically between the pharynx and the internal jugular vein and enters the cranium through the **carotid canal**. It has **four parts**:

items: **Cervical part** — up to the base of the skull; **gives off no branches**.
**Petrous part** — in the carotid canal of the temporal bone; gives off the caroticotympanic arteries and the artery of the pterygoid canal.

**Cavernous part** — inside the **cavernous venous sinus** (with nerve VI beside it and nerves III, IV, V~1~ and V~2~ in its lateral wall); it bends in an S shape, forming the **carotid siphon**; gives small branches to the pituitary gland, the trigeminal ganglion and the dura mater.

**Cerebral part** — pierces the dura mater and enters the subarachnoid space beside the optic nerve; gives off the **ophthalmic artery**, the **superior hypophyseal artery**, the **posterior communicating artery** and the **anterior choroidal artery**, and finally divides into the **anterior** and **middle cerebral arteries**.

blocks.text: The **ophthalmic artery** (*a. ophthalmica*) enters the orbit together with the optic nerve through the **optic canal** and runs forward along the medial wall of the orbit. Its branches: the **central retinal artery** (within the optic nerve to the retina; an **end artery** — its occlusion causes blindness), the **lacrimal artery**, the long and short **posterior ciliary arteries** (choroid), the muscular arteries (anterior ciliary arteries), the **posterior and anterior ethmoidal arteries** (ethmoidal cells, nasal cavity, dura mater of the anterior cranial fossa), the **supraorbital** and **supratrochlear arteries** (forehead), and the medial palpebral arteries; its terminal branch is the **dorsal nasal artery** (anastomosis with the angular artery of the facial artery — a route between the external and internal carotid systems).

blocks.text: The brain receives blood from two systems: the **carotid system** (both internal carotid arteries — ≈70–80 % of the blood reaching the brain) and the **vertebrobasilar system** (both vertebral arteries). The **vertebral artery** (from the subclavian artery; topic 27) ascends through the transverse foramina of vertebrae C~VI~–C~I~, bends backward above the atlas and enters the cranium through the **foramen magnum**. Inside the cranium it gives off the **anterior and posterior spinal arteries**, the **posterior inferior cerebellar artery** (its largest branch) and meningeal branches. The two vertebral arteries unite at the **lower border of the pons** to form the unpaired **basilar artery**; it lies in the basilar groove of the pons, gives off the **anterior inferior cerebellar**, **labyrinthine** (inner ear), **pontine** and **superior cerebellar arteries**, and at the upper border of the pons divides into the two **posterior cerebral arteries**.

blocks.text: The **arterial circle of the brain** (the **circle of Willis**, *circulus arteriosus cerebri*) lies on the base of the brain **around the sella turcica and the pituitary gland**, encircling the optic chiasm and the tuber cinereum. It is formed by: both **anterior cerebral arteries** (A~1~ segments) and the unpaired **anterior communicating artery** that connects them, the terminal parts of both **internal carotid arteries**, both **posterior communicating arteries** and both **posterior cerebral arteries** (P~1~ segments). By uniting the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems and the right and left sides, the circle provides **collateral circulation** when one artery is narrowed. The circle has the "classic" form in ≈50 % of people; in the rest some of its parts are thin or absent.

parts.text: **Ischemic stroke** most often occurs in the territory of the **middle cerebral artery**; its thin **lenticulostriate branches** ("arteries of stroke") rupture in hypertension, and blood is shed into the region of the **internal capsule** — **hemiplegia** and hemianesthesia on the opposite side. **Saccular (berry) aneurysms** form at the branching points of the circle of Willis (most often the anterior communicating artery); if they rupture, **subarachnoid hemorrhage** results (a sudden "worst headache of my life"). An aneurysm of the **posterior communicating artery** compresses the oculomotor nerve (III) passing beside it, causing ptosis and a dilated pupil.

items: **Between the external and internal carotid systems**: the angular artery (from the facial artery) ↔ the dorsal nasal artery (from the ophthalmic artery); the superficial temporal artery ↔ the supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries.

**Between the two sides**: the right and left branches of the facial, lingual (few), occipital, superficial temporal and superior thyroid arteries across the midline; at the base of the brain — the anterior communicating artery.

**Between the carotid and subclavian systems**: the posterior communicating arteries of the circle of Willis; the superior ↔ inferior thyroid arteries; the occipital artery ↔ the vertebral and deep cervical arteries.

In the newborn the diameter of the aorta is 18–20 mm, and ≈4 cm at 15–16 years; the descending aorta lengthens ≈4 times by the age of 50. Because the heart lies high in the newborn, the ascending aorta passes into the arch at a higher level; the aortic arch lies at the level of T~I~ and descends to the level of T~II~ at 17–20 years and T~III~ at 25–30 years.

The diameter of the common carotid artery is 3–6 mm until 1 year, 6–7 mm at 15–16 years and 9–14 mm in adults; in the newborn the bifurcation is at C~III~–C~IV~ (C~IV~ in adults). The intracranial part of the internal carotid artery and the middle cerebral artery grow rapidly in infancy and early childhood in step with the growth of the brain.

In children the muscles and fasciae of the neck are thin, so the large arteries lie more superficially; the arterial walls contain many elastic fibers (they are distensible), and by 12–16 years the length and diameter of the arteries increase 3–5 times. In the elderly the aorta and carotid arteries undergo atherosclerosis and become tortuous and rigid.

skills.title: Practical skill: taking the pulse of the arteries of the head and neck and the points for temporary arrest of bleeding

items: **Common carotid artery**: palpate with 2–3 fingers at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (never press both sides at the same time!); in bleeding, press the artery against the **carotid tubercle** of C~VI~.
**Facial artery**: at the anterior border of the masseter, above the lower border of the body of the mandible — it is pressed against the mandible.

**Superficial temporal artery**: in front of the external acoustic meatus, 1 cm in front of the anterior border of the auricle — it is pressed against the root of the zygomatic process of the temporal bone.
At each point assess the rhythm and volume of the pulse and compare the two sides (weakening on one side is a sign of stenosis).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 20-year-old man was struck hard on the temple by a football, lost consciousness for a few minutes, then came round and felt well. After 3 hours he developed a severe headache and vomiting and lost consciousness again; his right pupil is dilated. CT shows a fracture of the temporal bone and a lens-shaped collection of blood between the bone and the dura mater.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? Which artery is injured? State its origin and course.
cases.answer: **Epidural hematoma**. The injured artery is the **middle meningeal artery**: it arises from the mandibular part of the **maxillary artery** (a terminal branch of the external carotid artery), enters the middle cranial fossa through the **foramen spinosum**, divides into frontal and parietal branches and lies in grooves on the inner surface of the skull bones, outside the dura mater. Its anterior branch passes under the thinnest bone, in the region of the **pterion**, so it tears in a temporal fracture. Arterial blood strips the dura mater from the bone and compresses the brain after a "lucid interval"; displacement of the temporal lobe compresses nerve III and dilates the pupil. Treatment — emergency trephination and ligation of the artery.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 67-year-old woman suddenly developed paralysis of the left arm and the lower left half of the face, with reduced sensation on the left; the leg is relatively spared. Speech is preserved (she is right-handed). CT/MRI shows a focus of ischemia on the lateral surface of the right hemisphere.
cases.ask: Which arterial territory is affected? Explain its area of supply and why the arm is affected more than the leg.
cases.answer: The affected artery is the **right middle cerebral artery**. It is the largest terminal branch of the internal carotid artery; it enters the lateral sulcus, winds around the insula and supplies the **superolateral surface** of the hemisphere, including the **face and arm** areas of the precentral and postcentral gyri; its lenticulostriate branches supply the internal capsule. The **leg** area (paracentral lobule) lies on the medial surface and receives blood from the **anterior cerebral artery**, so it is less affected. The signs are on the opposite (left) side because the motor and sensory pathways cross. In a right-handed person the speech centers are in the left hemisphere, so there is no aphasia.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient's left common carotid artery is completely occluded by an atherosclerotic plaque, yet the neurological signs are minimal. On angiography the left middle and anterior cerebral arteries fill with contrast.
cases.ask: By what routes does blood reach the left hemisphere? Explain the anatomy of these routes.
cases.answer: The main route is the **arterial circle of the brain (of Willis)**: 1) from the right internal carotid artery, the right anterior cerebral artery → the **anterior communicating artery** → the left anterior cerebral artery and the terminal part of the left internal carotid artery → the left middle cerebral artery; 2) the vertebral arteries → the basilar artery → the left posterior cerebral artery → the **left posterior communicating artery** → the cerebral part of the left internal carotid artery. Additional routes: since the left external carotid artery is also occluded, the external carotid branches of the opposite side (facial, superficial temporal, superior thyroid) anastomose across the midline, and then blood passes through the **angular artery ↔ dorsal nasal artery** and the supraorbital artery into the **ophthalmic artery** and, by reversed flow, from it into the internal carotid artery. Because the structure of the circle varies between individuals, collateral flow is not equally adequate in everyone.

topics.title: The brachiocephalic trunk. The subclavian artery and its branches. Arteries of the upper limb: the axillary, brachial, radial and ulnar arteries, the palmar arches

goals.text: To teach the student the parts and branches of the subclavian artery, the topography and branches of the axillary, brachial, radial and ulnar arteries, the palmar arches, the anastomoses of the arteries of the upper limb (the scapular, cubital and dorsal carpal networks), and their age-related features and clinical significance.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the parts of the subclavian artery and the branches arising from each part;
the three parts of the axillary artery and their branches;
the branches of the brachial artery and the deep artery of the arm;
the course and branches of the radial and ulnar arteries;
the superficial and deep palmar arches and the dorsal carpal networks;
the arterial anastomoses around the scapula, the elbow joint and the hand;
the age-related features of the arteries of the upper limb.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the subclavian artery and the arteries of the upper limb in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
take the pulse of the subclavian, axillary, brachial, radial and ulnar arteries in a living person;
show the points at which the arteries are compressed for temporary arrest of bleeding.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In bleeding, the **subclavian artery** is pressed downward against the **1st rib** in the supraclavicular fossa, above the middle of the clavicle; its pulse is also taken here. In **thoracic outlet syndrome** (a cervical rib, hypertrophy of a scalene muscle) the artery and the brachial plexus are compressed in the interscalene space — numbness, pain and a weak pulse in the arm. If the subclavian artery is occluded proximal to the origin of the vertebral artery, blood for the arm is "stolen" **from the vertebral artery by reversed flow** — dizziness when the arm is exerted (**subclavian steal syndrome**). The **internal thoracic artery** is used in cardiac surgery for **coronary artery bypass grafting**.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The **pulse** of the brachial artery is felt in the medial bicipital groove and in the **cubital fossa** (medial to the aponeurosis) — **blood pressure** is measured here with the stethoscope of a sphygmomanometer (Korotkoff sounds). In bleeding the artery is pressed against the **humerus** in the medial groove. In children with a **supracondylar fracture of the humerus** a bone fragment may injure or compress the brachial artery — risk of ischemic contracture of the forearm muscles (**Volkmann's contracture**). If the brachial artery is ligated **below** the deep artery of the arm, blood circulates well through the cubital network.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The **radial artery** is the main site for taking the pulse (over the styloid process of the radius, lateral to the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis); it is also the site for **arterial blood sampling**, **coronary angiography** (transradial access) and the **arteriovenous fistula** for hemodialysis (radial artery + cephalic vein). Before puncturing the radial artery the **Allen test** is performed: the radial and ulnar arteries are compressed at the same time, then the ulnar artery is released — if the palm flushes quickly, collateral flow through the arches is adequate. In wounds of the palm both ends must be ligated, because the arches receive blood from both sides.

blocks.text: The **subclavian artery** (*a. subclavia*) arises on the right from the **brachiocephalic trunk** (behind the right sternoclavicular joint) and on the left directly from the **aortic arch** (so the left one is ≈4 cm longer and has a thoracic part). It arches over the cupula of the pleura, passes through the **interscalene space** (between the anterior and middle scalene muscles, together with the brachial plexus; the subclavian vein lies in front of the anterior scalene muscle), lies in the groove of the same name on the **1st rib** and at the lateral border of the 1st rib continues as the **axillary artery**. In relation to the anterior scalene muscle it is divided into **three parts** (Table 27.1). The main arterial trunk of the upper limb is named in sequence: subclavian → axillary → brachial → radial and ulnar arteries → palmar arches.

blocks.text: The **axillary artery** (*a. axillaris*) is the continuation of the subclavian artery; it extends from the lateral border of the 1st rib **to the lower border of the pectoralis major** (or to the lower border of the teres major) and lies in the axillary fossa. It is surrounded by the **cords of the brachial plexus**, with the axillary vein medial to it. In relation to the **pectoralis minor** it is divided into **three parts**:

blocks.text: **The scapular arterial anastomosis**: the **suprascapular artery** (from the thyrocervical trunk; over the scapular notch to the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae), the **dorsal scapular artery** (from the subclavian artery; along the medial border of the scapula) and the **circumflex scapular artery** (from the axillary artery) unite around the scapula. This network connects the subclavian artery with the distal part of the axillary artery — if the axillary artery is ligated **above** the subscapular artery, blood reaches the arm by this route.

blocks.text: The **brachial artery** (*a. brachialis*) is the continuation of the axillary artery; it runs from the lower border of the pectoralis major **to the cubital fossa**. In the arm it lies in the **medial bicipital groove** (*sulcus bicipitalis medialis*); beside it are the **median nerve** (lateral above, crossing in front in the middle, medial below) and two brachial veins. In the cubital fossa it lies under the biceps **aponeurosis** and at the level of the **neck of the radius** (≈2 cm below the elbow joint) divides into the **radial** and **ulnar arteries**. Its branches:

items: **Deep artery of the arm** (the largest) — winds around the back of the humerus with the radial nerve in the **radial groove** and supplies the triceps; it ends as the **middle collateral** and **radial collateral arteries** (to the cubital network); it gives off a nutrient artery of the humerus and a deltoid branch.
**Superior ulnar collateral artery** — with the ulnar nerve, behind the medial epicondyle.
**Inferior ulnar collateral artery** — in front of the medial epicondyle.
Muscular branches and the **nutrient artery of the humerus**.

In bleeding the artery is pressed against the **humerus** in the medial groove. If the brachial artery is ligated **below** the deep artery of the arm, blood circulates well through the cubital network.

blocks.text: The **arterial network of the elbow joint** is formed by the union of the following arteries: from above — the **middle** and **radial collateral** arteries (from the deep artery of the arm) and the **superior** and **inferior ulnar collateral** arteries (from the brachial artery); from below — the **radial recurrent**, the **ulnar recurrent** (anterior and posterior branches) and the **recurrent interosseous** arteries. This network supplies the forearm with blood when the brachial artery is ligated.

items: The **superficial palmar arch** is mainly the continuation of the **ulnar artery**, completed by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery; it lies under the palmar aponeurosis, over the flexor tendons, at the level of the **distal border of the fully extended thumb** (Kaplan's line). 3 **common palmar digital arteries** arise from it; they divide into **proper digital arteries** to the adjacent borders of fingers II–V; a separate artery goes to the medial border of finger V.

The **deep palmar arch** is mainly the continuation of the **radial artery**, completed by the deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery; it lies under the flexor tendons, at the bases of the metacarpal bones, ≈1–1.5 cm proximal to the superficial arch. From it 3–4 **palmar metacarpal arteries** arise and join the common digital arteries; the **perforating branches** connect with the dorsal metacarpal arteries.
The **princeps pollicis artery** and the **radialis indicis artery** — from the radial artery.

**The carpal networks**: the **palmar** one (palmar carpal branches of the radial and ulnar arteries, anterior interosseous artery) and the **dorsal** one (dorsal carpal branches, posterior interosseous artery); from the dorsal network arise the **dorsal metacarpal arteries** → **dorsal digital arteries**.

parts.text: The **radial artery** is the main site for taking the pulse (over the styloid process of the radius, lateral to the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis); it is also the site for **arterial blood sampling**, **coronary angiography** (transradial access) and the **arteriovenous fistula** for hemodialysis (radial artery + cephalic vein). Before puncturing the radial artery the **Allen test** is performed: the radial and ulnar arteries are compressed at the same time, then the ulnar artery is released — if the palm flushes quickly, collateral flow through the arches is adequate. In wounds of the palm both ends must be ligated, because the arches receive blood from both sides.

items: In the newborn the arteries of the upper limb are relatively thin but well developed relative to the size of the limb; the diameter of the subclavian artery grows rapidly from birth **to 4 years**. The length and diameter of the arteries increase 3–5 times by 12–16 years.

In children the muscles, fasciae and grooves of the arm and forearm are poorly developed — the large arteries lie **more superficially** and are easily palpated, but the risk of injury is also higher.

In the newborn the superficial palmar arch is often formed also by the **median artery** (the artery accompanying the median nerve) (in the fetus the median artery is the main artery of the forearm and hand, then it regresses); the shape of the arches varies.
In youth the arterial walls contain many elastic fibers; in the elderly the walls thicken and the vessels become tortuous (for example, the brachial artery).

skills.title: Practical skill: taking the pulse of the arteries of the upper limb and the points of compression

items: **Subclavian artery** — in the supraclavicular fossa, above the middle of the clavicle, it is pressed against the 1st rib.
**Axillary artery** — with the arm abducted to 90°, in the axillary fossa, along the medial border of the coracobrachialis, it is pressed against the head of the humerus.
**Brachial artery** — against the humerus in the medial bicipital groove; it is palpated in the cubital fossa medial to the aponeurosis (the site for measuring blood pressure).
**Radial artery** — at the distal end of the radius, lateral to the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis (counting the pulse); it is also palpated in the **anatomical snuffbox**.
**Ulnar artery** — lateral to the pisiform bone, beside the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris.
Perform the Allen test and interpret the result.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: An 8-year-old child fell on his arm and sustained a supracondylar fracture of the humerus. In the emergency department no pulse can be felt at the wrist, the hand is cold and pale, and passive extension of the fingers causes severe pain.
cases.ask: Which artery may be injured? Explain its topography and the complication. By what routes can circulation be restored?
cases.answer: The **brachial artery** has been injured or compressed by a bone fragment. It lies with the median nerve in the **medial bicipital groove**, distally in front of the humerus and in the cubital fossa under the biceps aponeurosis, and is close to the bone in the supracondylar region. Ischemia of the forearm flexors soon leads to **ischemic contracture (Volkmann's)** (pain on passive extension is a sign of compartment syndrome). Collateral flow is via the **arterial network of the elbow joint**: from above, the deep artery of the arm (the middle and radial collateral arteries) and the superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries; from below, the radial, ulnar and interosseous recurrent arteries. But because the injury is in the region of the network, the collaterals may be inadequate — urgent reduction and exploration of the artery are needed.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A cardiologist intends to perform coronary angiography on a patient via the radial artery. Before the puncture he performed the Allen test: after both arteries were compressed and the ulnar artery was released, the palm stayed pale even after 15 seconds.
cases.ask: What is the anatomical basis of the Allen test? What does the result show, and what decision is made?
cases.answer: The hand receives blood from two arteries: the **ulnar artery** mainly forms the **superficial palmar arch** and the **radial artery** mainly the **deep arch**; the arches anastomose with each other (through the palmar metacarpal and common digital arteries) and through the carpal networks. The test checks whether, if the radial artery became occluded (thrombosis after puncture), the hand could receive enough blood through the ulnar artery and the arches alone. If the palm does not flush within 5–10 seconds the test is **positive (abnormal)**: the arches are incomplete (for example, the superficial arch is not closed) or the ulnar artery is diseased. In this patient radial access is dangerous, and access through the femoral artery (transfemoral) is chosen.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient with a stab wound in the axillary region is bleeding heavily from an artery. The surgeon had to ligate the axillary artery below the origin of the subscapular artery. After the operation the blood supply of the arm is unsatisfactory.
cases.ask: Why is ligation at exactly this site dangerous? In which region is ligation of the axillary artery relatively safe, and why?
cases.answer: The main collateral route of the axillary artery is the **scapular arterial anastomosis**: branches of the subclavian artery (the **suprascapular artery** from the thyrocervical trunk, the **dorsal scapular artery**) connect with branches of the **subscapular artery** arising from part III of the axillary artery (the **circumflex scapular** and thoracodorsal arteries); by this route blood flows backward into the subscapular artery and returns to the distal part of the axillary artery. So if the artery is ligated **above the subscapular artery** (in parts I–II), collateral flow is preserved. When it is ligated **below** the subscapular artery this route does not work — the remaining collaterals (the anastomosis between the circumflex humeral arteries and the deep artery of the arm) are few, so the risk of ischemia of the arm is high; repair of the artery (suture or a graft) is preferable.

topics.title: Branches of the thoracic and abdominal aorta. Blood supply of the internal organs

goals.text: To teach the student the topography and the parietal and visceral branches of the thoracic and abdominal aorta, the branching of the celiac trunk and the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries, the blood supply of the organs of the thoracic and abdominal cavities, the arterial anastomoses and the age-related features.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the topography and the parietal and visceral branches of the thoracic aorta;
the course and anastomoses of the intercostal arteries;
the parietal and the unpaired and paired visceral branches of the abdominal aorta;
the celiac trunk and its three branches;
the branches of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries;
the blood supply of the stomach, liver, spleen, pancreas, intestines, kidneys and gonads;
the anastomoses between the branches of the abdominal aorta and the age-related features.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the branches of the thoracic and abdominal aorta in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
show the skeletotopy of the branches of the abdominal aorta (the vertebral levels);
draw and explain the arterial arcades of the stomach and colon on a diagram.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Pleural puncture** is performed along the **upper border** of the rib, so as not to injure the main intercostal neurovascular bundle in the costal groove (posteriorly, in the scapular line — the 7th–8th intercostal space). In coarctation of the aorta the dilated intercostal arteries erode the lower borders of the ribs and produce "rib notching" on radiographs.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: A **gastric ulcer** on the lesser curvature may erode the left gastric artery, and an **ulcer on the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb** may erode the **gastroduodenal artery** passing behind it, causing heavy bleeding. In **cholecystectomy** the cystic artery is found in **Calot's triangle** (between the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver) and ligated; variants of the hepatic arteries (for example, a right hepatic artery arising from the superior mesenteric artery) are common — care is needed. In liver operations blood flow can be stopped temporarily by compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament between the fingers (the **Pringle maneuver**).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Acute thrombosis or embolism of the superior mesenteric artery** (often in atrial fibrillation) leads to necrosis of almost the whole small intestine and the right half of the colon — the risk of death is very high; at the onset there is severe pain while the abdomen remains soft. In the acute angle between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta the **left renal vein** (**"nutcracker" syndrome** — hematuria, left varicocele) or the **horizontal part of the duodenum** may be compressed. In appendectomy the **appendicular artery** is ligated in the mesoappendix.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: An **abdominal aortic aneurysm** usually forms below the renal arteries (infrarenal); it is palpated as a pulsating mass in the umbilical region; if it ruptures — retroperitoneal bleeding. When the aorta is clamped below the renal arteries, the blood supply of the inferior mesenteric artery territory is maintained through the arc of Riolan and the rectal arteries. Renal artery stenosis (atherosclerosis, fibromuscular dysplasia) leads to **renovascular hypertension**.

blocks.text: The **thoracic aorta** (*pars thoracica aortae*) is the continuation of the aortic arch; it lies in the **posterior mediastinum** from T~IV~ to T~XII~: above, to the left of the esophagus; below (T~VIII~–T~IX~) it passes behind it; to its right are the thoracic duct and the azygos vein, to its left the hemiazygos vein and the left pleura. It passes into the abdominal cavity through the **aortic hiatus** of the diaphragm (T~XII~). Its branches are divided into two groups:

It gives off the **dorsal branch** (back muscles and skin; from it the **spinal branch** passes through the intervertebral foramen), the **collateral branch** (along the upper border of the rib below), the lateral cutaneous branch and mammary branches; anteriorly it anastomoses with the **anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery**.

In coarctation of the aorta the dilated intercostal arteries erode the lower borders of the ribs and produce "rib notching" on radiographs.

blocks.text: The **abdominal aorta** (*pars abdominalis aortae*) lies from T~XII~ to L~IV~ in front of the bodies of the lumbar vertebrae, behind the peritoneum, slightly to the left of the midline; to its right is the **inferior vena cava**, and in front of it are the pancreas, the inferior horizontal part of the duodenum, the root of the mesentery of the small intestine and the **left renal vein** (which passes between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery). At the level of L~IV~ (slightly below the level of the umbilicus) it divides into the **common iliac arteries**; its continuation is the thin **median sacral artery**.

blocks.text: The **celiac trunk** (*truncus coeliacus*) is a short (1–2 cm), thick unpaired trunk; it arises from the anterior surface of the aorta at the level of T~XII~, where the aorta emerges from the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm; above the upper border of the pancreas it divides into **three branches** (**Haller's tripod**):

items: The **left gastric artery** — upward and to the left to the cardia of the stomach, then to the right along the **lesser curvature**; it gives off esophageal branches; it anastomoses with the right gastric artery to form the **arterial arch of the lesser curvature**.

The **common hepatic artery** — to the right, along the upper border of the pancreas; it divides into the **proper hepatic artery** and the **gastroduodenal artery**. The **proper hepatic artery** runs to the porta hepatis in the hepatoduodenal ligament (to the left of the common bile duct, in front of the portal vein), gives off the **right gastric artery** and divides into the **right** (from which arises the **cystic artery**) and **left branches**. The **gastroduodenal artery** passes behind the superior part of the duodenum and gives off the **right gastro-omental artery** (greater curvature) and the **superior pancreaticoduodenal (anterior and posterior) arteries**.

The **splenic artery** (the largest, tortuous) — to the left along the upper border of the pancreas to the hilum of the spleen; it gives off **pancreatic branches**, the **short gastric arteries** (fundus of the stomach), the **left gastro-omental artery** (to the right along the greater curvature; with the right artery it forms the **arch of the greater curvature**) and splenic branches.

In liver operations blood flow can be stopped temporarily by compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament between the fingers (the **Pringle maneuver**).

sections.title: 4. The superior and inferior mesenteric arteries

blocks.text: The **superior mesenteric artery** (*a. mesenterica superior*) arises from the aorta at the level of L~I~, descends behind the neck of the pancreas, passes between the gland and the inferior horizontal part of the duodenum (in front of the latter) and runs within the **root of the mesentery of the small intestine** toward the right iliac fossa. Its branches:

items: The **inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries** — anastomose with the superior arteries (a route between the celiac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery).

The **jejunal** and **ileal arteries** (15–20) — arise from the left side and form **arterial arcades** with one another in the mesentery (1–5 tiers; more in the ileum); from the arcades **straight arteries** (vasa recta) run to the intestinal wall.
The **ileocolic artery** — the cecum (anterior and posterior cecal arteries), the **appendicular artery** (in the mesoappendix), the end of the ileum and the beginning of the ascending colon.
The **right colic artery** — the ascending colon.
The **middle colic artery** — in the transverse mesocolon; the transverse colon.

blocks.label: Figure 28.8
blocks.caption: The superior mesenteric artery and its branches, transverse colon removed (Figure No. 421): 1 — posterior cecal artery; 2 — anterior cecal artery; 3 — ileal branch of the ileocolic artery; 4 — its colic branch; 5 — ileocolic artery; 6 — right colic artery; 7 — inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery; 8 — anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery; 10 — right gastro-omental artery; 12 — gastroduodenal artery; 15 — cystic artery; 17 — proper hepatic artery; 19 — portal vein; 20 — inferior vena cava; 22 — common hepatic artery; 23 — splenic artery; 24 — abdominal aorta; 25 — renal artery; 26 — superior mesenteric artery; 27 — middle colic artery; 28 — jejunal arteries; 29 — ileal arteries; 30 — straight arteries. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **inferior mesenteric artery** (*a. mesenterica inferior*) arises from the aorta at the level of L~III~ and runs to the left and downward behind the peritoneum. Its branches: the **left colic artery** (descending colon and the left part of the transverse colon), the **sigmoid arteries** (2–3) and its terminal branch, the **superior rectal artery** (descends into the lesser pelvis and supplies the upper part of the rectum; anastomoses with the middle and inferior rectal arteries).

The **marginal artery of the colon** (artery of Drummond) is a continuous arcade formed along the intestine by the joined branches of all the colic arteries. The large anastomosis between the **middle and left colic arteries** is the **arc of Riolan** (it links the territories of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries). The left flexure of the colon (splenic flexure) is the "critical point" at the border of the two territories: the collaterals are weak, and **ischemic colitis** most often occurs here.

Labels in the figure are in Latin, English and Russian. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

parts.text: **Acute thrombosis or embolism of the superior mesenteric artery** (often in atrial fibrillation) leads to necrosis of almost the whole small intestine and the right half of the colon — the risk of death is very high; at the onset there is severe pain while the abdomen remains soft. In the acute angle between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta the **left renal vein** (**"nutcracker" syndrome** — hematuria, left varicocele) or the **horizontal part of the duodenum** may be compressed. In appendectomy the **appendicular artery** is ligated in the mesoappendix.

items: The **renal arteries** arise at the level of L~I~–L~II~; the **right renal artery is longer** and passes behind the inferior vena cava. At the renal hilum the artery lies behind the vein and in front of the pelvis (between the two); it divides into anterior and posterior branches, then into **segmental arteries** (5: superior, anterosuperior, anteroinferior, inferior, posterior). The segmental arteries are **end arteries** — they do not anastomose. **Accessory renal arteries** are common (≈25–30 %).
**Suprarenal arteries**: superior (from the inferior phrenic artery), middle (from the aorta), inferior (from the renal artery).

The **testicular arteries** arise at the level of L~II~, cross in front of the ureter behind the peritoneum, and pass through the **deep inguinal ring** in the **spermatic cord** to the testis; the **ovarian arteries** reach the ovary in the suspensory ligament of the ovary and anastomose with the ovarian branch of the uterine artery.

**Anastomoses**: celiac trunk ↔ superior mesenteric (superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries); superior ↔ inferior mesenteric (arc of Riolan, marginal artery); inferior mesenteric ↔ internal iliac (superior, middle and inferior rectal arteries); internal thoracic ↔ external iliac (superior and inferior epigastric arteries — anterior abdominal wall); intercostal ↔ lumbar arteries.

parts.text: An **abdominal aortic aneurysm** usually forms below the renal arteries (infrarenal); it is palpated as a pulsating mass in the umbilical region; if it ruptures — retroperitoneal bleeding. When the aorta is clamped below the renal arteries, the blood supply of the inferior mesenteric artery territory is maintained through the arc of Riolan and the rectal arteries. Renal artery stenosis (atherosclerosis, fibromuscular dysplasia) leads to **renovascular hypertension**.

items: In the newborn the diameter of the aorta is 18–20 mm, and ≈4 cm at puberty. In children the descending aorta extends from T~IV~ to **L~V~** (in adults it bifurcates at L~IV~); it lengthens ≈4 times by 50 years, and the thoracic part grows faster than the abdominal part.

The origin of the abdominal aorta is at the level of T~XI~ in the newborn; in the second period of childhood it descends to the middle of T~XII~, and in adolescence to the lower 1/3 of T~XII~. In the newborn the abdominal aorta is ≈5 cm long, with a diameter of 5.5–6.8 mm.

The diameter of the **superior mesenteric artery** is 2.5–3 mm in the newborn; it increases 2 times by the end of early childhood and increases 4.4 times by the end of the first period of childhood. The **inferior mesenteric artery** in the newborn has a diameter of 1.5–2 mm and a length of 1–2 cm.

The superior suprarenal artery in the newborn is ≈0.9 mm wide and 2.4 cm long; at 20 years, 1.5 mm and 3.26 cm. The arteries of the internal organs change in step with the growth and changes in position of the organs (for example, the testicular artery lengthens as the testis descends into the scrotum).

In children the density of the intraorgan vessels is higher than in adults; in the first year the intraorgan vessels mature rapidly. In the elderly the aorta and its branches undergo atherosclerosis, become dilated and tortuous.

skills.title: Practical skill: showing the skeletotopy of the branches of the abdominal aorta

items: On a skeleton or a radiograph, count T~XII~ and the lumbar vertebrae (using the 12th rib).

T~XII~ — the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm, the celiac trunk and the inferior phrenic arteries; L~I~ — the superior mesenteric artery and the middle suprarenal arteries; L~I~–L~II~ — the renal arteries; L~II~ — the testicular (ovarian) arteries; L~III~ — the inferior mesenteric artery; L~IV~ — the aortic bifurcation.
In a living person the aortic bifurcation projects 1–2 cm below and slightly to the left of the umbilicus, at the level of the line joining the highest points of the two iliac crests.
In a thin person, palpate deeply for the pulsation of the abdominal aorta above the umbilicus, slightly to the left of the midline.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 55-year-old man has had a duodenal ulcer for 10 years. Today he passed black stools (melena) and vomited coffee-ground material; his blood pressure is 85/50 mmHg. Endoscopy shows a deep bleeding ulcer on the posterior wall of the bulb.
cases.ask: Which artery is bleeding? State its origin and topography. What anastomoses does this artery have?
cases.answer: The source of bleeding is the **gastroduodenal artery**. It arises from the **common hepatic artery** (a branch of the celiac trunk), descends **behind** the superior part (bulb) of the duodenum and divides into the **right gastro-omental artery** and the **anterior and posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries**. A deep ulcer on the posterior wall of the bulb erodes the arterial wall directly. Its anastomoses: the superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries with the inferior ones arising from the **superior mesenteric artery**; the right gastro-omental artery with the left one arising from the splenic artery (the arch of the greater curvature). So when the ulcer is sutured, the artery must be ligated above and below the ulcer — otherwise blood arrives from both directions.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 72-year-old patient has atrial fibrillation. Suddenly unbearable pain developed around the umbilicus; on examination the abdomen is soft and the pain is out of proportion to the physical findings. After 6 hours signs of peritoneal irritation and bloody stools appeared.
cases.ask: Embolism of which artery is suspected? State the area supplied by this artery and explain the collateral routes.
cases.answer: **Embolism of the superior mesenteric artery** (mesenteric ischemia). The artery arises from the aorta at the level of L~I~ at an acute angle and runs almost parallel to the aorta, so emboli lodge in it easily. It supplies the lower half of the duodenum, the head of the pancreas, **the whole jejunum and ileum**, the cecum and appendix, and the ascending colon and right 2/3 of the transverse colon. Collaterals: from above — branches of the **celiac trunk** (superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries ↔ inferior ones); from below — the **inferior mesenteric artery** (left colic artery ↔ middle colic artery, the **arc of Riolan** and the marginal artery). In acute occlusion these routes are inadequate, so intestinal necrosis develops; urgent embolectomy is needed.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: During a laparoscopic cholecystectomy the surgeon noticed that the vessel he was about to ligate as the cystic artery was in fact a larger artery running to the porta hepatis.
cases.ask: Which anatomical landmark is used to find the cystic artery? Which variants of the hepatic artery are dangerous?
cases.answer: The cystic artery usually arises from the **right branch of the proper hepatic artery** and is found in **Calot's triangle** — the area bounded by the cystic duct (below), the common hepatic duct (medially) and the inferior surface of the liver (above). The surgeon must not divide anything until the "critical view of safety" is established (only two structures — the cystic duct and the cystic artery — entering the gallbladder in the triangle). Dangerous variants: the **right hepatic artery** passing in front of the common hepatic duct or forming a loop in Calot's triangle ("Moynihan's hump") — it may be ligated in mistake for the cystic artery; a right hepatic artery arising from the **superior mesenteric artery** (≈10–15 %); an accessory left hepatic artery arising from the **left gastric artery**; two cystic arteries. If the right hepatic artery is ligated, ischemia of the right lobe of the liver may develop.
