topics.title: The common, internal and external iliac arteries. Arteries of the lower limb: the femoral, popliteal, leg and foot arteries

goals.text: To teach the student the topography and branches of the common, internal and external iliac arteries, the blood supply of the pelvic organs and walls, the course and branches of the femoral, popliteal, tibial and fibular arteries and the arteries of the foot, the arterial anastomoses of the lower limb, and their age-related features and clinical significance.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the topography and division of the common iliac artery;
the parietal and visceral branches of the internal iliac artery;
the external iliac artery and its branches;
the topography (femoral triangle, adductor canal) and branches of the femoral artery, and the deep artery of the thigh;
the popliteal artery and the arterial network of the knee joint;
the anterior and posterior tibial and fibular arteries;
the dorsal and plantar arteries of the foot and the plantar arch;
the age-related features of the arteries of the lower limb.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the iliac arteries and the arteries of the lower limb in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
take the pulse of the femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis arteries in a living person;
show the point at which the femoral artery is compressed for temporary arrest of bleeding.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In **hysterectomy**, when the uterine artery is ligated there is a risk of injuring the **ureter**, which crosses below and lateral to it (≈1.5–2 cm lateral to the cervix). In **severe postpartum hemorrhage** the uterine arteries or the internal iliac arteries are ligated or **embolized** — because the pelvic organs have many anastomoses through the branches of both sides and the ovarian and rectal arteries, necrosis is rare. **Aberrant origin of the obturator artery** (from the inferior epigastric artery, ≈25–30 %) — the "**corona mortis**" (crown of death): it may be injured when the lacunar ligament is divided in a femoral hernia operation, causing heavy bleeding.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The inferior epigastric artery is the landmark for distinguishing inguinal hernias: in an **indirect (lateral) inguinal hernia** the hernial sac emerges **lateral** to the artery (through the deep inguinal ring), and in a **direct (medial) hernia** — **medial** to the artery (through Hesselbach's triangle).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The pulse of the **femoral artery** is felt slightly medial to the middle of the inguinal ligament (midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis — the **midinguinal point**); in bleeding it is pressed here against the **pubis**. This site is the main access for **angiography** and **coronary angiography** (Seldinger technique): the artery is punctured below the inguinal ligament, over the head of the femur. The femoral vein lies medial to it — the site for central venous catheterization. Injury to the **medial circumflex femoral artery** (fracture of the femoral neck) leads to **avascular necrosis** of the head of the femur.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Because the **popliteal artery** lies close to the bone, it is injured in **knee dislocation** and distal femoral fractures; its pulse is palpated deeply with the knee flexed. **Popliteal aneurysm** is the most common peripheral aneurysm. If the popliteal artery is ligated, collateral flow through the genicular network is poorer than when the femoral artery is ligated (the risk of gangrene is high).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In **peripheral arterial disease** (atherosclerosis, diabetes mellitus) the degree of ischemia of the foot is assessed by taking the pulse of the **dorsalis pedis artery** (lateral to the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus, below the midpoint of the line between the malleoli) and the **posterior tibial artery** (midway between the medial malleolus and the Achilles tendon); the ankle-brachial index is measured. In ≈10 % of people the dorsalis pedis artery cannot be palpated or arises from the perforating branch of the fibular artery. In **compartment syndrome of the leg** (fracture, crushing) the pressure in the fascial compartments rises and the anterior tibial artery and nerve are compressed — fasciotomy is needed.

blocks.text: The **common iliac arteries** (*aa. iliacae communes*) begin at the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta at the level of **L~IV~**, run downward and laterally (5–7 cm long) and in front of the **sacroiliac joint** divide into the **internal** and **external iliac arteries**. The **ureter** crosses in front of the point of division. The common iliac arteries give off no large branches (only small branches to the peritoneum, the ureter and the psoas muscle).

blocks.label: Figure 29.1
blocks.caption: The common iliac artery and its branches, anterior view (diagram; Figure No. 424): 1 — internal pudendal artery; 2 — inferior gluteal artery; 3 — appendicular artery; 4 — superior gluteal artery; 5, 6 — posterior and anterior cecal arteries; 7 — ascending branch; 8 — ileocolic artery; 9 — aortic bifurcation; 10 — superior mesenteric artery; 11 — inferior mesenteric artery; 12 — lumbar arteries; 13 — median sacral artery; 14 — left colic artery; 15 — superior rectal artery; 16 — sigmoid arteries; 17 — common iliac artery; 18 — internal iliac artery; 19 — external iliac artery; 20 — obturator artery; 21 — femoral artery; 22 — common, external and internal iliac arteries. Source: Sh.J. Teshaev, E.A. Xaribova. Human Anatomy. Atlas, vol. 2.

blocks.text: The **internal iliac artery** (*a. iliaca interna*) descends from the level of the sacroiliac joint into the **lesser pelvis** and at the upper border of the greater sciatic foramen usually divides into **anterior** and **posterior trunks**. It supplies the pelvic walls, the pelvic organs, the external genitalia, the perineum, the buttock and the medial group of thigh muscles.

parts.text: In **hysterectomy**, when the uterine artery is ligated there is a risk of injuring the **ureter**, which crosses below and lateral to it (≈1.5–2 cm lateral to the cervix). In **severe postpartum hemorrhage** the uterine arteries or the internal iliac arteries are ligated or **embolized** — because the pelvic organs have many anastomoses through the branches of both sides and the ovarian and rectal arteries, necrosis is rare. **Aberrant origin of the obturator artery** (from the inferior epigastric artery, ≈25–30 %) — the "**corona mortis**" (crown of death): it may be injured when the lacunar ligament is divided in a femoral hernia operation, causing heavy bleeding.

blocks.text: The **external iliac artery** (*a. iliaca externa*) runs from the sacroiliac joint along the medial border of the psoas major to the inguinal ligament and, passing to the thigh through the **vascular lacuna**, takes the name **femoral artery**. Near the inguinal ligament it gives off two branches:

items: The **inferior epigastric artery** — ascends medial to the deep inguinal ring (within the **lateral umbilical fold**), rises inside the rectus sheath and anastomoses with the **superior epigastric artery** (from the internal thoracic artery) — a collateral between the subclavian and external iliac arteries. Its branches: the **pubic branch** (to the obturator artery), in men the **cremasteric artery**, in women the **artery of the round ligament of the uterus**.
The **deep circumflex iliac artery** — laterally behind the inguinal ligament along the iliac crest; the broad muscles of the abdominal wall and the iliacus.

parts.text: The inferior epigastric artery is the landmark for distinguishing inguinal hernias: in an **indirect (lateral) inguinal hernia** the hernial sac emerges **lateral** to the artery (through the deep inguinal ring), and in a **direct (medial) hernia** — **medial** to the artery (through Hesselbach's triangle).

blocks.text: The **femoral artery** (*a. femoralis*) emerges in the middle of the vascular lacuna (lateral to the femoral vein, medial to the femoral nerve — **NAV**: nerve, artery, vein from lateral to medial), descends in the **femoral triangle** (between the inguinal ligament, the sartorius and the adductor longus), then enters the **adductor canal** (Hunter's canal; between the vastus medialis, the adductor magnus and the lamina vastoadductoria) and, passing through the **adductor hiatus** into the popliteal fossa, becomes the **popliteal artery**. Its branches:

items: The **superficial epigastric artery** — the skin of the anterior abdominal wall (as far as the umbilicus).
The **superficial circumflex iliac artery** — the skin over the iliac crest.
The **external pudendal arteries** — the skin of the scrotum or the labia majora.

The **deep artery of the thigh** (*a. profunda femoris*) — its largest branch; it arises from the posterolateral side 3–5 cm below the inguinal ligament; it gives off the **medial circumflex femoral artery** (the hip joint and **the main blood supply of the head of the femur**, the adductor muscles), the **lateral circumflex femoral artery** (ascending, transverse and descending branches — the quadriceps) and **3 perforating arteries** (which pierce the adductors to reach the posterior thigh muscles).
The **descending genicular artery** — arises in the adductor canal; branches to the genicular network and along the saphenous vein.

parts.text: The pulse of the **femoral artery** is felt slightly medial to the middle of the inguinal ligament (midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis — the **midinguinal point**); in bleeding it is pressed here against the **pubis**. This site is the main access for **angiography** and **coronary angiography** (Seldinger technique): the artery is punctured below the inguinal ligament, over the head of the femur. The femoral vein lies medial to it — the site for central venous catheterization. Injury to the **medial circumflex femoral artery** (fracture of the femoral neck) leads to **avascular necrosis** of the head of the femur.

sections.title: 5. The popliteal artery and the genicular network

blocks.text: The **popliteal artery** (*a. poplitea*) lies deepest (closest to the bone) in the popliteal fossa: superficial to it is the **popliteal vein**, and most superficial is the **tibial nerve** of the sciatic nerve (**NVA** — from behind forward). At the lower border of the popliteus it divides into the **anterior** and **posterior tibial arteries**. Its branches forming the **arterial network of the knee joint** are the **superior lateral** and **superior medial**, **middle** (to the cruciate ligaments), **inferior lateral** and **inferior medial genicular arteries**; the descending genicular artery (from the femoral artery), the descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery and the anterior and posterior tibial recurrent arteries also take part in the network. Muscular branches — the **sural arteries** (to the triceps surae).

parts.text: Because the **popliteal artery** lies close to the bone, it is injured in **knee dislocation** and distal femoral fractures; its pulse is palpated deeply with the knee flexed. **Popliteal aneurysm** is the most common peripheral aneurysm. If the popliteal artery is ligated, collateral flow through the genicular network is poorer than when the femoral artery is ligated (the risk of gangrene is high).

blocks.text: The **dorsalis pedis artery** (*a. dorsalis pedis*) lies lateral to the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus and passes to the sole as the **deep plantar branch** in the **1st intermetatarsal space** (completing the plantar arch). Its branches: the **lateral** and **medial tarsal arteries**, the **arcuate artery** (over the bases of the metatarsal bones; from it the **dorsal metatarsal arteries** → **dorsal digital arteries**), and the 1st dorsal metatarsal artery.

The **medial plantar artery** (the smaller) runs along the abductor hallucis; the **lateral plantar artery** (the larger) runs laterally between the flexor digitorum brevis and the quadratus plantae, then turns medially from the base of the 5th metatarsal and forms the **plantar arch** with the **deep plantar branch**. From the arch arise the **plantar metatarsal arteries** → **common** and **proper plantar digital arteries**; perforating branches anastomose with the dorsal metatarsal arteries.

parts.text: In **peripheral arterial disease** (atherosclerosis, diabetes mellitus) the degree of ischemia of the foot is assessed by taking the pulse of the **dorsalis pedis artery** (lateral to the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus, below the midpoint of the line between the malleoli) and the **posterior tibial artery** (midway between the medial malleolus and the Achilles tendon); the ankle-brachial index is measured. In ≈10 % of people the dorsalis pedis artery cannot be palpated or arises from the perforating branch of the fibular artery. In **compartment syndrome of the leg** (fracture, crushing) the pressure in the fascial compartments rises and the anterior tibial artery and nerve are compressed — fasciotomy is needed.

sections.title: 7. Arterial anastomoses of the lower limb and age-related features

items: **Gluteofemoral anastomoses** (the "cruciate anastomosis"): the superior and inferior gluteal and obturator arteries (internal iliac) ↔ the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries and the 1st perforating artery (femoral artery). When the external iliac artery or the proximal part of the femoral artery is occluded, blood reaches the limb by this route.
**In the abdominal wall**: inferior ↔ superior epigastric arteries; deep circumflex iliac ↔ iliolumbar artery; obturator ↔ inferior epigastric (pubic branches).

The **genicular network**, the **malleolar networks** (medial and lateral malleolar branches), the **calcaneal network**; in the foot — the **plantar arch** and the deep plantar branch and perforating branches between it and the dorsalis pedis artery.

In the fetus the **umbilical arteries** are the main continuation of the internal iliac arteries and carry blood to the placenta; after birth they are obliterated and become the **medial umbilical ligaments** (their proximal parts remain as the superior vesical arteries). So in the newborn the internal iliac artery is thicker than the external one; with age, as the limb grows, the **external iliac artery** predominates.

In children the aortic bifurcation is lower (down to L~V~) and the angle between the common iliac arteries is smaller. The arteries of the lower limb lie more superficially in children; their length and diameter increase in step with the growth of the limb, especially rapidly during puberty.

In the elderly the arteries of the lower limb (especially the femoral and popliteal arteries) are the ones most often affected by atherosclerosis — "intermittent claudication," and in severe cases gangrene.

skills.title: Practical skill: taking the pulse of the arteries of the lower limb

items: **Femoral artery** — palpate below the inguinal ligament, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis; in bleeding, press here with the fist against the superior ramus of the pubis.
**Popliteal artery** — with the patient lying prone and the knee slightly flexed, palpate deeply in the middle of the popliteal fossa with the fingers of both hands.
**Posterior tibial artery** — in the hollow between the medial malleolus and the Achilles tendon.
**Dorsalis pedis artery** — on the dorsum of the foot, lateral to the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus, between the bases of the 1st and 2nd metatarsal bones.
Compare the pulses in the two legs and record the result (present, weakened, absent).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 65-year-old man who smokes complains of pain in his left calf after walking 200 meters, forcing him to stop (intermittent claudication). On the left side the femoral pulse is good, but there is no pulse in the popliteal, posterior tibial or dorsalis pedis arteries.
cases.ask: Determine which artery is narrowed and where. By what collateral routes is blood reaching the leg?
cases.answer: There is a pulse in the femoral artery but none in the popliteal — the narrowing is in the **distal part of the femoral artery**, most often in the **adductor (Hunter's) canal** (a typical site of atherosclerosis). Collateral routes: branches of the **deep artery of the thigh** (which arises higher up from the femoral artery) — the **perforating arteries** and the **descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery** — anastomose through the **arterial network of the knee joint** with the genicular arteries of the popliteal artery (superior lateral and medial); the descending genicular artery also takes part in this network. At rest the collaterals are sufficient, but on walking the demand of the calf muscles rises and ischemic pain appears. Treatment — stopping smoking, walking exercise, and in severe cases femoropopliteal bypass or angioplasty.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: After coronary angiography a painful pulsating swelling appeared in the patient's right groin (a false aneurysm). The doctor found that the puncture site had been well above the inguinal ligament.
cases.ask: Where is the correct site for puncturing the femoral artery? Why is a puncture above the inguinal ligament dangerous? State the order of the structures in the femoral triangle.
cases.answer: The correct site is 1–2 cm below the inguinal ligament, at the **midinguinal point** (midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis), where the artery lies **over the head of the femur** — after the puncture, bleeding can be stopped by pressing the artery against the bone. Above the inguinal ligament the artery is the **external iliac artery** and lies behind the peritoneum — it cannot be pressed against bone, so the risk of **retroperitoneal hemorrhage** and false aneurysm is high; too low, there is the origin of the deep artery of the thigh or the crossing with the femoral vein, with a risk of arteriovenous fistula. In the femoral triangle, from lateral to medial: the **femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein** (NAV), and medial to the vein the femoral canal (lymph nodes).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: After childbirth there is heavy bleeding because the uterus fails to contract, and conservative measures are ineffective. The surgeon ligated the anterior trunks of the internal iliac arteries on both sides; the bleeding stopped, and no necrosis of the uterus or bladder was seen.
cases.ask: From which arteries does the uterus receive blood? After the internal iliac arteries are ligated, how do the pelvic organs remain supplied with blood?
cases.answer: The uterus receives blood mainly from the **uterine artery** (from the anterior trunk of the internal iliac artery; at the base of the broad ligament it crosses over the ureter and ascends along the lateral border of the uterus); it anastomoses with the **ovarian artery** (from the abdominal aorta). After ligation the blood pressure falls and the bleeding lessens, but the organs receive blood through the following collaterals: the **ovarian arteries** (from the aorta); the **superior rectal artery** (from the inferior mesenteric artery) ↔ the middle and inferior rectal arteries; the **median sacral artery** (from the aorta) ↔ the lateral sacral arteries; the **lumbar arteries** and the **deep circumflex iliac artery** ↔ the iliolumbar artery; the **inferior epigastric artery** (from the external iliac) ↔ the obturator artery; the **circumflex femoral arteries** ↔ the gluteal arteries; the branches of the two sides also join at the midline. That is why there is no necrosis.

topics.title: The venous system: the superior and inferior venae cavae, the portal vein. Venous anastomoses. The fetal circulation. The lymphatic system. Organs of the immune system. Age-related features

goals.text: To teach the student the general principles of the venous system, the superior and inferior vena cava systems, the dural venous sinuses, the veins of the upper and lower limbs, the hepatic portal vein, the cava-caval and portocaval anastomoses, the fetal circulation and the changes after birth, and the structure, age-related features and clinical significance of the lymphatic system and the organs of the immune system.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the structural features of veins and the venous systems;
the superior vena cava, the brachiocephalic veins, the internal and external jugular veins, the azygos and hemiazygos veins;
the dural venous sinuses and their connections with the external veins;
the superficial and deep veins of the upper and lower limbs;
the inferior vena cava, the portal vein and their tributaries;
the portocaval and cava-caval anastomoses;
the fetal circulation and the changes after birth;
the lymphatic vessels, trunks, ducts and lymph nodes; the primary and secondary immune organs and their age-related features.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: find the main veins, sinuses, lymphatic ducts and immune organs in an atlas and on specimens and name them in Latin;
show the subcutaneous veins of the upper and lower limbs and the venipuncture sites in a living person;
draw and explain the portocaval anastomoses and the fetal circulation on a diagram;
show the palpable groups of lymph nodes.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Emissary veins** and **diploic veins** connect the sinuses with veins outside the cranium, and the **ophthalmic veins** connect the cavernous sinus with the **facial vein** (angular vein). That is why squeezing a boil in the nasolabial triangle (the "**danger triangle**") can carry infection into the cavernous sinus and cause **cavernous sinus thrombosis** (exophthalmos, paralysis of the oculomotor nerves) and meningitis. Injury to the superior sagittal sinus causes heavy bleeding.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: **Varicose veins of the leg** — due to incompetence of the valves of the great saphenous vein (especially the ostial valve where it joins the femoral vein) and of the valves of the perforating veins; complication — trophic ulcers. **Deep vein thrombosis** (prolonged bed rest, after surgery, pregnancy) is dangerous — a thrombus may break off and pass via the inferior vena cava → the right heart → causing **pulmonary embolism**. The great saphenous vein is harvested as an **autograft** for coronary artery bypass and peripheral bypass (it is reversed because of its valves). **Left varicocele** is more common: the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In **cirrhosis of the liver** the pressure in the portal vein rises (**portal hypertension**): bleeding from esophageal varices (one of the main causes of death), hemorrhoids, "caput medusae," **splenomegaly** and **ascites** are seen. One method of treatment is **TIPS** (creating an artificial portocaval shunt within the liver between the portal vein and a hepatic vein by means of a stent).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Congenital heart defects: **patent ductus arteriosus** (shunting of blood from the aorta into the pulmonary artery, a "machinery murmur"; common in premature infants — closed with indomethacin or ibuprofen), **atrial septal defect**, **ventricular septal defect** (the most common), **tetralogy of Fallot** (pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta, right ventricular hypertrophy — cyanosis). A patent foramen ovale in adults may cause **paradoxical embolism** (passage of a venous thrombus to the brain).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Enlargement of the lymph nodes (**lymphadenopathy**) is seen in infections, tumor metastasis and blood diseases; to know which nodes a tumor will metastasize to, the **regional lymphatic drainage** of the organ is important: for example, breast cancer — mainly the **axillary** nodes (the first being the "sentinel node"), gastric cancer — the left supraclavicular node (**Virchow's node**, beside the point where the thoracic duct ends). When the thoracic duct is injured (mediastinal operations) lymph collects in the pleural cavity — **chylothorax**. When lymph flow is obstructed — **lymphedema** (for example, swelling of the arm after mastectomy).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Although the spleen is protected by the ribs, it **ruptures** in fractures of the lower left ribs or in abdominal trauma — heavy internal bleeding (in children a spleen-preserving operation is performed if possible). After splenectomy, especially in children, the risk of severe infection with encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus) increases — vaccination is needed. Normally the spleen is not palpable; if it is palpable — splenomegaly (portal hypertension, blood diseases, infections). Tumors of the thymus (thymoma) may be associated with **myasthenia gravis**.

blocks.text: **Veins** carry blood from the organs to the heart. Compared with arteries their walls are **thin** (the middle muscular layer is scant), their lumen is wide and they are more numerous; ≈70 % of the blood is in the veins (**capacitance vessels**). Most medium-sized veins have folds of endothelium — **valves** (especially in the veins of the lower limb); they prevent the backflow of blood. There are no valves in the venae cavae, the portal vein, or the cerebral, renal and pulmonary veins. Veins are **superficial** (subcutaneous, without arteries) and **deep** (accompanying arteries; 2 each for medium and small arteries); they are connected by **perforating veins** and form many **venous plexuses**. Venous return is aided by the **muscle pump**, the negative pressure in the thorax (inspiration), the suction effect of the heart and the pulsation of neighboring arteries.

The veins of the systemic circulation unite into three systems: the **superior vena cava system**, the **inferior vena cava system** and the **hepatic portal vein system** (part of the inferior vena cava system); separately — the **cardiac veins** (coronary sinus). In the pulmonary circulation — the **4 pulmonary veins**.

blocks.text: The **superior vena cava** (*v. cava superior*, 5–6 cm long, ≈2 cm in diameter) is formed by the union of the right and left **brachiocephalic veins** behind the junction of the right 1st costal cartilage with the sternum; it descends to the right of the ascending aorta and drains into the **right atrium** at the level of the 3rd costal cartilage. Before it enters the pericardium the **azygos vein** drains into it from behind. It collects blood from the head, neck, upper limbs, thoracic walls and part of the abdominal wall.

items: The **brachiocephalic veins** are formed on each side by the union of the **internal jugular** and **subclavian veins** behind the sternoclavicular joint (the **venous angle** — where the thoracic and right lymphatic ducts drain); the left one is longer (5–6 cm) and passes obliquely in front of the branches of the aortic arch. The **vertebral**, **internal thoracic**, **inferior thyroid** and **supreme intercostal** veins drain into them.

The **internal jugular vein** begins at the jugular foramen (the continuation of the **sigmoid sinus**; at its start is the superior bulb) and descends in the carotid sheath lateral to the common carotid artery; it has an inferior bulb. **Intracranial tributaries** — the dural sinuses (cerebral, ophthalmic and inner ear veins); **extracranial tributaries** — the **facial vein**, the **retromandibular vein**, and the **pharyngeal**, **lingual**, **superior** and **middle thyroid veins**.

The **external jugular vein** is formed below the auricle from the posterior auricular vein and the posterior branch of the retromandibular vein, descends obliquely **over the sternocleidomastoid** (under the platysma) and drains into the subclavian vein; it bulges on coughing or in heart failure. The **anterior jugular veins** begin below the hyoid bone and unite in the suprasternal space by the **jugular venous arch**.

The **subclavian vein** is the continuation of the axillary vein; on the 1st rib it passes **in front of the anterior scalene muscle** (the artery lies behind the muscle); because it adheres to the fasciae its lumen is always open — the site for **central venous catheterization**.

The **azygos vein** (the continuation of the right ascending lumbar vein) and the **hemiazygos vein** (on the left) ascend along the vertebral column in the posterior mediastinum; the **posterior intercostal**, esophageal, bronchial and mediastinal veins drain into them. The hemiazygos vein crosses to the right at the level of T~VII~–T~X~ and drains into the azygos vein; the azygos vein arches over the right bronchus and drains into the superior vena cava at the level of T~IV~. They form an important **cava-caval** route between the superior and inferior venae cavae.

blocks.text: The **dural venous sinuses** are valveless venous channels between the layers of the dura mater whose walls do not collapse; they collect blood from the brain, the eye, the inner ear, the skull bones and the meninges and carry it mainly to the **internal jugular vein**. The **superior sagittal** (in the upper border of the falx cerebri; cerebrospinal fluid is absorbed into the blood through the arachnoid **granulations**), **inferior sagittal**, **straight** (receives the great cerebral vein) and **occipital** sinuses meet at the **confluence of sinuses** (at the level of the internal occipital protuberance); from it the **transverse** sinuses → the **sigmoid** sinuses → the jugular foramen → the internal jugular vein. Beside the sella turcica are the **cavernous sinuses** (the internal carotid artery and nerve VI pass through them, and nerves III, IV, V~1~ and V~2~ run in the lateral wall); they drain through the **superior** and **inferior petrosal** sinuses into the transverse sinus and the jugular vein, and connect with the facial veins through the **ophthalmic veins**.

parts.text: **Emissary veins** and **diploic veins** connect the sinuses with veins outside the cranium, and the **ophthalmic veins** connect the cavernous sinus with the **facial vein** (angular vein). That is why squeezing a boil in the nasolabial triangle (the "**danger triangle**") can carry infection into the cavernous sinus and cause **cavernous sinus thrombosis** (exophthalmos, paralysis of the oculomotor nerves) and meningitis. Injury to the superior sagittal sinus causes heavy bleeding.

blocks.text: **Veins of the upper limb**: the **superficial veins** — the **cephalic vein** (*v. cephalica*; lateral side of the forearm, lateral bicipital groove, through the deltopectoral groove to the axillary vein) and the **basilic vein** (*v. basilica*; medial side of the forearm, pierces the fascia in the middle of the arm to join the brachial vein); in the cubital fossa they are connected by the **median cubital vein** — the main site for **venipuncture** and intravenous injection. The **deep veins** — the paired radial, ulnar and brachial veins accompanying the arteries → the **axillary vein** → the subclavian vein.

The **inferior vena cava** (*v. cava inferior*) is the largest vein; it is formed by the union of the right and left **common iliac veins** at the level of L~IV~–L~V~ (to the right of and below the aortic bifurcation), ascends to the right of the aorta, lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the liver, passes into the thoracic cavity through the **opening in the central tendon** of the diaphragm (T~VIII~) and drains into the **right atrium**. Its tributaries:

items: **Parietal**: the **lumbar veins** (4 pairs; connected with the ascending lumbar veins), the **inferior phrenic veins**.

**Visceral**: the **testicular (ovarian) veins** (the right one drains into the inferior vena cava, **the left one into the left renal vein** at a right angle), the **renal veins** (the left one is long and passes in front of the aorta; it receives the left testicular and left suprarenal veins), the **suprarenal veins** (the right one directly), the **hepatic veins** (3–4; they carry the blood that arrived through the portal vein and hepatic artery out of the liver into the inferior vena cava on the posterior surface of the liver).

**Common iliac veins** = the **internal iliac vein** (pelvic walls and organs; the **rectal**, **vesical** and **prostatic/uterovaginal venous plexuses**) + the **external iliac vein** (the continuation of the femoral vein; the inferior epigastric vein).

**Veins of the lower limb**: **superficial** — the **great saphenous vein** (*v. saphena magna*; **in front of** the medial malleolus — the site for venesection; along the medial surface of the leg and thigh, it drains into the **femoral vein** through the **saphenous opening** 3–4 cm below the inguinal ligament) and the **small saphenous vein** (from behind the lateral malleolus, along the posterior surface of the leg to the **popliteal vein**); **deep** — the paired veins of the foot and leg → the **popliteal** → the **femoral vein**; they are connected by **perforating veins**.

parts.text: **Varicose veins of the leg** — due to incompetence of the valves of the great saphenous vein (especially the ostial valve where it joins the femoral vein) and of the valves of the perforating veins; complication — trophic ulcers. **Deep vein thrombosis** (prolonged bed rest, after surgery, pregnancy) is dangerous — a thrombus may break off and pass via the inferior vena cava → the right heart → causing **pulmonary embolism**. The great saphenous vein is harvested as an **autograft** for coronary artery bypass and peripheral bypass (it is reversed because of its valves). **Left varicocele** is more common: the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle.

blocks.text: The **portal vein** (*v. portae hepatis*, 5–6 cm long) carries blood from the **unpaired organs** of the abdominal cavity (the stomach, the small and large intestine as far as the upper part of the rectum, the spleen, the pancreas, the gallbladder) **to the liver**. It is formed behind the head of the pancreas (at the level of **L~II~**) by the union of the **superior mesenteric** and **splenic veins** (the inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic vein); it ascends in the **hepatoduodenal ligament** behind the common bile duct and the proper hepatic artery and divides at the porta hepatis into right and left branches; within the liver: **interlobular veins** → **sinusoidal capillaries** → **central veins** → **hepatic veins** → the inferior vena cava. The **left and right gastric veins**, the **cystic vein** and the **paraumbilical veins** (along the round ligament of the liver) drain directly into it.

blocks.text: **Portocaval anastomoses** are connections between the portal vein system and the caval systems; normally they are insignificant, but in **portal hypertension** (cirrhosis of the liver) blood bypasses the liver through them and the veins dilate:

blocks.text: **Cava-caval anastomoses** — between the superior and inferior venae cavae: 1) **in the anterior abdominal wall** — superior ↔ inferior epigastric veins, the thoracoepigastric vein ↔ the superficial epigastric vein; 2) **in the posterior abdominal wall** — the **azygos and hemiazygos veins** (through the ascending lumbar veins) ↔ the lumbar veins and the inferior vena cava; 3) **the internal and external vertebral venous plexuses** (intercostal ↔ spinal branches of the lumbar veins). When the inferior vena cava is occluded, blood flows to the superior vena cava by these routes.

parts.text: In **cirrhosis of the liver** the pressure in the portal vein rises (**portal hypertension**): bleeding from esophageal varices (one of the main causes of death), hemorrhoids, "caput medusae," **splenomegaly** and **ascites** are seen. One method of treatment is **TIPS** (creating an artificial portocaval shunt within the liver between the portal vein and a hepatic vein by means of a stent).

blocks.text: The fetus obtains oxygen and nutrients from the mother's blood through the **placenta**; its lungs do not function. The course of the blood:

items: Arterial (oxygen-rich) blood from the placenta comes through the **umbilical vein** (unpaired), within the umbilical cord, to the porta hepatis.

Part of the blood passes into the portal vein (to the liver), but most of it bypasses the liver through the **ductus venosus (of Arantius)** and drains into the **inferior vena cava**, where it mixes with venous blood from the lower part of the body.

Blood arriving in the right atrium from the inferior vena cava is directed by the **valve of the inferior vena cava** (Eustachian valve) through the **foramen ovale** into the **left atrium** → left ventricle → aorta; through the branches of the aortic arch the relatively oxygen-rich blood goes **to the head and upper limbs** (which is why they are relatively well developed).

Venous blood from the superior vena cava passes to the right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary trunk; a small part of the blood goes to the lungs, and most of it passes through the **ductus arteriosus (of Botallo)** into the part of the aorta beyond the arch (the descending aorta).
The mixed blood in the descending aorta goes to the lower part of the body and returns to the placenta through the two **umbilical arteries** arising from the internal iliac arteries.

parts.text: Congenital heart defects: **patent ductus arteriosus** (shunting of blood from the aorta into the pulmonary artery, a "machinery murmur"; common in premature infants — closed with indomethacin or ibuprofen), **atrial septal defect**, **ventricular septal defect** (the most common), **tetralogy of Fallot** (pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta, right ventricular hypertrophy — cyanosis). A patent foramen ovale in adults may cause **paradoxical embolism** (passage of a venous thrombus to the brain).

blocks.text: The **lymphatic system** absorbs tissue fluid to form **lymph** and returns it to the venous system; it carries **fats** (chylomicrons) from the intestine, filters the lymph in the lymph nodes (a barrier) and produces lymphocytes. Its components: **lymphatic capillaries** (closed at one end, with a wall of a single layer of endothelium; absent from the brain, cartilage, cornea, lens, epithelium, splenic parenchyma and bone marrow) → **lymphatic vessels** (with many valves, "beaded"; superficial and deep) → **lymph nodes** → **lymphatic trunks** → **lymphatic ducts** → the **venous angles**.

items: **Lymphatic trunks** (paired): **jugular** (head and neck), **subclavian** (upper limb), **bronchomediastinal** (thoracic organs), **lumbar** (lower limbs, pelvis, abdominal wall, paired organs); unpaired — the **intestinal trunk** (unpaired abdominal organs).

The **thoracic duct** (*ductus thoracicus*, 30–41 cm long) is formed at the level of T~XII~–L~II~ by the union of the right and left lumbar trunks (and the intestinal trunk); at its start is the dilated **cisterna chyli**; it passes through the **aortic hiatus** of the diaphragm into the posterior mediastinum, ascends between the aorta and the azygos vein, deviates to the left at the level of T~V~–T~VII~, forms an **arch** at the level of C~VI~–C~VII~ and drains into the **left venous angle**. It collects lymph from **3/4 of the body** — both lower limbs, the abdomen, the pelvis, the left half of the thorax, the left upper limb and the left half of the head; it has 7–9 valves.

The **right lymphatic duct** (10–12 mm; often absent — the trunks drain separately) is formed from the right jugular, right subclavian and right bronchomediastinal trunks; it drains into the **right venous angle** and collects lymph from the upper right **1/4 of the body**.

**Lymph nodes** (500–1000 in number, with a total mass of ≈1 % of body mass) are bean-shaped, 1–15 mm; 4–6 **afferent** lymphatic vessels enter on the convex side, and 2–4 **efferent** lymphatic vessels leave from the **hilum** on the concave side. They have a capsule, trabeculae, a **cortex** (lymphoid follicles — B lymphocytes), a **paracortical zone** (T lymphocytes, postcapillary venules) and a **medulla** (medullary cords); lymph passes through the **sinuses** (subcapsular → cortical → medullary → hilar sinus). Groups: the superficial and deep cervical, submandibular, submental, axillary, cubital, inguinal, popliteal, mediastinal, bronchopulmonary, abdominal, iliac and others.

parts.text: Enlargement of the lymph nodes (**lymphadenopathy**) is seen in infections, tumor metastasis and blood diseases; to know which nodes a tumor will metastasize to, the **regional lymphatic drainage** of the organ is important: for example, breast cancer — mainly the **axillary** nodes (the first being the "sentinel node"), gastric cancer — the left supraclavicular node (**Virchow's node**, beside the point where the thoracic duct ends). When the thoracic duct is injured (mediastinal operations) lymph collects in the pleural cavity — **chylothorax**. When lymph flow is obstructed — **lymphedema** (for example, swelling of the arm after mastectomy).

blocks.text: The organs of the **immune (lymphoid) system** produce lymphocytes and other immune cells that protect the body from genetically foreign substances and microorganisms. They appear early in fetal life and are mature in the newborn; their total mass (excluding the marrow) is 1.5–2 kg.

blocks.text: The **thymus** lies in the upper **anterior mediastinum**, behind the manubrium of the sternum, in front of the pericardium, the superior vena cava and the left brachiocephalic vein; it consists of right and left **lobes**, divided into lobules by the capsule and septa; each lobule consists of a **cortex** (densely packed T lymphocytes) and a **medulla** (Hassall's corpuscles). It develops from the endoderm of the **3rd–4th pharyngeal pouches**.

blocks.text: The **spleen** (*splen, lien*) lies under the left costal margin at the level of the **9th–11th ribs**, with its long axis along the 10th rib; it is 10–14 cm long and weighs ≈190 g in men and ≈150 g in women. It has **diaphragmatic** and **visceral** (gastric, renal and colic) surfaces, upper (notched) and lower borders, and a hilum; it is covered on all sides by peritoneum (gastrosplenic, splenorenal and phrenicosplenic ligaments). Inside are the **red pulp** (venous sinuses, ≈80 %) and the **white pulp** (periarterial lymphoid sheaths and lymphoid nodules). Blood arrives through the splenic artery and leaves through the splenic vein to the portal vein.

parts.text: Although the spleen is protected by the ribs, it **ruptures** in fractures of the lower left ribs or in abdominal trauma — heavy internal bleeding (in children a spleen-preserving operation is performed if possible). After splenectomy, especially in children, the risk of severe infection with encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus) increases — vaccination is needed. Normally the spleen is not palpable; if it is palpable — splenomegaly (portal hypertension, blood diseases, infections). Tumors of the thymus (thymoma) may be associated with **myasthenia gravis**.

items: In the newborn the venous system is less mature than the arteries: the veins run straight, the venous plexuses are poorly defined, there are subcutaneous venous plexuses in the limbs, and the large subcutaneous veins become clearly visible only **after 2 years**. In early childhood the length and cross-section of the veins increase 2 times, and by 8–12 years they increase 7–8 times; the number of anastomoses increases up to 16 years.

In the newborn the superior vena cava has a diameter of 10–12 mm and is short; its point of entry is at the 1st intercostal space and descends to the level of the 2nd rib at 1–3 years and the 3rd rib at 4–10 years. In the newborn the inferior vena cava is formed at the level of L~III~–L~IV~ (L~IV~–L~V~ at puberty) and is short and wide (≈6 mm). In the newborn the portal vein is 16–44 mm long and 3–4 mm wide.
The fetal circulation changes after birth (Table 30.2); in the newborn the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus sometimes remain open for several days (the foramen ovale for up to 6–8 months).

In the newborn the lymph nodes are small, their capsule thin and their lymphoid nodules poorly formed; in childhood they grow rapidly and increase in number and size; in children the lymph nodes respond quickly to infection and enlarge; in the elderly the number of nodes decreases and they are replaced by fatty tissue.

In the newborn the **thymus** is relatively large (≈13 g), its upper border 1–2.5 cm above the manubrium; it grows rapidly in the first 3 years and is **largest at puberty** (≈37 g); it then undergoes **age-related involution** and is replaced by fatty tissue (≈6 g at 70–75 years). Until 10 years the cortex predominates; after that the medulla increases.

In the newborn **red bone marrow** is present in all bones; from 4–5 years it turns into yellow marrow in the diaphyses of the long bones, and by 20–25 years the medullary cavity is filled with yellow marrow; in adults the mass of the marrow is 2.5–3 kg.

In the newborn the **spleen** is rounded and lobulated and weighs ≈9.5 g; 24–28 g at 1 year, 2 times that at 6 years, and 165–171 g at 16–17 years. The (palatine) **tonsils** are largest at 8–13 years; the pharyngeal tonsil may enlarge in children (adenoids) and obstruct nasal breathing; after puberty the tonsils and lymphoid nodules shrink.

skills.title: Practical skill: showing the superficial veins and lymph nodes

items: Apply a tourniquet to the arm and show the cephalic and basilic veins and the **median cubital vein** in the **cubital fossa** — the venipuncture site.
Show the **external jugular vein** over the sternocleidomastoid (it bulges when the patient strains to breathe out).

Show the **great saphenous vein** in front of the medial malleolus (the venesection site) and its point of termination in the thigh below the inguinal ligament, and the **small saphenous vein** behind the lateral malleolus.

Palpate the lymph nodes in order: occipital, retroauricular, submandibular, submental, anterior and posterior cervical (along the sternocleidomastoid), supraclavicular (on the left — Virchow's node), axillary, cubital, inguinal and popliteal nodes; assess their size, tenderness, mobility and consistency.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 52-year-old man has been drinking alcohol for 15 years. He was brought in vomiting blood. On examination the abdomen is enlarged (ascites), there are dilated tortuous veins around the umbilicus, and the spleen is enlarged. Endoscopy shows ruptured varices in the lower esophagus.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? How is the portal vein formed? Explain the signs on the basis of the portocaval anastomoses.
cases.answer: This is **portal hypertension** resulting from **cirrhosis of the liver**. The **portal vein** is formed behind the head of the pancreas by the union of the **superior mesenteric** and **splenic veins** and carries blood from the unpaired abdominal organs to the liver; in cirrhosis flow through the liver is impeded, the pressure rises and blood flows into the caval veins through the **portocaval anastomoses**: 1) the **left gastric vein** (portal) ↔ the **esophageal veins** → the azygos and hemiazygos veins (superior vena cava) — esophageal varices, and hematemesis if they rupture; 2) the **paraumbilical veins** (along the round ligament of the liver to the portal vein) ↔ the superior and inferior epigastric veins — **"caput medusae"**; 3) the superior ↔ middle and inferior rectal veins — hemorrhoids; 4) the retroperitoneal anastomoses. **Splenomegaly** results from congestion in the splenic vein, and **ascites** from the increased hydrostatic pressure in the portal system and reduced protein synthesis by the liver.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In a premature newborn (32 weeks), on day 3 there is shortness of breath and a continuous "machinery" murmur (in systole and diastole) over the heart; the pulses in the legs are "bounding."
cases.ask: What defect is suspected? What is the function of this structure in the fetus, and how should it have closed after birth?
cases.answer: **Patent ductus arteriosus (of Botallo)**. Because the lungs do not function in the fetus, most of the blood in the pulmonary trunk passes through the **ductus arteriosus** into the **aorta** (the part beyond the aortic arch), bypassing the lungs. After birth, with the first breath, pulmonary vascular resistance falls, the pressure in the aorta exceeds that in the pulmonary trunk, blood oxygen rises and prostaglandins fall — the wall of the duct contracts, it closes **functionally in 1–2 days** and **anatomically in 8–10 days**, and becomes the **ligamentum arteriosum**. In premature infants this process is delayed; if the duct remains open, blood is shunted **from the aorta into the pulmonary trunk** (left-to-right shunt) — the lungs become congested and heart failure develops. Treatment — drugs that block prostaglandin synthesis (ibuprofen, indomethacin) or surgical/endovascular closure.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a 48-year-old woman a hard, fixed, painless lymph node is palpated in the left supraclavicular fossa. The patient says that in recent months she has lost weight and her appetite has decreased.
cases.ask: Disease of which organs could be associated with enlargement of this node? Explain on the basis of the anatomy of the lymphatic system.
cases.answer: This is **Virchow's (Troisier's) node** — the left supraclavicular lymph node. It lies near the point where the **thoracic duct** drains into the **left venous angle** (the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins). The thoracic duct begins at the **cisterna chyli** (from the lumbar and intestinal trunks) and collects lymph from the abdominal organs (stomach, intestines, pancreas, liver), the pelvic organs and the lower limbs. That is why **cancers of the abdominal organs**, especially **gastric cancer**, metastasize to this node through the lymphatic duct. In a woman tumors of the ovary and other pelvic organs are also considered. The patient needs endoscopy and abdominal investigations.
